Now, precepts are the fundamental basis for universal cultivation because they can purify immeasurable defiled karma and establish immeasurable pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
If one lacks the virtue of the precepts, how could the defiled mind be made clear and pure? How could pure conduct...
Thus it was successfully accomplished. Therefore it is said: "The precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed bodhi; one should single-mindedly uphold the pure precepts.
Now, the mind that upholds the precepts has essentially two paths: first, the observance through abstention (*śīla-vidhāraṇa*); second, the observance through performance (*kriyā-vidhāraṇa*).

While the observance through abstention has been propagated by those of later generations from the Tang dynasty until the present day, the observance through performance has remained silent and without promotion for over several hundred years. Since the year Yihai...

In the spring, he received the full precepts in Runzhou and constantly attended upon the Elder Master [Zhuanfeng], assisting him in spreading the teachings throughout various regions. He frequently requested instruction on the practice and maintenance of the Vinaya.
The Elder said, "Since your aspiration lies in the *vinaya*, I wish for you to restore the severed threads of the tradition.

Within the Tripiṭaka, there is the *Tánwúdébù shānbǔ suíjī jiémó* (The Tánwúdé School’s Revised and Supplemented *Karmavācanā* According to Circumstances), which was compiled by the Patriarch Nanshan [Daoxuan]. It is complete in both ritual procedures and legal principles; it is truly..."

It serves as a model; yet, because it has long been submerged in obscurity, it is ultimately difficult to restore by forceful means. I await the day when you will propagate it for the sake of the assembly.
Alas! The earnest instructions of my teacher still ring in my ears. In the summer of the year Wuyou, the Elder retired to his chamber and entrusted me with the mountain retreat.

Reflecting that I could not disobey his final testament and moved by the desire to repay his compassionate grace, I burned oil lamps to continue through the night, exhausting myself in the study of the Vinaya section.

Regarding its profound subtleties, he led the assembly in personal practice and expounded the grand principles of the *Karmavācanā*. That which was established must be followed; that which was improper was immediately reformed.

However, the original texts of the *Karmavācanā* Piṭaka contain only outlines and headings, so that while the procedures are listed, the methods are incomplete. Furthermore, there are textual passages that are archaic, such that their meaning is not evident.
Out of compassion for beginners who find themselves at a loss when facing these scrolls, I have relied upon the Vinaya to expand upon these ritual methods and provide an explanation.
Its hidden subtleties are titled *The Continued Commentary on the Vinaya* (*Bini zuoxi chushu*), intended to ensure that the unfolding and collapsing of its volumes make everything perfectly clear.
It is my hope that fellow practitioners may understand the boundaries between what should be done and what should be stopped, discern right from wrong, and weigh matters as they arise.

Thus, they shall do what ought to be done, together bathe in the ocean of the precepts to wash away all mundane minds, and tread the stages of the Path to perpetuate the lineage of the Sages. How could this possibly be compared to—?
What a display of empty talk, filling scrolls and volumes with nothing but vanity!
On the day of the preceding *anvaya-vāsa* (the first retreat) in the year of Kāngxī Yisi (1705), the junior student of the *Vinaya*, Duti from Yunnan, recorded this at Jin.
Preface to the Continued Commentary on the *Sifen lü shanfan buque xingshi chao* (The Vinaya of the Four-Part Dharmaguptaka School with Supplements and Omissions) by Lü Bao Huashan at Xixuan.
The Vinaya prescribes the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures). All monastic affairs are accomplished in reliance upon them;

if there were no *karmavācanā*, no actions could be performed or completed. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Where there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and those who explain its practice, this is called the True Dharma abiding in the world.
It further says: "One who does not recite the *jñapti-karman* (motion) shall never be permitted to leave their *niśraya* (dependence)."
Thus one should know that for a bhikṣu, no essential duty takes precedence over this; one should strive to master and uphold it.

The various *karmavācanā* rules originated from specific circumstances and were gradually established according to events; later, due to the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*), they were categorized and divided into the *khandhakas*.
Although Wen Hao has compiled this work for the purpose of investigation, if it were not thorough and penetrating, the fault would be difficult to avoid.

As for the great Vinaya masters of antiquity who upheld the True Dharma and strictly purified the *vinaya*, they all extracted and abridged from extensive sources, constantly reciting them without omission.
Within the present canon, there are three collections belonging to the Dharmaguptaka school; however, two of these have not yet harmonized the various [sections].

The ritual protocols of this school were incomplete; there was only the four fascicles of the *Suiji Jiemó* (Manual of Rituals for Occasions) compiled, edited, and supplemented by the founding patriarch Xuansu of the Nanshan school.

This work incorporated the *duīshǒu* (confession before another) and *xīnniàn* (mental recitation) rites from other traditions along with the *jiémó* (ritual procedures) for the Saṃgha, making them fully conform to the original school’s standards.

Regarding the application of rituals and practical matters, they were adapted according to circumstances based on their underlying principles; thus, the added protocols were put into practice, differing in two respects from the other [two schools]. Therefore...

Now, specifically continuing the practice and examining the original scrolls in detail, there were originally one hundred and eighty-four items listed in the table of contents; these have been reduced by sixty-five.

Since this is described as a "supplementary collection," what was the intention behind the omissions? Furthermore, within the text itself, it is redundantly stated that [the work] has been "fully expanded."

The compilation of this work is such that one cannot understand it without study; otherwise, one would merely waste time and effort without accomplishing the preliminary task. Therefore, it was omitted and not included here.

Should one need to apply these principles in practice, the *Great Compendium* (*Daocao*) provides detailed instructions. Alas, the *Great Compendium* has disappeared from the world and its whereabouts are unheard of.

For this reason, I have exhaustively researched the extensive sections, collated them, and established this manual for preservation. This should be followed according to the catalog and as a continuation of the Dharma.

A single character "Continuation" (續) is marked at the top [of a section] where the meaning should be explained according to the Vinaya. A single character "Explanation" (釋) is marked at the top where faults and errors should be exposed.

A single character "Incorrect" (非) is marked at the top where [an error] should be pointed out. A single character "Appendix" (附) is marked at the top where corroborating evidence or incidental practices should be added.
If none of these four categories—continuation, explanation, incorrect, or appendix—are present, it is entirely the original text of the canon volume. All...

In the method of maintaining the white [original] texts, all titles are written at the top margin; the remaining single character below serves to clarify the ancient edition and distinguish it from new continuations.
Should one read this and harbor doubts, please consult the *Cun* (存) volume of the Northern Canon, where the evidence is clear and verifiable.
A separate collection of the characteristics of the precepts is titled *The Compendium of the Cessation and Maintenance of the Vinaya*.

If there are matters that should be conducted through formal acts (*jñapti-karman*), these are all clearly explained within the section on "Active Maintenance" (*zuo-chi*); because this work distinguishes between cessation (*zhi*) and activity (*zuo*), they are not combined.

The original title within this fascicle remains as it was; however, for the sake of facilitating study and investigation, I have provisionally added the title *Commentary on the Continuation of the Vinaya* (*Pini zuoxi chishu*).

Zongshao composed this work with the primary intent of rekindling the light and extinguishing the flames [of the tradition]. It is my hope that his former efforts will surely bear fruit in the future. Thus, (the body of the text).

I personally labored on this for over twenty years. The reason I did not hasten to publish the completed manuscript was to ensure that those who rely on this study would refine their knowledge and views, and establish firm faith;
now that they have come to believe with joy and respectfully practice it, I have thus carved it into woodblocks for circulation.
May future generations rely upon this to repay the Buddha’s kindness and requite the virtue of my teacher. If, after receiving full ordination, one does not... [text ends]
I understand. Because the transmitted teachings have been lost, one studies but does not practice; how can such a fault be excused?

Even if one has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is only right that they be admonished and rebuked for perusing the Vinaya sections. If you claim that the Vinaya rules must be known beforehand before receiving full ordination, [this is incorrect].
This is like giving a person a drink of poison;
is one not being cautious? *Vinayakārikā-vṛtti-ṭīkā-mukha*, Volume One.

Following this, the *ekapudgala-dharma* (dharmas for a single person) and the *saṃgha-dharma* (dharmas for the community) are clarified, wherein the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) are complete with the seven types of invalidity (*saptavidha-asamyak*).
First, a formal act that is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya;
second, a formal act that is contrary to the Dharma performed by a separate assembly;
third, a formal act that is contrary to the Dharma performed by a harmonious assembly.
Fourth, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that is according to the Dharma but performed by a separate assembly;
fifth, a formal act that is similar to the Dharma but performed by a separate assembly;
sixth, a formal act that is similar to the Dharma and performed by a harmonious assembly.
Seventh, regarding the meaning of the formal act of admonishing without cessation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*), seven types of invalidity are established:
first, invalidity of the person; second, invalidity of the dharma; third, invalidity of the matter.
1. Four persons regarding the Dharma; 2. Five persons regarding the matter; 3. Six persons regarding the Dharma;
4. Seven persons regarding the matter; 5.

Seven persons regarding both the Dharma and the matter—these constitute the *pratimukha-karman* (face-to-face ritual), with all seven types of invalidity as described above; 6. The *pratimukha-karman* for the community, with all seven types of invalidity as described above.

△ First, the Explanation of Weighing the Prior Matter:
"Weighing" (*chēngliàng*) means measuring and assessing. There are approximately two ways of performing this weighing and holding: first, that which should be...
First, within a single matter, one must weigh the three factors of person, dharma, and circumstance against the three types of error.

Second, one should, for each individual *karmavācanā*, weigh the three conditions of person, dharma, and circumstance. If one weighs them skillfully, then merit will accrue to oneself and others, and the Dharma will flourish and endure for a long time.
If one does not weigh them skillfully, then blame will fall upon those presiding over the assembly, and the task will fail to be accomplished. Therefore, this is clarified at the outset.
Weighing [the matter] and acting with single-minded persistence is the secret essence of the Vinaya school.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "The 'matter' refers to the person and the dharma.

*Explanation:* In any task to be accomplished, these three—person, dharma, and matter—must be present. Although the current manual simply refers to them as "the preceding matter," [it implies all three].
Regarding those things hidden within the "Dharma of persons" (pudgala-dharma): it is because affairs arise dependent upon persons, and persons are able to uphold the Dharma to accomplish affairs.
Therefore, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* is cited to reveal these hidden meanings. The treatise states: "Affairs are persons, and they are also called 'Dharma'."
The Vinaya states: "To 'weigh' means to weigh the bhikṣu and the layperson, as well as the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the offense.
**Explanation:** This clarifies that within a single matter, one must weigh three types of faults: the person, the dharma (the ritual), and the matter itself.
Whenever a matter arises and the time comes to perform the formal ritual (*karman*), one must first weigh the gravity of the matter: whether it pertains to the public or to private affairs.
How should the three types of formal procedures (*karmas*) be performed? Are they for the sake of establishing what is wholesome or for the sake of disciplinary punishment?

How should one judge the suitability of the person acting? Is it within the same assembly (*saṃgha*) or a different assembly? How should they be convened? If one discusses the arising of a matter, it cannot be treated as a single instance;
this text alone cites from the *Ekottarika-khaṇḍa* (The Section on the Numerical Increase) the specific case of prohibiting [monks] from going to the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).

This refers to a person who, for this matter, possesses both the monastic and lay lineages and the three types of non-proper conduct; because these are clearly weighed and evident, the case taken as an example applies to others as well.
The Buddha said: "A bhikṣu who possesses ten qualities should be granted the *karmavācanā* of prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadhāna-gṛhapraveśana-karman*):
first, he speaks ill of and reviles the homes of laypeople; second, he employs means to cause the decline of the homes of laypeople."
Third, performing what is of no benefit; fourth, having no place of abode; fifth, inciting strife among laypeople;
sixth, slandering the Buddha in the presence of laypeople; seventh, slandering the Dharma; eighth, slandering the Sangha; ninth, using vulgar and insulting speech toward laypeople in their presence.
If there are ten such dharmas that a layperson claims to possess but does not actually fulfill, and if they possess even a few of these ten dharmas, one should perform the *karmavācanā* for them;
therefore, it is said that one "weighs" the bhikṣu. If a layperson possesses five dharmas, one should not perform the *karmavācanā* for them:
first, not respecting their father; second, not respecting their mother; third, not respecting śramaṇas; fourth...
They do not show respect to brahmins. They do not firmly uphold the five things that ought to be upheld.
If a layperson possesses these five qualities, they should perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) against the bhikṣu; thus it is said, "weighing the layperson.

*Explanation:* This clarifies that one must weigh three kinds of conditions for each individual ritual action (*karmavācanā*).

Among these, there are cases where the conditions that give rise to a formal act belong to that very formal act itself; and there are cases where the conditions that give rise to a formal act belong to another formal act.

For example, in the formal act of receiving the precepts (*upasampadā-karman*), when the assembly of monks performs the rite of the fourth motion, the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) immediately becomes a bhikṣu. This is also the case with the rite of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).

they should perform the task. The *karmavācanā* for disciplinary expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) is measured according to the circumstances, employing methods of subduing and restraint to reform past faults and cultivate new virtues.

Since its original purpose was to initiate action for the sake of others, it is said to be "for the sake of others," as in the case of the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
The *pāṭimokkha* recitation for the fortnightly *poṣadha* consists of a single formal motion (*jñapti*). One simply recites the *prātimokṣa*.

The regulations are as stated above. As for the expressions "separated at times" and "united at times," one who wishes to understand their separation must first measure their union;

Such as the rituals for clearing offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*) or releasing suspension (*pravāsanīya*), these are all termed "belonging to the combined" because they still share the same legal status and food with the pure assembly. These constitute the one hundred and eighty-four kinds of *karmas*.
This refers to the distinction between being separated from and united with the central [time].

△ Second, the explanation of the locus upon which the dharma arises: "Arising" (qi) means to emerge and establish; "relying" (tuō) means to entrust or depend upon. This means that whenever a dharma is produced, there must necessarily be a locus upon which it relies.

Regarding the location: the previous section has already explained in detail the measurements to demonstrate that there is a basis for the ritual procedure. If the site chosen deviates from the regulations, then the Dharma will likewise be difficult to establish.
Therefore, the second section further clarifies the location upon which the Dharma arises.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "In a place that is not a site for formal ritual acts (*karmabhūmi*), one may not receive the consent (*chanda*) to perform monastic affairs.
According to the Vinaya, if a formal ritual act is to be performed, one must first establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*)."
The commentary cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stating that all monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) vary in size and have no fixed boundaries.
Prior to the formal demarcation of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), such a place is termed "non-ritual ground" (*akarmabhūmi*).

One may not receive the consent (*chanda*) or perform monastic affairs there, as it is a location unsuitable for the entrustment of legal acts; this clarifies the prohibition. It further cites the *Mūla-vinaya*, stating that all...
When the saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) or carries out monastic affairs, they must first reach a consensus through a motion with one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Although the sacred teachings have their boundaries in terms of spatial extent and direction, the procedures for monastic residence rely on the presence of those with a connection to the site;
those who receive the proxy consent (*chanda*) do not personally attend when there is no business requiring it, lest they constitute a separate assembly. This clarifies the established rule.
However, there are two types of locations for reliance. If it is within a natural boundary (*jātideśa*), there is only the single rite of formal boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha-karman*);
all other monastic legal acts (*saṃghadharma*) must be performed within a ritual boundary (*kṛtadeśa*).
**Commentary:** Regarding the two types of sites for ritual construction (*karmabhūmi*): these refer to the constructed site (*kṛtrimabhūmi*) and the natural site (*prakṛtibhūmi*).

Generally, affairs arise from people, and the Dharma relies on people for its propagation. Since people have unstable conditions regarding their movement and dwelling, the sites for constructed rituals are likewise not fixed.
For instance, a constructed site is originally established for the purpose of providing a basis for monks to perform legal acts (*dharmakarma*). However, if...

When circumstances arise that lead one beyond the boundaries [of the monastery], one cannot simply follow them; yet when such events suddenly occur, how could one leave them unaddressed? It is for this reason that one is called a "precept-holding bhikṣu.
Therefore, the World-Honored One established the Dharma in accordance with specific conditions, further instituting the four kinds of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*).
If one travels by boat, there is the method of establishing a boundary by splashing water;
if one travels by land, there is the limit of six hundred paces. Upon encountering a village, there is a fixed rule regarding what may be distinguished and what may not;
upon encountering an araṇya, there is a demarcation based on whether there are difficult circumstances or no difficult circumstances.
Because it is not necessary to erect markers or perform the ritual of proclaiming boundaries to establish it, each has its own fixed limits;

this is collectively termed the "natural boundary" (*dharmatā-sīmā*) and is also called the "boundary of non-action" (*akṛta-dharmatā-sīmā*). This serves as the basis for the ritual procedures of wandering bhikṣus.
If one performs rituals within this natural boundary, it is exempt from the formal act of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha-karman*).

The *mārga* (preparatory rite) for one dharma may not be performed; as for all other monastic *karmavācanā* rites, their performance within the ritual boundary (*sīmā*) is identical and no different from the formal proclamation (*jñapti*).
However, regarding the two dharmas of face-to-face communication (*saṃmukha-vinaya*) and mental recollection (*manasikāra*), these apply to both types of boundaries.

Commentary: This clarifies the application of the rules regarding the *dharmas* based on the location of entrustment (*pratisthāna*). Fearing that future generations might doubt whether it is possible to perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) separately from the assembly within the two boundaries (*sīmā*), he immediately adds:
"If the entrustment is made through the *pratyekamukha* (face-to-face) or *manasikāra* (mental) methods, then it applies to both boundaries;

one may perform formal acts separately from the assembly in accordance with the Dharma, even if the rest of the assembly performs them improperly. However, if it concerns a formal act of the Saṃgha [performed by the whole assembly], then [it must be done] within the two boundaries."
In the midst [of the assembly], it is *dharmic* when one acts together with the multitude, whereas it is *adharmic* when acting apart from the multitude; therefore, this is discussed in detail.
△ Third, the explanation of the method for assembling the *saṃgha*.

"Assembling" (*ji*) means gathering. "*Saṃgha*" refers to the full number of the four types [of monastics]. The citation of the Vinaya above has already established that [the assembly] is based upon...
Regarding the location: there must be two groups of monks for the assembly of the Dharma. If there were no basis for such an agreement, upon what could the gathering rely?
Therefore, the third section further clarifies the method for assembling the Saṃgha.
The Vinaya states: The Buddha said, "One should spread out seats and strike the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong), so that everyone may assemble in one place.
Commentary: This cites the second section of the *Prātimokṣa*, the *Poṣadha-ghaṇṭā-vastu*. Regarding "spreading out seats":
in the monasteries of the Western Regions, monks do not possess chairs or benches. Whenever they wish to assemble, the junior *bhikṣus* first purify the area and spread mats upon the ground.

It is used to await those who have taken their seats. As for the *gaṇḍī* (wooden gong), there is no standard translation [for its name]. When it is time to summon [the assembly], one follows the treatises on phonology (*śabdavidyā*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whichever material it may be made of—wood, tile, copper, or iron—one should have a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) strike it so that it rings."
If there is no *śrāmaṇera*, a *bhikṣu* may also do so, provided he does not exceed three strikes.

[Commentary: To further explain the meaning of the *gandī* as being "from sound," this passage from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is cited; it clarifies both the person who beats it and the act of sounding.
Regarding "sounding" (*míng*), any object that produces sound is said to "sound. For example, striking a bell, beating a drum, knocking on a board, or tapping [an instrument].
*Qing*. Whatever object it strikes that produces a sound is the *ghanṭā* for assembling the Saṃgha.

A *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) is a member of the monastery who constantly serves as an agent for the Saṃgha. Because they were granted by a king and rely upon the pure assembly, they are called "pure persons."
The śrāmaṇeras share two points of similarity with the bhikṣus: this refers to similarity in dharma, not similarity in form. Regarding "similarity in dharma":

although it is permitted for a bhikṣu to strike [a śrāmaṇera], this applies to one who has newly entered the summer retreat; it does not apply to one whose seniority (*vassa*) is greater. The rule is fixed by the three-fold [striking]. As for "one must not exceed [this limit]":
this clarifies that the Buddha’s regulations are such that they must not be transgressed. Should one transgress them, one shall be punished for the offense of violating the *vinaya*.
In the *Fofazang zhuan* (Biographies of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury), there is a method for "long-striking" [the drum].
This four-fascicle work appeared during the Later Wei period. Because it records instances where one ascends the seat at the request of others, it prescribes long-striking;
this is similar to how, nowadays, when ascending the hall to preach the Dharma or confer ordination, the drum is struck before the abbot’s incense burner.

Regarding these protocols: what is cited here is intended to ensure that those who preach the Dharma understand that they must not assemble the community with three rounds of strikes, nor may they strike the bell for an extended duration.
Within the *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-vinaya* (The Three Thousand Rules of Deportment), the exact number of strikes for the mallet is clearly specified.
Commentary: The preceding section mentioned three rounds (*tōng*), but did not yet specify the number of subsequent strikes. Therefore, this is clarified here.
These three fascicles on ritual protocols (*weiyi*) were translated by An Shigao of the Later Han. As for the "mallet" (*chǔ*), it refers to a wooden mallet used with a block.

In that tradition, fifty-four strikes constitute one round. Regarding what is called "fully manifesting" [the signal]: excluding the three rounds for summoning the assembly, if it is not a time of death, one strikes accordingly (that is, to send [the message]).

[This refers to] deceased monks). If a magistrate arrives, or there is a great fire, a great flood, or bandits—these four occasions also require striking [the bell] according to the time, without a fixed number of blows.
If a *śrāmaṇera* is assembled, strike three times; if an *upāsaka* is assembled, strike twice; if the "private children" (*si'er*) are called, strike once.
As for the term "private children," this distinguishes them from the commoners who belong to the monastery as gifts from the king; these are the private property of the community.
Cattle are kept as laborers for the young novices. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"In the matter of summoning the Saṃgha with the *gandī* drum, there must always be a fixed standard; they may not be interchanged."
Commentary: To cite this treatise again is out of fear that the number of *śalākā* (voting sticks) might be confused;
it serves to clarify that the monastic agreement must never be altered. "Constant standard" refers to a fixed and perpetual rule.

If the numbers were interchanged, then when those [monks] arrive at this or that assembly, the agreement of faith would be lost, resulting in errors in the *karmavācanā*. Therefore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Ānanda..."
Ascending the lecture hall, he strikes the mallet. The mallet is the drum of faith of the Tathāgata.
△ Fourth, the assembly of the *saṃgha* and the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmā*).

"Delimitation" (*yue*) means to set a limit or agreement. The preceding section clarified the ritual procedure for entrusting the boundary; the boundary is generally categorized into two types. [Now] the *saṃgha* assembles.

There is a method. This method establishes the *gandī* (wooden gong). Now, examining the detailed demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā*) and their separate collections, these also differ. Fourth, it further clarifies the assembly of the Saṃgha with respect to boundaries.

Generally, there are two types of boundaries; if they are formalized boundaries (*karmabhūmi-sīmā*), they correspond to three kinds: namely, the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the Precept Platform (*śīlāmaṇḍala*), and the Small Boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).

If one discusses a small boundary (*kṣudrakasīma*), there is no external area to assemble from. If it is a boundary for the precept-platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) or a great boundary (*mahāsīma*), one must chant the restrictions and assemble everyone within them.

Commentary: Now, there are two kinds of boundaries; this sentence provides the general heading, which will be explained in detail below. According to the Vinaya, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is as follows:

There are three types of boundaries (*sīmā*). The first is the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), which is further divided into six kinds: (1) the simple great boundary; (2) the great boundary for the storage of robes (*cīvarasīmā*);
(3) the great boundary containing an inner *śīmaṇḍala*; (4) the great boundary where both the Dharma and the food are shared;

(5) the great boundary where the Dharma is shared but the food is separate; and (6) the great boundary where the food is shared but the Dharma is separate. Second, regarding the *śīmaṇḍala*: this is due to...
The boundary of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*) is vast and wide; when the assembly has become exhausted from gathering there, they listen for the formal act of binding it.

This is precisely what is meant by the site for receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā-śālā*). Regarding the third type, the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*): as for the small boundary, the boundary does not exist permanently, nor do the *saṃgha* reside within it.

It was originally established because the assembly did not agree [on a larger area], so this ritual procedure was temporarily opened. Furthermore, no outsiders can be gathered there. If it is a site for the precept-platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*), [the same applies].
Regarding the "Great Boundary" (mahā-sīmā): it exists only as that which was proclaimed at the time of its formal establishment, each having its own demarcated limits.

All monks must assemble within these prescribed boundaries. This applies only to the shared legal acts (*dharmas*) performed within a distinct Great Boundary; if one performs monastic legal acts here, [they must be conducted within this boundary].
The Saṃgha should assemble at this location. If the formal acts of the Saṃgha are to be performed there, the Saṃgha must assemble there;
for if they act according to the Dharma, it does not constitute a schism. If the Saṃgha receives a gift, the assembly should divide it equally; one may not form a separate faction.

If one considers the natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*), they are divided into four types: namely, the village (*grāma*), the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the path (*adhva*), and the water boundary (*udaka*).

Regarding the first, the village, there are two kinds. If the village boundary cannot be clearly distinguished, it is calculated according to the measure of seven trees from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, totaling six intervals of sixty-three steps. If there are no other groups present, the formal act (*karma*) may be accomplished.
*Mo* (Explanation).
According to the Vinaya regulations, the *jñapti-kṣetra* (natural boundary) is divided into four distinct types, namely: the village and so forth. This indicates the categories;
the following provides the explanation. "Village" (*grāma*) refers to a place where people reside together, similar to a hamlet. There are two kinds of these. If...

The boundaries of the village were so vast that they could not be clearly distinguished; therefore, the measurement of seven trees according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was adopted as the demarcation.
That Vinaya states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who questioned the World-Honored One, saying:
"What kind of *āmra* tree has firm roots and trunk, and luxuriant branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit?"
[The trees] grew successfully, spreading out and flourishing without obstructing one another. The Buddha said, "Plant one tree every seven bows of five cubits each.
By planting in this manner, the roots and trunks will become firm and solid, and they will not obstruct one another.
Having heard this, he was filled with joy, paid his respects, and departed. At that time, Upāli, knowing the proper moment, addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have already heard [the instruction]."

Regarding the boundaries for planting trees, I now ask again: if the boundaries of a city or a village settlement cannot be determined, when performing a *karmavācanā*, to what extent should it be defined so that it is called a properly performed *karmavācanā* and one does not incur the offense of a separate assembly? The Buddha said:

The measurement of seven *śimśapā* trees permits the performance of a *karmavācanā*. Although there may be other members of the assembly who see one another, there is no offense of a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*).
Therefore, the present text states that the measure of seven trees totals six intervals and sixty-three paces.
If we calculate this according to the current standard, using a bow of five cubits where seven bows equal one tree, the total amounts to forty-two bows.
One *hasta* (cubit) is one foot eight inches. Five *hastas* constitute one *dhanus* (bow).
Each *dhanus* is nine feet, totaling thirty-seven *zhang* and eight feet. This is the measurement of the bow used in the Western Regions (*Sīyù*).

If compared with the measurements for paddy fields and pacing in steps used during the Tang dynasty in this land—where six feet constitute one step—sixty-three steps exactly correspond [to that distance].
In the Western Regions, the measure of seven trees is forty-two *dhanus*. Within this measurement, there are no separate groups, and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) can be accomplished.
Beyond this measurement, even if separate groups are present and see one another, there is no offense of having a distinct assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
This clarifies that within an indistinguishable village or natural boundary, one may not establish the regulations for performing monastic legal acts (*saṃghakarma*).
As for a distinguishable village, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one must assemble the entire community of that village.
Explanation: That which can be distinguished refers to a village that is not extensive, such that its boundaries can be known.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "At that time, the bhikṣus were in a village where there was no monastery (*saṃghārāma*). They first constructed a monastery, but had not yet performed the formal demarcation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
At that time, how large should the boundary be? The Buddha said: 'The boundary of the village is the boundary of the monastery. The bhikṣus did not..."
One should perform the *poṣadha* and the *saṃgha-karman* separately; if one acts otherwise, one commits an offense, as stated in the *Mūla-ekottara-karman*:

"The Buddha said: 'If there are bhikṣus staying in a village, they must all assemble in one place—including those within the walls and platforms, as well as those within the external boundary—to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and the *pravāraṇā*, using a simple motion (*jñapti*)."*

Both types of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and three proclamations) must be performed [within this area]. If they do not assemble there, the ritual procedure will not be valid, and they will incur the offense of acting as a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).
This clarifies the regulation that the legal procedures of the Saṃgha may be performed within the demarcated natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) which is subject to distinction.
Second, regarding the term *araṇya*, there are also two types. If it is free from obstacles, most schools state it should be one *krośa*.
According to the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*, this refers to five *li*. This is traditionally accepted as the standard definition.
Commentary: The first two phrases provide a general heading; the subsequent text provides a detailed explanation.

*Araṇya* is also called *āraṇya*, which is translated as "empty and tranquil" (*kōngjì*) or "leisurely and tranquil" (*xiánjì*). Because it is empty and leisurely, there is no contention; it is a place that is secluded from clamor and profoundly still.
The first type is the *araṇya* free from difficulties, meaning a location where there are no predatory beasts or bandits, and where coming and going is safe.
Peaceful. Many schools state that one *krośa* [is the extent]. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:
"At that time, the bhikṣus were constructing a monastery in a desolate place where there was no village. Before the boundary had been established, how large should the boundary be? The Buddha said:"
It is one *krośa* square. Within this area, the bhikṣus should not perform the *poṣadha* or the *saṃghakarma* separately from the assembly.
The *Fanyi ji* (Collection of Translations) states: "The Sanskrit term *krośa* is translated here as 'five hundred bows,' also as 'the roar of a great bull,' or 'the sound of one drum.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says it is two *li*. Now, according to the *Zabaozang jing* (Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels), it says:"
Five *li*. Traditionally, the translators have handed down this as the fixed standard; therefore, it is what we rely upon.
This clarifies that within the natural boundary (*prakṛtisthiti*) of a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) free from obstacles, one may perform the legal acts of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the difficulty of practicing in an araṇya, as stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
"If the distance between seven pāṭakas is fifty-eight paces, four chi, and eight cun, one may perform the karmavācanā."
Commentary: Regarding the "forest hermitage with obstacles" (*araṇya-sa-vighna*): this refers to a location where there are many wild beasts and bandits, and the roads are terrifying.
It cannot be categorized as a forest hermitage without obstacles. This boundary is as explained in the *Sudarsana-śāstra*:
the Sanskrit term is *paṇḍa*, which here means twenty-eight cubits (*hasta*). The measure of seven *paṇḍas* totals one hundred and ninety-six cubits. Each...
One *zhǒu* is one chi and eight cun. Altogether, this amounts to thirty-five *zhàng*, two *chí*, and eight *cùn*.
Since each step is six feet (*chí*), thirty-five *zhàng*, two *chí*, and eight *cùn* does not reach fifty-nine steps;
therefore, it is said to be fifty-eight steps and four feet and eight inches. Within these measurements, one may perform the *poṣadha-karman*. This clarifies...
In a wilderness (araṇya) where there are obstacles, one may perform the formal acts of the Saṃgha within the natural boundary (jātīya-sīmā).
Third is the boundary for the practice of the Path (mārga-caryā-sīmā). According to the Sarvāstivāda Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya, it measures six hundred paces in length and breadth.

Commentary on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (The Ten Recitations): Regarding the boundary (*sīmā*), according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two causes and conditions by which it is permitted [to establish one].

First, on the day of the *poṣadha*; second, on the day of the *pravāraṇa*. This is because when various bhikṣus are traveling together on the same road, they may not reach the assembly of the Saṃgha in time.

One should establish the boundary for the path through skillful means for the purposes of the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*. East and west are called "width" (*vistāra*), while north and south are called "length" (*āyāma*).
The square or circular area measures six hundred paces; each pace being six feet, this totals three hundred and sixty *zhang*.

Within these dimensions, one may perform the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*. According to the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), when establishing a boundary for walking on the path, one must first demarcate two [sides].
First, regarding the path: one must exclude places for drawing water and fields, as these are frequented by laypeople.
If it is a desolate road with no people passing, it cannot serve as a valid boundary because it is not known [to all].

However, if a road is cut off where people and carts still travel, it may serve as a boundary even if it separates three or four villages. This clarifies the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) established along a traveled path.
One may perform the ritual for establishing a *saṃgha* boundary.
Regarding the water boundary (*udakasiṃā*), as described in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: among the assembly on a boat, a strong person throws water or sand in the four directions;
the area reached by these is the limit of the boundary.
The *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Wufen lü) states: When various bhikṣus were traveling by boat together and encountered the day for the *poṣadha*, they wished to recite the precepts.

Therefore, it was permitted to recite the precepts within the boat. Having moored the boat in shallow water, one strong bhikṣu from among the assembly was ordered to go out and stand at the prow of the boat, splashing and throwing water in all four directions; wherever the water reached, [that area was considered the boundary].
It serves as the boundary. The remainder is within. One should observe the four directions; if one throws sand, it is likewise.
This clarifies that within the natural boundary of the water-course, the formal acts of the Saṃgha may be performed.
These six characteristics all refer to the area within the boundaries of the directions toward which one’s body and face are oriented;
only when no one is gathered within this space can the ritual be performed in accordance with the Dharma.
*Explanation:* This text concludes the preceding section, meaning that the six types of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*) explained above are not the same as those [established by] proclamation.

They establish boundary markers to define the limits of the *dharmadhātu*. Since these boundary markers are established according to the cardinal directions facing the body and face at that time, the Saṃgha assembles within this area for the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*.
If even one person does not assemble [within this boundary], [the ceremony is not valid].
Then the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā* will not be valid; they may only be performed according to the Dharma when there is no one [else present].
△ Five: Explaining the Harmony of the Assembly According to the Dharma.

As stated above, regarding the gathering of the Saṃgha, it is defined by the boundary (*sīmā*). Only those within the *śīlākṣetra* (precept-field) and the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) must gather. If they have gathered but...
"Harmony" (saṃgha) is still the same as being a separate assembly (nānāsaṃgha). Therefore, the fifth [section] further clarifies what constitutes harmony and concordance according to the Dharma.
The Vinaya states: "Those who should come have come; those who should give their consent (chanda) have given their consent;
those present who are entitled to censure do not censure. This is called harmony. Conversely, the three factors opposite to these constitute a separate assembly.
Commentary: This cites the third section, the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (The Section on Reprimands).

It means that when the wooden gong (*gandi*) is struck once within the boundary, those dwelling together who hear the sound and immediately arrive are said to be acting according to the Dharma and are fit for the business before the Saṃgha. The first phrase refers to those whose bodies and minds are both assembled;
the second phrase refers to those whose bodies have other affairs or conditions but whose minds are assembled; the third phrase refers to those whose bodies and minds are manifest [in assembly].
Previously, even if one encounters those who would rebuke them, they remain joyful and patient in mind, remaining silent and not rebuking in return; this is called "being in harmony.
Conversely, if the three aforementioned conditions are absent, one constitutes a "separated assembly" (nānāsaṃvāsika).
*Vinaya-jishu-chi-shu*, Scroll One: Phonetic Explanations and General Rules.
"General" (*fan*) refers to the general outline. "Rule" (*li*) refers to a standard for comparison. The *Preface to the Zuo Zhuan* states: "To establish the general rules... (Fafa).
To initiate an analogy.
"Lian" (斂) is pronounced with the upper tone; it means to gather and to collect.
It also means to investigate and seek out.
"Huan" means to flee.
"Hao-hao" describes the vast appearance of great waters; it is used here as a metaphor for the profound and expansive nature of written words.
"Zhui" means to append redundantly.
"Bingyu" (秉御) refers to the proclamation and dissemination of the Buddha's regulations, much like proclaiming the edicts of a human sovereign.
"Wei" (委) refers to the source and the flow: the "yuan" (原) is where the spring originates, and the "wei" (委) is where the current gathers.
"Yanqiong" means to investigate thoroughly.
"Jiàochóu" refers to collating two versions against one another. "Fùjiào" (re-examination) is like viewing [the text] as an enemy.
"Kuī" means to look at something narrowly or scrutinize it.
"Sou" (搜) means to seek out; it means to search for. "Qu" (足) means to be full; it means to have no deficiency.
"Sui" (遂), with the departing tone, means to approach; it means to follow; it means because of or by means of.
"Bō" (Extensive) responds to both the holy and the ordinary; "bō" (pervasive) means universal. *Karma* is the solemn regulation of the Dharma King, universally covering all members of the Sangha.

Even those who are stainless noble monks (*anāsrava-ārya-bhikṣu*), whose residual physical forms have not yet passed away, or Bodhisattvas manifesting their traces among the ranks of the monastic community—all without exception revere and comply with it, none daring to transgress.
*Chán* (禅) is pronounced with a departing tone; it means "to transmit.
*Luǎnlián* (輦连) is pronounced with an entering tone; it refers to a hand-pulled carriage.
*Gǔ* (毂) has the phonetic value of *gǔ*; the hub is the very center of the wheel where the spokes converge.
To avoid mentioning a person's name by calling it their "taboo" (huì) when they are alive; to call it their "taboo" after they have died.
*Yùn* (pronounced yìn) means to conceive or carry a fetus in the womb.
*Yūn* (pronounced jūn).
"Śì" (諡) is pronounced "shì. It is the record of one's deeds. A "lèi xíng" (讄行) is the establishment of a title to replace one's given name. This practice began with the Duke of Zhou.
In ancient times, when a high minister or noble died, the ruler would command the relevant officials to accumulate accounts of their merits and virtues, composing a written text to commemorate them;
this was called the "posthumous title based on the record of deeds" (讄行之諡). Thus, Emperor Yizong of the Tang dynasty, in order to honor his grandfather’s virtue, bestowed upon him a posthumous title.
The Vinaya Master Chengzhao’s stupa is named Jingguang (Pure Light). His eulogy is identical to [the previous] lü (eulogies). The sound [of the name] is *lěi*.
When the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa between the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara at Heilin (Crane Forest), the forest trees all turned white; therefore, it is called Heilin.
The first ordination was that of one hundred and ten people, namely: the five headed by Cunda;
Yaśas along with his fifty friends; and the fifty people from the city of Vārāṇasī who were his marriage associates.
These were the very first one hundred and ten members of the Sangha Jewel in the world, all of whom realized the fruit of Arhatship.

Preface: Regarding the five abodes of afflictions, the first is the "abode of all views" (*sarvadṛṣṭi-sthānīya-kleśa*). This refers to the afflictions of conceptual discrimination within the three realms.

That is to say, sentient beings, through the faculty of mind (*manas*) confronting mental objects (*dharmas*), engage in discrimination and give rise to various false views, thereby remaining [in this state].

They are attached to the three realms. Second is the delusion of the ground of abiding in craving for desire (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*), which refers to the afflictions of volition in the desire realm.

This means that all sentient beings, through the five sense organs encountering the objects of the five dusts, give rise to craving and attachment, thereby dwelling and clinging to birth and death within the desire realm.
The delusion of the dwelling-place of craving for the three realms of form (*rūpārāga-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) refers to the afflictions of volition (*cetanā*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Because sentient beings do not understand this delusion, they dwell attached to meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and are unable to achieve liberation.

The delusion of the dwelling-place of craving for existence (*bhavārāga-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) refers to the afflictions of volition in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Because sentient beings do not understand this delusion, they dwell in meditative concentrations and are unable to achieve liberation.
The fifth is the delusion of the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*), which is precisely the fundamental delusion of ignorance.
This means that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, failing to comprehend this delusion, remain submerged in true emptiness and dwell in the land of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*).

The "land of expedient means" refers to the realm inhabited by those who have cultivated the path of expedient means to sever the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*). Only Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas are able to eliminate and sever it. Because...
Other afflictions remain unexhausted as one dwells in the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kṣetra*). The "Land of True Reward" refers to receiving retribution in accordance with reality.
Thus, there is the dwelling-place of ignorance and the dwelling-place of non-ignorance. To speak of them collectively, the afflictions of view within the three realms constitute one dwelling;
the afflictions of thought within the three realms constitute three dwellings; and fundamental ignorance constitutes one dwelling. Therefore, they are called the five dwellings (*pañca-vāsa*).
The second is the death of the limited portion (*prādeśika-vaiparītya-maraṇa*). "Limited" (*prādeśika*) refers to a fixed limit; "portion" (*prādeśika*) refers to physical segments.

This means that according to the karmic power of sentient beings in the six realms, the retributive fruits they experience result in bodies that are either long or short, and lifespans that are either full or premature.
Because they all thus transmigrate through birth and death, it is called the death of the limited portion. The second is the death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*).

Birth and death refers to the birth and death of transformation (pariṇāma-maraṇa) that exists for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, even though they have abandoned the birth and death of fragmentation within the triple world.
This [transformation] occurs in lands such as those of skillful means (*upāya*). For example, the first stage serves as the cause and the subsequent stages serve as the fruit;
furthermore, the subsequent stages serve as the cause and the following stages serve as the fruit. Because the cause shifts and the fruit changes, it is called "transformation."
Birth and death.
"Body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of "aggregation. It refers to the formation of a body through the aggregation of various phenomena (*dharma*).

The first, the aggregate of the principle-dharma (*dharmadhātu*), is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This means that from the initial stage of the first *vihāra* (abode), the principle of the *dharmatā* is manifested, and so on until the Sublime [Stage].
The collection of principles of the ultimate fruit of awakening, being square and round, is the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha), which is the collection of dharma-principles.

The collection of the two wisdoms is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya). That is to say, from the first stage (prathamabhūmi) up to the ultimate fruit of wondrous awakening, the collection of wisdom is square and round because wisdom accords with principle;
one obtains this body as a reward for that wisdom. This collection of wisdom-dharmas is called the Reward-body Buddha. Third, the collection of merit...

The "aggregate of merit and dharma" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). This means that from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the aggregate of merit becomes complete;
thus, it is able to manifest in response to the capacities of beings and preach various teachings to deliver all sentient beings.
This aggregate of merit is what is called the *nirmāṇakāya*.
"Wanghuang" (vast and boundless) means deep and expansive.
"Yi" (upper tone: yì) means moistening and saturating.
"Yi" (overflowing) means full to the brim.

*Lànshāng* (濫觴): the upper character is pronounced *làn*; the lower character is pronounced *shāng*. This refers to when a spring first begins to flow, not exceeding the volume of a cup of water, yet gradually becomes a widespread flood.
*Shì* (碩): pronounced *shí*, meaning "great."
