△ 6. Explanation of Distinguishing the Assembly from the Non-Assembly. "Distinguish" means to differentiate. "Assembly" refers to the five groups of monastics as well as laypeople.

As stated above, they should be in harmony according to the Dharma, and those who ought to come should come; however, there is concern that among those who have come, there may be those who do not belong to the assembly. Therefore—
The sixth section further clarifies the distinction between those who are qualified and those who are not for the assembly.
The Vinaya states: "Those who have not received full ordination must leave," and so forth.

Explanation: This cites the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on the Recitation of Precepts) from the second division (*Dvitiyabhāga*) of the Vinaya. "Those who have not received full ordination" refers to the three types of novices (*śrāmaṇera*).

The assembly: because a śrāmaṇera eavesdrops on the *karmavācanā* of the bhikṣus and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), participating in the communal monastic rites, he is termed a "thief-dweller" (*steyasaṃvāsika*).
At the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), this constitutes an obstacle (*antarāyika-dharma*) that disqualifies him; therefore, he must be expelled. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:

"If, at the time of the *poṣadha*, one sends a śrāmaṇera to a place where he neither sees nor hears [the proceedings], one should inspect under the beds and illuminate the area thoroughly with lamps."
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it includes laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Because King Piṃśala had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, he dispatched men to guard the *saṃghārāma*.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, fearing they might disobey the king’s command, [the monks] did not dare to go far away. The Buddha said:
It is well if one employs skillful means to have a layperson leave. If this is not possible, the bhikṣus may go outside the boundary to perform the poṣadha;
however, they must not perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) or recite the precepts in the presence of a layperson.
It is further said: There are four types of persons who possess "full status" (pūrṇa-saṃkhyā) and should not be censured.
These are those for whom the formal acts of censure, banishment, dependence, or prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople have been performed; these four persons are such individuals.
Commentary: This citation from the third section, the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Pravāraṇa-vastu*), clarifies the fourfold analytical examination regarding the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*).

The first sentence provides a general heading; what follows is a detailed explanation. "If the Saṃgha has already performed the formal act of censure" refers to cases arising from quarrels, disputes, or insults within the assembly.
"If it has already performed the formal act of banishment" [refers to those who have committed such offenses].
This is because he dwells in dependence upon a village, engages in evil conduct, and defiles the families of others.

If the *niśraya-karman* (act of formal dependence) has already been performed against him, it is because of his delusion and ignorance, whereby he commits many offenses, lives in close association with laypeople, and does not accord with the Buddha’s Dharma.
If the *chanda-anāgamanīya-karman* (act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople) has already been performed against him...

"Grinding" (mārjanā) refers to this: because one has reviled and insulted a faithful donor with base and contemptuous words, these four types of persons, although they have undergone the formal act of *karmavācanā* and been subjected to harsh disciplinary punishment, may still request release from it. Since they have not yet committed a root offense (*mūlāpatti*), they may continue to dwell together with the Saṃgha;
if they assemble with the community, they merely count toward the required quorum for the presence of members, but they are not permitted to obstruct the proceedings.

Regarding the *saṃghakarma*: if one obstructs it, one commits one of the offenses involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). "Obstruction" (*pratikṣepa*) is precisely what is meant by "reproaching" (*ākrośana*).
Therefore, it is said that when a person has attained full [ordination], they should not be reproached.
Second, there are those who, though not yet having reached the full number, should be censured; that is to say, one who intends to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
Explanation: One who intends to receive the full precepts is called a *śrāmaṇera*. Therefore, they do not count toward the full number of the Saṃgha.

Regarding those who should be rebuked: when one is about to receive the precepts and, at the very moment the formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha*) is being performed, says, "I will not receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*)," this is termed an obstruction (*paripantha*).
This is because it renders the Saṃgha’s *karmavācanā* ineffective. This is based on the *Vinayamātṛkā* of the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*.

The Buddha said: "If a śrāmaṇera, at the time of receiving full ordination, feels regret in his heart and does not wish to receive it, saying, 'I do not wish to receive the full precepts,' this statement constitutes an obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that such a person cannot count toward the required number and should be rebuked."

Third, regarding "not being permitted to complete the quorum and not being permitted to object": if a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed for a *bhikṣu*, one may include a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī* to complete the required number.
Commentary: In this third section, there is an extensive citation of Vinaya evidence. First, it clarifies the case of bhikṣuṇīs and the three junior groups [śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās].

If the great saṃgha assembles harmoniously within the boundary (sīmā) to perform a *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣu—most often concerning matters such as the formal accusation of faults or disciplinary punishment—the bhikṣuṇīs and the three junior groups may not serve as members to complete the quorum; they may neither voice criticism nor obstruct the proceedings.
The *Mahāsaṃghika-karman*.
Regarding the statement that one who has committed a "border offense" (*antarakṛtya*) or any of the thirteen obstacles (*trayodaśāvaraṇa*) is [ineligible]:
Commentary on the Thirteen Obstacles: 1. One who has committed a border offense; 2. One who has violated a bhikṣuṇī; 3. One who has received ordination with a thieving mind (*caura-citta*).

1. One who has broken the precepts; 2. One who belongs to an internal or external non-Buddhist path; 3. A eunuch; 4. One who has murdered his father; 5. One who has murdered his mother; 6. One who has murdered an Arhat; 7.
One who has disrupted the Saṃgha’s performance of the *karmavācanā* or its turning of the Wheel of Dharma;

8. One who has shed the blood of a Buddha; 9. A non-human being; 10. An animal; 11. One with dual sexual organs. If one possesses any such conditions, they are called a person subject to the thirteen obstacles (*trayodaśa-antarāya*).
If one has received the precepts and maintains them, it is known that there is room for them to receive [the full ordination].

Even if the assembly does not know this at the time, if they become aware of it after the reception has occurred, they must immediately expel the individual and shall no longer dwell together with them. What is here called an "offense" refers to an offense committed after the reception [of the precepts].

One who commits an offense is no longer a member of the Saṃgha; therefore, they cannot complete the quorum of the fourfold Saṃgha, nor can they obstruct a formal act (*saṃghakarma*) within the assembly.

This applies whether they have been subject to the three types of suspension (*tri-utkṣepa*), have been expelled (*pravāsanīya*), are subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya-arha*), or are undergoing the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*).

**Explanation:** Regarding the "three types of formal suspension" (*ukkhepanīyakamma*): these refer to suspension for not seeing [one's offense], suspension for not confessing [one's offense], and suspension for not relinquishing a wrong view.

As for "expulsion" (*pabbājaniya*): "extinguishing" (*pabba*) refers to severing one's traces; "banishing" (*bājanīya*) refers to casting one out from the boundary. One is excluded from the distribution of the Dharma and the food, and shall never dwell in community again.
This is the proper legal procedure due to having committed an irredeemable offense (*āpatti-ānantarika*). That which should be subject to expulsion refers to the matter itself.

This constitutes a manifest offense; according to the Dharma, he should be expelled. However, as the Saṃgha has not yet assembled to perform the formal proclamation of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations), one speaks of "separate residence" (*parivāsa*).

This means that while residing within the same boundary (*sīmā*), the community gathers to perform the ritual, yet [the offender] dwells separately on one side and does not participate face-to-face in the assembly.
Such a person does not count toward the full number of the Saṃgha, nor can they obstruct a *karmavācanā*.

This applies whether they are on the boundary of the precept-platform (*sīmā*), or if, by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they remain visible or become invisible, staying beyond the range of sight or hearing; or if it concerns the person for whom the *karmavācanā* is being performed.

Commentary: The above has fully and clearly explained both [the full and the incomplete]. Below this, only the incomplete is explained. The boundary markers for the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) and the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) are each distinct.

When one possesses the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), one dwells in space and is not comprised within the earth. To vanish from the midst of the assembly and manifest a miracle is to be formless;

to be beyond hearing yet within sight, or to hold forth a formal motion (*jñapti*) that is not heard, or to be beyond sight yet within hearing while shielding oneself with a screen—such as these cases, if they were to occur...
If others are present performing the ritual procedure, but the number of the Saṃgha is incomplete, one may not take them to fulfill the required number.
Therefore it is said: "Regarding those who perform the *karmavācanā*..."
Commentary: These twenty-eight types are merely illustrative and not exhaustive.

This phrase concludes the preceding section. It refers to nuns and the three groups of minor ordination, those subject to the thirteen *ānantarya* offenses, those who have been subjected to the three types of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), the two types of banishment (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), and those living in separate residence (*parivāsa*).

Furthermore, it includes those in a boundary where the *sīmā* is suspended in the air, those who have vanished, and those who are beyond the range of sight or hearing. These constitute the twenty-eight classes of persons.
Because among the four types of Saṃghas, none of them can fulfill the required quorum.

Furthermore, it is said: regarding those who practice *parivāsa*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *mānatva*, as well as those undergoing the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation of the offense), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When the *parivāsa* is completed, the *mūlāpakarṣa* is completed, and the six-night [mānatva] is completed—concerning these seven persons above, the Buddha declared that they do not constitute a valid quorum."
Commentary: This cites the third section, the *Pārājika-pācittiya* (the Chapter on Concealment). It was established because of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargīya*).
While they themselves practiced concealment followed by the *mūlāpakarṣa-mānāpya*, they granted others concealment followed by the *mūlāpakarṣa-mānāpya*.

The *naṭṭha* (one who has fallen away) and those who have completed twenty days [of probation] may grant another the rite of absolution (*āpattivyutthāna*). The origin story (*nidāna*) in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise:

having completed the period of concealment (*parivāsa*), and having completed the period of penance for returning to the original status (*mūlāpakarṣa*), there still remain six nights and the rite of absolution to be performed.

Having completed the six nights but not yet performed the rite of absolution, one should not act as a member of the quorum to perform the rite of concealment (*parivāsa-karman*) for another. Rather...

Up to the point of the "expiation of the offense" (*āpattivyutthāna*), the text of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* lacks the description of the performance [of the rite]. Therefore, I have cited the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to supplement it.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states: "A sleeping person, a person speaking incoherently, a person in a state of agitation, a person in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), a mute person, a deaf person, a person who is both mute and deaf, a mad person, a person with a disturbed mind, a person whose mind is impaired by illness, a bhikṣu on a tree, and a layperson (*avadātavasana*)."
These twelve types of persons do not constitute a quorum for the conferral of the precepts. Commentary:

One who is asleep is one whose mind has fallen into a state of non-defined neutrality (*avyākṛta*), while their body merely occupies its seat. One who speaks incoherently is one whose mouth lacks restraint and whose speech excessively disturbs the assembly.
One who is agitated is one whose mind is disordered and restless, with the mental faculty (*manas*) directed toward various external objects. One who has entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*)...

Gathering the mind and reflecting inwardly, one does not perceive the questions and answers. One who is mute should undergo the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) formal act, yet being unable to speak, they cannot provide testimony.
One who is deaf finds it difficult to observe and listen; thus, they are ignorant of right and wrong. One who is both mute and deaf lacks both speech and hearing, providing no benefit to others.
One who is insane has lost their fundamental mind, and their perception is clouded and dim. One with a distracted mind speaks perversely. [This applies to those] sitting...
Those who act contrary to proper decorum; those whose minds are impaired by illness, their four elements being in disharmony and lacking self-mastery;
"monks in trees," meaning those who observe the rainy season retreat while perched in trees, whose dwelling is distinct and who are not in communion with the assembly;

and "laypeople," meaning those who, though having shaved their hair, have not yet been moistened by the categories of precepts—these twelve kinds of persons receive the precepts in either central or peripheral lands.

One must not count toward the required number for the preceptor or the *saṃgha*. This applies not only to the reception of the precepts, but because one cannot fulfill the required number for any *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) either.
The *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Those who are seriously ill, those from border regions, and those who are dull-witted—these three [categories]" [are excluded].

Explanation: A person who does not fulfill the requirements of the assembly refers to one who is gravely ill; such a person’s mind is preoccupied with suffering, making it difficult to wait for the matter to conclude.

One from a frontier region refers to someone whose national language differs and whose speech cannot be understood. One who is dull-witted refers to one who is ignorant and lacks knowledge, such that they do not recite the Vinaya. Thus are the three.
A person also does not constitute a full assembly for the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one has given their consent (*chanda*), or if there is a physical barrier, or if there is a partial covering and exposure with a barrier between them."

If it is half-covered and half-exposed such that one cannot reach another with an outstretched hand; or if it is entirely an open space such that one cannot reach another with an outstretched hand while seated.
Commentary: "One who gives their consent" refers to anyone who completes the quorum of the assembly, all of whom serve as witnesses within the ritual procedure.

Clarification: One person shall hold the *jñapti-karman* (motion), while the rest of the assembly examines whether it is lawful or unlawful. If it is in accordance with the Dharma, they should grant their consent;

if it is not in accordance with the Dharma, they must object. Therefore, the person in question must be present before the assembly. It is permissible for the rest of the assembly to grant their consent (*chanda*) through a proxy.

However, it is not permitted to appoint a person who has granted their own consent as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the instructor (*ācārya*) for bestowing full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, whether in the center or at the borders of the assembly. As for those separated by a barrier, this refers to such a person...
Even if they have assembled, if there are further obstructions such as screens, curtains, or canopies that hinder sight and hearing, the assembly cannot be considered complete.
If it is "half-covered and half-exposed," meaning half-hidden and half-visible, it remains equivalent to a separate group and does not count toward the number present before the assembly.
Therefore, it is not permitted for the assembly to be complete [if these conditions exist]. Regarding "obstructed by an intervening barrier":

this refers to when people have already gathered and their bodies are not concealed, yet there is an object intervening between them that obstructs their faces so that they cannot see one another; thus, the assembly cannot be considered complete.
If it is half-covered and half-exposed such that one cannot reach across with the hands, then even though there is no physical object intervening, the covered and exposed areas remain distinct;

therefore, the full assembly is not constituted. If all are seated on open ground such that one cannot reach across with the hands, then even though there is no covering or obstruction and the seating area is one, they are still distant from the rest of the assembly and their hands do not reach one another; therefore, the full assembly is likewise not permitted.
It is further stated: "If the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* while sitting, it is contrary to the Dharma; this applies even when they alternate between standing, sitting, walking, and lying down.

The fourth division (*Caturvargika*) states: "I went to the place where the precepts were being recited and did not sit, thereby causing the assembly to be divided. The Buddha said, "This is contrary to the Dharma."

Commentary: Generally, when one enters the assembly to serve as a full member of the *saṃgha*, one’s sitting, rising, walking, and coming must be identical to those of the assembly; to differ would constitute disharmony.

To be in the assembly yet not part of the assembly is improper; thus, it is said that one should lie down [only] so as to fulfill the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and avoid lacking the required ritual count.

Therefore, the following citation from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* clarifies the reasons for the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule regarding separate assemblies. The incident originated with the group of six bhikṣus who, on the day of the *poṣadha*, thought to themselves:
"I shall not sit in the place where the precepts are recited, fearing that other bhikṣus might perform a *karmavācanā* against me.
If they obstruct the recitation of the precepts, it will prevent the assembly from successfully completing the *karmavācanā*. The Buddha knew this.
[The Buddha] rebuked them. The group of six [monks] said, "To act in such a manner is contrary to the Dharma.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In all cases of sick monks, the *poṣadha* is to be performed through a formal motion (*karmavācanā*).
Commentary: That Vinaya says that on the day of the *poṣadha*, if a sick person comes, or if there are many sick persons within the Saṃgha...
If they are able to come, the Saṃgha should assemble at the patient’s location to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts;
this clarifies that even for a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), there is no exemption when one is ill, let alone for other minor reasons to violate the noble regulations.

The Buddha said: "The meaning of 'a separate assembly' is like that of a drunken person, or when one speaks and the person before them does not understand, such that mind and object do not correspond;
these are all termed 'unlawful. Therefore, within the *Vinaya* concerning the methods for receiving and relinquishing the precepts, it says:
'If one is asleep, intoxicated, insane, or enraged such that there is no mutual understanding—as in the aforementioned circumstances—it is not accomplished.'"

**Commentary:** The first three phrases establish the meaning based on the Vinaya; the following sections provide an explanation according to the Vinaya. The *Upasampadā-vastu* (Chapter on Receiving Ordination) states:
At that time, there were bhikṣus who conferred full ordination upon those who were asleep. When they woke up, they returned home. The bhikṣus said to them, "Stop! Do not return home;
you have already received the precepts. They replied, "I did not receive the precepts. There were also those who conferred [ordination] upon people intoxicated by alcohol.

There are cases where one receives full ordination while insane, or where one receives full ordination while in a state of rage. When the intoxication has cleared and the original mind has been regained, or when the rage has subsided, it is likewise so.
This refers to the time when the precepts are formally received; at that moment, the state of the mind does not correspond [to the formal ritual].
Having received [the precepts], he returned home; as he was not included within the Saṃgha, it is said: "The meaning of being a separate assembly is like a drunken person," and so forth.

Regarding the method for relinquishing the precepts in the first section, it says: "If one relinquishes the precepts before a person who is insane, before a person with a disturbed mind, before a person in pain, before a deaf or mute person, before a person from the central lands before a person from the borderlands, or before a person from the borderlands before a person from the central lands..."

To renounce the precepts in the presence of others refers to the actual moment of renunciation. Even if one’s own words are not understood by the person before them, although the formal act of renunciation has not yet been completed, because the intention to renounce has already been resolved, one is no longer a bhikṣu in substance. The final two phrases provide a summary:

thirdly, such a person cannot complete the required number [for a quorum], and they may not be censured. This refers to the various obstructing conditions, as explained in detail according to the Vinaya cited extensively above.
This is not established, because the number of monks must fulfill the requirements of the Dharma.

Furthermore, one must understand the distinctions of the four propositions, such as "a separate assembly" being insufficient for the count, and so forth. One should be clear and practiced regarding the conditions for success and failure when facing specific circumstances.

Commentary: The preceding text only excluded those who complete the quorum for a formal assembly (*saṃgha*). This section further clarifies the case of a separate assembly (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, it says:
"Furthermore, one must know the distinctions among the four propositions, such as 'the separate assembly does not count toward the quorum,' and so forth.

The first proposition means that there are persons who are not permitted to participate in the formal acts (*karmavācanā*) of receiving precepts, absolving transgressions, receiving repentance, or undergoing disciplinary punishment; thus, they do not count toward the quorum within the *saṃgha* because they have been... [excluded].

Regarding disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍakarma*): as long as one has not yet sought resolution for it and has not yet repented for the offense committed, one may count toward the required quorum (*sāmagrī*) in other formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
However, if one is outside the range of sight or hearing—such that one cannot reach another by stretching out the hand—one does not constitute part of the quorum;
this constitutes the fault of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa-doṣa*). These refer to the four types of persons subject to censure (*tāḍana*) and so forth. The second phrase refers to...

There are persons who, during the conferral of precepts and even throughout all *karmavācanās*, do not count toward the required quorum; although they remain within the boundary (*sīmā*), they do not constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

These are precisely those such as the four types of *bhikṣuṇīs*, as well as those subject to the thirteen heavy obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*), the three types of formal accusations (*tṛtīya-karman*), the two types of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), and so forth. The three phrases refer to those persons who, regarding the conferral of precepts and all...

Within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), none of these individuals may count toward the quorum. If they do not attend or provide their consent (*chanda*), one commits the offense of acting in a separate assembly (*pṛthag-varga-dosa*).
These include those who are mute, deaf, mentally dull, confused, suffering from serious illness, or residing in border regions;

for they are unable to testify as to what is right or wrong, and thus none are permitted to count toward the quorum. Nevertheless, because they are originally bhikṣus, if they fail to attend, they commit an offense.

Regarding "being apart from the assembly" (*bhedasaṃgha*): there are four cases where a person, from the time of receiving the precepts up to all formal acts (*karmavācanā*), is counted as fulfilling the quorum for the assembly;

yet, by not being present and not having granted their consent (*chanda*), they commit the offense of being apart from the assembly. This refers specifically to a bhikṣu who is pure and without fault.
If one can thus examine each case individually according to the Dharma, it is said that the formal act is accomplished. Not...

To be able to distinguish each of these as non-Dharma in this manner is called the "corruption of the *karmavācanā*. This constitutes the meaning of the distinctions among the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

If one convenes the assembly and presides over the formal motion (*jñapti*), thereby being clear and lucid when facing the immediate situation, this is what it means to be well-versed [in the ritual].
The Vinaya is thoroughly proficient regarding the two conditions for formation and destruction.
Fourth, there are those who have attained the full number [of the quorum] and are also entitled to censure.
If virtuous bhikṣus dwell within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and do not remain beyond the range of sight or hearing, even down to speaking to bystanders—such persons possess both of these factors.

Explanation: This means that bhikṣus who abide within the same boundary according to the Dharma assemble for the performance of the ritual (*karmavācanā*), remaining within range of sight and hearing, even as far as those near the officiating monk (*karman-kāraka*) such that their speech can be heard. Therefore, it is called "excellent" (*kuśala*).
Because of this excellence, there is no fault; one attains the full number of the Saṃgha and is also able to block the ritual. Hence it says, "and so forth."
A person is endowed with both dharmas.
△ Seventh, the explanation of the purity of the *chanda* (consent).
Having already distinguished whether the prior *saṃgha-karma* was in accordance with the Dharma or not, if there is anyone who should grant their *chanda*, they shall grant it.
Since it was not known what the rules for granting and declaring *chanda* (consent) were, the seventh section further clarifies the declaration of *chanda* and *pārisuddhi* (purification).
The Vinaya states: "The monks who do not attend shall declare their *chanda* and *pārisuddhi*. Within this, there are three categories, namely:
the methods of granting *chanda*, receiving *chanda*, and declaring *chanda*.
Commentary: Herein, the second section of the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Precepts) is cited in its entirety. First, three dharmas are indicated; subsequently, they are explained individually.
All are subsumed under the category of "confession before another" (*pratyekapratideśanā*), while the dharma of granting consent (*chanda-dāna*) pertains to both public and private matters.
First, the procedure for granting consent (*chandadāna*).
Explanation: "Granting" (*dāna*) means to bestow or entrust. "Consent" (*chanda*) means the desire or inclination [to participate].

If one resides within the same boundary (*sīmā*), then in all formal monastic proceedings (*saṃghakarma*) conducted according to the Dharma, everyone desires to participate; thus, they act in harmony together to accomplish the task at hand due to that specific occasion.

Being bound by circumstances, I am unable to attend in person. Therefore, with my own heart’s desire, I shall set forth this matter with proper decorum before a learned bhikṣu who understands the Dharma.
I beg that he convey it to the Saṃgha when the time comes, so that they may know our minds are one and not different.

Based on the principle of assembling the community in person, if there are circumstances that prevent the opening of the heart for a collective gathering, then the capacity of the recipient and the teaching will not coincide;
how then could one provide salvation? Therefore, it is permitted to transmit the mind through speech. Only when the matters before the Saṃgha are thus addressed can both parties' needs be fulfilled.
It is for this reason that [the practice of] granting consent (*chanda*) was established as a skillful means.

If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, or matters concerning the sick or those tending to the sick, it is permitted to grant consent; however, the single method of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*) is the sole exception.

Commentary: According to this fundamental Vinaya, it is permitted to grant one’s consent (*chanda*) regarding matters concerning the Three Jewels and illness. However, the specific conditions for granting consent in the two cases of legal matters and illness are not detailed.
Now, I shall clarify them by drawing from the Mūlasarvāstivāda school. That text states: "If one grants consent for a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*)."
Either one currently has an illness; or fears that an illness is about to arise; or has recently recovered from a new illness;

or is exhausted from attending to a sick person; or encounters hunger, thirst, cold, or heat; or by nature is prone to excessive drowsiness and sleep, and thus practices other wholesome qualities in the hope of dispelling lethargy;
or recites the *Prātimokṣa* in a quiet room; or listens to and receives the meaning of the precepts from another; or...

For one who guards the words and phrases and fixes the mind on their meaning, fearing they might be forgotten; or for one who, having newly begun cultivation, attains a sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) manifesting before them in order to subdue the mind;

or for one who, regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and wholesome qualities, does not allow them to be interrupted—fearing that if they were mixed with other objects, right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) would be lost;
or for one who at times attains the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*): in all these cases, there is no offense in granting consent (*chanda*). However, if one grants consent [inappropriately]:
[The assembly] is large, while those gathered together are few. An elderly bhikṣu should set aside other virtuous activities and proceed to that place.
If a bhikṣu is indolent or gives his consent (*chanda*) for the sake of a base practice, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (i.e., *dukkaṭa*).

With the sole exception of the single rite of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), in performing any monastic legal procedure (*saṃghakarma*), one must necessarily possess ten conditions. Only then...

It is established. Only the *karmavācanā* for establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*) possesses exactly seven conditions: first, there is no place to rely upon; second, there is no boundary to delimit.
Since there is no encompassing boundary, the formal consent (*chanda*) is not mentioned. Furthermore, when establishing a boundary, one first proclaims its cardinal directions.

One must certainly know the limits of its length and breadth for its establishment; therefore, all members must assemble in full. For this reason, it is not permitted to grant one's consent (*chanda*) [by proxy].

According to the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on the Settlement of Disputes), when settling a dispute through the method of "majority decision" (*yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*) or the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*), it is likewise not permitted to grant consent, for fear that the assembly is not present in person and the dispute might subsequently arise again.
There are five ways of giving consent (*chanda*). These are: saying "I give you my consent"; saying "I speak my consent"; saying "speak my consent for me";
manifesting it through physical gestures; or speaking it at length so that the giving of consent is accomplished.
If one neither manifests it through physical gestures nor speaks it verbally, it is not accomplished; one must then give consent to another.
Commentary: Regarding the manifestation of bodily signs: At one time, there was a sick bhikṣu who, on the day of the poṣadha, was unable to verbally express his purity (*śuddhika*).
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "One should grant him purity through the body (*kāya-śuddhika*). If he raises his hand..."
If one raises a finger, shakes the body, shakes the head, or even lifts a single eye, it is called "giving the desire for purity" (*śuddhikāmatā*).
However, if a sick person does not manifest physical gestures, or if the four types of vocal utterances are indistinct and so forth, these do not constitute a valid giving of the desire.
One should instead give the desire to another; that is, one must wait until the sick person has recovered from their stupor and can manifest [the gesture] once again.
Regarding physical gestures and the other four [modes of communication], if one clearly articulates them to another person, both constitute the granting of consent (*chanda*).
Furthermore, it is said that the expression of consent and the declaration of purity must be stated simultaneously; they may not be stated separately.

**Commentary:** Regarding the causal conditions established in the Vinaya: because the group of six bhikṣus gave their consent (*chanda*) but did not give their purity (*śauca*), when a matter arose within the Saṃgha, the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) could not be performed.
The bhikṣu who held the consent said, "I have brought the consent, but I did not bring the purity," yet they proceeded with the *karman* of detention and the recitation of the precepts.
He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "When giving consent, one should say as follows:"

"I grant my consent (*chandadāna*); my purity (*śuddhi*) is likewise. This means that one person informs [the assembly] of their own desire and intention, while another informs them of their half-monthly purity and freedom from transgressions.
Although these individuals are not present in person, this does not obstruct the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha.
Therefore, it is said that the granting of consent and the declaration of purity must both be stated together at once; they may not be stated separately.
If one wishes to explain this in detail, one should properly maintain the deportment and go to the person to whom the consent is to be transmitted, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. [I], the bhikṣu [Name], regarding the legal matters of the Saṃgha, grant my consent and purity" (saying this once and then ceasing).

**Commentary:** "Fully practicing the dignified deportment (*airyāpatha*)" means that "fully" (*samanvāgata*) implies being without deficiency, and "practicing" (*bhāvita*) implies being properly composed.

Whenever entering among the Sangha or performing formal rituals (*karmavācanā*) before a single person, one should adjust one's robes and maintain a solemn countenance; the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) must be respectful to manifest utmost sincerity.

The subsequent requirements for dignified deportment follow this principle and need not be elaborated upon here. "Venerable One" (*bhadanta*): the Sanskrit term is *bhadanta*. According to the Vinaya...
The *Śāstra* says: These are words of respectful address. One should not call a bhikṣu by name or clan, whether they be junior or senior.
A senior addresses a junior as "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*), while a junior refers to a senior as "Worthy Sir" (*bhadanta*).
As for the phrase "with a focused mind," this is a request for their compassion and mindfulness toward oneself. Regarding "matters of the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma," this...

This is the general statement. In the Vinaya, it is said that because the group of six monks spoke of giving their consent (*chanda*) with reference to a specific matter, saying, "I give my consent to you regarding this matter," and because matters arose within the pure assembly of monks, the monk holding the consent said, "I bring the consent and purity regarding this specific matter;
I do not bring the consent and purity regarding any other matter. Consequently, the monastic affairs were delayed. Thus [it was said] by the various monks.

He informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should not grant consent by referring to specific matters. From this day forward, I authorize the granting of consent and purity for monastic affairs conducted in accordance with the Dharma. This is now a fixed rule."
The Buddha said: "If one can remember their clans, physical characteristics, names, and categories, one may accept as many as one wishes.
If one cannot remember them, it is also permissible to simply say, 'Many bhikṣus grant their consent and purity.'"

Commentary: This passage clarifies the conditions for receiving [consent]. It is prepared according to the Vinaya: after a bhikṣu has received the consent of one person, he doubts whether he may receive that of two;
and so on, until after receiving the consent of three, he doubts whether he may receive that of four. The Buddha said:
"If you can fully remember and recognize the names [of the individuals], you may receive as many as you wish. If you cannot remember their names, you should..."
One should address them by their clan name. If one cannot recall the clan name, one should address them by their physical characteristics.

If one cannot recall their physical characteristics, it is also permissible to say, "The many bhikṣus," and then grant the *chanda* (consent) and *viśuddhi* (purity) for the legal business of the Saṃgha.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the *poṣadha* is to be held tomorrow, giving one's consent (*chanda*) today does not constitute the valid giving of consent.

It further states: "When the assembly meets at the proper time, one should give the consent for purity (*śuddhi-chanda*); when the assembly meets at an improper time, one should give the consent for formal ritual action (*karma-chanda*).

(Text). The original text cited here only clarifies the timing of consent based on this fundamental Vinaya. Regarding ordinary monastic affairs, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they should be conducted in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*) for monastic affairs: the remainder of the *karmavācanā* formula is the same as above.
Second, the explanation of the method for receiving consent:
"Receiving" (*pratigraha*) means to accept, take in, and retain in memory. As for the giver, they may grant it either extensively or in brief, provided it is done according to the Dharma. Its...
If the recipient does not maintain the mindfulness [of the precepts] properly, or if they have committed an offense, the reception is not accomplished.
The Buddha said: "If one who has received the *kāmacchanda* (desire) passes away immediately after receiving it; or if they go outside the boundary;

or if they abandon the path and join the ranks of non-Buddhists or other sects; or if they arrive at the site of the *sīmā* (boundary); or if the dawn appears—these seven conditions and others like them [render the reception invalid]."

If one declares oneself to be a person who has committed one of the thirteen obstacles, such as a transgressor of the boundary offenses (*sīmā-aticāra*), or if one has been subject to the three types of formal accusation (*tri-udghāta*) or the two types of expulsion (*dvividha-niḥsaraṇa*),
or if one remains in a secluded place out of sight and hearing— such cases, together with the twenty-eight preceding conditions, all render the reception of a proxy vote (*chanda*) invalid.
If one reaches the middle of the path, or likewise reaches the midst of the Saṃgha, one should further grant one's *chanda* (consent) to another.
Commentary: Regarding "having already granted *chanda* and then passing away," birth and death and the breath do not wait for man.

Regarding "going out of the boundary," one is suddenly pulled by circumstances; the body follows the matter at hand. Regarding "one who has abandoned the path," their craving and desire are intensely blazing, and their precepts...
"Returning home while emaciated" refers to entering the ranks of non-Buddhist sects (tīrthika), wherein one's knowledge and views are inverted, abandoning the correct for the false.

"Members of a separate faction" refers to those who have reconciled after the four types of disputes but whose groups have subsequently split apart. "Arriving at the boundary of the precept-platform" (sīmā-maṇḍala) refers to walking about within a different territory and thus forgetting or erring regarding what has been received [of the precepts].
"The appearance of the dawn light" means that the latter part of the night has already passed and the time belongs to the following morning. In the Vinaya, there are such cases as these.
There are seven conditions. After the bhikṣus have given their consent (*chanda*), each one individually gives rise to doubt, thinking:

"Has the consent been lost, or has it not been lost? They go to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha says: "In all cases, the consent is lost for those who possess the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*), and so on, up to those who have moved beyond the range of sight or hearing.

The meaning is to be interpreted according to the previous explanation. Together with the seven types previously mentioned, such as death, these twenty-eight conditions do not [constitute a valid transmission].
The formal consent (*chanda*) is not established. When people such as these receive [the consent], it is not established;

even if they do hold the consent, should they reach the midpoint [of the journey] or arrive among the Saṃgha, it is in all cases not established. Therefore, it is said: "it is likewise. One should instead grant the consent to others.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are five ways of losing a formal authorization (*chanda*). These are as explained in the section on 'insufficiency of the quorum. Furthermore, it says: (1) receiving an authorization while outside the boundary;

(2) the one holding the authorization goes outside the boundary; (3) the person giving the authorization goes outside the boundary; (4) having given the authorization, one returns to the midst of the Saṃgha and then leaves the assembly;
(5) the one holding the authorization is in the midst of the Saṃgha when, due to an emergency, everyone rises in alarm and not a single person remains."
These and others like them are all termed "loss of the consent" (*chanda-vināśa*).
Regarding the explanation of the five kinds of loss of consent mentioned among those who do not count [as present]:

they are as follows—when the person giving the consent is separated by a barrier, or by a partial covering and exposure, or when there is an intervening barrier or partial covering and exposure such that one cannot reach out one's hand to the other.
If, among those sitting in an open space, one cannot reach another by stretching out the hand, this is called the five kinds of loss of consent (*chanda*).

Regarding one who receives consent outside the boundary (*sīmā*): the Vinaya prescribes that the assembly of monks must gather based on the boundary; thus, the giving of consent must occur within the boundary, not in a place not encompassed by the boundary.
It is not included in the assembly. If, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one has previously left the boundary due to some business, there is no need to grant consent (*chanda*) from outside the boundary.
If one who holds consent or maintains consent leaves the boundary, this constitutes a personal cause for error regarding the consent of others.

Regarding those who have granted their consent (*chanda*) and then depart from the boundary: this is an allowance made because of the person; when the person departs, the legal act (*dharma*) is lost.

Furthermore, if one has already granted consent and then goes among the Saṃgha but subsequently leaves the assembly, there is a case in the Vinaya of a sick bhikṣu who, having granted his consent, heard the Saṃgha reciting the Dharma and the Vinaya.
He exerted himself to go and listen, but after sitting for a long time, he became weary and exhausted. Because he had previously granted his consent, he departed in silence.
The seat is vacated. If one who holds the *chanda* (consent) is among the Saṃgha, and due to a calamity they are startled and rise up so that not a single person remains—

meaning the person holding the *chanda* has already arrived among the Saṃgha, but both he and the assembly encounter calamities such as water, fire, bandits, or wild beasts and are all startled and rise together,
scattering in all directions to seek refuge so that there is not a single bhikṣu within the boundary— all such cases are termed "loss of *chanda*."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one grants [the formal act] to three types of persons, such as those who conceal their offenses (*paryuṣita*), they lose their consent (as do those undergoing *mūlaparivāsa* and *mānāpya*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one grants it to four types of persons, such as nuns; or to three types of persons, such as those who are insane; or if the assembly departs in disorder—all these render the consent invalid."
The four persons, namely nuns and so forth, refer to the *śikṣamāṇā*, the *śrāmaṇera*, and the *śrāmaṇerī*.

The three persons, namely those who are insane and so forth, refer to the person who is mentally deranged, the person with a disturbed mind, and the person who is dull-witted. Regarding "one who leaves the assembly in reverse":

this refers to a person who has received the *chanda* (consent) with the intent of causing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) to be invalid; having received the *chanda*, they arrive in the midst of the Saṃgha and then again leaves in reverse. Thus it is said.
None of these constitute the valid reception of the *chanda* (consent).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a person who has received the *chanda* and purification (*pariśuddhi*) declares themselves 'I am not a bhikṣu' either at the time of receiving it or after it has been received, the *pariśuddhi-chanda* is not established."
**Explanation:** "To take" means to seek. This refers to when a bhikṣu is correctly seeking the *kāma* (consent/vow) from another person, and that person says:
"I have already abandoned the precepts; I am now a śrāmaṇera, an upāsaka, or a layman (*avadātavasana*). I have entered among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); I am no longer a bhikṣu.
Since he has spoken thus himself, he is no longer part of the Saṃgha, and therefore the *poṣadha* is not shared with him. For this reason, one does not give him the *kāma*.
Because it has been accomplished. If the request is completed, the same applies to such speech.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one is the presiding elder (*sthavira*), one should say: 'I am the presiding elder of the Saṃgha; I should not accept [this task].'"
If one is a preceptor of nuns, or a reciter of the Prātimokṣa, one should say, "I shall speak for myself; I will not receive [the instruction] on behalf of others.
If one is a caretaker of the vihāra or a sick person, one should say, "I will not go into the Saṃgha; I shall give it to another person.
If one says, "I am a beggar," "I am an araṇyaka," "I wear rag-robes," or "I am a person of great virtue," one should not accept [the assignment].
"Desire" constitutes a *vinaya*-offense. Regarding "Elder" (*sthavira*):
one whose years since ordination (*varṣāgra*) surpass the multitude and whose virtuous deeds are peerless. According to the Vinaya regulations, four types of elders are established within the Saṃgha.
Whenever they preach the Dharma to provide guidance, receive offerings, or perform any activity, the entire assembly must show them respect.

If those who instruct or recite the precepts have been duly appointed and possess the requisite virtues, they have their duties to perform; thus, these three types of persons should not logically accept a formal delegation of consent (*chanda*).
Since even those guarding the dwellings or those who are ill still grant consent, one should properly decline such requests.

If one says, "I am a mendicant," this refers to manifesting one's own ascetic practices (*dhūta*); it is an act of self-aggrandizement and contempt for others, and therefore constitutes an intentional offense.

The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu holding the *chanda* (consent) has personal business arise and is unable to go to the Saṃgha to hear the formal act, he may transfer it to another bhikṣu. He should speak as follows:

Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, together with many other bhikṣus, grant our consent and purity for the formal acts of the Saṃgha performed according to the Dharma.
Both they and I hereby grant our consent and purity. (Having spoken once, one ceases.)

Commentary: If one’s own person is bound by circumstances and another wishes to offer their consent (*chanda*), both parties will lose their intended purpose because the matter of the Saṃgha is delayed.
Therefore, the Noble One’s compassion, responding to the needs of the occasion, again permitted the transfer of consent. The present text is for receiving the consent of multiple persons;
if one were to receive the consent of only a single person, simply replace the two characters "many" (*zhòngduō*) with the name of that individual, while the rest of the wording remains unchanged.
The *Tripiṭaka* states that one may express the *chanda* (consent).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "One must not give consent to another person haphazardly; it should be given to one capable of conveying the consent and expressing it within the Saṃgha."
Commentary: This clarifies that one should not quickly grant the *kāmacchanda* (desire/consent) to those who lack wisdom; rather, it should be granted to one who is capable of upholding it.

That is to say, it should be given to one who has approached with a general protection of the categories of precepts (*śīlaskandha*), possesses wisdom and mindfulness so as not to forget, and is endowed with the proper decorum expected of others.
Only such a person knows what constitutes the proper time for desire and what does not, and is well able to maintain it until they reach the midst of the Saṃgha to act according to the Dharma.

The reason for citing this from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is to demonstrate that the aforementioned faults regarding the transmission of the *chanda* (consent) all arise because the giver acts precipitately and fails to discern the recipient.
If there is one who speaks [the consent], after the *karmakāraka* has questioned him as described above, that holder of the *chanda* should respond, "It is so."

Commentary: *Karma* is a general term. It refers to those who gather at the proper time to recite the precepts (*śīla*), and those who gather at an improper time to perform formal legal acts (*dharmakriyā*).

Having asked as above—meaning that the assembly is gathered according to the Dharma and in harmony, and having distinguished between those who belong to the assembly and those who do not—the person performing the *karma* asks:
"Is the Saṃgha assembled? Is it in harmony? Have those who have not received full ordination departed? Have those who are absent sent their consent (*chanda*)?"
And whether it is pure or not. If it is, that person holding the *chanda* (consent) shall respond with palms joined while at their original seat, saying:

"It is so. Having answered, they rise from their seat, properly maintain their dignified demeanor, and approach the one performing the *karmavācanā*. Before him, they perform one prostration, kneel with their right knee on the ground, join their palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have received his consent and purity. He has granted his consent and purity for the Dharma-accordant business of the Sangha.
(Having spoken thus once, one should stop.)
If it is the time for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), one should say, "I grant my consent for the *pravāraṇā*. The remaining wording is the same as above. [Commentary:

when one dwells upon that restlessness and feels distress in the mind, it is "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*). Regarding the "hindrance of doubt" (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) has the meaning of hesitation and indecision; it is, in essence, delusion (*moha*).

It is delusion (*moha*). Being darkened and dull by ignorance (*avidyā*), one cannot distinguish between the true and the false; with a mind of hesitation, one is constantly unable to reach a decision.
By means of these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and other such delusions, the mental consciousness of all sentient beings is shrouded, such that they cannot clearly perceive the Noble Path.

They are unable to give rise to the wholesome dharmas of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and remaining stagnant within the three realms (*tridhātu*), they fail to attain liberation. Therefore, it is so named.
It serves as a canopy.
The "five hundred years of the final dharma" refers to the first five hundred years of the ten-thousand-year period of the final dharma.
During these five hundred years, although bhikṣus lack cultivation and realization, they still possess liberation, meditative concentration, and the observance of precepts in great measure.
Regarding the mention of "giving": the Buddha knew that the Dharma was gradually declining, and therefore he taught this sequence.
In the first hundred years, liberation will be firm; in the second hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm;

For five hundred years, one should remain firm in giving.
