When traveling through a wilderness where there is no village, if the community of monks is unable to assemble, they should follow their respective teachers and virtuous friends;
leaving the main path, they should gather at one place, establish a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.

It is further stated that on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, if traveling on a road in a non-village area such as an *āraṇya* and the assembly cannot be brought together, they should follow their respective teachers and close associates and move [to a suitable location].

In a different location, they establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; thus we know that it is not difficult [to do so], and one may freely establish such a boundary even when various obstacles are absent.
If one violates this regulation, one commits an offense.

Explanation: This passage first cites the conditions for exemption (*anujñāhetu*). That is to say, regarding the establishment of a small boundary for receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), this refers to...
The opening of the *dharmakarmika-mahā-sīmā* (the great boundary established by formal ritual) is permissible, just as when one establishes the two small boundaries for the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*.

This is permitted specifically regarding the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) for those traveling on a road. According to what is clarified in the Vinaya, unless there is the difficulty of being outside a *mahā-sīmā*, where there are obstructions and no path, or where the traveling companions on the road are in discord;
even if one were to set up a rule based on their own arbitrary views, it would be comparable [to the aforementioned cases].

To take such cases as examples and, clinging to them as being correct, to hastily establish such small boundaries (sīmā) is to contravene the Buddha’s intended regulations and violate the chapters on prohibitions.
Therefore, I now cite the Vinaya as proof; one must skillfully investigate and uphold [the rules].
Furthermore, none of these have external boundaries; rather, the very place where the body sits constitutes the substance of the boundary. Therefore, it is said in the *Upasampadā-vidhi*:
"This community of monks has gathered in one place to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*). In the *Poṣadha-vidhi*, it says: "Now, so many bhikṣus have gathered to establish a small boundary.
And in the *Pravāraṇā-vidhi*, it says: "The places where the bhikṣus sit are already full; [the boundary extends] as far as the seats of these bhikṣus."

In such locations, the Saṃgha establishes small boundaries (*sīmā*) and so forth; thus we know that in both cases there is no external boundary marker (*bāhya-nimitta*). This is for the purpose of preventing those who would object;

as the *Upasampadā-vidhi* (Method for Receiving Ordination) concerning the small boundary states: "An objection raised outside the boundary does not constitute a valid objection. This text clearly explains the absence of an external boundary marker.

Commentary: This clarifies the essential substance (*bhāva*) of the boundary. It refers to the binding of three minor boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*), which takes as its substance the places where the various bhikṣus present at that time walk, stand, or sit.
No external markers are required to manifest the demarcations of the interior and exterior.

Even if someone with a differing opinion should come and attempt to perform a formal act of censure (*codanā-karman*), if they do so from outside the boundary, their censure is not valid. This is based on the following precedent: [text follows].
The Vinaya texts explain that it is clear there are no external boundary markers.

Now, if one establishes boundary markers for a hall or courtyard and performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) within it, the ritual is not accomplished. This is because the markers for the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) were not proclaimed according to the Dharma;
furthermore, the Small Boundary (*khuḍḍakasīmā*) has no [fixed] markers. Since the markers were established contrary to the Dharma, the Great Boundary must be proclaimed by individuals separately.

Regarding the boundary markers (*lakṣaṇa*): these are recorded within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure). Since there is no formal proclamation (*jñapti*) for a minor boundary (*kṣudrakasīma*), the markers are made manifest by the *karmavācanā* itself;

therefore, they are again set forth clearly and explicitly so that there may be no doubt or confusion. If one were to proceed with the binding [of the boundary] without this, it would constitute multiple offenses: first, it would not be a case of a permitted exception (*anujñāta-vaipulya*);
second, it would be a case of arbitrarily establishing markers; and third, the location would remain fixed and permanent. As the text says: "One should not fail to dissolve [the boundary]..."

The four types of false claims (*mṛṣāvāda*) apply to other dharmas as well; these are cases where one prescribes what was not previously prescribed. The text for the *karmavācanā* is as usual. Commentary: This explains the characteristics of what is improper.

There are those who establish boundary markers (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*) within a monastery compound and then perform the formal act of binding [the area]; this is not called "binding a *śikṣādattaka* site" (*śikṣādattaka-maṇḍala*) or "constructing an altar.

This is intended to serve as a permanent model for posterity. This refers to the binding of three small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) and the establishment of markers while maintaining the existing rooms.

Therefore, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is not accomplished. Why? Because when establishing the boundary markers for a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), it is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*) not to announce them;
yet when binding a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), there are no such markers. If one were to establish markers and then announce them, it would likewise be contrary to the Dharma.

When binding a great boundary, one must specifically have a single person announce the markers. In the text of the formal ritual act (*jñapti-karman*), it is recorded as follows: "The bhikṣus of this residence announce..."

Regarding the characteristics of the boundaries of the four directions: since there is no established procedure for proclaiming the marks of a small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*), the *karman* itself makes the defining marks manifest, as described in the "Three Dharmas" section that follows.
Therefore, I have again provided a detailed and clear explanation so that there may be no doubt or confusion. These two sentences are words of concluding admonition;
they mean that the efficacy of the *karman* achieves a preeminent success, and even a slight deviation from the Buddha’s intent will render it ineffective.
What is beneficial may instead result in harm; for this reason, I have repeatedly cited scriptural evidence and explained the matter with meticulous detail, reaching the ultimate point of clarity.

I hope you will no longer harbor doubts and will strictly adhere to the correct regulations. If one were to act lightly according to one's own whims and form bonds [of ordination] at will, then many transgressions would ensue.
Therefore, four faults are set forth, as the text states: "One should not depart without understanding," and so forth. The term "and so forth" refers to the three minor [precepts].
Regarding the phrase "the legal procedure for simultaneous presence within the realm," which states that its *karmavācanā* text is as usual: this sentence merely indicates a general outline.
Since the full ritual procedure for the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* has not yet been clarified, it is now appended here for practical use.
The Method for Establishing and Dissolving the Small Boundary for Receiving Precepts, continued:
These two methods follow the outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation). Now, they are included here following the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*.

As for the conditions for opening [the boundary], it must rely upon ten monks who are in agreement and pure [of offenses] (in border regions, five may suffice). Regarding the person about to receive the precepts:

Having gone outside the boundary, establish a place where [the sound] can be heard from afar. Once the community of monks has quickly gathered at one location, they shall bind a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).

Having performed the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakarmika*), they respond by saying, "We are binding a small boundary. Then, for the *karman* of receiving the precepts, they make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This Saṃgha has assembled in one place to establish a small boundary (sīmā). If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent to establish this small boundary.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This Saṃgha has assembled in one place to establish a small boundary (sīmā). Which elders consent to the Saṃgha’s assembly to establish the small boundary?
Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented, and the assembly has completed the establishment of the small boundary.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus maintained.
This *karmavācanā* was performed for the sake of an individual; thus it belongs to the private sphere.

First, it is invalid because there is not one person [to perform it], the assembly of preceptors is insufficient, and it is subject to interference and obstruction. Second, it is invalid because of errors in the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Third, it is invalid because there is no cause for its dissolution. The latter four cases are to be understood by analogy.
The method for dissolving the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for receiving the precepts:

Once the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) has been completed, one should immediately dissolve it by employing another expedient means. In response, one says: "The *karman* for dissolving the boundary.

Although the assembly has not yet dispersed, because the procedures for binding and dissolving differ, the wording is changed from "binding" (*bandhana*) to "dissolving" (*vimocana*), while the remaining phrasing remains unchanged. Below...
The method for dissolving the two small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) may be understood by analogy with the preceding cases.
The procedures for establishing and dissolving the small boundary for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) are both included here.

These two methods follow the general outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (formal motion followed by one proclamation). Now, they are incorporated here following the *Poṣadhavastu* (Section on the Recitation of Precepts). This is the opening.

The conditions are as stated above. One should perform the preliminary rites (*pūrvakalpa*). The response is: "The formal act (*karmavācanā*) for establishing a small boundary (*sīmā*) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. Thus one should announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to establish a small boundary..."
The boundary is thus announced. Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
So many bhikṣus have assembled to establish a small boundary (sīmā). Which elders among you consent to so many bhikṣus assembling to establish a small boundary?
Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak. The Saṃgha has consented to so many bhikṣus...
The demarcation of the small boundary (sīmā) is completed. Because the Saṃgha remains silent, it is accepted; this matter is thus maintained.
This single *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the Dharma; it belongs to the public.
It is not [the case that] non-humans are [bound by this]. This refers to those who have not gathered in a mixed assembly and so forth. The other forms of destruction are as stated above.
If one understands this boundary, the subsequent procedures for receiving the precepts should be conducted according to the above.
The method for establishing the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, together with its dissolution, follows.
These two methods are based on the framework of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Now, they are incorporated here following the *Pravāraṇā-vastu*.

The conditions for their application are as stated in the text. One should perform the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*) and respond by saying: "The *karman* for establishing the small boundary for the *pravāraṇā*."
Make the following announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, listen. The seating places for the bhikṣus are already full, extending as far as these seating places of the bhikṣus.
If it is the proper time for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let the Sangha establish a small boundary (sīmā) within these seating places. Thus is the announcement made.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The seating places for the bhikṣus are already full. The Saṃgha now establishes a small boundary (sīmā) within these seating places.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a small boundary within these seating places should remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus settled:
the Saṃgha has completed the establishment of the small boundary within these seating places. The Saṃgha consents by its silence; therefore, this matter is as [stated].
This is the *dhāraṇī*.
Explanation: This single *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the Dharma; thus, it belongs to the public. Within this, it is clearly shown to be different from the aforementioned.
The Method for Establishing and Dissolving the Hall for the Recitation of the Precepts.

Continued. These two methods follow the framework of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation). Now, they are incorporated here following the *Poṣadha-vastu* (Section on the Recitation of the Precepts).
The Vinaya-mūla states: "The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to recite the precepts in a single location, or to wait for one another in the mountains, or..."

In the forest, or among the burial mounds, or in a large hall, a dining hall, a walking path, by a river, or even on a patch of soft grass, they waited for one another until the assembly became weary. They reported this to the Buddha, who said:

"Whether it be in a large hall, on an upper story, in a walking path, or even on a patch of grass, you should state the name of the location. I authorize a formal motion with a second (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."

[The procedure for] *mārjanā*. From among the assembly, one who is capable and competent shall be appointed to preside over the ritual. He should perform the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakalpa*) and state:
"I shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the establishment of the *Poṣadha-hall*. The officiant then makes the following formal motion (*jñapti*): [text follows].
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. [We] shall establish a Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a location.

This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Now the community of monks is establishing a Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a location. Which elders consent to the Saṃgha’s [action]?
"Those who approve of establishing a *poṣadha-śālā* at [this] location, remain silent. Whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and authorized the establishment of the *poṣadha-śālā* at [this] location. Since the Saṃgha remains silent, it is so; this matter is thus upheld."

Commentary: This one *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the Dharma; it pertains to the public. Within it, it is clearly distinguished from the aforementioned explanation of the rules for the *śīla-śālā* (precept hall).
Continued: At that time, the bhikṣus had previously established a *poṣadha* hall on Vulture Peak Mountain, but later wished to establish one in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
For this reason, they informed the Buddha, who accordingly permitted them to dissolve the previous boundary and re-establish it through a formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Among the assembly, a capable person should be appointed to perform the preliminary procedure, responding by saying: "I shall dissolve the *śīla* [boundary]."
The formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) regarding the hall has been completed through question and answer. It is announced as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I shall dissolve this place as the hall for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Thus it is announced.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Now the *poṣadha* hall at [place name] is being dissolved. Which elders among you consent to the dissolution of the *poṣadha* hall at [place name] by the Saṃgha?
Those who consent remain silent. Those who do not consent speak. Since the Saṃgha has consented and remains silent, the dissolution of the *poṣadha* hall at [place name] is concluded.
Because the Saṃgha consents through silence, this matter is thus upheld.
Commentary: This section distinguishes errors and clarifies what is incorrect; all seven cases follow the previous pattern.

Furthermore, according to the Vinaya: At one time, there was a monastery where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the assembly gathered but the hall for the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃghāta*) was too small to accommodate them.
The bhikṣus reported this fully to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said: "The Saṃgha has the authority to act as it sees fit. If [the boundary] is not..."
**Explanation on the Binding for the Recitation of the Precepts:** This means that once [the boundary] has been established within the ritual action zone (*karmabhūmi*), it need not be bound again.
The items listed in the outline are provided so as not to omit any monastic laws; here, too, the procedure continues in order to ensure that the permissions granted are known.

**The Second Method: Binding and Unbinding the Garment Boundary** There are three types of monasteries (*saṃghārāma*): those where the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) coincides with the monastery itself; those where the boundary is smaller than the monastery; and those where the boundary is larger than the monastery.

In the first two cases, it is unnecessary to bind the boundary. If the boundary is larger than the monastery, one should bind it according to the Dharma, and then [the garments] will be contained within that boundary.
[This refers to] the robe.
Explanation: This means that whether a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) is large or small, its construction is first established and fixed.
However, if the boundaries are later demarcated such that they are not equal, there are thus three differences. If one establishes markers according to the site of the monastery...
Regarding the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*): this refers to boundaries shared with monasteries (*ārāma*) and the like.

If there are many small huts within a single large monastery and the residents dwell separately, each person may establish a boundary marker according to the foundation of their own dwelling; this is called a boundary smaller than the monastery.
These two types of boundaries do not require formal ritual delimitation. If, outside the monastery, the area is vast and unobstructed, or if there are [natural] markers...

Whether it be a meditation cell, a layperson’s house, or a village, one may establish boundaries as appropriate. Regarding those within the boundary, one should set up markers according to their distance and demarcate them collectively;
this is called a boundary larger than a monastery (*ārāma*). One should establish it in accordance with the Dharma, so that the robe is contained within the boundary.

However, there are those who establish a *karmavācanā* for the "non-village" boundary (*amūla-sīmā*). According to the Vinaya texts, one first establishes a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) that includes the village within it;
subsequently, due to the arising of certain circumstances, the village is then excluded. Now, a single method is established universally:
regardless of whether a village exists or not, the exclusion must be performed as a matter of course.

Commentary: The preceding section clarified that there are three types of *ārāma* (monasteries). This citation from the Vinaya serves to establish the formal procedures. Regarding the establishment [of boundaries] where no village exists:
this refers to the *Karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) compiled by the Vinaya Master Tandi of the Cao Wei dynasty, which states:

"If there is a village, the village must be excluded; if there is no village, it is not necessary to proclaim the exclusion of the village or the external boundary of the village. If one follows the Vinaya...

The text states: First, the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) was established such that robes were contained within the village. Later, due to a specific incident, the village boundary was subsequently removed. The *Mūla-vinaya* says:
"It was permitted for the bhikṣus to first establish a non-contained robe-boundary, with robes contained within the village.

Later, because a bhikṣu took off his robe and placed it in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), at the moment he put on the robe again, his body was exposed, leading to public censure. For this reason, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha... [text continues].
It was said: "From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to establish the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe), excluding the 'outer limit of a village' (*grāmabāhya*).
This is established through a formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Therefore, now synthesizing the various schools, a single fixed rule is established:
regardless of whether a village exists at the time of the establishment or not, it must naturally be excluded. 'Naturally' (*dharmatā*) means that it is so by its own inherent principle."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sa-p'o-to lun) correctly establishes this principle, excluding [the robe] due to five reasons for the arrival of a village.
Explanation: This citation from the treatise proves that the doctrine established is not without basis. As for the five reasons:

first, the village is a state of distraction and instability, whereas the boundary of the robe (*cīvara-sīmā*) is fixed; second, it is to eliminate censure and slander; third, it is to eliminate... [text fragment].

1) Because of quarrels and disputes; 2) for the sake of protecting the holy life (*brahmacarya*); 3) for the sake of removing suspicion; 4) for the sake of protecting the holy life; and 5) for the sake of removing suspicion.
The following text, based on the treatise, provides a detailed explanation of the intent behind the prohibition of [staying] in a village.
If there was originally no village and the boundary has been established through formal ritual, then from the dwelling of the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) outward, wherever a village enters,
all such areas are not the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā).
**Commentary:** This clarifies the principle that what did not previously exist may later come into being.

It means that after the *saṃgha* has already performed the ritual of boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandha*), if a layperson subsequently resolves to serve the community by performing manual labor and enters the boundary to reside there, they first construct dwellings.
Because the locations where those dwellings are situated are not included within the "robe-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*) of the bhikṣus, this principle is based on the *Śāstra*.

It is said: When a king enters within the boundary and sets up a canopy to encircle the area, with food-preparation sites established nearby on the left and right, these are all not part of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
However, if he returns to his original village, it is still included within the robe-boundary.
**Commentary:** This clarifies the principle of "previously existing and subsequently non-existing. According to the treatise:

if there was originally a village and, after the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) has been established, one moves out and leaves the boundary, then this empty space is called the "boundary where one is not separated from the robe" (*acīvaravippavāsa-sīmā*).
"If there was previously a village that was not included [in the robe boundary], and the village moves away from the ground, the robe boundary returns to its full extent.
Explanation: This clarifies the principle of prior existence followed by increase or decrease. The first phrase, according to the treatise, states:
"If one has previously demarcated a robe boundary and there is a settlement that was originally small but later becomes large, [the boundary] extends as far as the settlement reaches."

It is not the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīma*). According to the treatise, the second phrase states: "If a village was originally large and, after the boundary has been established, the village subsequently becomes smaller, then wherever there is empty space, it all remains the robe-boundary."
This is because the village comes and goes; it is not due to the binding and unbinding [of the boundary]. This same intent is found throughout the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Commentary: This explains the preceding discussion on the meaning. That is to say, whether a village exists or not, and whether it is large or small, depends on the coming and going of people from that village;

thus its dimensions increase and decrease without fixed limit. It is not the case that once bound it is then unbound, or once unbound it is then bound again, for the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-boundary) is fixed.
Regarding the citation from the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*): the *Five-Part Karmavācanā* was compiled by the Vinaya Master Aitong of Kaiye Monastery during the Tang dynasty.
That text states: "In both the *Four-Part Vinaya* and the *Ten-Recitation Vinaya*, villages are entirely excluded; that we do not exclude them here is because their fundamental tenets differ.

This follows the principle of non-exclusion, yet it serves as indirect evidence for the existence of a rule regarding the exclusion and binding [of boundaries]. Since it mentions "tenets" (*mūla*),...
The essential points differ. Now, since we have established the exclusion of villages and areas outside the village, what further doubt could there be?
△ Regarding the method for binding the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*):
At one time, there was a monk who felt a sense of renunciation. Seeing an *āraṇya* (wilderness) site, he saw a fine cave and thought to himself: "I..."

If one is permitted to stay overnight separated from one’s robe, one may reside in this cave accordingly. The Buddha said: "I allow you to establish the *acchinnaka* (non-forfeiture) rule, except in the case of a swift-flowing river.

[Commentary: This first clarifies the conditions for the regulation. "Disgusted and detached" means contemplating that the five aggregates are without self, and that the world and the body [are likewise].

Excessive pleasure is a cause of suffering. One should cultivate weary detachment and non-attachment, dwelling alone far from the crowds, gathering the mind in seated meditation to aspire toward right concentration;
such is the practitioner of the dhūta ascetic practices. "Cave" refers to a hollow or opening in a rock. Regarding the description of a "good cave," according to the Vinaya:

it must be such that when standing, the head does not strike the ceiling; when sitting, there is enough room for the knees; and it must also be sufficient to shield against wind, rain, and water. Only then may it be used.
Sitting therein, the Buddha permitted the establishment of a *acīvarāpattika-sīmā* (a boundary where one is not guilty of being separated from one's robes) for such a cave.

However, the square boundaries of this *cīvara-saṃgraha-sīmā* (robe-holding boundary) are determined according to the outer boundaries of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), with no addition or subtraction. The text on establishing the robe boundary in the Mūlasarvāstivāda school states:
"If the Saṃgha deems the time has come and grants its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish a *bhikṣu-śeyyāsana-sīmā* (boundary for monks' bedding and seats) upon this *mahā-sīmā*."

Regarding the *kṣetra* (boundary) for not losing one's robes (*a-cīvara-apahāra*): it is stated in the original Vinaya that this place constitutes a single residence with a single recitation of the precepts (*ekoddeśa*), without distinction.
However, both [versions] clarify this in accordance with the literal text. "Swift current" (*sārī*) refers to a rapid flow.

In the Vinaya, there is a case where a boundary for not losing one's robes is established outside of a river with a swift current. At that time, a bhikṣu went to retrieve his robe, but because of the water...

[The Buddha said: "It is subject to being swept away. Knowing this, the Buddha did not permit the establishment of a *naivāsika-sīmā* (a boundary for not losing one's robes) across flowing water, except where there is a permanent bridge.

When establishing it, the *karmakāraka* (the officiant) shall assemble the community and perform the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakalpa*), responding as follows: 'I shall perform the *karmavācanā* for establishing the *acīvaramuṣitaka-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robes).

If it is established simultaneously with the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary), one should follow the previous question and answer; it is not necessary to perform the preliminary formalities again. The *karmakāraka* [should proceed].
Thus he makes this announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This place is a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let it authorize the establishment of a 'no-loss-of-clothing' boundary (akathina-sīmā), excluding villages and the external boundaries of villages. The announcement is made thus."

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. At this place, which is a single residence and a single place for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the Saṃgha now establishes a *akappiyacīvarasīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept with one), excluding the villages and the space outside the villages.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a *akappiyacīvarasīmā* at this place—a single residence and a single place for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa—excluding the villages and the space outside the villages, remain silent. Who does not consent?

The motion is made: "The Sangha has already consented to this place as a single residence for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, having bound the 'non-loss-of-clothing' boundary, excluding the villages and the space outside the villages.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

● Chapter Three: The Method for Receiving the Various Precepts.

The principles of the precept-dharma are universal, and its significance encompasses both the monastic and the lay. Since the violation of the five precepts makes the attainment of full ordination difficult, it is necessary to systematically organize them from beginning to end and to have a clear and thorough mastery of their essence and characteristics. The precepts received by the seven classes of followers are listed below.
Commentary: Regarding the term "various" (*zhū*) used in reference to the precepts (*śīla-dharma*), this section summarizes them into three categories, while enumerating forty-two specific rules.

The first two sentences cite the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* (Shansheng jing) to present the essential meaning. In that sutra, Upāli asks the Buddha: "How does a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva achieve the precepts?
How does he achieve the virtuous precepts? How does he achieve the precepts for benefiting sentient beings?"
The Buddha replied, "One must first fully possess the upāsaka precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the bhikṣu precepts.
It is impossible for one who does not possess the upāsaka precepts to obtain the śrāmaṇera precepts;

it is likewise impossible for one who does not possess the śrāmaṇera precepts to obtain the bhikṣu precepts. If one says that without possessing these three kinds of precepts, one may [obtain them]..."
The same applies to the Bodhisattva precepts; such a thing is impossible. It is like a four-storied tower where one ascends by stages:
it is impossible to reach the second story without first passing through the first, and likewise impossible to reach the fourth story without passing through the third.
Therefore, it is said that the principle of the Dharma of the precepts is universal and its meaning encompasses both the monastic and the lay. The following two lines cite [this analogy].
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) clarifies the aforementioned meaning. That treatise states:

"If one violates a grave precept among the five precepts, even if one subsequently receives the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts, the dhyāna-precepts, or the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts, none of these will be obtained.

If, after having violated a grave precept among the five precepts, one discards the five precepts and attempts to receive them again, such a thing is impossible. This applies to the eight precepts and the ten precepts as well."
The same applies to the full precepts (*upasampadā*). Now, this treatise states: "If one commits an offense against the five precepts, it becomes difficult to attain the full precepts.

Therefore, one must proceed from the three refuges at the beginning to the full precepts at the end, following the systematic rules of the Dharma. Within this process, one should beforehand master both the essence and the characteristics [of the precepts].
The precepts received by the seven classes of followers are listed below in order.

**Exegesis on the Method for Receiving the Three Refuges** Regarding this reception of the three refuges, along with the methods for the five precepts and eight precepts that follow, I shall now provide an explanation of the meaning based solely upon the text.

As for the procedures for bestowing and receiving [the precepts], the guidance provided, and the ritual additions for repentance, these should be followed according to the separate collection of instructions for the transmission of the three refuges, five precepts, and eight precepts.
The correct principle is clearly explained in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*,
which states: "One takes refuge in the Triple Gem because one desires to be protected and shielded from them, so that one may not be subjected to oppression or violation."
Explanation: Those who take the Triple Gem as their refuge do so because the Triple Gem is endowed with immeasurable, true, and pure merit.
Desiring to earnestly invoke its compassionate protection for themselves, they seek to ensure that the four māras and various sufferings cannot inflict harm upon them. The *Xiantong lun* states:
"This is the meaning of rescue and relief. By taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one is able to extinguish the boundless sufferings of birth and death.
The wheel [of Dharma] is for the sake of distancing oneself from all great terrors; its meaning is the same as that in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "There are five kinds of taking refuge in the Triple Gem: first, the triple refuge for turning away from heterodoxy; second, the triple refuge for the five precepts; third, the triple refuge for the eight precepts..."
The forty precepts with the three refuges, and the five-fold full precepts with the three refuges—this is the first [category].

As for what is called "turning away from heterodoxy": before the Buddha appeared in the world, heterodox teachers preached the Dharma; their words were all false, and their teachings did not accord with principle.

Like the blind leading the ignorant, those who sought to ascend instead fell downward. When the Buddha appeared in the world, his wisdom and realization were peerless; he thoroughly penetrated cause and effect, and his titles...
He preached the Dharma by nature to rescue and deliver sentient beings and lead them into the Right Path; thus it is called the "Reversal of Heresy through the Three Refuges.
When the Tathāgata first traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, Yaśoda’s father was inspired to take refuge with faith.
To this day, all people continue to receive his gracious bounty.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha take refuge in the *dharmakāya*, which refers to the qualities of omniscience and the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), consisting of the five factors.

Commentary: Regarding those who take refuge in the *dharmakāya* Buddha: the Buddha possesses three bodies (*trikāya*). Within the *dharmakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) are subsumed.
Therefore, the Dharma-body is twofold. First is the Dharma-body of Principle (*li-fashen*). Principle is precisely the virtue of nature (*xingde*).

This refers to the essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity, which is fundamentally free from thought, equal to the realm of empty space, and all-pervading. Buddhas and sentient beings are identical in this single characteristic;

this is called the Dharma-body of Principle. Second is the Dharma-body of Merit (*gongde-fashen*), which refers to that which the Tathāgata cultivated over the course of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past.
Throughout kalpas, one cultivates the merit of the myriad practices of the six pāramitās as the cause, thereby accomplishing the fruit of the Dharma-body; thus it is called the "Dharma-body of Merit.
The text states that it is "accomplished by all-knowledge and so forth," which precisely clarifies the Dharma-body of Merit as it encompasses the Dharma-body of Principle.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess these two kinds of Dharma-bodies. What is now referred to as "Buddha" [refers to this].
This means taking refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The following two lines explain the preceding one. To elaborate:

"The Omniscient One" refers to one who is able to know and understand all internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) and their internal designations (*nāman*), as well as all external phenomena and their external designations.

Regarding "internal phenomena and designations": the phenomena refer to the characteristics of reality (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as elucidated within the Buddhist tradition, as well as the linguistic expressions that convey them.
Names. These refer to names within the principle (*li*), as Buddhism speaks in accordance with the principle; thus they are called "within the principle.

As for names of external dharmas, these refer to the phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) explained outside the principle, as well as the names that express them. These are the arbitrary conceptualizations of non-Buddhists and others that deviate from the principle.
Therefore, it is said to be "outside of principle. This refers to the functional application of the wisdom that is capable of contemplation. Regarding "untainted merit" (*anāsrava-guṇa*):

this means that when one arouses the mind and practices, one does not seek the minor fruits of humans or devas within that practice; rather, all is dedicated toward awakening (*bodhi*) for the sake of saving and delivering sentient beings.
Hence, it is called "untainted. The Buddha realizes the *dharmakāya* through these untainted merits, which consist of the five factors.
It constitutes the Dharmakāya. Regarding the "fivefold division," "division" (bhaga) refers to a distinct portion; "dharma" refers to the various dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom;
and "kāya" means an accumulation. It is the accumulation of these various dharmas that constitutes this body. First is the *śīla-kāya* (precept-body):

by maintaining pure precepts, the dharma of precept is perfected, and one attains realization of this body. Second is the *samādhi-kāya* (concentration-body): by cultivating untainted, pure dhyāna, one attains...

3. The body of realization (*adhigama-kāya*). By cultivating untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one attains the realization of this body. 4. The body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*). There are two kinds of liberation:
first, conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*), which refers to severing tainted afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*) by means of untainted wisdom;
second, unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), which refers to the total extinction of all afflictions without remainder. Once the afflictions are exhausted...

Principle is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). By means of two kinds of liberation, one attains realization of this body: the body of the fivefold knowledge and vision of liberation (*pañca-vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).
"Knowledge" refers to knowing through wisdom (*jñāna*), and "vision" refers to seeing with the eye (*cakṣus*).

That is to say, by means of this wisdom-eye, one realizes and clearly perceives that all phenomena are empty in their very essence and entirely like illusions. Because one attains realization of this body, it is called the "Dharma-body of the five parts."

The body. Regarding "taking refuge in the Dharma," it means taking refuge in the state where both self and other are exhausted; that is, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), which is Nirvana, characterized by the abandonment of desire and the absence of desire.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the state where self and other are exhausted," "self" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Within this, there are two types: first, that which is co-existent...

There is the innate grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the conceptual grasping at a self, as explained in the original preface. Others say that there are also two kinds of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*):
first, the innate grasping at phenomena, which refers to the false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated by sentient beings since beginningless time.
One gives rise to false attachments toward all phenomena, which are constantly accompanied by the body.

Second is the attachment to the discrimination of phenomena (*dharma-grāha-vikalpa*), which refers to the conceptualization and estimation of the teachings spoken by heterodox teachers and heterodox doctrines, grasping them as real phenomena. The two characters "exhaustion" (*jin*) and "place" (*chu*) refer to the contemplation of the principle of the two emptinesses:
first, the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The emptiness of persons is the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*); it is also called the emptiness of beings (*jīva-śūnyatā*).

This is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) grasp at a self as described above; therefore, the Buddha taught that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are without self in order to refute this conception.

The followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) realize this and enter the principle of selflessness; this is called "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Second is "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*):

it means that the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet reached the principle of the emptiness of phenomena and still reckon that phenomena such as the five aggregates truly exist. The Buddha taught this in order to refute this [view].
Because of grasping, it is said that the profound wisdom of *prajñā* penetrates and perceives that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is entirely empty.

When a bodhisattva awakens to this, they enter the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); this is called the emptiness of phenomena. The following two lines explain the preceding:

that which is the principle of the two kinds of emptiness is the cessation of desire, the absence of desire, the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and nirvāṇa. To explain this in detail, these two lines collectively encompass the four [truths].

The Truths of the Dharma: The cessation of desire and the absence of desire is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). By knowing that birth and death within the three realms are truly suffering, one investigates the truth of causes and examines them thoroughly;
thus, one realizes that afflictions, delusions, and karma are indeed what actually summon and accumulate the suffering of birth and death. If one cuts off all afflictions...
If the causes of suffering do not accumulate, then the wheel of birth and death ceases, and there will forever be no fruit of suffering.

Now, although the afflictions of the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*) are numerous, desire (*kāma*) is specifically singled out; this is because both the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) have desire as their root.

If desire is severed, the various delusions are easily eliminated. As for the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is Nirvana: "cessation" means quiescent extinction, resulting from the ultimate weariness with birth and death.

Suffering. One must carefully examine that Nirvana is indeed the bliss of quiescent extinction; it can only be reached by practicing the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, so that the principle of the two kinds of emptiness may manifest.

Regarding "taking refuge in the Saṃgha," this refers to taking refuge in the ultimate Saṃgha (paramārtha-saṃgha), namely the field of merit consisting of the virtues of the Śrāvakas who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
*Commentary:* Regarding the "ultimate Saṃgha," this is explained according to the fourfold ultimate truth (*catur-vidha-paramārtha-satya*) as set forth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
This refers to the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). That is to say, the śrāvakas realize the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two-fold emptiness;
this is the meaning of "supreme" (*parama*). The following two lines explain the above: the Saṃgha of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-saṃgha*) is a truly pure field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
The qualities it possesses can bestow blessings and protection upon sentient beings. If one takes refuge in them, one will obtain immeasurable benefit. However...
These qualities of the śrāvaka are further divided into those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

What is called a "śrāvaka" refers to one who hears the Buddha’s teachings and enters realization by relying on their cultivation. Those in training refer to the first three fruits and the four paths toward them.

Those beyond training refer to the fourth fruit, the arhat, whose outflows (āsrava) have been exhausted and who no longer possesses afflictions. According to the sūtras and vinayas, ordinary persons (pṛthagjana)...
Those monks who are able to uphold the prohibitive precepts are all designated as "Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*) monks, because the essence of the precepts constitutes a fertile field of merit.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that these must all be conferred by a teacher through verbal transmission. If the words are not articulated, or if they are incomplete, or if the name is not correctly pronounced, or if it is not understood, then [the ordination] is not accomplished. It must be said: "It is not accomplished."
I (so-and-so), for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Thus it is said three times. Having thus come under the protection of the Dharma:
Explanation: Regarding "belonging to the Dharma," all sentient beings, prior to receiving the Three Refuges, belong to Māra;
they are bound by the various sufferings of birth and death and thus cannot attain liberation.
Once they have returned to the Triple Gem with sincere faith, they then belong to the Buddha, for they are protected by the Dharma. No Māras, heterodox teachers, or the like can prevail over them.
Why is this? To conclude below that which is taken as refuge:
I (so-and-so), for as long as life lasts, have completed my taking of refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my taking of refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my taking of refuge in the Saṃgha.
After the three refuges have been completed, the Vinaya contains no formal rite for receiving the Dharma. All the treatises fully set this forth: one merely receives the Dharma of the Refuges;
there is no separate rite for the precepts. Thus, a treatise states: "Once the Three Refuges are concluded, if something further is added, one obtains both the Refuges and the Precepts;
if nothing is added, there are the Refuges but no Precepts."

Commentary: Once one has completed receiving the Three Refuges, one must understand what is gained and what is lost in order to observe them accordingly. However, this should be taught to those who receive them.

According to the *Śrāddhabrāhmaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Good Life), if there is a person who, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, does not formally receive the precepts yet cuts off all evil and cultivates all goodness, even while remaining a householder, they abide in accordance with the Dharma; such a person is likewise [a true practitioner].

He is called an upāsaka. Furthermore, it is said: if one performs various kinds of actions and cultivates wholesome deeds for the sake of experiencing pleasure, like the method of bartering in a marketplace, and his mind cannot feel compassion for sentient beings, such a person does not obtain the three refuges.
It is further said: if a person, in order to protect their home, body, or life, makes offerings and sacrifices to various spirits...
A person does not lose the Three Refuges if they hear that certain devas have previously seen the Buddha and possess virtues superior to their own, and thus pay homage to and make offerings to them.

Such a person does not lose the Three Refuges. However, if a person believes that these beings can save them from all fears and consequently pays homage to various non-Buddhist teachers—or at times pays homage to Maheśvara—they then lose the Three Refuges.
The Master should perform prostrations as one would toward the kings, elders, and nobles of the world; yet he must not thereby lose the Three Refuges.
Although he performs these prostrations, he must be careful never to cherish the false teachings that are spoken.
In various sutras, the Buddha spoke these verses to Maitreya: "Those in your three assemblies are those whom I previously transformed. [Of the ninety-six...]"
"Of those billions of people who received my Three Refuges, next were those three types of 'broken' persons.

As for the ninety-two billion who merely uttered 'Namo Buddha' once, they all attained the Way of the Buddha. (Text) This clarifies that although they received the dharma of the Refuges, they lacked the dharma of the Precepts.
Below this, according to the treatise, the Three Refuges are explained; from here on, by adding further elements, one attains the full Refuges.
...as well as the dharmas of the five precepts and the eight precepts. The *Sūtra on the Method for Receiving the Five Precepts* states:

"Suppose there were a son or daughter of good family who bestowed the four requisites of life upon all sentient beings throughout the four continents, making offerings to them until they were exhausted."

The merit of observing the precepts for a single day and night is superior to that of [other practices] for a hundred years. This is because the nature of the precepts extends to both sentient and non-sentient objects.
Commentary: Among all things sought by the world for peace and happiness, there is not one that does not arise from the Three Jewels. If there were no Three [Jewels...]
If one returns to the five precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas will be cut off.

Therefore, I first cite the scriptures for corroboration, stating that although this act of giving involves a vast scope, many recipients, offerings according to one's wishes, and a long duration of years, its merit may indeed be exceptionally superior;
yet it does not equal the merit of observing the precepts for even a single day and night. This is shown to demonstrate the benefits of the Dharma of the precepts.
This is because they apply to both sentient objects and non-sentient objects. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"One obtains the four precepts with respect to sentient beings, and one obtains the precept against drinking alcohol with respect to non-sentient objects.
Whether a sentient being may be killed or not killed, stolen or not stolen, sexually approached or not approached, or lied to or not lied to—[the precepts apply to all such cases]. (1)

All obtain these precepts. From those below in the Avīci Hell to those above in the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven, including the trichiliocosm and all sentient beings up to the Tathāgata—everyone obtains these four precepts.

This is because at the time of first receiving the precepts, one vows not to kill any being, up to and including not to speak any falsehood, without any limitation or restriction; thus they are obtained.

Regarding the precept against drinking alcohol: throughout the beginning and end of this one life, within the entire three-thousandfold world system, one obtains the "color of the precept" (śīla-rūpa) with every swallow of all existing alcohol.

Because at the time of receiving the precepts one vows never to drink any alcohol whatsoever, even if all alcohol were to be completely extinguished, the precept remains perpetually accomplished and is never lost. By virtue of this merit, it is twice as great as that of giving.
Regarding the statement that "sentient beings filling the four continents [are benefited]," the *Śāstra* says: "By means of precepts, giving becomes pure.
Commentary: The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) and the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* (Youposai jiejing) also contain this meaning; namely, for an upāsaka...
There are two kinds of purity in practicing generosity: first, purity of the object (*vastu-śuddhi*). This means that the object is not stolen, nor is it an item prohibited by the Noble Ones;
it is not property belonging to the community (*saṃgha*), nor property belonging to the Three Jewels (*triratna*); it is not something given to one person and then diverted to many;

it is obtained without causing distress to others, without deceiving others, and without cheating people. Second, purity of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*). At the time of giving, one does not do so for the sake of rebirth in cyclic existence, nor for the sake of favorable karmic fruits, nor for the sake of reputation.
They surpass others, attain physical strength and talent, and do not sever their family lineage; they possess many kinsmen and dependents.

They give solely for the sake of adorning the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit and for the sake of taming sentient beings. This clarifies that those who uphold the precepts are impartial and maintain their proper station;
they do not deceive in their livelihood, and whatever they give is all pure wealth. Among all forms of relinquishment, these are...
It encompasses both self-benefit and benefit for others. If one acts contrary to this, then the giving is not pure; therefore, this is cited as an example.

Prior to receiving the precepts, one must fully inquire regarding the obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*). Thus, the *Sūtra of Good Birth* (*Śraddhākaragāra-sūtra*) says: "Have you not stolen property belonging to the Saṃgha present before you?
Have you not committed impure conduct with your six types of relatives, or with bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs? [Have you not committed such acts] with your father..."
"Will you abandon a mother, teacher, or elder who is ill? Will you kill a sentient being who has generated the bodhicitta?
Having asked these and other such questions, if they have no [such intentions], one should say to them: "This precept is extremely difficult;
it serves as the very foundation for the śrāvaka and bodhisattva precepts."

Commentary: This clarifies the gravity of the precepts and their methods. One should exercise discernment regarding the recipient before bestowing them. If one fails to inquire thoroughly prior to the transmission and reception [of the precepts], it is feared there will be no benefit.
As for "property of the present Saṃgha," this refers to the merit resulting from the offerings made by those with pure faith and sincere reverence.
It is most preeminent. If one steals these objects, the retribution for the offense will likewise be preeminent. Regarding the six relations:
the father’s six relations refer to paternal uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons; the mother’s six relations refer to maternal uncles, aunts, brothers, and grandsons.

As for parents, the father’s kindness is equal to heaven, and the mother’s kindness is matched by earth; they give birth, nourish, and shelter us, such that even grinding one's bones would not suffice to repay them.
"Master," O Elder, there are two kinds of teachers: first, the worldly teacher who provides instruction and benefits;
second, the monastic teacher who instructs in the Buddha-dharma. "Bodhi" is an abbreviation;
in full it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which translates as "Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Right Enlightenment. One who generates this mind is determined to achieve supreme realization.
The Buddha-way transforms sentient beings from below. If one were to kill this person, it would be to sever the seed of the Buddhas.
Having thus inquired individually regarding each of these seven difficulties, if the answer is that there are none, one should say:
"These five precepts for an upāsaka are extremely difficult to receive and difficult to maintain; they serve as the foundation for the śrāvaka and bodhisattva precepts. You ought to..."
Be cautious and reverent; by no means be careless.
Good son, there are five kinds of precepts, beginning with abstaining from killing and ending with abstaining from drinking alcohol.

If one receives even one precept, one is called a *śrāmaṇera-upāsaka* (a lay follower who observes a single part). One who fully maintains all five precepts is called a *paripūrṇa-upāsaka* (a lay follower who observes the complete set).
"What portion of the precepts do you now wish to receive? You may receive them according to your inclination. At that time, the wise person should receive them in accordance with those words.
[Commentary: Regarding the five precepts, it is permitted to receive one part, a small portion, a half-portion, a large portion, or the full portion. The recipient who wishes—

This is because it reveals the merit of maintaining and upholding [the precepts]. If one observes the five precepts in their entirety, the characteristics of a human being are fully realized; if one additionally practices the ten wholesome actions, the retribution of rebirth as a deva will constantly follow.
Even with only one or two precepts, one still attains a human body; whether one's lifespan is long or short, or one's status high or low, depends upon the number of precepts observed.

If one does not deliberate at the time of undertaking [the precepts], one will frequently commit transgressions after receiving them. To maintain even a single precept is superior to not receiving them at all.
The Buddha’s compassion guides sentient beings skillfully in this manner.
As the *Āgama* and other sūtras state: "One should repent of one's offenses prior to receiving [the precepts], and only then receive the dharma. It should be conferred in this way.
He says:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
For one day and one night, or for as long as life lasts, I shall be an upāsaka (or upāsikā). The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One."

After the threefold administration has been completed, he says: "The Three Refuges just administered constitute the very essence of the precepts. Now, by repeating them three times, I demonstrate the refuge to which the precepts belong.
I, [Name], have already taken refuge in the Buddha; I have taken refuge in the Dharma; I have taken refuge in the Sangha—for one day and one night, or for as long as life shall last."
[Whether possessing] one part of the precepts or the full five precepts, the Upāsaka (or Upāsikā) [should declare]: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One.
Regarding the Sanskrit term *Tathāgata*: it is translated here as "Thus Come" (*Rúlái*). If it is said that he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, he is therefore called "Thus Come";
this is an explanation based on the *dharmakāya*. Alternatively, it may mean "according to the self-nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

"Coming to achieve perfect enlightenment" is explained in reference to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). If it says "riding upon the path of suchness to come and deliver sentient beings," this is explained in reference to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
In Sanskrit, *arhat*; here it is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*yìnggòng*), and also translated as "One Who Corresponds to Truth" (*yìngzhēn*).

Now, translated as "Ultimate Truth" (*tathāgata*): because he serves as a field of merit for the world, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*); because he is in profound accord with his own true nature, he is called "Ultimate Truth.

Because he is in profound accord with the truth, he is capable of acting as a field of merit. The Sanskrit term *samyaksambuddha* is translated here as "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*zhengbianzhi*).
"Perfectly" (*zheng*) carries the meaning of "complete" (*bian*); it refers to one who fully elucidates the various distinct Dharma-gates. This is called... [name].
This constitutes their equality. This distinguishes [the Buddha] from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who possess deep knowledge of the nature of non-differentiation;

this is termed "correct. This distinguishes him from ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists. Now, among the ten titles, only three are explicitly mentioned, while the remaining seven are subsumed therein to manifest the three virtues (*guṇa*).
"Tathāgata" is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Arhat" is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*); "Samyaksaṃbuddha" is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).
If it is virtuous, the three preceptors shall then address him, saying: "Now we shall show you the characteristics of the precepts. Listen attentively and receive them.
For as long as life lasts, one must not kill living beings. This is the precept of an upāsaka (or upāsikā). Are you able to uphold it? [He] replies: "I am able to uphold it."
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not steal. This is a precept for an upāsaka/upāsikā. Are you able to observe it? [He/She] replies, "I am able to observe it.
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not engage in sexual misconduct. This is a precept for an upāsaka/upāsikā. Are you able to observe it? [He/She] replies, "I am able to observe it."
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not speak falsely. This is a precept for an upāsaka (or upāsikā). Are you able to uphold it? [He] replies, "I am able to uphold it.
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not drink intoxicants. This is a precept for an upāsaka (or upāsikā). Are you able to uphold it? [He] replies, "I am able to uphold it."

The preceding questions and answers have been completed as detailed above. As for the remaining six grave and twenty-eight light offenses, along with their various miscellaneous characteristics, they are explained extensively in the *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Good Life) and the *Xingshi chao* (Commentary on Monastic Practices). One should then make vows to practice the eight precepts together.

**Commentary:** Regarding the phrase "having completed the questions and answers as above," this concludes the section on merely receiving the five precepts. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"One who wishes to receive the five precepts first receives the three refuges. Once the three refuges have been received, at that moment one has already obtained the five precepts.
The reason for stating the names of the five precepts is to ensure that the person recognizes the names of those five precepts. This [concludes the discussion].

Regarding the five precepts, the first four are actual transgressions (*dosa*), while the one precept concerning the consumption of intoxicants is a prohibitive transgression (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

The reason this single precept on drinking alcohol is grouped together with the other four as a category of precepts is that drinking alcohol is the root of heedlessness (*pramāda*), which enables one to violate the other four precepts.
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, because he had drunk alcohol, committed adultery with another's wife and stole and killed another's rooster.
When others asked him, "Why did you do this? he replied, "I did not; it was because I was deranged by the wine.
Thus, in a single moment, he was able to destroy four precepts. The text further notes: "After the question and answer, there remain six grave offenses and twenty [lesser ones]."

Regarding the eight light precepts: this refers to a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, having thus received the five precepts, wishes to give rise to the Great Mind and seek to receive the householder bodhisattva precepts.
One should rely on the *Sūtra of Good Birth* (*Śraddhā-pratiṣṭhāna-sūtra*) to receive these six grave and twenty-eight light precepts.

This is done first to demonstrate the ritual procedures for practical application, and secondly to allow the recipient to observe their own capacity in relation to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. That is to say:
The various aspects of these miscellaneous practices are explained at length in the *Śāṅgīti-sūtra* (or *Sujāta-sūtra*) and the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu-śīla-viniścaya* (Xingshi chao).
However, since the *Chao* (the *Śīla-viniścaya*) composed its text based on the sūtras to clarify points of gain and loss, as well as right and wrong, it has no original sūtra to rely upon;

nevertheless, I shall now record two or three passages from it so that one may understand the general outline. That sūtra says: The Buddha said, "Among all forms of giving, the gift of fearlessness..."
Fear is the foremost [of what is to be abandoned]. Therefore, when I speak of the five great gifts, they are precisely the five precepts.
These five precepts enable sentient beings to leave behind the five fears. Furthermore, it is said that there are five wholesome dharmas that surround these precepts:
first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; fourth, patience; and fifth, faith. If a person can destroy grave and false views...
Seeing this, one’s mind becomes free from the net of doubt and thus possesses right mindfulness. It is adorned with purity; it is fundamentally pure, being free from evil thoughts and reflections.
If one can distance oneself from these five unwholesome matters, this is called receiving the precepts.

To distance oneself from all evils of body, speech, and mind—if one claims that one can transcend birth and death after merely leaving the five precepts—such a thing is impossible. [If one wishes] to transcend...
In this great ocean of birth and death, one should with a sincere heart receive and uphold the five precepts.
Among these five precepts, four become the unmanifested precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) in future lives; only craving is difficult to sever, and thus they cannot be fully realized.
For this reason, being entangled by the bonds of desire and craving, one should with a sincere heart be cautious and never be negligent. It is further said: "These five precepts have five [aspects]."

There are four kinds of fruits: first, the fruit of non-action (*avijñapti-phala*) (meaning that taking the pure five precepts as the cause, one gradually attains renunciation and receives full ordination, thereby accomplishing the essence of the *avijñapti* precepts);

second, the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*) (meaning that by taking the five precepts as the cause while concurrently practicing the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions, one is reborn in the heavens as retribution and experiences various sublime pleasures; yet one is still unable to transcend [samsara] because the third category of precepts has not been purified);

third, the fruit of remainder (*niṣyanda-phala*) (meaning that taking the observance of the five precepts as the cause, one obtains the human realm; because the merit of the precepts is not yet exhausted, one is born again among humans to experience worldly pleasures); fourth, the fruit of action (*kriyā-phala*) (meaning that those who uphold the five precepts can...).
By guarding one precept, one experiences the virtuous retribution of that one precept; likewise, by violating one precept, one experiences the karmic retribution of that one precept.

Fifth is the fruit of liberation (meaning that in future lives, through practicing and entering the Path, one attains liberation from saṃsāra and realizes the fruits of sainthood—all of which take these five precepts as their fundamental and direct cause). It is further said:
"If an upāsaka can regularly go to temples and monasteries, and having arrived, approach the bhikṣus and others to inquire about the flavor of the Dharma and listen [to its teachings]..."
Having already received and upheld [the teachings], they remember them without forgetting and are able to discern their meaning and transform sentient beings; such a person is called an upāsaka.

They benefit themselves and others. If they are unable to practice and study what has been taught, yet go to listen to the Dharma with the intent of disparaging bhikṣus and seeking out their faults, lacking faith and reverence, and instead serving non-Buddhists while regarding their merits with deep conviction—[this is not the mark of a true upāsaka].
If such a lay follower (upāsaka) [worships] the sun, moon, the five planets, and the various lunar mansions, he is not called one who dwells firmly according to the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said:
although he does not personally commit the five evil karmas, he may incite others to do so; or he may first take another's property under the pretext that it is for the sake of performing a ritual;
or he may serve as a warden at a pass or ferry, taxing and appraising goods for sale; or he may calculate fees for treating illnesses and sell them once the treatment is finished.
Regarding material things: if one violates public or private regulations, such instances are all considered not abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
If one does not commit evil oneself, does not instruct others to do so, and does not harbor evil thoughts in the mind, this is called abiding in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said:

if an upāsaka commits an offense arising from adventitious afflictions and yet does not give rise to a sense of shame, remorse, or a mind of repentance, he is not abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
If one commits various evil deeds for the sake of one's body and life, this is not abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is said that an upāsaka is permitted to engage in trade and commerce, provided he does not perform five types of activities:
first, he must not engage in the trade of livestock as his primary occupation; second, he must not engage in the trade of bows, arrows, swords, or staves.
These are the occupations [to be avoided]: third, one must not make the sale of alcohol one’s profession;
fourth, one must not make the pressing of oil one’s profession, because there are many insects in oil; fifth, one must not make the dyeing with the five primary colors one’s profession.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the *Cāo* (Excerpts) based on the sūtras and śāstras. The text says: "Those who vow to practice the eight precepts together" refers to following the subsequent eight [precepts].
The Vow Text for the Precepts: Change only the three characters "eightfold fast" (bāguānzhāi) to "five precepts" (wùjiè); the rest of the wording remains unchanged.
○ The Method for Receiving the Eight Precepts.
The *Sūtra on Good Birth* (*Śāṇakavāsin-sūtra*) in the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

The Buddha told the upāsakas, "On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, you should go to where the elder bhikṣus are and receive the eight precepts one by one. Receive them one by one;
do not let their sequence be lost."
Commentary: This first clarifies the duration for receiving the precepts and the teacher who bestows them.
According to the *Buddha-bhāṣita-poṣadha-sūtra*, a follower of the Way receives the eight precepts on the six fast days (*ṣaḍ-poṣadha*).
The six fast days refer to the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month.

In the *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*, the Buddha taught that on the six fast days—specifically the eighth and twenty-third days of the month—the Four Heavenly Kings dispatch their messengers to descend and inspect the good and evil among human beings.
On the fourteenth and twenty-ninth days, the sons of the Four Kings descend to inspect the human world. On the fifteenth and thirtieth days, the Four Kings [themselves]...

Descending from there to the human realm, he observed sentient beings. When those who practiced giving, maintained the precepts, and were filial toward their parents were few, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and informed Śakra.
The hearts of all the devas were displeased, and they said, "The race of asuras is increasing, while the race of the devas is diminishing.
[They continued,] "If those who practice giving, maintain the precepts, and are filial toward their parents were many, the devas..."
Śakra, his heart filled with joy, said: "The asuras are diminished, and the hosts of devas are increased.
As for the mention of only the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, it is because the singular includes the pair.
"Approaching the elder bhikṣus" refers to those who honor seniority by years of ordination (*vassa*).

The *Śāstra* states that one should have the fivefold assembly confer it. The *Tattvasiddhi* says: "If no person is present, one may simply recite it mentally and verbally, even saying 'I observe the eight precepts,' and the reception will still be accomplished."
Commentary: Regarding the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that the five groups of renunciants are permitted to bestow [the precepts], this allowance has two meanings:

first, to meet specific occasions; second, to select the appropriate persons. Furthermore, these eight precepts must necessarily be observed on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) and the eight *rāja* days.
If one receives [the precepts] beyond the appointed time, there will be little benefit. If there is no bhikṣu available, one may receive them from a bhikṣuṇī;
likewise, if there is no śrāmaṇera, one may receive them from a śrāmaṇerī. This is what is meant by "observing the time. As for "selecting the person":

One who bestows the precepts must personally observe them before they may act as a teacher. If there is a bhikṣu who does not observe the precepts, one should receive them from a bhikṣuṇī who observes them;
even if there is a śrāmaṇera who does not observe the precepts, one should receive them from a śrāmaṇerī who observes them.
Furthermore, citing the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "If no person is present, one should simply recite them with mind and mouth."

It is said: Although one who receives [the precepts] may also have urgent needs that require their immediate application, the mental faculty cannot grasp the initial resolve; it must be developed over a long period.
Only those who constantly observe the eight precepts for a time come to know the characteristics of the precepts and can speak of them without confusion.

Even if there is a person who conforms to the Dharma, if they deliberately harbor thoughts of doubt or arrogance, then even if they explain the teachings clearly, the precepts will not be established.

Regarding the reception [of the precepts], the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "If one first forms the intention and receives them on the day of the fast, one obtains them even after having finished eating.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* also contains this statement. Now, judging by this explanation, that text says: "If a person wishes..."
If one receives the eight precepts after first indulging in thoughts of female beauty, or engaging in music, or craving food and drink, or various forms of merriment—

having performed such acts of negligence with all one's heart and only thereafter receiving the precepts— one does not obtain the precepts regardless of whether it was before, at, or after midday. Furthermore,
if one has no original intention to receive the precepts yet engages in various acts of negligence, [the same applies].

Regarding the matter: if one later encounters a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and receives the precepts for the fast (*upavāsa*), one attains the merit of the fast regardless of whether it is before, during, or after midday.
If one wishes to receive the fast but is hindered by difficulties and lacks the freedom to do so, once those difficulties have been resolved—
As for those who receive the fast (upavāsa), it does not matter whether it is before or after midday; they all obtain the fast.
The citation from the *Abhidharmakośa* refers precisely to this latter point, and therefore I shall now elaborate upon it.

The one who is to receive the precepts first lowers their mind, joins their palms, and follows the words of the person bestowing the precepts; they must neither precede nor speak simultaneously with them.

If they violate this, the rite is not accomplished. [Commentary: This clarifies the ritual procedure. "The one who is to receive the precepts" refers to those such as the elder bhikṣus mentioned previously. They have attained...
Regarding the precepts received by the five assemblies, one must invariably give rise to a mind of reverence for the Dharma and humility.
One should offer incense and prostrate, then kneel long with palms joined, following the words of the person bestowing the precepts. One must wait until they have finished speaking before responding;

it is not permitted to respond before they have concluded, nor may both parties speak at the same time. If these rules are violated, the reception of the precepts is not accomplished. This refers to the person...
All such ritualistic practices are incorrect.
The *Śāstra* states: "If one receives the eight precepts, one should say 'for one day and one night,' so as not to confuse them with lifelong precepts.
