The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The five precepts and eight precepts vary according to the length of the days and months; they may last for a year, a month, or [a shorter period]."
By midday or midnight, one may again receive the precepts of reduction and receive them all once more.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states: "The Buddha originally established that one day and one night must not exceed the limit.
If one has the strength to receive them, once the first day has passed, one may receive them again in succession. In this way, according to one's capacity, one takes the lifelong precepts."
This refers to the five precepts received for as long as one lives. Furthermore, citing the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it says: "According to the length of days and months.
This means that once they have been received, they endure through years and months; there is no need to receive them repeatedly every day. The present [text] also follows this view.
This is done to ensure that there is a basis for future observance. As for the statement that one may receive [the precepts] for half a day or half a night, such is not the rule of the Dharma;

it is spoken thus to manifest the virtue of the precepts. Regarding "receiving again": if the year or month has expired and one wishes to receive them once more, this is called receiving again. Regarding "receiving a reduced amount":

this refers to when the years or months are insufficient, and one receives them by agreeing upon a specific period according to one's own wish. Provided there is a heart of utmost sincerity, all such cases are valid. If...
Regarding the bestowal of the precepts at the time of receiving them, one should speak as follows:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha—for one day and night, or for one year, or for one month—as a pure-practice Upāsaka (or Upāsikā).
(Thus, it is bestowed three times.)

I (so-and-so) have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha. For one day and night [or one year, or one month], I have become a pure-practice Upāsaka [or Upāsikā].
(Having completed the three recitations, next state the characteristics of the precepts:)
Just as all Buddhas refrain from taking life for the duration of their lives, [so shall] (Name) refrain from taking life for one day and one night.
Can you maintain this? (He answers: I can maintain it.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from stealing for the duration of their lives, [Name], will you be able to refrain from stealing for one day and one night? (Answer: I am able to observe it.
"Just as all Buddhas refrain from sexual misconduct for the duration of their lives, will you, [Name], refrain from sexual misconduct for one day and one night? Can you maintain this? (He replies:
"I can maintain it.
"Just as all Buddhas refrain from false speech for the duration of their lives, will you, [Name], refrain from false speech for one day and one night? Can you maintain this?"
[The preceptor] says: "Can you maintain it?
Just as all Buddhas do not drink alcohol for the duration of their lives, [Name], can you maintain the practice of not drinking alcohol for one day and one night?
[The candidate] replies: "I can maintain it."

Just as all Buddhas, for the duration of their lives, abstain from flowers, perfumes, necklaces, and the anointing of the body with fragrant oils, (Name), can you maintain the precept of abstaining from flowers, perfumes, necklaces, and the anointing of the body with fragrant oils for one day and one night? (He answers: I can maintain it.

"Just as all Buddhas, for the duration of their lives, abstained from sitting on high or luxurious beds and from going to watch or listen to singing, dancing, and music—[so too shall you,] [Name], abstain from sitting on high or luxurious beds and from going to watch or listen to singing, dancing, and music for one day and one night.
Are you able to maintain this? [He] replies, "I am able to maintain it."
Just as all Buddhas, for the duration of their lives, abstained from eating at improper times, so shall [Name] abstain from eating at improper times for one day and one night.
Are you able to maintain this? (He replies: I am able to maintain it.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state: Having conferred [the precepts] in the sequence described above, one should instruct them to make this vow, saying:
"By the merit of these Eight Precepts of the Fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), may I not fall into the evil realms, the eight difficulties, or the borderlands.
Taking this merit, may I absorb all the evils of all sentient beings; and bestowing all my own merits upon them, may they attain Buddhahood."

[One should] ascend to the path of the supreme, true reality. Furthermore, [one should ensure that] in the three assemblies during the era of the future Maitreya Buddha, one may attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Śākyamuni said: "In practicing any spiritual discipline, one ought to make a vow. If there is practice without a vow, that practice will surely be solitary."
If there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty. If practice and aspiration support one another, they will then constitute the function of wisdom.
Regarding the Eightfold Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-śīla), the essence of the fast consists in not eating at improper times, while the eight items serve to shut out evil and assist in perfecting the fast.
This is because, among the primary causes of birth and death, none is like sexual desire; and among the auxiliary conditions for birth and death, none is like...

Regarding food and drink: the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that all sentient beings depend upon sexual desire to sustain their lives, and all sentient beings depend upon food to dwell in their households.

Because the two groups [of lay followers] cannot forever abandon household affairs, kin, and worldly entanglements, they observe the five precepts for the duration of their lives, excluding only illicit sexual conduct while not prohibiting eating at improper times.

If one receives the eight precepts, which are observed for only one day and night, one strictly prohibits eating after noon so that food does not enter the throat, and one must not allow even the slightest movement of lustful thoughts.
In every respect, one acts as the Buddhas do, firmly maintaining these merits for the remainder of one's life;
therefore, they surpass the five precepts. As for not falling into the evil realms or the eight difficulties, this—
This clarifies that one distances oneself from evil through one’s own vow and maintains these merits.
To "gather in the evils of all sentient beings" means that one also vows for all sentient beings to be free from evil. As for the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*):
first is the difficulty of being in hell. This refers to five hundred *yojana*s beneath Jambudvīpa, where there are the eight cold and eight hot hells. Sentient beings, due to...
Impelled by evil karma, one falls into that place and suffers incessantly through the long night of darkness;

being obstructed from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma is called the "difficulty of hell. Second is the difficulty of being among animals, meaning that the species of animals are manifold and diverse.
Each also receives retribution according to their respective causes, constantly suffering flogging and slaughter, or devouring one another, enduring endless pain.

Because it obstructs the seeing of the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, it is called the "difficulty of the animal realm. Third is the difficulty of the hungry ghosts (*preta*). This refers to three types of hungry ghosts:
first, those whose karma is most heavy, who for long eons do not even hear the names of water or drink. [The second type... due to their karma...
Next, regarding the "heavy" [obstacles]: these exist only among humans. They constantly seek out and consume pus, blood, excrement, and filth.

Those whose three karmas are light may occasionally find a single meal; furthermore, they are driven and coerced with swords and staves, filling rivers and blocking seas, undergoing immeasurable suffering.

Because this obstructs seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, it is called the "difficulty of the hungry ghosts. Fourth is the "difficulty of the long-lived heavens," which refers to this heaven because—
Their lifespan is five hundred kalpas; this refers to the Heaven of Non-conception within the fourth dhyāna of the form realm.
It is called "non-conception" because mental activity and thought do not function there, like fish in ice or hibernating insects.

Many non-Buddhists who practice meditation are reborn in that place, which obstructs their seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; therefore, it is known as the "difficulty of the long-lived heavens. Fifth is in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.

Difficult [to reach]. In Sanskrit, it is called Uttarakuru; in the language of China, it means "Superior Place" (Shengchu). This refers to the fact that the retribution experienced in this place is superior to that of the three continents of the east, west, and south.
The people there have a lifespan of one thousand years and do not suffer premature death. However, because they are attached to pleasure, they do not accept instruction or transformation.
For this reason, the Sages do not appear therein, and the people cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma; thus it is named Uttara-kuru.
The difficulty of being born among the Mlecchas; and the sixth, the difficulty of being blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired.

This refers to those who, though born in a central land, possess such heavy karmic obstructions that they are blind, deaf, mute, or lack their sensory faculties; thus, even when a Buddha appears in the world, they are unable to see him.

7. The obstacle of being born before the Buddha: Although the Buddha preached the Dharma, one was unable to hear it; hence it is called the obstacle of being blind, deaf, and mute. 8. The obstacle of worldly wisdom and eloquence:

This refers to those in the world who possess sharp and clever worldly intelligence but devote themselves solely to the study of non-Buddhist (tīrthika) scriptures, having no faith in the supramundane Dharma of the King of the Dharma;
hence it is called the obstacle of worldly wisdom and eloquence. 9. The obstacle of being born after the Buddha.

The "Difficulties After the Buddha" refers to the following: When a Buddha appears in the world as a Great Teacher, he causes all sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvana. Only those with the requisite conditions encounter his appearance;
however, those who exist before or after the Buddha’s era possess heavy karma and meager conditions. Since they neither see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma, this is termed "birth."
Regarding the difficulty [of encountering] the Buddha before and after [his appearance], one bestows all merit upon others so that they may achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment;
this clarifies that one plants the causes for attaining Buddhahood through vows for both oneself and others.

Furthermore, it ensures that in the future world of Maitreya Buddha, one shall attain deliverance during his three assemblies from birth, old age, sickness, and death; this clarifies that one attains the meeting [with the Buddha] for both oneself and others.

This is the vow for the Buddha’s liberation. Regarding the three assemblies, according to the *Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born* Sūtra (*Maitreyavyākaraṇa-sūtra*), on the very day Maitreya Bodhisattva leaves the household life, he shall attain Buddhahood and sit beneath the Dragon Flower tree (*nāgapuṣpa*) in the Flower Grove Garden (*puṣpavana*).
There, he will preach the Dharma in three assemblies. In the first assembly, he will deliver nine hundred and sixty billion śrāvakas. [It is so recorded.]
It is said: If there are kings, ministers, elders, householders, men, women, or any other donors who,
within the True Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform the work of a Buddha— whether planting roots of goodness themselves or teaching others to plant them—
using the seven treasures of gold, silver, brass, copper, iron, wood, stone, or clay, or using silk threads or colored fabrics.
One should paint images of the Buddha and stūpas, whether large or small, even as small as a finger-joint.
One may offer worship with incense, flowers, and various exquisite offerings.
By the power of such roots of goodness, when the Tathāgata Maitreya attains perfect enlightenment, one will obtain a human body and be present at his first assembly.
Having shaved his head and left the household life, he attained *nirvāṇa* by virtue of the power of his past vows.
At the second assembly, he delivered ninety-four hundred billion *śrāvaka*s. The record states:

"If kings, ministers, or commoners, within the True Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform deeds for the Dharma—namely, regarding the various Mahāyāna sūtras, or the Vinaya, or..."

Treatise: Whether reading or reciting [this scripture], or reverently making offerings to it, or adorning the scroll with various colored silks—by the power of these roots of goodness, when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, one will obtain a human body and, within his second assembly, shave one's head and leave the household life; by the power of past vows, one shall immediately attain nirvāṇa.
At the third assembly, he delivered [the Dharma] to nine hundred and twenty billion śrāvakas. The record states:

"If kings, ministers, commoners, and others, within the True Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform services for the Saṃgha, plant roots of merit themselves, or teach others to plant them, on the first day of each month, or on the eighth or fifteenth day..."
Every day they established a vegetarian feast (*śramaṇa-bhakta*), making offerings to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; or they made offerings to those practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
or they made offerings to those preaching the Dharma; or they bestowed gifts such as seats and bedding, making offerings to the Saṃgha.

By the power of these roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), when Maitreya Buddha attains perfect enlightenment, they will successfully obtain a human body and, within his third assembly, shave their heads [to enter the monastic order].
Having left the household life by shaving their hair, they immediately attained *nirvāṇa* through the power of their past vows.
Therefore, the present text states that they shall also, in the future world of Maitreya Buddha, attain deliverance from birth, old age, sickness, and death during his three assemblies.
The Sūtra states: "Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, without having made this vow, observe the eight precepts of the fast;
they will obtain a small measure of the field of merit. To corroborate this with ancient precedent, it says:
Commentary: This refers to the aforementioned generation of vows. According to the sutras, this cites ancient precedents as proof to produce the text.
If one does not thus dedicate and generate such vows, it is a mind of self-interest that does not seek liberation; consequently, one will only obtain a small measure of merit-field (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Therefore, for all who receive the five precepts or the eight precepts, they should daily, by means of the merit of upholding the precepts...
When the evening recitation is concluded, one should burn incense and prostrate before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Kneeling upright with palms joined, one should sincerely make vows and pray for the holy ones to bear witness and grant their seal of approval, so that one’s aspirations may be fulfilled. Now, I shall again briefly clarify the specific practices.
This is intended to make known whether merit exists or not, and to ensure that one’s observance is not in vain. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:

"If, after having received the eight precepts, one beats sentient beings, the fast is not pure. Even if one does not beat them on that very day, if one intends to beat them the following day, it is likewise not pure.
To state the essential point: if one performs acts of improper conduct with body or speech [the fast is not pure]."
Although one may not break the fast, the fast is not pure. Even if body and speech are pure, if the mind gives rise to thoughts of greed, anger, or malice, the fast is likewise called impure.
If, after receiving the eight precepts, one diligently cultivates the six recollections, this is called a pure fast.
As for what are called the six recollections: first is the recollection of the Buddha, which means recollecting the Buddha’s perfection.
The Ten Epithets, Great Compassion and Great Mercy, the Radiance of Wisdom, and Immeasurable Supernatural Powers, who are able to uproot all sufferings.
With a pure and upright mind, I have been able to draw near to the Buddha; my heart gives rise to joy.
Because of this joy, my body attains happiness. Because of this happiness, my mind attains concentration. Because of attaining concentration, my mind becomes equanimous.

And so forth. By practicing the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), one will certainly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*; this is called "mindfulness of the Buddha. Second is mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
This refers to being mindful that the Dharma consists of all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata, namely the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so on.
With a pure and upright mind, one attains proximity to the Dharma, and joy arises in the heart. One proceeds in this manner until practicing the contemplation of mindfulness of the Dharma.
One will certainly proceed toward Nirvāṇa; this is called mindfulness of the Dharma. Third is mindfulness of the Saṅgha:

that the Saṅgha are the disciples of the Tathāgata who have attained the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom, and are able to serve as a fertile field of merit for the sentient beings of the world;
they should be revered. With a pure and upright mind, I am able to draw near to the Saṅgha, and my heart gives rise to joy.
...up to the cultivation of the mindfulness of the Saṅgha, which necessarily leads to Nirvāṇa; this is called mindfulness of the Saṅgha.

Fourth is mindfulness of the precepts, which means being mindful of all prohibitive precepts that can obstruct all evil afflictions. With a pure and upright mind, one attains intimacy with the precepts, and joy arises in the heart.
Up to the cultivation of the mental image of mindfulness of the precepts, it necessarily leads to Nirvāṇa; this is called...
Contemplating the precepts. Fifth, contemplating generosity: that is, reflecting that the merit one has bestowed brings benefit to all the world;

that while formerly I was shrouded by stinginess and envy, I have now become free from such stains of greed and have dwelt in a mind of equanimity, giving away all things without any sense of attachment or regret. Having thus practiced giving, I—
The mind should be joyful. Because of this joyful mind, the body attains happiness. One should even cultivate the perception of the recollection of generosity (*dānānusmṛti*);

one will certainly proceed toward Nirvāṇa. This is called the recollection of generosity. Sixth is the recollection of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*), which refers to the recollection of the devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.
All have been born in those places due to the roots of merit from their past discipline and generosity, where they experience celestial happiness. I, too, see that such is the case.

Through the merit of precepts and giving, at the time of death, one will certainly be reborn in that heaven. Because of mindfulness of the heavens, one is freed from unwholesome states and the mind gives rise to joy.
Because the mind is joyful, the body attains happiness. Because of this happiness, the mind attains concentration.
Because concentration is attained, the mind becomes equanimous. By cultivating the perception of mindfulness of the heavens, one will surely proceed upon the path to heaven. This is...
This is called "Recollection of the Devas. Here, observing the eight precepts serves as the cause, while the six recollections serve as the support.

It should be understood that although the sixth recollection—the recollection of the devas—has non-nirvāṇa as its cause and results in tainted (sāsrava) fruits, it nonetheless causes the practitioner to recollect; regarding this, there are two meanings.
First, it is to manifest that the merit of giving precepts has a specific destination; second, it is to clarify that mindfulness is focused on the fast so as to remain untainted.

For these reasons, various sutras universally elucidate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). [Next is] the ritual for the bestowal and reception of the precepts for those who have left the household life.

The seven clarifications are as follows: first, clarifying that the merit of renunciation originates with the Bodhisattva; second, clarifying that there is benefit that transcends the world; third, clarifying that obstacles to renunciation cause great harm;
fourth, clarifying that having already renounced, one may still commit sinful deeds; fifth, clarifying that having already renounced, one may practice ordinary meritorious deeds;
sixth, clarifying the essential practices for cultivating the Path after renunciation; and seventh, clarifying the correct practices of both the Great and Small Vehicles.
The Three Studies are the foundation. This is explained at length in the *Chao* (Commentary).

This constitutes a general presentation of the primary meaning. Regarding the statement that a detailed explanation is found in the *Chao*, I shall now provide a brief exposition based on the Sūtras and Vinaya;
thus, the meaning of the *Chao* will not be lacking.
First, to clarify that the merit of renouncing the household life originates with the Bodhisattva: The Bodhisattva is none other than the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha (Huming).
He descended to be born in the palace of King Śuddhodana and was named Prince Siddhārtha, which is the causal name of Śākyamuni Buddha.

When Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma were traversed, and as for the people...
The lifespan gradually diminished until it reached one hundred years. The sentient beings of the world remained in a state of long-term ignorance and darkness;

they did not hear of the Triple Gem, but committed only various evils and were beset by manifold sufferings. They took the three miserable realms as their permanent home and underwent the four modes of birth as if changing clothes.
Bodhisattva Rāhula, pitying those who were thus submerged and sinking, was about to succeed to the Buddha’s position to appear in the world and benefit living beings.
Transversely across all realms of existence, one who is free from thought and detached from defilement plants the seeds for renunciation.

Delighting in secluded tranquility, if there is any attachment, it will ultimately become a golden shackle. This single path is the expedient means for leading others forth. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"If there are those who do not understand the dharma of renunciation, who delight in and cling to birth and death, and do not seek liberation—for this reason, the Bodhisattva abandons his kingdom and wealth."

For this reason, he left the household life to seek tranquility. According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata first desired to renounce the world, he made these four vows to deliver sentient beings:

first, he vowed to rescue sentient beings from their distress and calamities, saying, "When I have attained perfect enlightenment and acquired all-knowledge, if at that time sentient beings are beset by distress and afflicted by various sufferings, I shall [deliver them]."
First, to deliver and liberate them, causing them to sever their bonds of affection. Second, to vow to eliminate the afflictive obscurations of sentient beings;

that is, because sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering of birth and death, obscured by the darkness of ignorance, and entirely lacking knowledge, I shall manifest [the truth] for them, like a pure eye with no obstruction internally or externally, enabling them to emerge from it. Third, to vow to sever the false views of sentient beings.

It means that sentient beings dwelling in the world are conceited with self-importance, exalting themselves and disparaging others; their minds harbor false views, and they do not aspire to the Noble Path.
I shall transform and guide them, causing them to enter the True and Right Way. Fourth, it means vowing to deliver sentient beings from the wheel of suffering:
that sentient beings dwell within the wheel of birth and death, which revolves without end, and whose cessation cannot be reached by themselves because their eye of wisdom is unable to see.
I shall preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain liberation; thus it is said that the merit of leaving the household life originates with the Bodhisattva.

Second, to clarify those who benefit by transcending the world: this refers to those who leave the household life with true sincerity, fearing the suffering of the four enemies, and contemplating non-transmigration.
In nature, one is included among the ranks of the Buddhas; how could it be that there is no self? Within the retributions of various classes of beings, why would one willingly endure them?

To abandon the deep attachment to the five desires and leave behind the most beloved of six kin—only through such renunciation can one cause the Three Jewels to flourish and deliver the four modes of birth.
One should know that shaving the head and donning the dyed robes is not merely a superficial flow toward transcending the mundane; it requires a supreme aspiration. Thus it is said:
It is beneficial and transcends the world.

Regarding the three types of obstacles that greatly harm one’s progress toward liberation: these refer to those who leave the household life with a sincere heart, thereby continuing the lineage of the sages and saints and serving as eyes for sentient beings.
If there were no Sangha in the world, the Three Jewels would be severed. In the vast and surging sea of suffering, who then could launch the compassionate vessel? In the boundless expanse...

Regarding the path of karma, who can point out the way for those lost in delusion? According to the *Pravrajyāpuṇya-sūtra*, if one can permit others to leave the household life and receive the precepts, the merit is immeasurable.
It is like making offerings for a hundred years to as many arhats as would fill the four continents.

It is not equal to the merit of someone who, for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, goes forth from home and receives the precepts for even one day and one night (meaning that although the aforementioned giving was abundant, it was still subject to exhaustion and bound to the desire realm; whereas going forth for the sake of the Dharma is not an action belonging to the three realms, and thus it is said to surpass the former). Furthermore, it says:

"If one obstructs another’s going forth and creates difficulties for them, due to the retribution of this sin, one will fall into the three evil paths and be perpetually blind and sightless; if one is born as a human, [one will suffer likewise]."
While in the mother’s womb, he was conceived without eyes; throughout a hundred years, even with unimpeded wisdom, he could not exhaustively describe the retribution for these sins.
Among the four realms of existence, he remained perpetually blind until his death, for it is recorded that this person did not attain liberation because they obstructed their own renunciation.
Furthermore, the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), citing a sutra, states: "If one intends to renounce the world..."
To create obstacles, cause destruction, and suppress [the Dharma] is for this person to sever the seed of the Buddha. All manner of evils will gather in their body like the great ocean;
they will manifest leprosy in this life and, upon death, enter the Black Darkness Hell with no prospect of escape.

According to the sutras, the harm to the meaning [of the Dharma] comprises two aspects: first, self-harm; second, harming others. Therefore, it is said that obstructing the emergence [of the Dharma] is a great harm.

As for those in the Four Clarities who, having already left the household life, engage in sinful conduct: this refers to those who, at the outset of their path toward the Way, seek peace while avoiding suffering;

yet by shaving their heads and donning the black robes, they turn their backs on peace and head toward suffering. With four mouths and three [monastic] precepts broken, how can they allow themselves such license?

Like the grass tied to a goose or the pearl in its beak, how could they not be imitating [the foolish]? Now, failing to remember the ancients, they wish to ascend but instead fall—this is entirely due to their own ignorance and lack of resolve.
Do not transgress the ordinary. Lacking a teacher as a virtuous guide, consult the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Yijiao jing), which states:

"One must not engage in buying and selling, trading, compounding medicinal decoctions, or divining good and bad fortune. One should restrain the body, eat at the proper times, and maintain a pure livelihood.
One must not involve oneself in worldly affairs, act as a messenger, practice incantations or elixirs, cultivate intimacy with the noble, or become familiar and disrespectful. All such things...
One should not do so. One should instead rectify one's own mind and seek deliverance through right mindfulness, without concealing faults or manifesting wonders to delude the masses.
Regarding the four types of offerings, one should know moderation and contentment; whatever provisions are obtained should not be hoarded.
If one practices in accordance with the sutras, this is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*). If one acts contrary to the teachings, it is called unwholesome action (*pāpakarman*). Therefore...
It is said that once one has left the household life, one may still commit sinful deeds.
As for the five types of worldly merit performed by those who have left the household life, this refers to the true mind detaching from sensory dust and the household transcending the two deaths.

Generally, the diligent cultivation of merit is not the teaching of the Noble Vehicle. To speak of the three untainted states (anāsrava) is for those within the school who study and cultivate the Vinaya;
as for the seven types of conditioned merit (saṃskṛta-puṇya), they are performed by the lay assemblies outside. Otherwise, one abandons nirvāṇa of one's own accord and seeks only temporary pleasure.

Pleasure ends and suffering arises; the paths of humans and devas are perilous. If one can take wisdom as the precursor and dedicate every action toward the adornment of sentient beings and the Buddha-lands, without grasping or attachment and with no thought of seeking reward, then one’s conduct will encompass that of Samantabhadra.

It is even more difficult to praise those who are deluded, for through the functioning of ignorance, their conduct results in that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, it is said: "Having left the household life, one performs the conduct of an ordinary person.

Sixth, regarding the essential practices for cultivating the Way after leaving the household life: this means that as long as ordinary sentiments are not exhausted, the accomplishments of the Way will be difficult to achieve. Not yet...
The essence of all things has love and desire as its root; the Way that is difficult to accomplish has pure precepts as its foundation.

The essential practice for one who has left the household life is solely the observance of the precepts, with the severing of desire as the primary task. The Sutra in Forty-two Sections states: "When a person harbors love and desire..."
Those who do not see the Way are like people looking down at clear water that has been stirred by hand; though many gather around it, none can see their own reflections.
Because people’s minds are turbid due to the entanglement of craving and desire, they do not see the Way. One should abandon craving and desire;
when the defilements of craving and desire are exhausted, the Way can be seen. The *Śāriputra-śīla-sūtra* says: "By relying on this precept, one attains..."
One gives rise to the various dhyānas and concentrations, as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering; for this reason, one should maintain pure precepts.
Since the precepts are the foremost dwelling place for the merit of peace and security, it is said that they are the essential practice for leaving the household life and cultivating the Way.
Seventh, it is explained that the Great and Small Vehicles take the three trainings as the foundation of right practice. These three are precept, concentration, and wisdom.

All are called "trainings" (*śikṣā*); "training" is like adornment. Just as a vessel cannot achieve beauty without adornment, so too, if one observes people who do not train, they cannot achieve the virtues of a sage.
Therefore, those who cultivate according to these principles will necessarily realize the fruit of sainthood; this is termed "right practice. Indeed.
Sentient beings take deluded minds as afflictions; when thoughts stir, karma is formed. Through karma, retribution is induced, and birth and death continue without end.

Desiring to escape the fruit of suffering, one must eliminate its cause. Therefore, one first uses precepts to govern karma, and subsequently uses concentration and wisdom to clarify both afflictions and karma.
Because they distinguish between good and evil, the two practices of cessation and action are used to overturn delusions; [only] obscurity and distraction remain.
Therefore, the two dharmas of meditative concentration and wisdom are applied as an antidote; as the illness is cured by medicine, the faculty relies upon the teaching for cultivation.

Only then are karma exhausted and delusions eliminated, such that emotional attachments perish and the true nature is revealed. Although the gates of the teachings are vast, they do not transcend this; both the Mahayana and Hinayana cultivate them in common.
There are distinctions among those who have realized [the truth]. Therefore, it is said that for both the Great and Small Vehicles, the three trainings constitute the foundation of right practice.
○ Regarding the method for requesting ordination:

at that time, the bhikṣus would arbitrarily ordain people without knowing how to provide instruction; because they were themselves ignorant and deluded, those [ordinands] did not receive [proper guidance].
The instructors did not observe the rules of decorum; their robes were not properly adjusted; they went for alms in an improper manner;
they accepted impure food in their bowls from various places; and at both the great and small meals, they raised their voices and shouted loudly, like the assembly customs of the Brahmins.
The bhikṣus reported these matters to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow the Saṃgha to confer the full ordination upon them."

This is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. One who wishes to ordain others should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and should make this formal request as follows:
Commentary: In accordance with the ritual procedures, one should first strike the gavel to assemble the community. Those who wish to ordain others should fully observe the dignified deportment;
having first prostrated before the senior monks in the assembly, they should kneel with palms joined and make their request.
Venerable Sangha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], seek the Sangha’s permission to ordain a person and bestow the full precepts upon them.
May the Sangha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], permission to ordain a person and bestow the full precepts.

In the *Tri-kaṭhina-vinaya*, according to the text of the *Karmavācanā*, one who is to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) must formally request the method for maintaining a following (*gaṇa-parigraha*).
If one consults the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, after the virtues of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) have been fully enumerated, the concluding text states:
"The maintenance of a dependent (*niśraya-parigraha*) is likewise for the maintenance of a śrāmaṇera. Thus, it is known that in both cases, one who lacks these virtues is ineligible.
[End of section].
Commentary: This explains the method for applying the precedents as clarified in the Vinaya. Regarding the prior detailed listing of the preceptor’s virtues:

according to the Vinaya, the Buddha stated that there are five qualities whose fulfillment renders one ineligible to bestow the full ordination (*upasampadā*): lacking faith, [lacking shame, lacking dread of blame, being ill-tempered, and being ignorant].

Lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame, being indolent, and being forgetful—one who possesses these five qualities may be granted the full ordination (the opposite of the aforementioned five qualities).

Furthermore, there are five other qualities by which one is not permitted [to grant it]: violating the higher training in ethical discipline, violating the higher training in view, violating the higher training in conduct, and having little learning.
Lacking wisdom (the opposite of the five aforementioned dharmas results in receiving the precepts). Furthermore, there are five other dharmas by which one does not receive them:
first, failing to attend to a sick disciple, or failing to have someone else attend to him, until he recovers or passes away;
second, if a disciple is unhappy with his dwelling place, failing to employ skillful means to move him to another location; third, if a matter of doubt arises, failing to resolve it.
Understand their meaning. If they are removed according to the rules and laws, [they may be ordained]. Fourth, one who is unable to instruct another to abandon evil views and abide in right views.

Fifth, one who is less than ten years [of standing]—[if these five conditions are met, one may receive ordination]. Furthermore, there are five things that must not be unknown: the increase of morality (*adhiśīla*), the increase of mind (*adhicitta*), [the increase of wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), the training in higher conduct, and the training in higher discipline].

Increasing wisdom; not knowing how to perform the *jñapti* (motion); not knowing how to perform the *karman* (formal act)—[these five conditions entitle one to receive ordination]. [These points are recorded here only briefly, four or five in number; they are detailed in the Vinaya.
One may not grant dependence (*niśraya*), yet one may grant dependence. One may not keep a *śrāmaṇera*, yet one may keep a *śrāmaṇera*.

Regarding the qualities required for those who are ordained, they are all the same as those for a *upādhyāya*. Thus, it is not easy to be a teacher, and it is truly difficult to possess these qualifications.

Regarding the method for ordaining others, the Buddha said: "One should examine this person. If they are incapable of being instructed, and one does not wish to sustain them with two things—first, the Dharma;
second, food and clothing—one should say: 'Venerable One, stop! Do not ordain others. If, however, they possess wisdom..."
The wise one is capable of providing instruction. Furthermore, regarding the inclusion by means of two matters, one should perform the *karmavācanā*.
Having had those three [persons] make their requests, they pay homage and stand up. The officiant, having performed the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*), replies as follows:
Regarding the method for ordaining others: the one who presides over the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) makes this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] now requests the Saṃgha to grant ordination and bestow full admission (*upasampadā*) upon another person."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha now grants the bhikṣu [Name] permission to ordain others and bestow the full precepts.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. This bhikṣu [Name] now requests from the assembly of monks permission to ordain others and bestow the full precepts.
The Saṃgha now grants [the authorization] to the bhikṣu [Name] to ordain others and bestow full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting [the authorization] to the bhikṣu [Name] to ordain others and bestow full ordination should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.

The Saṃgha has already consented to grant [the authorization] to the bhikṣu [Name] to ordain others and bestow full ordination. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is settled.
"Maintain it thus. Commentary:
To bestow the full ordination upon one seeking admission is to act as an *upādhyāya*. In the Sanskrit original, the correct name is *upādhyāya*;
when transmitted to Khotan, it was translated as "Upāsaka," and when transmitted to this land [China], Master Kumārajīva translated the name as "Lì" (Power).
Regarding this meaning, it accords with the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, which states:

"Now, one who leaves the household life abandons the house of birth-and-death belonging to their parents and enters into the gateway of the Dharma to receive the subtle and wondrous Dharma. This is nurtured by the power of the Teacher;

the Dharma-body gives rise to the wealth of merit and nourishes the life of wisdom. There is no greater achievement than this. If there were no Buddha-Dharma, there would be no Dharma-body or wisdom."
Life cannot grow or flourish [without them]. If one lacks food and clothing, the physical substance and the vessel for the Path cannot be sustained.
If these two matters are not lacking, and once ten years of ordination have been completed, the Saṃgha must perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and grant their consent.
This single *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the person’s own benefit; thus, it belongs to the private sphere.

Non-validity due to the person: not being one [qualified member], not being from the same boundary (*sīmā*), being less than ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), having little learning, being unvirtuous, being largely ignorant of the Vinaya, or having committed offenses, and so forth.

Non-validity due to the two factors: errors or omissions in the formal request (*jñapti*), inversion in the *karmavācanā*, unclear speech, or confusion regarding the preliminary procedures (*pūrvakalpa*).
Non-validity due to the three matters: deficiencies in the two types of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), and so forth. Non-validity due to the four persons.
The Dharma is not [correct]. Up to the seven cases where three are incorrect, taking the preceding and combining them with the succeeding fully reveals what is incorrect.
Regarding the legal procedures for ordaining śrāmaṇeras, the ordination of Rāhula was the first.
Commentary: This explains the origin of the rule. "Rāhula" is translated here as "obscuring" (fùzhàng).
It refers to the Asura Rāhu, who obscures the moon's light when he devours it. Because he remained in his mother’s womb for six years, obscuring her, he was named after him.
Formerly, he was called "Lohula. According to the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya* (Jiè duàn), while the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu...
At that time, when the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Monastery in the kingdom, he arrived at the proper hour, donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Having finished his meal, he returned and departed the city. At that moment, Rāhula and his mother were atop a high tower;
seeing the Buddha approaching, she said to her son, "The one coming there is your father. Thereupon, Rāhula quickly descended from the tower and went to where the Tathāgata was.

He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. The World-Honored One stroked his head with his hand, and he thought to himself, "Since my birth, I have never experienced such fine, smooth, soft, and pleasant sensation.

The Buddha asked him, "Are you able to leave the household life and study the Way? He replied, "I am able to leave the household life. The Buddha extended a single finger and gave it to Rāhula, leading him away.
Within the saṃghārāma, he addressed Śāriputra, saying: "You must ordain this youth, allowing him to leave the household life and receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
This was the occasion for that regulation.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one is seven years of age and understands what is good and what is evil, they may be granted ordination. If one is over seventy and requires assistance for rising and reclining, they must not be ordained.
However, if they are able to cultivate various practices, their ordination is permitted. If one first desires to leave the household life, they should be told of the hardships:
eating once a day, dwelling alone, and sleeping alone; and that there is much study and answering of questions. Only if they can maintain these should they be ordained."
Commentary: This citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies the weighing of a candidate’s suitability.
In that Vinaya, it was because various bhikṣus ordained individuals aged eighty or ninety who had white hair, hunched backs, and failing faculties, such that they could not restrain their movements.
If one requires assistance for spitting and expectoration, they will defile the pure grounds of the Sangha and incur the reproach of worldly people; therefore, the Buddha established this rule.

If a person is seven years of age and understands what is wholesome and unwholesome, their ordination is permitted—meaning they know that the world is suffering and that renunciation leads to tranquility.

Such a person, though young in years, possesses the roots of past cultivation and right view, and will ultimately perfect the factors of the Path. If, however, one is over seventy and requires assistance for rising and lying down, [they must not be ordained].
Such a person may not be ordained. This is not due to a lack of compassion or a refusal to admit them; rather, it is out of pity that they are barred.

This refers to those who come seeking what is required for the homeless life; because they follow the path of the Dharma yet do not cultivate the practice of giving, they would fail to repay the costs of their lodging and sustenance.

Even if one were to employ human labor and effort, it would ultimately be impossible to provide for them. Furthermore, if one is over seventy, although their physical form may be decrepit, their vitality and strength may still be robust.

If one’s resolve is not indolent, such a person may also be permitted to receive ordination. Generally, for those wishing to leave the household life, regardless of whether they are old or young, one should first explain the hardships of renunciation so that they may deliberate upon its feasibility.
If, when questioned, they respond with joy and say they are capable, then their faith is certain and free from regression.
If, however, they remain silent out of anxiety, this indicates they are terrified and unable to endure it; thus, the matter is described as being difficult.
This means that one is not moved by cold or heat, is diligent and never indolent, and understands that only the Way is worth cultivating and that the body is not to be spared.

This suffering is, in fact, the cause for the bliss of transcending the world. "One meal" means not eating at improper times. "One dwelling" means sitting cross-legged to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"One sleep" means applying effort during the first and last of the three watches of the night to compensate for what was not accomplished during the day.
It is sufficient. When the mid-night spirit grows weary, listen to its teachings on cherishing and nurturing; sleep in peace and study extensively.

This means reading the Vinaya to cultivate practice, receiving the Sūtras to inquire into their meaning—these four are to be cultivated through meditation and recitation. Use eating and sleeping to refine the physical substance.

If one can truly achieve this, then there will be no dread regarding any of the various karmic practices. In Sanskrit, *śrāmaṇera*; here it is translated as "Cessation of Worldliness" (Xici), meaning to cease worldly affairs.
The sentiment of defilement is countered by using compassion to save all living beings. It is also said that when first entering the Buddha-dharma, one often retains worldly sentiments;
therefore, it is necessary to cease evil in order to practice compassion. Those from the youngest age of seven up to thirteen are all called "crow-driving śrāmaṇeras.
If they are between fourteen and nineteen years of age, they are called "dharma-conforming śrāmaṇeras. If they are twenty...
The above are all designated as *śrāmaṇera* by name.
Regarding the method for shaving the hair:
because the bhikṣus would occasionally ordain people on their own initiative, the Saṃgha was unaware [of the status of those individuals]. The Buddha said: "If you wish for the Saṃgha..."

When shaving the hair in the midst of the blue-robed community, one should announce it to the entire Saṃgha. If they cannot assemble, one should go from room to room to inform them before shaving the hair.
If they can assemble, one should shave the hair after making the formal announcement.

Commentary: This introduces the circumstances for the establishment of the rule. According to the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya* (Section on Receiving the Precepts), there was once a skilled artisan who went to a monastery and requested the bhikṣus to allow him to leave the household life to practice the Path. The bhikṣus immediately ordained him.
At that time, his parents came to the monastery weeping and asked the bhikṣus [about their son], but they all replied that he was not to be seen. His parents...
He immediately searched within the monastic quarters; having found it, he reviled the community of monks. It was for this reason that this regulation was established.
One should know that once one has left the household life, one’s residence is shared with the monks and one partakes in the monks’ portion of offerings.

If the assembly is unaware of the source of such items, and the matter is explained but the request for tonsure is not yet granted, this is not merely a matter of avoiding secular reproach; there is also the fear of defiling the Dharma-gate, as well as the charge of theft.

If monastic property is used, the responsibility for the offense falls upon the preceptor; how can one not exercise caution? Furthermore, instructing each individual room to inform others makes it difficult for the assembly to gather.

If the Sangha assembles in harmony, one should perform a *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion) first, and only then perform the tonsure. This is because the rule regarding those who are not present was established for laypeople.
One should have the person seeking ordination move away from the place where they can hear the proceedings, while a capable person within the assembly performs the *karman*.
Having performed the preliminary formalities, he replies, saying: "The Saṃgha of venerable ones, please listen.
This person [Name] wishes to have his hair shaved by the bhikṣu [Name]. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. I announce this: the shaving of [Name]'s hair."

After the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, he is summoned into the midst of the assembly and given the ritual for shaving the head and ordaining a person, as detailed at length in the *Śrī-vinaya-saṃgraha*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "First one receives the five precepts, and afterwards one receives the ten precepts."

Commentary on the Ritual for Ordaining Others: I have previously compiled the *Zhishan Shami Zhengfan* (The Correct Model for the Tonsure of Śrāmaṇeras), within which the ritual procedures for conferring the five-part precepts are detailed and clearly explained.
With evidence provided to refute errors, one may understand them through reading alone. As a guide for practical application, this work truly supplements the profound transformation [of the Dharma].
I shall not cite further sources here at length.
○ The Method for Bestowing the Ten Precepts:
The Buddha said, "If one intends to ordain someone within a monastery to allow them to leave the household life, one should inform the entire Saṃgha.
Once permission has been granted for the ordination, one should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) in this manner."

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This [person, so-and-so] seeks to go forth from the bhikṣu [so-and-so]. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and allow [so-and-so] to go forth. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Commentary: Regarding these two *śuddha-ekajñapti-karmas*, there is a sequence in their establishment so that one may understand their general and specific applications.

If the hair is shaved on the first day and the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*) are conferred on the following day, although the two dharmas occur sequentially, both require the formal ritual procedure (*karma*). One should perform the preliminary preparations (*purva-kalpa*) for each:
the first response is for the *karma* of shaving the hair, and the subsequent response is for the *karma* of going forth (*pravrajyā*). This is what is meant.
The application differs. If, after shaving the hair, one immediately bestows the ten precepts, one performs only the initial announcement (*jñapti*) and omits the subsequent announcement;

since the Sangha has already granted its consent, there is no fault in either case. Because the reception of the precepts is subsumed within the act of shaving the hair, this is called "the application being collective.
These two *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) are performed for the sake of an individual and both pertain to private matters.

It is not otherwise, nor does it conform to the above; the only difference therein is that the person is not [qualified]. This refers to cases where the recipient is too young or old, violates the regulations, and so forth.
○ The Method for Receiving the Precept-Substance.
The *Sudarsana* states: The Ācārya says, "Follow my words; I shall instruct you in the reception of the Three Refuges. He replies, "So be it.

Furthermore, one must inquire regarding the obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*) and the conditions for the arising of the precepts (*śīla-samutthāna*), following the examples set in the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Only after conducting the inquiry in its entirety should one confer them, saying:
Explanation: In the Sanskrit language, *ācārya* is translated here as "model" (*guifan*) and also as "right practice" (*zhengxing*).

This means that he is able to cause his disciples to emulate his rules and regulations in order to rectify their mental conduct. When the *upādhyāya* presides over the seat, he briefly inquires regarding the prohibitions and obstacles;

these matters are all contained in detail within the *Zhantan Chuanjie Zhengfan* (The Correct Model for the Transmission of Precepts at the Three Altars). Here, we clarify only the role of the *ācārya*.
The ritual for bestowing the precepts of taking refuge is as follows: "I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
I now follow the Buddha into homelessness, with [Name] as my Upādhyāya. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One."
Having received the threefold [refuge] conferral, one immediately obtains the precepts:
"I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
I have now followed the Buddha forth into homelessness. [Name] is my preceptor (upādhyāya). The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One."
Having completed the three formal declarations, the characteristics of the precepts are now conferred:

"No. [He] replies, "I can uphold it.

[He] replies, "I can uphold it."
These are the ten precepts of purity for a śrāmaṇera. For as long as one lives, not a single one may be transgressed. Can you maintain them? (He replies: "I can. Commentary:
Of these ten precepts of the śrāmaṇera, the first four are the fundamental roots of essential gravity (*garuka*); if one transgresses them, one should...
Exclusion by expulsion (*pārājika*): one may not perform religious rites together with pure *śrāmaṇeras*, nor stay overnight in their company.

Furthermore, unlike other *śrāmaṇeras*, one may not stay with a *bhikṣu* for more than two nights. The final six [offenses] are offenses of concealment (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). If there is an offense, confession is permissible;

depending on whether the transgression was intentional or accidental, the gravity of the resulting offense—whether heavy or light—is determined. Only in the interim cases is it treated as a single *duṣkṛta*. Explanation.

In principle, one should read the *Yunqi Yaolue* (Essentials of Yunqi). To understand what is permitted and what is prohibited, one should study the majestic deportment according to the Vinaya, as in the *Sengfutian Jing* (Sutra on Inviting Monks as a Field of Merit). A śrāmaṇera should know the five virtues:

first, having resolved to leave the home life, he cherishes and wears the Way within his breast; second, he alters his physical appearance to accord with the dharma-robes; third, he forever severs affection for kin.
Fourth, because they cast aside their own lives to honor and follow the Way. Fifth, because they resolve to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.
[Commentary: This citation is from the *Sarvadeśaguṇa-puṇyakṣetra-sūtra*. However, these five virtues are not merely for those of limited capacity throughout their entire lives.
Practice it. From beginning to end, it penetrates the five aggregates; together they are capable of being sustained by material offerings and serve as models for humans and devas.
Therefore, one should recite and uphold it, and must not treat lightly the physical body or the monastic robes. That sutra says: At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha:

"If a person plants virtue and desires to seek great blessings, what excellent field of merit and retribution could there be that would yield infinite results from planting even a single hair's breadth?"
"Virtuous Root, one shall obtain immeasurable merit. The Buddha told Śakra Devendra: "The Sangha possesses pure virtue and is called a 'Field of Merit.
These five matters—from the first moment of resolve to leave the household life, up to the aspiration to seek the Mahāyāna—are termed the 'Field of Merit.
It is excellent, beautiful, and free from drought or decay; the merit gained by making offerings to it is beyond comparison. These five..."
The latter phrase is annotated in *Seonjo siseo* (The Record of Master Seonjo).

First, "one who has left home with the resolve for enlightenment wears the Way upon their breast" means that those who have left the household life generate a courageous mind to transcend the mundane world and practice the *bodhi* of the Buddha;
being able to wear the wondrous Way upon their breast, they become a field of merit for the world—this is the first pure virtue. Second, "to disparage... [text continues].

"Because their physical appearance accords with the Dharma robes" means that those who have left the household life shave off their hair and beards, destroy the marks of worldly beauty, cast off the dust of the mundane world, and don the Dharma robes of the Tathāgata. Possessing the majestic deportment of a Buddha, they serve as a field of merit for the world;
this is the second pure virtue. Third, because they have forever severed affectionate attachments and harbor neither favoritism nor aversion.

This means that having already surrendered to the Buddha and left the household life, one has severed the affectionate bonds with parents and no longer holds primary responsibility for worldly affairs.

If one is still attached and unwilling to renounce them, one should instead practice the Way with single-minded diligence to repay the virtue of one’s parents who gave birth and raised one, while simultaneously being able to serve as a field of merit for the world; this is the third pure virtue. Fourth, entrustment...

Regarding "discarding body and life to honor and revere the Way": this refers to those who have left the household life and are able to relinquish their bodies and lives without any regard or attachment, devoting themselves single-mindedly to seeking realization of the Buddha-way, while simultaneously serving as a field of merit for the world;
this is the fourth pure virtue. Regarding the fifth, "aspiring to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering others": this refers to those who have left the household life...
Such a person constantly harbors the intention to save all beings and is single-mindedly devoted to earnestly seeking the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
They deliver all sentient beings and serve as a field of merit for the world; this is the fifth pure virtue that a śrāmaṇera should practice and fulfill.
As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one should explain ten enumerations: first, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink; second, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

third, sensation, perception, and volition (*vedanā-saṃjñā-cetanā*); fourth, the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*); fifth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*); sixth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*);
seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*); eighth, the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārgaḥ*); ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings (*nava sattvāvāsāḥ*); tenth...

These ten "all-encompassing" [contemplations] are included within this enumeration. The explanation of their mutual counteraction and the manifestation of the correct [practice] is as extensively detailed in the *Xing-shi chao* (The Manual of Ritual Practice).

Regarding these ten items, I shall now follow the scriptural authorities to list the categories of phenomena; by explaining their characteristics, I aim to facilitate understanding for the purpose of contemplation.
This is the counteractive measure regarding the objective sphere (*ālambana*), which clarifies correct practice and does not obscure the sacred injunctions.
First, as for the statement that all sentient beings rely upon food and drink:

according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, "In this world, the twelve classes of living beings cannot sustain themselves by their own power; they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment. The *Yanyi Chao* states: "A single morsel..."

*Āhāra* (food). *Kavaḍa* means "divided into portions. Food has the sense of providing nourishment and benefit. It is defined as having the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its substance;

upon entering the stomach, it undergoes transformation and decay, thereby nourishing and benefiting the various sense faculties (*indriya*). In ancient translations of the sūtras and vinaya, this was rendered as *piṇḍa-āhāra* (lump-food), based on the meaning of "lumping together" with the hands.
Later translators, noting that liquids such as drinks cannot be lumped together, subsequently translated it as *kavaḍa-āhāra* (portion-food).

Second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). "Contact" (*sparśa*) means "encounter" (*pratigha*). This refers to the various objects (*viṣaya*), such as forms and so forth, which are encountered by the six consciousnesses—namely, qualities such as softness, smoothness, coolness, and warmth.
Because contact with these gives rise to joy and pleasure, and because they are all capable of sustaining and benefiting the sense faculties (*indriya*), it is called the nutriment of contact.
If contact were not nutriment, why would one watch theatrical performances and the like? One could remain hungry all day without eating. Regarding "nutriment through reflection":

reflection is mental volition (*manas-karman*), specifically the volition of the sixth consciousness. When directed toward an agreeable object, it gives rise to a sense of longing that can nourish and benefit the sense faculties.
It is like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who reaches a place where food and drink are available and looks forward to obtaining them.

It is called "nutriment of consciousness" because it sustains the body without causing death; thus, it is termed "consciousness-nutriment. "Consciousness" takes the sense of "grasping and maintaining" as its definition, referring specifically to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
It is through the support provided by the power and influence of the preceding three nutriments that this consciousness is able to flourish and prevail.
Because it sustains the sense faculties, it is called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). If analyzed according to the three realms:

edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the two objects of fragrance and taste do not exist in the form and formless realms; the remaining three nutriments pervade all three realms.
Therefore it is said: first, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink;
second, regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, among all phenomena there are only name and form.
If one wishes to contemplate them as they truly are, one should simply contemplate name and form, even though the deluded mind engages in manifold conceptualizations and discriminations.
Regarding the statement that there is not a single dharma other than name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "name" refers to the mind, which exists merely as words;

therefore, it is called "name. This consists of the mind and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Although they possess the function of being cognitive objects, they lack any substantial obstruction that can be perceived.
Since they differ from form (*rūpa*), they further include the mind, mentation, consciousness, and all the enumerated dharmas.

Because there are various distinct designations, they are called "names" (*nāman*). Second, as for "form" (*rūpa*): it refers to phenomena characterized by having shape and physical obstruction; thus they are called "form.
This includes all the environmental retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*) within the world and the first of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
All of these are phenomena of physical obstruction and lack the faculty of cognition. Since they differ from the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), they are so designated.
Because it refers to form (*rūpa*), it is said that "the two are name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).

Third, regarding "feeling, perception, and so forth": according to the *Aksayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra*, a bodhisattva observes their own feelings and observes the feelings of others, thereby attaining the stillness of mind (*citta-vyupaśama*), seeking out noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*), and aspiring to seek tranquility (*śānti*). Even if...

One encounters pleasure, yet it is not bound to desire. However, this perception of itching and pain is precisely the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) among the three types of sensation (*tri-vedanā*).
"Sensation" (*vedanā*) carries the meaning of reception; that is to say, the consciousnesses of the six sense faculties receive the objects of the six sensory realms. As for the three sensations:
First is the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*). This refers to the experience of oppressive suffering toward objects among the six sense-fields that are contrary to one’s inclinations;
this is called the sensation of suffering. Second is the sensation of pleasure (*sukhā vedanā*). This refers to the experience of gratifying joy toward objects among the six sense-fields;

this is called the sensation of pleasure. Third is the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*). This refers to that which is neither contrary to nor in accordance with the [objects of] the six sensations.

The object is that which is experienced as neither painful nor pleasant; this is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Therefore, it is said that the third is the perception of itching and pain.

The fourth refers to the Four Noble Truths. According to the *Sijiàoyí* (Outline of the Four Teachings), these are explained according to the four truths of arising and ceasing in the Tripitaka Teaching (*Zàngjiào*). The Tripitaka...

"Those" refers to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. "Arising and ceasing" means that these teachings explain the phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which possess both arising and ceasing.

"The Four Truths" (*catvāri satyāni*): *satya* carries the meaning of being examined and real. This refers to the Śrāvakas who, employing the contemplation of analytical emptiness (*vibhava-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), minutely examine the dharmas of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, each one being non-false.

Regarding "phenomena produced by causes and conditions": the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) act as the cause, and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) act as the condition. The organs and objects... [interact].

Regarding the mind that arises, it is called a "phenomenon of birth" (*jāti-dharma*). As for "analytical emptiness" (*vibhāga-śūnyatā*), "analysis" means to dissect; that is, to analyze phenomena such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and realize they are all empty. First is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Suffering" (*duḥkha*) has the meaning of oppression.
There are three types of suffering and eight types of suffering. In brief, these do not go beyond the cycle of birth and death within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Because Śrāvakas thoroughly examine and realize that birth and death are truly suffering, it is called the Truth of Suffering. Second is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). "Origination" (*samudaya*) refers to that which summons [suffering].

The meaning of *samudaya* (the truth of origination) is as follows: it refers to the fact that for a śrāvaka, one thoroughly examines how afflictions, delusions, and karma truly have the power to gather and bring about the suffering of birth and death;
therefore, it is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Third is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): "cessation" means tranquil extinction.

It means that once a śrāvaka has become weary of the suffering of birth and death, they thoroughly examine how nirvāṇa is indeed the bliss of tranquil extinction; therefore, it is called the Truth of Cessation.
The fourth is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). "Path" carries the meaning of that which enables passage.

This refers to the fact that for a *śrāvaka*, the path of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—when scrutinized with precision—is truly capable of leading to *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called the Truth of the Path. Thus, it is said that "four" refers to the Four Truths.
Regarding the fifth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): according to the *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, "aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of a collection or accumulation.
This means that by means of these five factors, sentient beings accumulate and form a body;

furthermore, based on this body, they accumulate conditioned phenomena such as afflictions (*kleśa*), which enable them to undergo immeasurable births and deaths. They are also called the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*).

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring," signifying that they can veil the true nature (*dharmatā*). When *skandha* and *āyatana* (or *rāśi*) are combined, it refers to the accumulation of conditioned existence.
It is because it covers over the true nature. First is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). "Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of material obstruction;

it refers to the combined accumulation of the various faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—and is therefore called the aggregate of form. Second is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

"Sensation" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of experiencing and receiving; it refers to the six consciousnesses corresponding with the six sense objects, resulting in the combined accumulation of the six sensations.
Therefore, it is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). Third is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): "perception" has the meaning of conceptualization.

This refers to the mental consciousness corresponding with the six sense objects, whereby the six perceptions are formed as a harmonious accumulation; therefore, it is called the aggregate of perception. Fourth is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*):
"formations" has the meaning of flux and volitional activity. This refers to the wholesome [actions] performed toward various objects due to the conceptualizations of the six consciousnesses.

One loathes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Because they are a combination and accumulation, they are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). As for the five aggregates of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), "consciousness" has the meaning of "discernment.
This refers to the six types of consciousness—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—with respect to their various objective spheres.
Because it illuminates, discerns, synthesizes, and accumulates, it is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, it is said that "five" refers to the five aggregates.
Regarding the sixth, the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), according to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), "base" (*āyatana*) carries the meaning of "entering.

This means that the six sense organs serve as the supports for the six consciousnesses and are able to enter the six sense objects; therefore, they are called the six bases. The first is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), which refers to the eye.

The sense-faculty (*indriya*) serves as the support for consciousness and is able to enter into form (*rūpa*). Second is the ear-base (*śrotra-āyatana*): that is, the ear-faculty serves as the support for consciousness and is able to enter into sound (*śabda*).
Third is the nose-base (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*): that is, the nose-faculty serves as the support for consciousness and is able to enter into odor (*gandha*).
Fourth is the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*): that is, the tongue-faculty serves as the support for consciousness and is able to enter into taste (*rasa*). Fifth is the body...
"Entry" (āyatana) refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) serving as the basis for consciousness, which is able to enter into contact (*spraṣṭavya*).

The six mental entries (*manāyatana*) refer to the mind-faculty (*manendriya*) discriminating the five sense-objects, which is able to enter into mental phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, it is said that "the six" refers to the six entries.

Regarding the "seven called the seven factors of enlightenment" (*saptabodhyaṅga*): according to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), they are also called the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven limbs of enlightenment.
"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means clear comprehension—that is, discerning whether the dharma being cultivated is authentic or spurious.
"Factors" (*aṅga*) refers to these seven types of dharmas, each having its own distinct branches and boundaries that do not intermingle; thus they are called "factors" and "limbs."

The three awakening factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-vicaya*), joy (*prīti*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) belong to wisdom (*prajñā*). The three awakening factors of energy (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) belong to meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The awakening factor of mindfulness belongs to both meditative absorption and wisdom. By cultivating these seven awakening factors, one enters the Path.

First is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena: "investigation" means discernment; that is, when using the wisdom of intelligence to observe all phenomena, one is well able to distinguish between the true and the false.

It is not erroneous. Because it takes up the dharma of non-falsity, it is called the awakening factor of investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Second is the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
"unmixed" is called *vī* (purity), and "uninterrupted" is called *rya* (progression). This means that when practicing the various path-dharmas, one is well able to discern and understand them.
One does not practice fruitless asceticism, but rather is able to constantly apply the mind with single-minded focus within the true Dharma without interruption;
therefore, it is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Third is the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); "joy" refers to gladness.
This means that when the mind accords with and realizes the true Dharma and attains gladness, one is well able to discern that this joy does not arise from inversion.

Having arisen, one abides in true *dharmaprīti*; therefore, it is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*). Fourth is the factor of enlightenment of exertion (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*);
"exertion" here means cutting off. That is to say, at the time of severing the afflictions of various views, one is well able to discern and eliminate false and deceptive phenomena.

It increases genuine roots of goodness; therefore, it is called the awakening factor of investigation (*pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Fifth is the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Equanimity means relinquishment;
that is, relinquishing the objects of attachment perceived by one's views. One is well able to discern them as false and unreal, never again recollecting them;

therefore, it is called the awakening factor of equanimity. Sixth is the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Concentration refers to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). That is to say, [to] give rise to...
At the time of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is skillfully able to discern all meditative states and does not give rise to afflictions or delusive thoughts;
this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Regarding the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): "mindfulness" refers to recollective thought.
