This means that when practicing the various methods of the Path, one is skillfully able to discern them, constantly ensuring that concentration and wisdom are balanced. If the mind becomes dull or drowsy, one should recollect and apply investigation (*pravicaya*).
The three awakening factors of dharma-discernment, energy, and joy involve the observation of all phenomena to prevent mental dullness.
When the mind becomes agitated, one should employ the awakening factor of investigation to eliminate it; one should employ the awakening factor of equanimity to remove faults of body and speech;
and one should employ the awakening factor of concentration to set aside discursive wisdom, enter right meditative absorption, and collect the scattered mind so that it does not become agitated.
This is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness. Thus it is said that the "seven" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

Regarding the "eight," which refers to the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), according to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), these eight dharmas do not rely on partiality or deviation;
therefore, they are called "Noble" (*ārya*). Furthermore, because they can lead one through to Nirvāṇa, they are called the "Path" (*mārga*). The first is Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), which means:

Cultivating the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to perceive the Four Noble Truths and clearly shatter the various false views of outsiders, such as those concerning existence and non-existence—this is Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Second is Right Thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*): when perceiving the Four Noble Truths, it refers to reflecting with right mindfulness, observing and deliberating so that contemplation may increase—this is Right Thought. Third is Right Speech (*samyagvāc*): namely, by means of the untainted...
Right Speech: By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one constantly restrains verbal karma and remains far removed from all false and unreal speech;

this is Right Speech. Right Action: By means of untainted wisdom, one cultivates and restrains the mind, abiding in pure right action and severing all wrong and deluded conduct; this is Right Action. Right Livelihood: Fifth is Right Livelihood.
This means that those who have left the household life should abandon the five kinds of wrong livelihood for gain and sustenance, and should always sustain their lives by begging for food;
this is called right livelihood. Sixth is right diligence, which refers to the diligent cultivation of the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
To be single-minded and focused without interruption is called right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).

Seventh is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), which refers to the recollection of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), the Noble Path, and the five methods for settling the mind (*pañca-vyupaśama-citta*) that assist the path; these enable one to advance toward Nirvāṇa. This is called right mindfulness. (Regarding the five methods for settling the mind:

for sentient beings with excessive distraction, there is the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*); for those with excessive greed, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); for those with excessive hatred, the meditation on loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*); for those who are deluded...)

The contemplation on sentient beings as causes and conditions (the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha for sentient beings with many obstacles). The eightfold right concentration: that is, gathering all distractions so that body and mind are tranquil.

Abiding correctly in the principle of true emptiness, remaining resolutely immovable—this is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Thus it is said that the eighth [member] is the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

As for the ninth, the "nine abodes of sentient beings" (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*), according to the *Shishi yaolan* (Essentials of the Śākya Clan), these refer to the nine stages (*bhūmi*) within the three realms (*tridhātu*). That is to say:
the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) constitutes one stage of mixed habitation; the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) consists of four stages, divided according to the four dhyānas.
The four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are divided into four stages (*bhūmi*), making nine stages in total. "Stage" (*bhūmi*) carries the meaning of supporting and sustaining;

sentient beings of the nine realms dwell in dependence upon them. From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven downward, as well as the four miserable destinies (*durgati*), all are considered earth-dwellers (*bhūmivāsin*).
From the Yāma Heaven upward, up to the Naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana Heaven, all are considered space-dwellers (*antarīkṣavāsin*). First, the five destinies are mixed together.
Regarding their abode: the five destinies (*gati*) consist of the six classes of gods and humans, hungry ghosts (*preta*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), and hell-beings (*naraka*).
Originally, these comprise the six destinies; however, because the asuras are included within those various destinies, only five are mentioned here. Regarding their mixed habitation:

although the fruits of retribution—the suffering and happiness—of the five destinies differ, they all collectively reside within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Second, the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

The "ground" refers to the first dhyāna heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). This means that the gods of this heaven have already abandoned the desires and unwholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and having attained the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of initial mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), they give rise to joy and bliss. Abiding in this concentration, no sufferings or afflictions can oppress them.

(Regarding *vitarka* and *vicāra*: when the initial mind is directed toward an object, it is called *vitarka*; when the subtle mind discriminates, it is called *vicāra*). The third ground, the "ground of joy and bliss born of concentration," refers to the form realm...
The realm of the Second Dhyāna heavens refers to those deities who have already transcended the *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) of the First Dhyāna.

Having gathered their scattered minds, they abide in a state of meditative concentration that is serene, tranquil, and born of stillness; they dwell in this concentration characterized by the joy and bliss of superior absorption (*samādhi*).

It is like a person emerging from a dark chamber and seeing the sun and moon, their radiance bright, clear, and penetrating. This is the stage of "Sublime Joy and Bliss Free from Rapture" (*prīti-virāga-sukha-bhūmi*).

This refers to the third dhyāna heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). It is said that the beings in this heaven have already abandoned the agitation caused by the exultation of joy found in the second dhyāna heaven.

By concentrating the mind and contemplating with clarity until all movement subsides, they enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and attain a supreme and wondrous bliss. Abiding in this concentration, their delight in the Dharma increases and pervades their entire bodies.
This is the fifth stage, the "Pure Ground of Equanimity and Mindfulness" (*upekṣāsmṛtipariśuddhabhūmi*), which corresponds to the fourth [dhyāna] of the form realm.
The Dhyāna Heavens: This refers to this heaven where one relinquishes the joy of the second dhyāna and the bliss of the third dhyāna.

The mind is free from aversion and attachment; in a single thought-moment it is equanimous, pure, and unmixed. Abiding in this meditative concentration, it is empty, luminous, and tranquil, wherein all phenomena manifest.
The Stage of Infinite Space is the first of the formless heavens; it is so called because the beings of this heaven are weary of...
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), material substance acts as an obstruction, preventing one from attaining mastery;

therefore, by applying effort and practice, one extinguishes all signs of form and enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Abiding in this absorption, the mind becomes luminous and pure, free from obstruction and characterized by mastery.
The stage of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-bhūmi*) is the second heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it is said that the beings of this heaven are weary of...
In the sphere of infinite space, one turns the mind to take consciousness as its object. In association with that consciousness, the mind becomes fixed and immovable;
the consciousnesses of the three periods of time all appear within this meditative concentration. Abiding in this concentration, one is pure and tranquil.

This is the eighth stage, the sphere of nothingness, which is the third heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is said that the beings of this heaven grow weary of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The cycle through the three periods of time is boundless. Abandoning these two states, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Abiding in this absorption, one is serene and tranquil, and no perceptions arise. Ninth is the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is the fourth heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This refers to the gods of that heaven who, weary of the sphere of nothingness as if it were delusion, abandon it.

One enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Abiding in this absorption, one perceives neither the characteristics of existence nor non-existence;

all things vanish into a profound stillness and cessation, pure and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, it is said that the ninth [stage] consists of the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*).

However, these nine realms are all not the state of a noble one (*ārya*); they cannot transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to attain great liberation. This is the aspiration of those who have left the household life for *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is made known that the nine elements (*dhātu*) are the abodes of sentient beings.

The tenth refers to the ten *sarvatragata* (all-pervading) bases, which are the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) meditative absorptions. According to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequence of the Dharma Realm), it says:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) constitute the initial gateway; the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*) constitute the middle;
and the practice that pervades all constitutes the fulfillment. These three types of contemplation fully embody the essence of dhyāna.

Only when they are first accomplished is it called "pervading all places" (*sarvatragata*), a name derived from the fact that the object of contemplation fills [the mind] everywhere. First, blue pervades one [direction].

The "Totality of Blue" (nīla-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi): This refers to within meditative concentration, taking up the blue color seen within the eight spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) and causing it to pervade all places so that everything becomes blue; therefore, it is called the "Totality of Blue.
The nine totalities—yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—are likewise. Hence, they are said to be ten.
The Ten Universal Bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*).
*Vini-zao-xu-chi-shi* (The Vinaya Continuation Commentary), Fascicle Four,
Phonetic Meanings.
Regarding the four *māras*, the Sanskrit term *māra* translates here as "life-taker" (*duōmìng*) or "slayer" (*shāzhě*).
This means they are able to seize the life-force of wisdom and destroy the roots of goodness of those who have left the household life. First is the *skandha-māra* (the demon of the aggregates).

This refers to the accumulation of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which together produce the bitter fruits of birth and death. Because these phenomena of birth and death can seize the life-force of wisdom, it is so called.
The Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). Second, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), which refers to all the delusive afflictions within the three realms.
Because practitioners have their minds and spirits disturbed by these, they are unable to achieve *bodhi*; therefore, it is called the Māra of afflictions.
Third, the death-māra (*mṛtyu-māra*): it refers to the dispersal of the four great elements, premature death, and passing away.

Because practitioners meet with such premature death, they are unable to prolong their "life of wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*); therefore, it is called the death-māra. Fourth, the celestial-māra (*devaputra-māra*):

this māra is the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If a person diligently cultivates supreme goodness and desires to transcend the birth and death of the three realms, yet this heaven...
Māra creates various obstacles and disturbances, preventing practitioners from accomplishing supramundane roots of goodness;
therefore, he is called the "Heavenly Māra" (devaputra-māra).
Regarding the four types of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: First is the ultimate truth of the world (*loka-paramārtha*).

This refers to the teaching of the sublime and excellent meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) with respect to the false phenomena of the five aggregates within the world. Second is the ultimate truth of principle (*yukti-paramārtha*).
This refers to the principle of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as contemplated by the Śrāvakas; this itself is the sublime and excellent meaning.
Third is the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which refers to the śrāvakas’ realization of the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness;
this is the meaning of "excellent" (*parama*). Fourth is the ultimate of the ultimate (*paramārthaparamārtha*), which refers to the principle of the single true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
this is known and realized in its entirety only by the Buddhas, and is thus the most supreme among all ultimate truths.
"Yu" (佑) means to assist the spirits.
"Wo" (沃) has the pronunciation of "wu" (屋); it means fertile.
"Rang" (壤) refers to soft soil that is free of clods.
"Diǎn" (典) means a steward.
"Yuè" (悅) means tax or rent.
"Zhí" (蟄), with the entering tone, means insects hibernating. "Chén" (沈) means to hide away.
The name *Trāyastriṃśa* is a term from the language of the *Tāvatimsa* devas; here it is translated as "Thirty-three. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
Formerly, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan who, together with thirty-two companions, collectively cultivated merit and virtue.
At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru. Kauśika became the Lord of Devas, named Śakra, while the other thirty-two became his ministers.
They served as ministers, residing in a surrounding circle while Śakra alone occupied the center.
"Mute" (*aṃga*) refers to having a mouth but being unable to speak.
The "Ten Virtues of an Elder" appear in the *Fanyi ji* (Collection of Translations). First is "noble lineage," meaning those of high rank and distinguished kinship, as commonly termed in the world.
"1. Families of high rank (*fǎyuè*). The pronunciation of *fǎ* is *fá*. The *Shiji* states: 'To clarify their status is called *fǎ*; to accumulate their merits is called *yuè*. 2. High positions:
this refers to those who occupy the offices of ministers, prime ministers, or imperial tutors, serving as the heads of the hundred officials. 3. Great wealth:
this refers to an abundance of treasures and goods, with all necessities fully provided. 4. Dignity and virtue: this refers to a gravity and majesty that is profound and imposing."
He is one whom people revere. Fifth is profound wisdom (*pañca-jñāna-gambhīratā*): this means his intelligence and deliberation are far-reaching, transcending the ordinary and excelling the masses;

whatever he plans is always appropriate. Sixth is venerable age (*ṣaḍ-varṣa-vṛddhatā*): this means his years are advanced and his reputation is weighty; he serves as a model for all beings and is honored and looked up to by others.
Seventh is purity of conduct: this means upholding the precepts, restraining oneself, being frugal, impartial, and pure, acting exactly as one speaks, and remaining entirely free from blemish.
Eighth is the perfection of etiquette: this means possessing dignified and orderly deportment that serves as a model for the world to gaze upon. Ninth is receiving praise from superiors.
This means that his talent and virtue are both complete, and his words and deeds serve as a model for others; thus he is one whom those above him delight in, praise, and admire.
"Ten below take refuge" means that he dwells in humility and governs the multitude with broad-mindedness; thus he is one toward whom those below look up and turn in devotion.
*Pī* (坯) means unbaked clay tiles. *Yīng* (嬰) means to be bound.
Regarding the five desires, the first is the desire for wealth, which refers to all worldly material resources; that is to say, people [use] wealth and goods...
For the sake of providing the means to sustain oneself, one gives rise to greedy seeking and attachment, refusing to let go.

Second is the desire for form (*rūpa-rāga*), which refers to the forms of the world such as blue, yellow, red, white, male, female, and so forth; it means that people find pleasure in these forms and their minds are satisfied by them.
Therefore, one gives rise to craving and attachment, unable to transcend the three realms. Third, the desire for food and drink refers to the various flavors of worldly delicacies;
it means that humans must rely on food and drink to sustain their lives, and thus they give rise to craving and become attached to them without satiety.
Fourth is the desire for fame; "name" refers to worldly reputation and renown. This means that humans—
Because one’s reputation and fame can manifest one’s personal glory, one gives rise to greedy seeking and attachment, not knowing when to stop.
Fifth is the desire for sleep: this refers to the state of sleep wherein the mental consciousness is clouded and obscured. It is said that human sleep also has its proper seasons;
if one is indolent and unrestrained, delighting in it without satiety, this is called the desire for sleep.
The "three destructions" refer to the destruction of precepts, views, and dignified deportment.
"Xièmàn" (媟嫚) has the first character pronounced *xiè* and the second *màn*; it means to defile.
The "two deaths" refer to the two kinds of birth and death: fragmentation and transformation.
Regarding "Tying with Grass": Once, there was a bhikṣu who encountered a band of thieves while traveling on a road. The thieves seized his belongings and were returning home;
fearing that the bhikṣu might reveal their location, they intended to kill him. Among the thieves was one who understood the dharma of the bhikṣus.
He immediately led the bhikṣu to a patch of living grass and tied his dharma-robe to it with the grass. The bhikṣu, observing the precepts, would rather die of hunger than violate them.
This is a story about a goose and a pearl. Long ago, there was a bhikṣu who, while begging for alms, came to the house of a pearl-maker. The pearl-maker was a person of deep faith;
he immediately rose to take food and gave it to the bhikṣu. However, a red pearl fell to the ground. The family kept a goose, and when the goose saw it—
The red pearl was immediately swallowed into his belly. Later, when the pearl-maker brought food, he could not see the pearl;
suspecting that the bhikṣu had stolen it, he demanded its return. The bhikṣu said, "I have not taken your pearl. He became enraged and beat the bhikṣu so severely that he was on the verge of death.
Because this bhikṣu guarded the precepts, he would rather die than speak of the goose having swallowed it, fearing that he might cause harm to a living being. He...
The jeweler was filled with extreme rage. A goose was swimming ahead of him; the jeweler struck it dead with one foot.
When the bhikṣu saw that the goose was dead, he said, "This jewel was swallowed by this goose. The jeweler cut open the goose and recovered the jewel. He then sought repentance, his faith increasing.
The seven types of conditioned merit are: first, the construction of Buddhist stūpas, monastic quarters, halls, and pavilions;
second, the provision of gardens, fruit trees, bathing pools, and cool groves; third, the constant distribution of medicine to cure and relieve various ailments;
fourth, the making of sturdy boats to ferry people across; fifth, the establishing of bridges to assist the weak and infirm in crossing over; sixth, [the proximity to...]
To construct wells so that those suffering from thirst may drink; and to construct latrines and provide facilities for the convenience of defecation—these are the seven acts of giving.
By virtue of receiving the karmic reward for these deeds, one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven after this life.
Raw leather is called *ge* (革); processed leather is called *wei* (韋). These refer to leather footwear.
*Lou* (瘻) is pronounced like *lü* (閭); it refers to a hunched back.
*Qin* (寢) means to lie down and sleep.
"Jing" (景) means "great.
"Shi" (適) has the pronunciation "di" (的) and means "exclusive focus.
There are twelve classes of sentient beings; the first is oviparous, namely those such as fish, birds, turtles, and snakes. The second is viviparous.
1. Those born from human wombs include humans, animals, dragons, and immortals. 2. Those born from moisture include insects and crawling creatures. 3.
Those born by transformation include metamorphic beings and flying spirits. 4. Those with form include those possessing auspicious or ominous spiritual clarity.
5. Those without form include those who are ethereal, dispersed, or dissolved. 6. Those with perception include spirits...
1. Ghosts, spirits, and similar beings; 2. The eight classes of non-percipient beings, whose spirits are transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone;

3. Those without form, such as the *vampira* (water-jelly) that uses a shrimp for its eyes—meaning that the water-jelly itself lacks its own inherent form and characteristics, and is thus said to be "without form," taking foam for its body and the shrimp for its eyes.

It is for the sake of the eye; therefore, it is said that they "accomplish" form. The ten [types] are not formless; they are the class of those produced through incantations and *yāna* (malevolent rites).
Incantation is simply summoning. *Yāna* is prayer. It is like a frog which attaches its body to an egg, whereupon it grows and develops;
were it not for the sound, it would perish. It is also like the peacock: when the female hears the cry of the male, she immediately becomes pregnant.
They give birth to chicks. These types of beings arise through the power of incantations and prayers. Eleventh is "non-identical with thought" (*na saṃjñin*):

this refers to categories such as the *pulu* (the *gongling*, or mud dauber wasp), which achieve their form through the transformation of different substances. The *pulu* is the *gongling* wasp; it takes a green insect to serve as its own offspring.
Since the green insect is not of the same category as the *pulu*, it is said to be "non-identical with thought," yet it is nonetheless able to be transformed [into the wasp].

Because they take their own offspring as their children, this constitutes the perception [of self]. The twelve non-perceptions include such beings as the *tuccha-kāka* (the "empty-crow"), which incubates a clod of earth to produce young, and the *bimba-pakṣin* (the "mirror-bird"), which incubates the fruit of a poisonous tree to produce its offspring; in these cases, the offspring eventually devour their parents.
Such are the various types [of beings] encountered.
"Extreme sound" (*jù yīn jí*) means "increasing," "excessive," or "playful.

Regarding the three types of suffering, the first is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). This refers to the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) with outflows (*sāsrava*); because its nature is constantly oppressive, it is called suffering.
Furthermore, it is associated with painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*); thus, suffering upon suffering is called "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Second is the "suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), which means that when the aspect of pleasure (*sukha-lakṣaṇa*) disintegrates, the aspect of suffering immediately arises; this refers to the fact that when pleasure reaches its peak, sorrow is born.

Third is the "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that constantly undergo the flux of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) and are never at rest.
It means peace and security.

The eight sufferings are: birth, aging, illness, death, separation from what one loves, encountering what one hates, failing to obtain what one seeks, and the intense burning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). These are the eight.
"Dàn" (澹然) refers to an appearance of tranquility and non-action (*wuwei*).
"Eight Liberations" (*bā bèishè*): "bèi" (背) means to turn away from; "shě" (捨) means to abandon. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Because one turns away from these pure five desires and abandons this mind of attachment, they are called 'liberations' (*bèishè*). By cultivating this contemplation, one gives rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state."
Through wisdom, one exhausts all afflictions of view and thought within the three realms and realizes the fruit of Arhatship.

The objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch in the desire realm are called the five coarse and debased sensual desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); the forms and other objects in the form and formless realms are called the five pure sensual desires.

First, there is the internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms. This means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as putrid, impure, and not to be desired;
with a mind settled in meditative concentration, they further imagine the skin and flesh falling away.
One merely sees white bones emitting light of eight colors. As for these lights of eight colors: one sees the color of earth as a pure ground, yellowish-white;
one sees the color of water as the clear, limpid water within a deep pool; one sees the color of fire as a pure fire from clean fuel and incense smoke;
one sees the color of wind as a dustless, clear breeze; and one sees the color blue as refined gold.
He sees yellow forms like *campaka* flowers; he sees red forms like the dawn clouds of spring; he sees white forms like jade or snow.

Therefore, it is said that "internally there are forms. Furthermore, because the greed of the desire realm is difficult to sever, even though one has already contemplated the impurity of internal forms, one must further employ the contemplation of impurity regarding the forms of others to bring [this realization] about.

One gives rise to revulsion in order to seek its abandonment; therefore, it is called "externally contemplating forms. This first liberation (*vimokṣa*) is situated in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the First Dhyāna Heaven.
Second is "internally having no perception of form, externally contemplating forms," which refers to the practitioner entering the Second Dhyāna.
Having already extinguished the internal perception of form within one’s own body, it is said that "internally there is no perception of form.
Furthermore, because the greed of the desire realm is difficult to sever, one continues to contemplate the signs of external impurity to engender revulsion and thereby seek its abandonment;

thus it is further said that "one contemplates forms externally. This is the second liberation (*vimokṣa*), which resides in the meditative concentration of the second *dhyāna* heaven. Third, the pure [liberations].
The "purified liberation" (*śubha-vimokṣa*) refers to the realization through direct experience of purity; that is, taking the aspect of purity as its object.

This means that after the practitioner has practiced the second liberation, they eliminate the impure aspects of external forms and instead train within meditative concentration upon the eight types of radiant light.
These are pure and brilliant, like the color of exquisite jewels; therefore, it is called the "purified liberation. Once the mind is thus clarified...
Purity increases gradually, pervading the entire body, such that it is entirely filled with joy; therefore, it is said that "one realizes it within the body. This is the third liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Its stage is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the third dhyāna heaven. Regarding the fourth liberation, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*):
this refers to when the practitioner, having subsequently discarded the impure form of their own body in the desire realm, [attains] the first liberation... [and so on].

Furthermore, having discarded the color of the white bones within one's own body after the second liberation (*dhyāna-vimokṣa*), and having further discarded all impure colors of the external body, there remain eight kinds of pure colors that abide dependent upon the mind. If the mind relinquishes form, form then ceases and perishes.
When the single mind takes emptiness as its object and accords with emptiness, it enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Because it is fixed upon the sphere [of infinite space], it is called the "liberation of the sphere of infinite space. This is the fourth liberation;
its stage is the meditative concentration of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. Regarding the "liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness":

when a practitioner relinquishes the sphere of space and enters concentration by single-mindedly taking consciousness as an object, they then contemplate this concentration, observing that, based on the five aggregates and so forth, all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Because it is false and unreal, the mind gives rise to revulsion and turns away from it, rather than accepting or clinging to it; therefore, it is called the "liberation by way of turning away from the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Sixth is the liberation by way of turning away from the sphere of nothingness. This means that if a practitioner relinquishes the sphere of infinite consciousness and focuses the mind single-mindedly on the sphere of nothingness, at the moment of entering meditative absorption, they contemplate this very concentration as being entirely impermanent, suffering, and empty, based upon the five aggregates and so forth.
It is selfless, illusory, and unreal. One gives rise to a mind of revulsion toward it and does not accept or cling to it;
therefore, it is called the "equanimity of the sphere of nothingness. Seventh is the "equanimity of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This means that if a practitioner relinquishes the sphere of nothingness and, with single-minded focus, takes as their object the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they then contemplate this upon entering meditative absorption.
In concentration, one relies on the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, realizing that they are entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and are false and unreal.

One gives rise to revulsion toward them and does not accept or cling to them; therefore, it is called the "liberation through the neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanavimokṣa*).

Eighth is the "liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception" (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhavimokṣa*). "Sensation" (*vedanā*) refers to experiencing, and "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to conceptualization; these are the two [aggregates] among the five aggregates.

It is the mind. This means that the practitioner, weary of this mental distraction and desiring to enter meditative absorption for rest, turns his back upon and extinguishes all mental states of sensation and perception;
this is called the "liberation through turning away from sensation and perception" (nirodhasamāpatti).
The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) refer to the state following the cultivation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).

When the contemplative mind has become thoroughly matured and one possesses mastery over its transformations, one can, at will, overcome objects whether they be pure or impure. The first two bases of mastery are situated in the first dhyāna;
the third and fourth bases of mastery are situated in the second dhyāna; and the fifth through the eighth bases of mastery are situated in the fourth [dhyāna].

Regarding the Dhyānas: as for why the "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana) are not established in the third dhyāna, it is because the bliss of the third dhyāna heavens is so abundant that the mind is entirely absorbed by it;

therefore, they are not established there. First: having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
This means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as decaying, impure, and unattractive.
Joyfully, with a mind settled in one-pointed concentration, he further visualizes the skin and flesh falling away, seeing only white bones emitting an eight-colored radiance;

thus it is said that "internally there is the perception of form. Furthermore, because the path of contemplation has not yet increased, if he were to contemplate many forms, he might find it difficult to maintain focus;
therefore, he contemplates few forms. For this reason, he contemplates his own body as impure, and likewise contemplates those who are dear to him.
The human body is likewise impure; therefore, it is said that one externally contemplates forms as being few. Regarding "whether beautiful or ugly," this refers to contemplating external forms:
those resulting from wholesome karma and wholesome fruits are called beautiful, while those resulting from unwholesome karma and unwholesome fruits are called ugly.
Alternatively, at times one fixes the mind on a single point and contemplates the forms within the desire realm that can give rise to craving; these pure forms are what are called beautiful.
That which gives rise to aversion is called "ugly" impure form. "Superior knowledge and superior vision" refers to the maturity of contemplation of the mind:
such that toward beautiful forms the mind feels no craving, and toward ugly forms the mind feels no aversion.
Second, having the perception of internal forms, one externally perceives many forms—whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge."
"Superior Vision" means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as decaying, impure, and not to be desired.
With a mind settled in one-pointed concentration, they further imagine the skin and flesh falling away, seeing only white bones emitting light of eight colors;
therefore, it is said that "internally there is the perception of form. Having thus contemplated the internal body until the perception of form is matured, one then contemplates the external.

Although forms are many, there is no obstruction. That is to say, when one contemplates a single corpse, and proceeds to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a million corpses—if one contemplates the single stage of bloating, one sees all of them bloated;
this remains the same up to the stages of putrefaction, lividity, and flaying. Therefore, it is said that one externally contemplates many forms, whether beautiful or ugly, and they are superior.

The superior knowledge and superior vision are as described above. Third, being internally without the perception of form, one externally perceives forms that are few—whether beautiful or ugly—with superior knowledge and superior vision.
This means that once the practitioner has entered the second dhyāna, the internal mental perception of form is extinguished; hence it is said, "internally without the perception of form.

Furthermore, because the path of contemplation has not yet increased, if one were to contemplate many forms, there would be a fear that they could not be maintained with ease; therefore, one contemplates [only a few].
A small amount of form. Thus, one contemplates one’s own body as impure and likewise contemplates the bodies of those one loves as impure;
therefore, it is said that one externally contemplates a small amount of form. Whether beautiful or ugly, one knows and sees them clearly as described above. Fourth:

being internally without the perception of form, one externally contemplates a large amount of form, whether beautiful or ugly, knowing and seeing it clearly as described above. This refers to the practitioner.
Having entered the second dhyāna, one extinguishes the perception of internal bodily form; hence it is said, "internally there is no perception of form.

When observing the internal body, since the perception of form is absent, even though external forms are numerous, they present no obstruction. The remainder is the same as above; there is no difference between these two [stages].
This is because practitioners find the afflictions of the desire realm difficult to overcome, and therefore they practice again within the second dhyāna.

The third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) extinguish the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) without remainder and cause the path of observation to progress, becoming firm and unshakable;
thus, one's skillful effort becomes increasingly superior. Regarding the fifth sphere of mastery, the blue:

this refers to the practitioner observing a brilliant blue color, which is superior to the [first] liberation (*vimokṣa*). It is the blue appearance perceived within the luminosity of the eight colors, which—[unlike the previous stage]—is not...

Because one gives rise to attachment to the phenomena [of the object], it is called a "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana). The sixth is the sphere of mastery of yellow: this refers to the practitioner contemplating a shining yellow color;
compared to the "deliverances" (vimokṣa), even the yellow sign seen within the radiant light of the eight forms does not give rise to attachment to the phenomena.

Therefore, they are called "Abhibhvāyatanas" (Spheres of Mastery). The seventh, the "Red Abhibhvāyatana," and the eighth, the "White Abhibhvāyatana," are explained as above in the section on the Blue and Yellow Abhibhvāyatanas.
*Tánwúdé bù sìfēn lǜ shānbǔ suíjí jiémó*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Chongyi Monastery in the Capital of Tang;
continued and annotated by the junior monk Duti of Huashan in Jinling.
Section Three, Part Two: The Method for Receiving the Various Precepts.

○ Regarding the Dharma for Receiving the Precepts of a Bhikṣu, the Buddha said: "The 'Welcome, Bhikṣu' [ordination]; the 'Destroyer of Fetters' (Saṃyojanavisaṃyoga) bhikṣu; the 'Three-Word' (Trivācika) bhikṣu;

the bhikṣu receiving precepts from five persons who uphold the Vinaya in border regions; and the fifth, the bhikṣu receiving precepts from ten persons in the Central Kingdom. These are the five listed above.

Regarding the *Upasampadā* (ordination) through the three words of "Welcome" (*ehi-bhikṣu*), these are restricted exclusively to the period when the Buddha was present in the world; the other three methods of ordination apply to the period after his parinirvāṇa.
Commentary: Regarding the "Welcome Bhikṣu," according to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra*, when the Buddha first traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī...
At the Deer Park, for the sake of the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he turned the Wheel of Dharma three times.
Kauṇḍinya and the others saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and deeply understood the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Having performed the proper rites, they paid homage to the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will allow us to go forth and practice the holy life. The World-Honored One replied: "Welcome, Bhikṣus! I permit you to follow me."

"Within the Dharma, one cultivates the holy life and reaches the end of suffering. As soon as these words were spoken by the World-Honored One, Kauṇḍinya immediately attained the going forth and received full ordination.
The Brahmin robes he was wearing fell away, along with his beard and hair;
the dharma-robes of a śramaṇa appeared naturally upon his body, and his deportment became dignified and orderly as he held [the alms bowl] in his hand.
The bhikṣus—such as those who had studied the Dharma for twenty years, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty in all—were all of noble birth and great wealth.

Originally followers of external paths, when the time came to receive the Buddha’s teaching after his appearance in the world, they all came to the Buddha, desiring to seek ordination. The last among them was named Subhadra. All such persons as these were together...
"Welcome, Bhikṣu. The fruits attained by such individuals are all untainted (*anāsrava*). As for those in their final existence (*caramabhavika*), why is this?
It is because it is spoken from the Buddha’s own divine mouth; it cannot be obtained from other persons.

A Bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is also called one who "receives full ordination through the superior [method]. According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is like a certain person who, having exhausted...
A certain bhikṣu who had not yet reached twenty years of age received full ordination. He then developed doubts regarding the status of the bhikṣu-dharma.
A fellow resident bhikṣu, perceiving that he had developed such doubts, went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣu whose outflows were exhausted.
"Do you count the years spent in the womb, including the intercalary months, as being complete? He replied, "They are not complete.
The Buddha then asked the bhikṣus, "Has this bhikṣu attained arhatship? The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, "He has attained arhatship.
The Buddha said, "This is the highest form of full ordination (upasaṃpadā). To explain clearly: 'breaking the fetters'—the fetters refer to..."

Bondage: Through objects, cognition is aroused; through the faculties, seeing occurs. When the faculties and their objects confront one another, craving and attachment arise as bondage, binding one to the cycle of birth and death within the three realms so that liberation cannot be attained.
"Latent tendencies" refers to the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). These afflictions are divided into five sharp and five dull types.
The five sharp ones are: first, the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which means that sentient beings falsely calculate the phenomena of the five aggregates to be...

First is the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Second is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which refers to grasping at either the extreme of annihilation or the extreme of permanence within the view of a self-entity.
Third is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which refers to apprehending principles with a distorted mind, denying cause and effect, and severing all roots of virtue.
Fourth is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This refers to falsely calculating that which is not truly superior to be *nirvāṇa*, thereby giving rise to attachment in the mind;
because one generates the notion of correctness within false views. Fifth is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

This refers to various non-Buddhists who falsely calculate what is not a true precept to be a precept—such as observing the "precepts" of cows or dogs—and regarding them as genuine precepts, taking them up for further cultivation. This...

The five kinds of delusive afflictions arise as soon as a thought stirs; because they are constantly present even in moments of haste, they are called the "driving forces" (*nīvaraṇa*). As for the five dull afflictions:
first is greed (*rāga*), which refers to being attached to the five worldly desires, indulging the mind and emotions, and seeking them out without satiety.
Second is anger (*pratigha*), which refers to giving rise to various forms of malice, resentment, and fury toward adverse objects, thereby disturbing oneself and others.
Therefore, there are three types of delusion (*moha*): namely, the mind being confused regarding its objects, such that one cannot clearly comprehend all phenomena.
Fourth is pride (*māna*), which means relying on one's own lineage, wealth, nobility, virtue, or talent to look down upon others.
Fifth is doubt (*vicikitsā*), which means the mind being confused and contrary to reason, such that one wavers and hesitates regarding all phenomena, failing to attain penetration. These five types—

Delusion arises from the prior five [afflictions] through inference; they are called "dull" in contrast to the "sharp. These ten are collectively termed *anuśaya* (latent proclivities), as *anuśaya* signifies the sense of driving and enjoining.
Because they can drive and enjoin the mental faculties of sentient beings, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms, they are all given the name *anuśaya*.
Based on the three realms, these are expanded into eighty-eight *anuśayas*, categorized according to the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Regarding this: it is said that under the category of Suffering (duḥkha), all [factors] are present, totaling thirty. Under each of Origination (samudaya) and Cessation (nirodha), three are excluded—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the adherence to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—leaving seven for each, totaling forty-two. When combined with the preceding thirty under Suffering, there are seventy-two in total.

The Path eliminates two views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Each of these consists of eight types, totaling twenty-four; when combined with the previous [sixty-two], they amount to ninety-six.
In the higher realms, anger (*vyāpāda*) does not operate; furthermore, in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the eight afflictions of anger are eliminated.

There are eighty-eight *anuśayas* (proclivities) in total. If one exhaustively eradicates these eighty-eight categories of *darśana-heya-kleśa* (defilements to be abandoned by vision) within the three realms, one immediately attains the first fruit, *srotāpanna*.

In the language of China, this is called "entering the stream" (*rùliú*) or "participating in the stream" (*yùliú*), meaning that this person has entered the flow of the Dharma of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Furthermore, within the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms, each stage contains nine grades of subtle thoughts.
Regarding the delusions of the desire realm: those of the highest degree (adhimātra-adhimātra) must be abandoned through two births;

those of the highest-middle and highest-lowest degrees together require two births to be abandoned—meaning either individually or both together. Among these two, those of the middle-high degree must be abandoned through one birth;
those of the middle-middle and middle-lowest degrees together require one birth to be abandoned—meaning either individually or both together. If one abandons this...
When the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exhausted, one immediately attains the second fruit, the *Sakṛdāgāmin*—which in the language of China means "Once-returner.
This refers to a person who, among the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, has completely severed the first six grades, while the remaining three grades still persist.
One must return once more to the desire realm to undergo one further birth. The lower-upper grade [of afflictions] requires half a lifetime to sever;
the lower-middle and lower-lower grades together require half a lifetime to sever—meaning that the former is severed alone, while the latter is severed in common with the former.
If these three lower grades of the desire realm's delusions of volition (*cetanā*) are completely severed, one immediately attains the third fruit, *Anāgāmin* (in Chinese, "Non-returner").
This means that this person has severed the final three grades of the desire realm and will no longer return to be born in the desire realm.

In the two higher realms combined, there are eighty-four grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation; if these are completely severed, one attains the fourth fruit, Arhatship—the Chinese term for which is *wuxue* (no-more-learning).
This means that this person has severed all afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms. [The four knowledges...]

He has already perfected [the path], has already transcended the three realms, and has already realized *nirvāṇa*; there is no further dharma to be learned. This is spoken in terms of gradual abandonment.
If, however, one possesses sharp faculties, then the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the three realms are abandoned all at once;

such a person does not require seven births returning through the desire realm. Therefore, they are called a "bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters" (*kṣīṇasaṃyojana*). As for the "bhikṣu by the three words": regarding—
The section on the "Formation of the Dharma through Conditions" within the *Duishou Jie-mo* (Face-to-Face Karmavācanā) has already clarified this.

Regarding the requirement of five monks who uphold the Vinaya for ordination in border regions: according to the *Carma-vastu* (Section on Leather), the Venerable Mahākātyāyana resided in the country of Aparantaka.
There was a man named Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa; after he had received the upāsaka precepts, he later requested ordination and the full admission (*upasampadā*).
In this country, there were few bhikṣus, making it difficult for the quorum of the Saṃgha to be reached;
it took two years to obtain one. Later, he reported this circumstance to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, I permit five persons in a border region to receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

In the central lands, ten persons shall receive the precepts. As for the "bhikṣu who receives the precepts," this refers to the method of bestowing them described below. However, regarding the five [categories] listed above...

The various methods of full ordination (*upasampadā*) are all consistent with the authentic texts of the various schools. Among them, the "Come Hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) ordination is that which was summoned by the Buddha’s divine voice;

the "Threefold Declaration" (*tri-avavāda*) was for the sake of those first sent forth to teach. These two are restricted exclusively to the period when the Buddha was in the world. The remaining three, however, apply both during the Buddha’s lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa.
The reason for listing all five types here is to ensure that one understands their origins and developments, even though they share the same name of "receiving [ordination]."
Because they are distinct.
○ Regarding the conditions for bestowing the *bhikṣu* precepts:

the precepts are the vessel for crossing the ocean of birth and death and the root of the True Dharma; they must necessarily depend upon the gathering of conditions. Should there be any discrepancy in their correspondence, even if...
It cannot be conferred. Now, I shall explain the two kinds of *karmavācanā*. It is only when five conditions are fully met that it is accomplished. Commentary:
This text is about to set forth the method for conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*).

First, it demonstrates that the virtue of the precepts is inconceivable and its merit surpasses all other practices, so as to cause one to understand the convergence of conditions and to carefully discern what constitutes a failure or a success. Regarding the statement, "The precepts are the vessel and rudder for crossing saṃsāra": this is because...
All sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms, their cycle of birth and death never ceasing; this is called sinking into the sea of suffering.
If one upholds the complete precepts and cultivates diligently in accordance with them, one can realize nirvana; this is called reaching the other shore. Therefore.
The Verses of the Extensive Vinaya state: "Just as a person crossing a river uses their hands and a float;

though the water be deep, they have no fear of sinking and can reach the further shore. Likewise, the disciples of the Buddha who practice the foundation of the prohibitive precepts will never turn back toward the flow of the heterodox or sink into the ocean of birth and death. Therefore, it is said that the precepts are..."

It is the vessel for crossing over birth and death. Regarding the root of the True Dharma: this refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when the final age has arrived and the Great Way is about to vanish, and the subtle words are on the verge of being lost.
At such a juncture, it is only the precepts that can provide support and maintenance, sustaining the life of wisdom.
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* states: "O bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should honor, treasure, and respect the *Prātimokṣa*..."
Prātimokṣa. This is your Great Teacher; it is no different from my remaining in the world. Therefore, it is said that the precepts are the root of the True Dharma.
Regarding the necessity of the convergence of conditions and their correspondence: even if one has received them, they are not truly obtained if there is a violation.

This means that the three "likewise" (trīṇi tathā) must be present when approaching the altar, and the seven "nots" (sapta na) must be strictly avoided during the bestowal and reception. These are the two types of *karmavācanā*.

"Regarding this: 'The formal ritual for bestowing full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the two divisions of the Dharma is established only when five conditions are complete'—this sentence serves as a general heading, which will be explained in detail in the following text."
First, regarding the person who is capable of receiving [the precepts], there are five types. First, because it is the human realm; as the Vinaya states:
"Heavenly beings, asuras, non-humans, and animals cannot obtain the precepts. As the Śāstra states: "The Three Refuges and Five Precepts exist only among humans;
they do not exist in other realms."
Exegesis: Regarding the first phrase, among the five conditions, one is specifically designated to clarify that there are five types of persons capable of receiving [the precepts].
First, among the sentient beings of the six realms, only those in the human realm are capable of receiving them—namely, by receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) and entering the Saṃgha;

by giving rise to faith through seeing and hearing; by serving as a field of merit for the world; and by transforming and benefiting others to inspire joy. Even if they lack noble lineage, they do not [fail] because of it.

This is born of parental affection; it differs from the norms of human relations and gives rise to worldly suspicion and fear. It is difficult to sustain the propagation of the Way and offers no benefit to the Dharma-gate;

therefore, I cite the Vinaya and Śāstras to provide proof. According to the treatises, if devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits receive the precepts of the five groups [of monastics], they may not receive the full major or minor precepts, yet all are permitted to receive the Three Refuges. Now, regarding the statement that "the Three Refuges and Five Precepts [apply to] the remainder..."

Regarding those who lack the Way, the fivefold monastic community returns to the precepts to restrain them. From the perspective of the Śrāvaka vehicle, these are the Saṃgha-ratna abiding in the world.
If it concerns Mahāyāna precepts, however, the fundamental doctrine differs once again; they do not fall under this same category.
Second, they must be complete in their sense faculties. The Vinaya states: those who are insane, deaf, or mute; those with incomplete physical characteristics;
and those subject to the "one hundred obstacles" and so forth—all such persons are incapable of bringing disgrace upon the Sangha, and therefore [are not qualified].
**Commentary:** "Those whose faculties are complete" means that their human characteristics are not deficient and the six [senses] are without impairment.

The previous statement that "only humans may receive [the precepts]" was made in contrast to other realms; this, however, refers to the fact that even among humans there are still those subject to prohibitions and obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), and thus they must be carefully examined.
For a jade stone with flaws is not a fine gem, and timber like the *chū* tree is unfit for a great pillar; therefore, the Vinaya is cited as proof.
The insane cannot discern gain or loss within their own minds; the deaf listen to the instructions before their teacher but do not know how to uphold or proclaim them;

the mute, though clear-minded, find it difficult to speak what they have received and understood; and those with physical defects or those subject to the hundred obstacles lack the requisite conditions.

The origins of this rule are explained in detail in the *Pravrajyāvastu* (Section on Ordination). Because it was subject to worldly censure and brought disgrace upon the monastic community, it was established as a definitive prohibition.
This remains observed to this day by all who receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Even if one can generate the most sublime resolve, such a mind can only be integrated within the Mahāyāna precepts; it is not permitted to be mixed with the Bhikṣu precepts.

The vessel of the three bodies is purified. Regarding the term *sarvadharmāḥ*: if one has previously received the five precepts or the eight precepts and has violated a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), one cannot receive the ten precepts again.
The Vinaya states: "If one who has previously received the precepts violates a grave precept and returns to receive them again, this is called the obstacle of the 'extreme offense' (*antya-avadya*).
Furthermore, if a layperson or a *śrāmaṇera* commits various grave deeds, these are all subsumed under the thirteen obstacles (*trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharma*).
Therefore, regarding the "body as a vessel": one takes the physical body born of parents as a Dharma-vessel for carrying the Way;
that is to say, the pure and wondrous precepts must be received only by those who have purified their body and mind. If it is a vessel that is broken and defiled, [it cannot hold them].
It cannot be contained. Since the preceding selection concerned external characteristics (*bāhya-lakṣaṇa*), this [section] simplifies the internal vessel;

thus, it first cites the *Śāstra* to clarify that violating the various precepts destroys the root. Once the multi-storied tower is barred from ascent, it next cites the *Vinaya* to clarify that violating the gravity of a bhikṣu’s nature makes the fundamental essence difficult to restore.
Furthermore, this includes the various grave offenses committed during one's time as a layperson (*avadātavasana*) or as a śrāmaṇera.

Regarding the karma that renders one ineligible for acceptance, this encompasses all thirteen grave obstacles (*trayodaśa-garuka-āpatti*), such as those strictly interrogated in two instances within the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Fourth, the complete observance of the characteristics of a renunciant: the Vinaya states that one should shave the hair and don the *kāṣāya* robe, being identical to other renunciants. If...
Wearing secular clothing, the robes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), various ornaments, or being naked, one is not said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Explanation: One who possesses the characteristics of a renunciant (*pravrajita*) is distinguished from those of the secular world. If the distinction between the monastic and the lay were not maintained, the Way of the Dharma would perish.
Therefore, citing the Vinaya regulations, it says: although one first leaves home and then seeks to receive full ordination, it is essential that one first undergoes the shaving of the hair.

The beard and hair [should be shaven], and the body should be clad in the *kāṣāya*, identical to those who have long left the household life to practice the *brahmacarya*; there must be no difference.
This is called "destroying the beauty of one's form," for one should wear the dharma-robes. As for wearing secular clothing:

in the Western Regions (India), householders all use white woolen cloth to cover the shoulders, wrap around the neck, and descend around the body. Regarding the clothing of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it refers to soft grass or tree [bark].

Regarding robes made from leaves, bird feathers, animal fur, skins, and the like, as well as various ornaments—namely, earrings, bracelets, necklaces, armlets, and so forth—it is said that the men and women of that country adorn themselves with these.
As for those who go naked, it means they are bare-bodied and lack any clothing to cover them. The Buddha declared: "People such as these are not said to have received full ordination. This also...
Because the world censured and rebuked this, it was prohibited and not permitted.

Fifth, obtaining only a partial portion of the Dharma: the Vinaya states that if one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) without having first received the *śrāmaṇera* precepts, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
Explanation: This refers to the recipient [of the precepts]. Because they receive them with utmost sincerity and without doubt, the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is accomplished.

If the regulations are violated or the proper order is disregarded, the fault and responsibility lie with the preceptor (*ācārya*). According to the Vinaya, all ten monks involved commit the offense of *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline).

The second [category] consists of seven objects of correspondence. First is the accomplishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). This is because if the boundary is not established, the ritual action (*karmavācanā*) lacks a basis.
[Commentary: The above merely clarified the person who receives [the precepts]; here, it clarifies that there are seven objects of correspondence, which further include internal [factors].
Third: First, it means that the *sīmā* (boundary) serves as the basis (*āśraya*), and all monastic legal procedures (*saṃghadharma*) serve as that which depends upon it (*āśrita*).
If the basis is not established, then all that depends upon it will likewise not be established. As the Vinaya states:

"If there are members of the assembly within the great boundary who do not agree, they are permitted to separately establish a small boundary outside the [great] boundary to confer the precepts, so that the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) may be effective."
Because it relies [upon the Sangha]:

secondly, there must be those capable of presiding over the ritual; for the Sangha performs the formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) according to the noble teaching, whereas those who are not in accordance with the Dharma are unfit to preside.
Explanation: This refers to the *upasampadā* *karmavācanā*, which is the Dharma King’s own pronouncement establishing the method for achieving goodness. It is required...
First, regarding the observance of the precepts: only one who knows the Dharma is capable of presiding over and proclaiming [the rites].

Even if one is familiar with the *karmavācanā*, if one is not personally pure, it is difficult to permit the formal announcement (*jñapti*). This is like proclaiming the edict of a Son of Heaven—how could one employ a minister who possesses transgressions?
The "three" in the phrase "the number of monks is complete" does not mean that the headcount must reach ten. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"The preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the two instructors (*ācārya*) must all be in accordance with the Dharma; the seven monks who serve as witnesses must all be pure and clearly knowledgeable. The Vinaya says:

"If there is no preceptor, or if the assembly of ten is incomplete, then according to what is explained regarding those cases where the required number is not met, [the ordination] is not accomplished."

Therefore, this passage correctly clarifies that ten persons in the Middle Kingdom receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, even among these ten, there are those who are prohibited and those who are permitted;
it does not mean that the number must simply be ten. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* is cited to clarify this point, stating that regarding the three masters (*ācāryas*), all [must be present].
This is in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the seven types of witnesses, it is stated that they must all be pure and clearly understanding.

This is because the translated texts complement one another: when divided, the phrasing differs; when combined, the meaning is identical. If one is not a person who is pure and clearly understanding, they are entirely incapable of serving as one of the ten masters of the Saṃgha.
According to the Ekottarika-āgama (Ekottara-khaṇḍaka), the Buddha said: "A bhikṣu who accomplishes five dharmas should be authorized [to confer ordination]."

One should know the great precepts; know the precepts of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*); know the increase of pure practice; know the *Prātimokṣa*; and know the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the ritual procedure (*karman*).
(One who lacks these five qualities should not confer the full ordination. Furthermore, there are another five qualities by which one should confer the full ordination:

knowing an offense; knowing how to repent; knowing that after repenting for an offense, one is purified; knowing the formal motion; and knowing the ritual procedure. (One who lacks these five qualities should not confer the full ordination. Furthermore...

There are five qualities by which one should be ordained: knowing what constitutes an obstructed situation (*sāntarāya-dharma*), knowing what constitutes an unobstructed situation (*anantarāya-dharma*), knowing the *jñapti* motion, knowing the *karmavācanā* formal act, and having completed ten years [of seniority].

Commentary: Regarding "begging for food": this refers to those who have left the household life to practice the path. If one lacks food and drink, the body will become exhausted and weary, and even life itself will not be sustained;

Furthermore, regarding the method of begging for alms, one day should be limited to seven households. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"When a bhikṣu begs for alms, he should divide [the food] into four portions. One portion should be offered to fellow practitioners of the holy life.
This means that whenever one begs for alms, there must be fellow practitioners who remain to guard the dwelling, or perhaps those who are elderly or infirm and thus unable to travel.

One portion should be given to the destitute beggars; that is to say, when obtaining food by begging, if one encounters a person in dire poverty seeking alms, one should give rise to a heart of compassion, regard them as if they were one's own hunger, and likewise share and bestow a portion.
Give to them so that they may be fully satisfied, and exhort them to cultivate virtue. Set aside one portion for the various spirits and deities;

1. To relieve the multitude of illnesses. 2. To construct sturdy boats to ferry people across. 3. To establish bridges for the weak and infirm to cross over. 4.
