These are the seven matters through which one attains the merit of Brahmā. In the present text, only the first is mentioned, yet it encompasses the remainder.
In the Vinaya, when bhikṣus teach and transform donors, they cause them all to perform these seven meritorious acts.
If the Upādhyāya and Ācārya provide any instruction in accordance with the Dharma, you must not disobey it.
You should diligently study, inquire, recite the sūtras, and seek skillful means. Within the Buddha-dharma, you shall attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts will not be in vain; the fruits of your reward will never cease. The rest...
What is not yet known, one should ask the Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
This explains the exhortation to study diligently and the encouragement to practice. One must not disobey any instruction that accords with the Dharma.

It is said that when humans are born into this world, who does not delight in ease and dread toil? Who does not weary of complexity and long for simplicity? When circumstances are favorable, one rejoices; when circumstances are adverse, one grieves.
Stirred by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the notions of "self" and "other" immediately arise; they spring up as soon as there is a collision with objects.

These are what are called "afflicted ordinary people" (*kliṣṭa-pṛthagjana*); they do not belong to the path of the renunciants. You have now attained full ordination (*upasampadā*) and dwell together with the Saṃgha.
The teaching must necessarily rely upon a master. In the conduct of the Saṃgha, one must not be coarse or frivolous; the four modes of deportment must conform to the standard of discipline.
One should be humble and respectful, yielding in virtue, and forget one’s own body for the sake of the Dharma.

If worldly habits persist and one defies the master’s instructions, then the Way will deviate from the Dharma, the laity will harbor contempt, and one will lose the human form beneath the kāṣāya, rendering oneself of no benefit whatsoever to the Gate of the Dharma.
Therefore, you should now study and inquire into the Vinaya, recite the sūtras, and diligently seek skillful means through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

By maintaining the purity of both abstention and performance, your mind shall become clear and wisdom shall manifest. Thus, within the Buddha-dharma, you will attain the fruits of the four paths and not be bound or detained by the fetters within the nine realms of existence.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, may the merits accumulated therein not be in vain.
Abandon [doubt]. It is said that such causes produce such effects; all of this arises from properly following the teacher’s instructions and practicing in accordance with the Vinaya.
Now, on this altar, I have provided only these brief teachings. Regarding anything else you do not yet know, after you descend from the altar, [you shall learn it].
One should inquire of each of one’s preceptors (upādhyāya), ācāryas, and like-minded senior monks (sthavira) regarding the Dharma;
if one hears their instructions yet fails to adopt them, one thereby betrays the sacred kindness of the sages and the compassionate heart of one’s teachers’ earnest teachings.
The Buddha said: "One who is receiving full ordination should be made to walk in front.

The disciple should inquire after the preceptor’s welfare three times each day—at dawn, midday, and dusk—and should perform two types of laborious service for the preceptor at those times, without showing reluctance or weariness:
first, the repair of dwellings; second, the mending and washing of robes. The preceptor shall [instruct] all matters as follows..."
The Dharma teachings must all be practiced accordingly; those who violate this shall be dealt with according to the law.
Commentary: Those receiving the precepts should walk in front, while the ten monastic masters should follow behind.
Regarding the instruction that "a disciple should inquire after the Master’s well-being three times a day," this is merely a brief citation of the method for attending upon a Master.

The full details are found at the end of the thirty-third fascicle of the Vinaya Piṭaka. If one sincerely accepts the specific regulations for revering one's teacher, I request that you read and practice them;
thus, one will deeply enter the name of filial piety, which is the essential purpose of the precepts. Within this [context]:

The three *jñapti* (formal announcements) and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one announcement and three proclamations) are all performed for the sake of others; thus, they pertain to the private [sphere].

The details regarding their distinctions have already been clarified in the preceding section on the five conditions for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), and therefore they will not be repeated here.
The fifth fascicle of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Commentary on the Vinaya).
Regarding the phonology and meaning: In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, within the borders of India, there is a river named Vārāṇasī. Not far from it [is the city].
He established a royal city named Gangāparikṣipta (City Encircled by the Ganges).
In the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī was the place where ancient kings used to keep deer.
When the Buddha first left home and entered the mountains to practice the Way, his father the king missed him deeply. The five companions, including Kauṇḍinya and the others, were there.
He then commanded the five men, including Cunda, to seek him out and attend upon him. When the Buddha attained enlightenment, he reflected that these five men should be liberated first;
therefore, at the Deer Park, he first cultivated their faculties and taught them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
And they attained liberation; these were the first five people to be delivered. First was Kauṇḍinya, which in the language of China means "Fire-vessel. He was of the Brahmin caste;
because he had served fire in his previous lives, he was the Buddha’s maternal uncle. Second was Aśvajit, also called Aśva-sena (Horse-teacher);
he was a member of the Buddha’s own clan. Third was Vāṣpa (Small-Wise); he was a member of the Buddha’s family.
They were of the same clan. Kāśyapa of the Forty Powers was also a maternal uncle of the Buddha, but he was neither Mahākāśyapa nor one of the three Kāśyapas.
The five Kuṇḍala princes were the eldest sons of King Droṇodana, and thus they were the younger cousins of the Buddha.
The turning of the Wheel of Dharma consists of teaching the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—in three successive cycles; this is called the "three turnings.
Just as a worldly wheel has the function of crushing and grinding, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma can crush and grind away the afflictions and karma of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "turning the Wheel of Dharma. The first is the "turning of demonstration," where "demonstration" means pointing out.
To say, "This is suffering; this is its origin; this is its cessation; this is the path," is called the turning of demonstration (*darśana-vartanā*).
Second is the turning of exhortation (*preraṇa-vartanā*); "exhortation" means to urge or encourage. To say, "This is suffering—you should know it;
this is its origin—you should abandon it; this is its cessation—you should realize it; this is the path—you should cultivate it," is called the turning of exhortation.
Third is the transformation through realization (*pratyakṣa*). This refers to verification; that is, to cite what one has personally realized in order to verify it. For example: "This is suffering;
I have already known it, and there is nothing further to be known. This is the origin; I have already abandoned it, and there is nothing further to be abandoned."
"This is cessation; it has been realized by me and need not be realized again. This is the path; it has been cultivated by me and need not be cultivated again.
This is called the turning of realization.
*Mei* (篾) refers to the slender twigs of bamboo.
Regarding the observance of the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* mentions six types of ascetic practitioners (*tīrthika*). First is self-starvation:
abstaining from food and drink, enduring hunger and emptiness for a long time, and adhering to this asceticism as the cause for attaining the fruit [of liberation].
Second, plunging into deep water: they cast themselves into deep abysses, enduring the suffering of cold and adhering to this asceticism as the cause for attaining the fruit.

Third, entering fire: they constantly scorch their bodies and fumigate their noses with heat, sweetly accepting the suffering of heat and adhering to this asceticism as the cause for attaining the fruit.
Fourth, sitting naked: they constantly remain in a state of nudity, unconstrained by [clothing].
5. Cold and Heat: Sitting in the open air, they maintain this ascetic practice as the cause for attaining the fruit [of liberation].
6. Fivefold Silence: Dwelling among charnel grounds and burial mounds, they remain silent and do not speak;
they maintain this ascetic practice as the cause for attaining the fruit. 7. Cow and Dog: They claim that in their previous lives they came from among cows and dogs. Thus...

They observe the precepts of cattle and dogs, eating grass and consuming filth, hoping only for rebirth in heaven. They cling to these ascetic practices as the cause for attaining the fruit [of liberation].
"Yōu" (猶) is the name of a beast;
it is full of doubt and suspicion. Whenever it hears the sound of a human voice, it immediately climbs a tree. After a long time, there is none...
A person [ascends] first, and then descends; after a brief moment, they ascend again. This occurs more than once; therefore, it is not definitively called "hesitation" (*yòuyù*).
Regarding the perfection of the four knowledges, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that an Arhat possesses four knowledges:

first, "my births have been exhausted," meaning that the Arhat has severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) and will no longer undergo birth and death within the triple world (*tridhātu*). Second, "the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been lived..."
1. Established: This means that by means of the practices of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), the Arhat achieves and realizes [the goal].
2. Having accomplished what was to be done: This means that the Arhat originally sought liberation from the three realms and cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Since birth and death have been exhausted and the holy life has been established, it is said that "what was to be done has been accomplished. 3. No further existence hereafter: This refers to the Arhat...
The Arhat has exhausted the delusions and karma of birth and death and will no longer receive a body in future lives; therefore, it is said that he "will not undergo further existence.
Kātyāyana means "Not Empty" in the language of China. He was of Brahmin descent from South India and was skilled in debate and exposition.
Among the ten great disciples, he was thus called the foremost in debate;
he was ranked among the preeminent ones.
"Yīxī" means indistinct, as if a mere semblance rather than the reality.
"Menglong" (朦朧) refers to the moon about to set and the moon about to rise; it signifies a state that is neither bright nor dark.
Regarding the "four castes" (四姓), these are the four types of people in the Western Regions who falsely reckon that they were born from the Brahmā Heaven.

First is the Brāhmaṇa (婆羅門), which in the language of China means "Pure Conduct" (淨行). Whether living as householders or having left the home-life, they have inherited this lineage through successive generations and take the Way (dharma) as their profession.
First are the Brāhmaṇas, who consider themselves born from the mouth of Brahmā and the descendants of Brahmā;

they maintain the Way and abide in integrity, purifying their conduct, and are therefore called those of "Pure Conduct" (Śuddhacaryā). Second are the Kṣatriyas, which in the language of China means "Land-Lord";
they are the lords of the great earth of the world and consider themselves born from the navel of Brahmā, being thus of royal lineage. Third are the Vaiśyas, that is, merchants.
The Vaiśyas consider themselves born from the side of Brahmā; the Śūdras, who are the agricultural caste, consider themselves born from the feet of Brahmā. These constitute the four castes.

The four rivers are as follows: first, the Gaṅgā River, also known as the Ganges, which flows from the silver ox-mouth on the eastern side of Lake Anavatapta; it circles the lake once and enters the southeastern ocean.
Second, the Sindhu River, which flows from the golden elephant-mouth on the southern side of Lake Anavatapta; it circles the lake once and enters the southwestern ocean.
Third is the Vakṣu River. It flows from the western side of Lake Anavatapta through the lapis lazuli horse-mouth, circles the lake once, and enters the northwestern ocean. Fourth is the Sītā River.
It flows from the northern side of Lake Anavatapta through the crystal lion-mouth, circles the lake once, and enters the northeastern ocean; some say it flows underground.
Flowing downward, it emerges from Mount Jishan and serves as the source of the Yellow River (Zhongguo).
*Zhi* (pronounced like *di*) means to sew.
*Rui* (pronounced like *wei*) means sharp.
Niè (pronounced like the "nie" in niè) means to bite; it is synonymous with *shì* (to gnaw).
Zì (pronounced like the "zi" in zì) means to soak;
it is synonymous with *qīn* (to immerse). Nǎi (pronounced like the "nai" in nǎi) refers to a wet nurse.
The large ants are called *bífú* (termites); the small ones are called *yǐzǐ* (ant larvae).
The character for "sting" (*chē*) has the phonetic *shì*; it refers to insects that discharge venom. The character for "chú" (a type of tree) has the phonetic *shū*.
*ǒu* (偶): A likeness or image. A wooden image is called a *mùǒu* (wooden puppet); an earthen image is called a *tǔǒu* (earthen puppet). *zhé* (酌): Pronounced like *zhuó*.
To take what is good and put it into practice is called *zhé*. It also means to deliberate or adjust (*zhēnzuò*).
*Pan* (with the departing tone) means to look back or to gaze.
*Jian* (with the rising tone) means a year of famine.
"Once every five days he went on inspection" refers to the World-Honored One’s practice of going on inspection once every five days for the sake of the five benefits.
First, a śrāvaka disciple does not cling to conditioned phenomena; second, he does not cling to worldly discourse;
third, he does not cling to sleep; fourth, he attends to sick bhikṣus;
fifth, having left home at a young age, he beholds the majestic and dignified deportment of the Tathāgata and gives rise to a heart of joy.
*Méng* (pronounced like *méng*) refers to the gadfly, a biting flying insect.
*Qì* (pronounced like *qī*) means sorrow.
*Kài* (with the departing tone) means to open.
*Tài* (pronounced *tài*) means intention, emotion, and coquetry.

Continued Explanation of the *Zhujie shoufa pian* (Chapter on the Method for Receiving the Various Precepts),
Part Three of Three, by the junior monk Duti of Huashan in Jinling:
The Method for Requesting an Upādhyāya (Preceptor).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose upādhyāya had passed away. Whether he had abandoned the path or resolved to go beyond the boundaries of the monastery, because there was no one to instruct him, he committed various violations of the precepts and acted in ways contrary to dignified decorum. The Buddha said: "I allow him to have an ācārya."
One should mutually honor, respect, and look after one another according to the rules for a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
[Commentary: This rule is derived from the *Pravrajyāvastu* (Chapter on Going Forth). One who has newly received full ordination (*upasampadā*) should always rely upon a preceptor.
He followed the instructions and studied and maintained the Vinaya. However, because his preceptor passed away, they were separated forever;

eventually, he resolved to cross the boundary and not return. Having lost his formal support (niśraya), various faults arose. The Buddha permitted that there should be an ācārya upon whom one must rely;
the ācārya should regard the disciple as a son, and the disciple should regard the ācārya as a father.
One should think: "We shall together honor, respect, and look after one another; thus the True Dharma will abide for a long time and increase and expand.
Therefore, it is said that this is according to the method of the *upādhyāya*.
One who seeks formal reliance (*niśraya*) should properly maintain dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
He should request as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mindfulness. I, [Name], now seek the Venerable sir to be my formal preceptor (*niśrayadātṛ*).

May the Venerable sir grant me formal reliance. I shall dwell in reliance upon the Venerable sir. (Having said this three times, and having accepted the request, he should reply: "So be it; I shall provide you with formal reliance."
Do not be negligent.
A disciple must perform two duties for you; you must not decline or shirk them. You should request the scriptures and inquire about their meaning until you have attained some understanding.

When five years have been completed, you may leave your dependence [upon your teacher]. If you know nothing and are not proficient in reciting the precepts, you must remain dependent for as long as you live.

[The Master] said, "Stop. [The Commentator] explains: This clarifies the conduct of serving one's teacher and the benefits of self-cultivation, establishing a fixed period for these duties. The Vinaya states:
"In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, one must perform two types of laborious service for the teacher and must not decline or feel weary. The first is the repair [of the dwelling]."
[The duties are: first, [the maintenance of] lodgings; second, the mending and washing of robes. One must carry out all matters as instructed by the teacher according to the Dharma.
If sent on a mission to travel through various regions, one must not decline the labor or remain by making excuses based on some pretext.

If one declines the labor, one shall be dealt with according to the law. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavācanā*, the Buddha said: "When five qualities are accomplished, [one may be ordained] after five years of summer retreat..."

[The period] is complete. One may then obtain release from formal dependence (*niśraya*) and travel among human communities. Regarding the five qualities (the first four being the same as those for a preceptor, with the fifth being):

one must be well-versed in the points of obstruction and non-obstruction regarding the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, and be capable of reciting and upholding it. The Venerable Upāli asked the World-Honored One:

"If one has completed four years of residence and accomplished these five qualities, but another has completed five years of residence yet has not heard these five qualities, [who may receive release from dependence?]"
"Is it not necessary to rely on a preceptor? The Buddha said, "It is not permitted. This is because the five-year period is fulfilled and the five qualities are accomplished;

these serve as the definitive criteria. Again he asked: "If a bhikṣu is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, has realized the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), and has already eliminated the three stains (*trimala*), even if he has only completed three years of summer retreat (*traivarṣika*), must he still rely on a teacher?
The Buddha said, "It does not depend on whether one has not yet attained or has already attained, or has not yet realized or has already realized..."

One who has realized [the truth] or already awakened, having attained freedom from dependence, may still be required to remain under the guidance of another due to the constraints of the prescribed rules;
specifically, one must fulfill five years of seniority (*pañca-varṣa*) and achieve the five qualities (*pañca-dharma*) before attaining independence.

Even if one is eighty years of age or has completed sixty years of seniority, if one has never recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* nor understood its meaning, one must likewise depend upon an elder. If there is no such person...
Whether one is old or young, it is likewise permitted; with the sole exception of prostration, all other duties must be performed. Such a person is called an "old or young bhikṣu.
An ācārya must possess five qualities:
he must know what constitutes an offense and what does not, he must know what is light and what is heavy, and he must have completed ten years [of standing].
Only then can one truly guide others. If one lacks these virtues and does not rely on faultlessness, [one cannot do so]. The virtues of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) are analogous to this.
Explanation: This refers to taking the virtues of the *upādhyāya* as a model for those who rely on a teacher (*niśraya*).

As clarified in the aforementioned method for requesting ordination, the *ācārya* (preceptor) must likewise request the method for maintaining a retinue (*gaṇa-parigraha*), just as in the procedure for the *upādhyāya*.
This is a distinction. One must possess the requisite dharmas and have food and clothing; only when the five virtues are truly complete may one take disciples under one's care.

If there is a deficiency in the five virtues and the two matters [of food and clothing] are not provided, it is no fault for them not to rely on such a teacher. However, if the teacher’s virtue is complete...
Having requested [to take] reliance, one must not stay overnight apart from the preceptor; if one stays apart, one incurs an offense.

Furthermore, according to the *Ekottarakarmaśataka*, if one does not feel a sense of settled mind, one may seek another reliance for up to five nights. The *Mūlasarvāstivādavinayakṣudrakavastu* states:
"If the preceptor has a mind of attachment [to the disciple], but the disciple has no mind of attachment; or if the disciple has a mind of attachment..."
If the preceptor has no mind of attachment, [the relationship] is not lost; if both have minds of attachment, neither loses the status of preceptor or disciple.
If both abandon [the relationship], it is called "losing the preceptor. This rite of formal act (*karmavācanā*) before another is performed for the sake of the Dharma.

This pertains to the private [sphere]. First, the fault of the person: it is not a single individual; the virtuous requirements for the rite are incomplete; and one accepts the invitation while gathering others [for the purpose]. Second, the fault of the dharma: the request and the granting of the gift are simultaneous;
the verbal expressions are unclear, and so forth. Third, the fault of the matter: when performing the ritual before the Noble Ones, the deportment is improper.
The phrase "cultivating [the factors] equally" and so forth, as well as the fact that the latter four are not [so], should be understood by analogy.
○ Regarding the continuation of the dwelling-dharma with non-Buddhists:
this follows the *綱目* (Outline) of the *Bia’er Jie-mo* (White Twofold Karmavācanā), but here it is continued according to the *Shoujie Jian-du* (Chapter on Receiving Ordination) of the Vinaya.
It is said: There was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who was skilled in debate and sought ordination as a monk.
After receiving full ordination (upasampadā), because his faith remained wavering, he returned to the fold of the non-Buddhists. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"I allow that a non-Buddhist be granted a four-month period of probation (*parivāsa*) within the community of monks through a formal act of two announcements (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), in order to test his faith. This is the root [of the rule].

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Baiyi jieben) states: One should request a bhikṣu to serve as one’s upādhyāya. For the duration of four months, one should wear the robes of an upādhyāya and partake of the regular food provided by the Saṃgha.
One should inquire about the obstructing dharmas (*antarāyika-dharma*). If [the candidate] is completely pure, he should be accepted. The Vinaya says:
Having first had his hair shaved, he puts on the kāṣāya, removes his leather sandals, places his right knee on the ground, and joins his palms.
He speaks as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, [Name], an outsider, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
I seek to go forth from the household life into the homeless state under the World-Honored One to practice the Path. The World-Honored One is my Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
(Thus three times. I, [Name], having taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as a follower of the non-Buddhist path, now go forth from home to study the Way under the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is my truly perfected and fully awakened one. (Thus three times.)
○ Next, the explanation for the instruction on receiving the precepts: This reception of the ten precepts is identical to those held by śrāmaṇeras and thus is not repeated here.
However, there is a difference in the procedure: while a śrāmaṇera receives the ten precepts before only two masters, this [reception] takes place within the assembly.
The Sangha serves as the witness and guarantor; therefore, it is said, "Venerable Sangha, please listen.
The Buddha said: "After those non-Buddhists have received the ten precepts, they should first go before the assembly of monks, baring their right shoulder."
Remove your leather sandals. Having prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, place your right knee on the ground, join your palms, and recite as follows: [Exegesis]:
Although it was previously stated that the Sangha serves as witnesses for the reception of the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts, the Sangha has not yet assembled in its entirety.

Since this is not a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed by the Sangha, but rather a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) constituting the actual proceedings of the Sangha, it is proper to ring [the bell].
[The officiant] strikes the gong and assembles the monks within the boundary. That preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya) should lead the outsider into the midst of the Saṃgha.
First, having fully prepared and cultivated the proper deportment, and after prostrating at the feet of the monks, they should cause [the outsider] to kneel with palms joined and speak as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, [Name], a follower of an external path, request from the Saṃgha a four-month period of co-residence.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me this four-month period of co-residence.
Having spoken thus three times, place that non-Buddhist in a location where he can see [the assembly] but cannot hear it.
From among the community, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed to make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) as described above.
Commentary: This is the *ajñapti-karman* (formal act not performed in the presence [of the offender]). Regarding the *karman*, one performs the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*) and replies:
"The *karman* for the four-month probationary residence with non-Buddhists. As above, one makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. That [so-and-so] non-Buddhist now requests from the community of monks four months of co-residence.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant it, let the Saṃgha grant four months of co-residence to that [so-and-so] non-Buddhist. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. That [certain] outsider has requested from the community of monks a four-month period of co-residence.
The Saṃgha now grants him a four-month period of co-residence. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting him a four-month period of co-residence, remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak. The Saṃgha has already approved the granting of the four-month probation to that outsider.
Since the Saṃgha is silent, it approves; this matter is thus upheld.

The Buddha said: "When those non-Buddhists have completed their period of co-residence and have caused the minds of the bhikṣus to be joyful, they shall then receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the community of monks through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

If those non-Buddhists, however, still persistently cling to the ways of the non-Buddhist laypeople, do not associate with the bhikṣus but instead associate with non-Buddhists, do not comply with the bhikṣus, and [do not] recite..."
They practice heterodox doctrines. If they hear someone speak of the unwholesome matters of non-Buddhists, or disparage the teachings of non-Buddhist masters, they immediately give rise to anger.
If they hear it said that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not the true Dharma, they leap for joy and exult.
If there are other non-Buddhists or non-Buddhist masters who come and praise the excellence of non-Buddhist matters, they likewise rejoice and leap for joy. If...
If it is thus, it will not bring joy to the bhikṣus. If one acts contrary to this, it is called dwelling together with those of external paths;
[one must instead] harmonize the mind and thoughts so as to bring joy to the bhikṣus.

Commentary: This *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed for the purpose of testing the mind of one who is to live in communal residence; thus, it pertains to the private [individual]. It is not [permissible] for a single person.

it is to simplify conditions and cultivate contentment. The nine-stripe, eleven-stripe, and thirteen-stripe [robes] are all [of two types].
One long [strip] and one short [strip] constitute the lower-grade *saṃghāṭī*. Fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen [strips], each having three longs and one short, constitute the middle-grade *saṃghāṭī*.
Twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five [strips], each having four longs and one short, constitute the upper-grade *saṃghāṭī*.
The reason the number of longs increases while the number of shorts decreases is as follows:
The Dharma robe is the field of merit for veneration; it is able to benefit all sentient beings, manifesting the increase of the holy and the decrease of the mundane.
The Vinaya states: "In accordance with the Dharma, it should have four borders, five strips with ten intervals. One should personally wash, dye, stretch, and press it.

The *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) and *antarvāsaka* (inner robe) must be made by cutting and piecing; if one lacks sufficient material, one may make them with fewer patches. The *pañcaka-paṭa* (five-patch robe) is likewise."
If the lower garment may be folded in pleats, it should be washed, dyed, and pressed by oneself.
According to the Vinaya regulations, a bhikṣu must not have a nun who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat his robes;
therefore, a robe in accordance with the Dharma must have borders on all four sides and consist of five strips and ten sections.

One should make the lower robe with one long side and one short side. Regarding the two larger robes, one should first measure the available material to see if it is sufficient for the pattern of cut-and-sewn strips;
if the length and width are adequate, it is well. Even if there is a slight deficiency, one need not cut it into strips;

instead, one should make a *saṃghāṭī* (patchwork robe) from this material. "Patch" (*saṃghāṭī*) means "layered," meaning that separate strips are applied as patterns upon it. This is the five-fold patchwork.

The same applies to robes (*cīvara*). This does not mean that five types of robes are permitted; rather, it means that one may take five kinds of refuse-rags (*pāṃsukūla*) and, by sewing them together, fashion them into the three dharma-robes.
Whether they are sufficient or insufficient, the method of cutting and patching is the same as for the two larger robes.

If the lower robe (*antaravāsaka*) is to be pleated, this refers to folding a small portion to form a leaf-like fold, just like the pleats on a robe. Although patching is permitted, [the specific method is as described].
The pleats should be fashioned like leaves. They must have internal channels for water to flow through freely without obstruction. At the points where they intersect, they must not be sewn together;
if they were sewn shut, it would not constitute the characteristic of a field-plot designed for the passage of water.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one makes it slightly less than the prescribed measure, or if one makes it plain (*maṇḍala*). Commentary:
Regarding "making it less than the measure," do not exceed [the limit] by reducing it by one or two inches; if it is reduced too much, it will not fit the body.
Regarding "making it plain," the Sanskrit term is *patta*, which in the language of Tang means "plain strip"; this refers to a single piece of cloth.

Woven cloth. There was no practice of wearing robes cut into patches. When the Buddha-dharma reached this place, one hundred and eighty-seven years had passed; those who had left the household life did not yet know how to cut and sew, and thus wore only this kind of cloth.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The leaf is at its widest four finger-widths; at its narrowest, it is like a grain of wild barley. The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"One should know this long strip, this short strip, this is the leaf, this is the first seam, and this is the second seam.

In this [sewing], the leaves are sewn in both directions; the sewing of the leaves is permitted to be done with 'bird's-foot' seams. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is necessary to back-stitch as one proceeds forward."
The four fingers [of width] serve as the basis for the hook; the subsequent eight fingers serve as the basis for the fastening loop.
Commentary: Regarding "the leaves being extremely wide, equal to four fingers," as stated in the section on purification in the subsequent text:

"If the width is equal to the four fingers of the Tathāgata and the length is eight fingers, it is sufficient to make a great robe (*saṃghāṭī*). The arrangement of the strips and the fluttering borders may be made according to one's preference, provided the material for the robe..."
The fringe at the edge is small; it is extremely narrow, like a grain of barley. Its shape is barely four-fifths [of the width].

In the original text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this long strip is divided in detail even down to the two sides of the leaf. This was likely because they feared that if cut into too many fragments, the strips would become disordered during sewing, thereby violating the Dharma.
Regarding the "bird's foot" seam (*pakṣipāda-sevana*): a bird's foot has toes both in front and behind; that is to say, one prong in front and another behind.
Stitching. Furthermore, one may not stitch forward; one must sew lengthwise in the conventional manner, which refers to the hook-needle stitch.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Stitching backward" means to retreat or move toward the rear. This is likewise the same as the bird-foot stitch; thus, one should leave a space of four finger-widths from the edge.
The "applied hook" (*śih-gou*) refers to the border four inches below the chest, extending eight finger-widths at the back.

The "applied knot" (*śih-niu*) refers to that which starts from behind the right armpit, wraps around the left shoulder, and measures eight inches between its upper and lower borders. These measurements are stated according to the fingers of an ordinary person.
The Sarvāstivādins say: "If the three robes are torn but the binding edges remain intact, the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) is not lost.

Commentary: This means that if among a bhikṣu’s three robes there is one that has been worn for many years and is damaged to the point where it cannot be repaired, provided that the binding edges around its four sides have not been severed, the formal undertaking is not lost.
This is intended for those with few acquaintances who find it difficult to obtain [new robes] as a provisional measure.
Open [the robe]. If there is something desired and wealth is to be obtained, how can one afford to be dilatory?
The *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Dignified Conduct) states: "Have it pasted at the four corners. The root Vinaya text states: "Have it sewn to cover stains and grease.
If the robe is damaged, patch it according to the size and shape of the hole—even if it is as large as two finger-widths.
Explanation: Regarding "sealing the four corners," this was originally established to ensure durability; today it has been corrupted and is called the "Four Heavenly Kings.

Regarding "sewing over greasy spots," this refers to when there is excess material in the robe fabric; one sews over the shoulders and the edges of the back to protect the garment and keep it clean, avoiding staining from sweat.
If the three robes suffer even slight damage or tearing, they must not be discarded; rather, one should seek better replacements.
One should repair it according to the size and shape of the hole—whether square or round—and even if it is only as large as two fingers, it should also be repaired.
According to the Buddha’s standard, his finger was four *cun* long, whereas an ordinary person’s finger is two *cun* long. There are two reasons for the regulation that one must perform such repairs.
First, it is for the purpose of counteracting the mind of craving; second, it is for the purpose of increasing the merit of giving.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should protect the three robes as one protects one's own skin. One who wears the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) must not carry stones, grass, wood, or other debris upon it.
If one enters a village without carrying the three robes, one commits an offense."
**Explanation:** Regarding the analogy that the three robes are like one's own skin: it is intended to give rise to a sense of protective affection for them.

As for "carrying": it means to transport or bear a burden. As for the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe): it is worn only when preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, entering villages to beg for food, or subduing non-Buddhists.
How could one possibly wear this honored garment for miscellaneous tasks? Therefore, it was established as improper to do so. **Explanation.**
A śramaṇa internally upholds the prohibitions and precepts, while externally he wears the kāṣāya. When entering the marketplace, he must remain distinct from the laity;

if he does not maintain the three robes, his physical form loses the dignity of a monk and nothing remains to represent his status. Therefore, the commission of such an offense results in the formal forfeiture of the robe (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should treat it with respect as if one were wearing it. If it is not being worn, one should fold it up and carry it.
When entering the dwellings of laypeople, if it is not fastened with its ties, one incurs an offense at every household."
Commentary: Regarding the statement that the three robes are like a Buddhist stūpa, it is because they inspire thoughts of reverence.
If one reverently makes offerings to a stūpa, one gains the merit of generating goodness and extinguishing evil; the same applies to honoring the robes.
When entering a village, if the two larger robes (the *saṃghāṭī* and the *uttarāsaṅga*) are not being worn, they should be folded and carried with one. Furthermore, for the sake of the bhikṣu...
When entering a village to beg for alms, his robe was blown by the wind and fell before laypeople, exposing his private parts and inviting ridicule.

Therefore, it was prescribed that when entering the presence of laypeople, one must wear fasteners. If one does not wear fasteners and passes beyond a single household, one incurs one *pācittiya* offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the lower part of the robe is damaged, one should also wear it inverted, with hooks and fasteners attached at the top and bottom."
Explanation: Because the robes of the bhikṣus frequently tore at the bottom, he prescribed that they be worn inverted.
Furthermore, because water would enter the folds of the robe when walking in the rain while wearing it inverted, he again permitted it to be worn in the regular manner.

Thus, hooks and toggles were provided for both the upper and lower parts. Now, a piece of cloth is attached to the top of the inner waistband (antarvāsaka), which is called the "Mount Sumeru. Moreover...
Two small pieces are placed upon the two side strips on the left and right; these are called the "Palaces of the Sun and Moon.
If they were placed upside down, the sun and moon would fall, and Mount Sumeru would hang inverted.

However, what has been corrupted is that the ritual talisman (*śāstrīya-paṭṭaka*) is placed with its greasy side facing inward, divided into three sections, and installed on the exterior. One piece is placed at the top edge; this is named—

Regarding the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe): A sutra states that in Rājagṛha there was a poor man who, seeing others making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, felt self-reproach for not having planted roots of merit in his past lives, whereby he now suffered various miseries of poverty in this life.

Thinking that he had nothing to offer, he immediately removed the old garment from his body and presented it as an offering to the Buddha. Out of compassion, the Buddha accepted it and caused [the monks] to...
The bhikṣus each divided a portion [of the cloth] and placed it upon their robes, establishing a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
Because they received a prediction (vyākaraṇa) that they would obtain the desired blessings and rewards in the future, it is therefore called the "Pīṇava robe. This has a scriptural basis.

In the Vinaya, it is prescribed that when outside the village one should wear the robes turned backward. Wherever a bhikṣu travels, his robe and bowl should always follow him, just like a flying bird.
The rest is as clarified in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*.
**Exegesis:** Regarding the first phrase, the Vinaya states: At that time, the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha did not permit them to wear their robes backward when entering a village.
Out of caution, they did not dare to do so outside the village, and consequently were covered by wind-blown dust and sun-scorched heat, as well as defiled by insects and birds.
On account of this, they informed the Buddha, who therefore granted permission. Wherever a bhikṣu travels, his robe and bowl must always follow him, just like...
Regarding the phrase "like a flying bird," other matters are clarified in the *Shuochao*. Now, according to the *Zimeng Jingxun*, it cites the *Shichao* as saying:
"In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one guards the three robes as one would protect one's own skin, and the alms bowl as one would one's own eyes.

It continues, stating that wherever one travels, one should be fully equipped with robe and bowl, remaining free from attachment or longing, just like a flying bird. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also says: "The bhikṣu’s three..."
One robe and one alms bowl must always be kept with one’s person; those who violate this are guilty of an offense upon crossing the boundary, except in cases of illness.

One should revere the three robes as if they were a stupa. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Guard the three robes carefully, as if they were the thin skin of one's own body; they must always be kept with one's person, like the feathers of a bird that follow it whether it flies or walks.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "When traveling, know the proper time and the improper time; do not engage in what should not be done."
Wherever one goes, one should be accompanied by the robe and bowl, just as a flying bird’s wings follow it. All schools have prescribed that these should be kept with one at all times;
nowadays, however, people merely guard against leaving them overnight, which is not the correct teaching. The reason the robe and bowl must always accompany the person is as follows:

Since the monastic life is fundamentally based on an empty mind, free from dwelling or attachment, one remains only as long as it is beneficial; therefore, the rule was established that [robes] must accompany the person.
If one were to leave them behind at will, it would further increase residual habits, and one would fail to exercise discernment regarding those factors conducive to the Path (*mārga-aṅga*).
Thus, there is a specific reason for this regulation, as clarified in the *Shan-chao*. The following text continues to cite the sacred teachings to manifest the merit of the three robes.
Because of its virtue.
According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, when the Tathāgata made his vows before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he prayed that upon his attainment of Buddhahood, his *kāṣāya* would possess five merits.
First, those who enter my Dharma—even if they have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views—[shall be purified]. Fourth...
First, if the multitude, in a single thought-moment, honors and respects [the wearer] with a reverent mind, they will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles.
Second, if devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits can respectfully honor even a small portion of this person’s *kāṣāya*, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression from the Three Vehicles.
Third, if any ghosts, spirits, or people obtain the *kāṣāya*, even if it is only four inches in size, their food and drink will become sufficient. Fourth, ...
If there are sentient beings who are at odds with one another, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Fifth, if one is amidst an army in battle, by holding even a small portion of this [robe] with reverence and respect, one will always be victorious over others.
If my *kāṣāya* did not possess these five powers, I would be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Provided that one is a śramaṇa by nature— even if one defiles the conduct and form of a śramaṇa—
anyone who is a śramaṇa wearing the kāṣāya shall, from the time of Maitreya Buddha up until Ruci Buddha, attain entry into nirvāṇa without remainder."

The *Yingluo jing* (Sutra on the Necklace) states: "If the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, engage in conflict, they should recollect this *kāṣāya* and give rise to a mind of compassion.

The *Hailongwang jing* (Sutra of the Naga King Sāgara) records: The Naga King addressed the Buddha, saying, "In this ocean, there are countless kinds of nāgas, among whom four types are constantly preyed upon by the garuḍas.
We pray that the Buddha will protect us and grant us peace and security. Thereupon, the World-Honored One removed his own [robe].
He put on his morning robes and addressed the Dragon King: "Take these robes and distribute them among all the dragons, ensuring they reach everyone.
Should any among them receive even a single thread, the King of the Garuḍas shall be unable to harm them. Furthermore, those who observe the precepts will surely attain their aspirations."

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the distant past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in a mountain forest of this Jambudvīpa, there was a lion named Caṇḍakalavi (the first syllable pronounced 'chá', translated as 'Firm Vow').
His body was golden in color, and his radiant marks were clearly manifest. At that time, a hunter had shaved his head and donned a kāṣāya robe, while secretly carrying a bow and arrows."
He shot him with a poisoned arrow. The lion was startled and immediately intended to charge and kill him. However, seeing that he was wearing a *kāṣāya*, he thought to himself:
"This person will surely attain liberation before long. Why is this? This *kāṣāya* is the distinguishing mark of the sages of the three periods of time.
If I wish to harm him, it would be as if I were directing an evil mind toward the holy ones of the three periods."

The *Dharmakṣaya-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, in an age of the five perversions and turbidity, the paths of Māra will flourish.
Māras will become śramaṇas and bring ruin and disorder to my Way.
They will don secular clothing and take pleasure in the five-colored robes of the kāṣāya, until even the kāṣāya itself turns white."

The *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance) records that a celestial being said: "For six or seven hundred years since the Buddha-dharma was transmitted to the East, the Vinaya masters of the North and South have never had such an intention.
Why use wealth obtained through the killing of living beings to make robes of compassion? Why has your Master alone been so exceptional? Nanshan replied:
"I once read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and saw that the Buddha wore a coarse cloth *kāṣāya*. Because of this, I conceived [this thought]..."
"It has always been in my heart; how could it have strayed from this? After he had heard the Vinaya, he saw silkworm-reared clothing and bedding.
Even if he obtained items already finished, he would cut them to pieces and use the scraps for plastering walls. Because of this, his reverence increased all the more.

Furthermore, seeing the Indian monks who had come from the West all wearing cotton cloth (*kārpāsa*), he inquired of them in detail, and they replied: "In the five regions of India, no one wears clothing made of silk. From this, a thought arose within him.
They wear cloth garments. Yet, those who are now monks do not contemplate the virtuous example of the ancients;

they act in remote accord with the prophetic signs of the extinction of the Dharma by frequently wearing purple-flowered or black-colored fabrics, all made of fine, soft silk and brocade, indulging their desires without restraint.

They disdain and discard the black robes (*kāṣāya*), yet conversely claim this is a source of merit and fortune. According to principle, this should be considered a fault. Alas! For every thread there are thousands of lives—how few are mindful of this!
To neglect compassion and cherish personal preference violates the monastic regulations.
○ Explanation of the Method for Receiving the *Antarvāsa*:
When about to receive the three robes, one must know their names; however, these specific names for the three robes do not appear in any of the various schools (*nikāyas*).

This is the correct translation. The *Shishi yaoyong chao* (Essentials for the Use of the Vinaya) explains it according to its underlying meaning: the *saṃghāṭī* is called the "garment of many fragments" because it consists of many strips.

If named according to its function, it is called the "garment for entering royal palaces and villages. When wearing the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) while begging for food or preaching the Dharma, it is called the "middle garment" (*antaravāsaka*).
Named according to its function, it is called the "garment for entering assemblies," used for rituals, recitation, vegetarian feasts, and lectures.

At that time, wearing the five-strip robe is called the "lower garment. Regarding its use, it is said to be for walking in the monastery grounds and for miscellaneous tasks. The following text clearly explains the method of formal acceptance (*parigraha*).

The Buddha said: "The three robes (*tricīvara*) should be formally accepted and maintained. If one has doubts, one should relinquish them and accept them again. If one possesses a robe, one must maintain it through formal acceptance."
This constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, as the procedure for receiving [the robe] has not been performed.

Now, according to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) rules of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a robe is dyed with the five primary colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—or with superior colors, neither the Vinaya nor the Śāstra permits its acceptance. If it is a robe that accords with the Dharma, one should say:

Commentary: Regarding this reception of robes (*cīvara*), what is stated as "it should be said" means that the Dharma must necessarily rely upon the Vinaya for its definitive form, while the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) should conform to its underlying meaning.
Now, it is added that whoever receives a robe should first approach a monk who maintains the precepts and understands the Dharma;
having performed the ritual gestures and completed the prostrations, one should stand up, hold the robe in one's own hands, and face the person before whom one stands. This is how one should proceed.

Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe, consisting of one long and one short panel, as a cut-and-sewn garment. (Recite three times.)
[The Master] explains: When the three recitations are finished, the person being addressed joins their palms and replies, "I have properly received the robe. [The donor] replies, "So be it.

They perform a prostration as before and then part ways. If the one receiving the robe is a senior elder (*sthavira*) and the person being addressed is a middle or junior elder, the recipient merely joins their palms and bows while standing;
once the ritual procedure is completed, the person being addressed should prostrate to him.

The *Upādhyāya-pāda* [text] contains the ritual procedures for receiving and relinquishing various robes and medicines when descending [from the seat]. Other seats are all to be regulated according to this. There are four types of lower robes (*antaravāsaka*):
namely, those made by cutting and piecing (*khaṇḍa-sīvana*), those with pleats (*patta-veṇi*), those with folds (*saṃghāṭi-veṇi*), and those made of a single strip (*ekāntara*).
Among these, there are two categories: the primary and the secondary. First, the primary type has three kinds; the secondary has twenty kinds. If one makes them with pleats or folds...
Regarding the two types of robes: when adding them to the text of the formal acceptance (*upasaṃpadā*), the remaining phrasing is the same as above;

one simply changes it to "I shall hold this robe with pleated folds" (*saṃvelliya-cīvara*). *Explanation:* "Category" (*piṇḍa*) refers to a class. To clarify that there are exactly three types, this refers to the four kinds of *antaravāsakas* (inner robes).

Of these, the first—the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa-sīva*)—has already been accepted. The remaining three are: the pleated (*saṃvelliya*), the stitched (*saṃsibbita*), and the seamless (*ekacciya*). If one makes it pleated...
Regarding the acceptance of robes made of two kinds of leaves: when adding the words for acceptance, the remaining phrasing is the same as above;

one simply changes it to "I shall hold this such-and-such robe. "From" (cong) means "in accordance with. If all four *antarvāsas* are lacking, one may temporarily accept a *saṃghāṭī* or *uttarāsaṅga* that is available to serve as an undergarment;
by maintaining it according to the Dharma, one avoids the fault of being separated from one's robes. This must be understood.

Regarding the formal undertaking (*dhāraṇa*) of robes, it is undertaken solely by their names and not by their physical characteristics; only wearing them on the body is permitted, while actually donning them [as outer garments] is not.
As for the statement that there are twenty types, this refers to the three grades of the *saṃghāṭī*, which consist of nine robes; these are permitted to be made in two ways:

either by cutting and patching (*khaṇḍika*) or by sewing strips together (*sūcaka*). There are eighteen *uttarāsaṅgas* in total, and these are likewise permitted to be made by either cutting and patching or by sewing strips together.
Because there are two ways of making [the robe], it is said that "there are twenty kinds of robes.
If one receives and maintains [the robe] by way of the robe itself, one should add the following words:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this twenty-five-fold *antarvāsa* robe."
"Four long and one short, this is the *khaṇḍa-sīvana* robe; I shall maintain it" (recite thus three times).
This applies analogously to the nine- and seven-strip robes. Regarding the *uttarāsaṅga* and *saṃghāṭī*, each has both primary and secondary forms;
their addition and reception may vary, as can be understood by reference to the above.
Commentary: Regarding "receiving [the robes] with mutual variation," this refers to the differences in the length and number of strips on the three robes (*tricīvara*).

If one follows the other in this manner, the wording for the formal undertaking (*upādāna*) may be inferred by adapting the preceding text accordingly. This uses the method of following one rule as an illustration to clarify all instances of following a rule.
If it is an unsewn *antarvāsa*, the remaining text should be recited as above, saying:
"I accept and maintain this unsewn *antarvāsa*" (three times).
If one intends to make it an *uttarāsaṅga* or a *saṃghāṭī*, both follow the same procedure as for the *antarvāsa*, with the sole exception of...
Regarding the upper and lower robes, the difference lies in their increase or decrease.
Explanation: This follows the regulation for making the three robes from a single strip of cloth (*kaṭhina*) according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

For one with limited resources who intends to make them by estimation, both the middle robe (*antarvāsaka*) and the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) follow the method for the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*): they are sewn as a single continuous piece without dividing the field-patterns (*kṣetra*).

Regarding length and shortness, this applies solely to the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*). It should extend below the middle robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) by a certain amount; the middle robe should extend below the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) by a certain amount.
If the upper garment covers the lower one, it is not permissible; rather, the lower garment must be longer than the upper.

By this, one should recognize that the wearing of the three robes all has its designated measurements. Therefore, it is said that they differ only in the increase or decrease of the upper and lower garments.
○ The Method for Receiving the Uṭtarāsaṅga: This robe has exactly two types;
that is, the *khaṇḍa-sīvana* (cut-and-sewn) seven-strip robe. There are twenty-two [types] from which it is derived. Commentary: Regarding "there are twenty-two from which it is derived":
there are nine each of the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), the *khaṇḍa-sīvana* (cut-and-sewn), and the *antaravāsaka* (inner robe). The *antaravāsaka*...
There are four types: cut-and-sewn, pleated, hemmed, and plain; together they total twenty-two.
If one receives a cut-and-sewn robe, the remaining texts follow the above pattern. The addition of the ritual formula in the subsequent text says:
"I receive this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe; it consists of two long strips and one short strip, a cut-and-sewn garment to be worn" (recite three times).
If it is a patchwork robe or a seamless robe, the wording should be adjusted accordingly.
○ The Method for Receiving the Saṃghāṭī:

This robe consists precisely of eighteen types; that is, there are nine grades each for both the cut-and-sewn (khaṇḍa) and the patchwork (saṃghāṭa) styles. Among these, there are six [types] based on size.

Commentary: Regarding the statement "there are six types," these refer to the four types of *antarvāsa* (inner robe)—namely, the cut-and-sewn, the pleated, the hemmed, and the seamless—and the two types of *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), which are the cut-and-sewn and the hemmed.
If one receives a *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe), the remaining wording is as above; following the previous model, the following should be modified:

Up to nine strips, they are received according to the preceding examples. If there are [additional] robes, they may be treated as before. ○ Regarding the legal procedure for receiving the *maṇḍala-cīvara* (unbordered robe):
