The second refers to the hand-washing basin. Desiring to cleanse one's hands before paying respects to the Saṃgha, one must be free from arrogance.

Water symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*); impurities are likened to the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*). Without relying on the power of concentration, the turbidity of worldly passions cannot be clarified and stilled.

*Śalākā* is translated here as "counting-stick" (*chou*); it is the method for recording numbers. It is at its shortest equal to five fingers and at its longest the length of a fist or an elbow; as for its thickness—
It is like the little finger; it is no thicker than a chopstick. Its functions are twofold: first, to determine the number of monks receiving the gift of robes;
second, to extinguish disputes by partaking of the communal meal. Regarding other times for the ritual: this excludes the striking of the gavel.
One may permit an assembly at a specific time, such as when the shadow reaches a certain length, or by making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) according to the established rule.
The number of those residing together determines the appropriate usage. ○ Regarding the Method for Continuing the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts):
The preceding text merely states, "Once the Saṃgha has assembled, members of neighboring seats should examine one another to ascertain who has arrived."

Regarding those who have come: as they have not yet clarified this rule, we shall now follow the "Single Proclamation" (jñapti) section of the *Karmavācanā* and continue according to the *Prātimokṣa-vastu*.
The Vinaya states: At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, there was a bhikṣu in a residence who entered his room, closed the door, and fell asleep.
When the bhikṣus had finished reciting the precepts, they rose from their seats and departed. Those who were sleeping woke up at the sound and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?
Are you not reciting the precepts? They replied, "We have already finished reciting the precepts."
"Where have you come from just now? he asked. He replied, "I was merely sleeping in my room with the door closed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One must not sleep in one's room on the day of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony).
From this day forward, I authorize those sitting nearby to examine one another, to know who has arrived and who has not. One should first announce [the absence], and only then recite the precepts."
Regarding the precepts, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today, on the tenth day, the Saṃgha shall recite the precepts. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
We shall recite the precepts in harmony. This is the announcement."
Commentary: It was stated above that "informing" (*jñapti*) is the *karmavācanā*. This refers to that very method. Having performed the informing, one proceeds according to circumstances;

the detailed or abbreviated recitation of the precepts is as prescribed by the Dharma. Regarding the seven types of invalidity (*saptavidha-akarmaṇya*), these have already been explained in detail within the section on the "Conditions for Assembling the Community."
I shall not repeat the selection here.

Subsequently, among the various recitations of the Vinaya-piṭaka during the fortnights of the white and black [moon], the Venerable Buddhayaśas separately translated the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa) for circulation.
At the beginning of the scroll, there are twelve stanzas that serve as the preliminary practice (*pūrvakaraṇīya*) for the questions and answers.

The *śuddhaka-śrāvaṇa* (single announcement) and the *saṃghakarma-samnipāta* (assembling for formal acts) are performed; the introduction to the *Prātimokṣa* is recited, followed by the sequential recitation of the two hundred and fifty rules of the precepts.
This is concluded with the seven verses of brief instruction from the Seven Buddhas and the verses of dedication. The opening and closing verses were added by the compilers;

because they categorized and subsumed the practices of restraint and performance into their respective sections, these [introductory and concluding] verses are omitted from the assembly for the practice of restraint (*vāraṇa-dhāraṇa*).

It is not included [in the formal texts]. I have now recorded it here appended to the *Seng shuo jie fa* (The Monastic Method for Reciting the Precepts) and briefly explained its meaning, so that one may understand the general outline of the extensive recitation.
As for the remaining ritual regulations for reciting the precepts, they are all clearly set forth within the *Liang cheng busa zhengfan* (The Correct Model for the Poṣadha of the Two Vehicles).
△ First, the twelve verses at the beginning of the scroll (divided into nine exegeses):
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, As well as the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; Now I expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may abide for a long time.

Commentary: This single verse consists of two lines at the beginning which are an act of homage to the Triple Gem, and two lines at the end which reveal that the precepts are to be explained, for they are capable of upholding the True Dharma.

Whenever one performs a ritual act, it is necessary first to pay obeisance to the Triple Gem in order to seek their empowerment, so that internal obstacles may be subtly eliminated and external māras may not cause disturbance. "Prostrating" (kai-shou) means lowering the head until it reaches the ground.

After a short while, he rose. "Li" (禮) means "to tread upon" (履). It refers to the ritual observances where advancement and retreat follow measured degrees, and honor and subordination maintain their respective divisions.
In the Western Regions, one pays the highest respect by prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground; in this land, one expresses the utmost reverence by bowing the head to the ground.
Now, following the local custom of the land, it is said "to bow one's head" (*kai-shou*). Furthermore, "bowing one's head" refers to paying respect through the action of the body.
When the body pays respect, the mouth invokes the virtuous title, and the mind maintains contemplative visualization; this constitutes the offering of the three karmas.
*Buddha* is the full term; here it is translated as "Awakened" (*jue*). This awakening possesses three meanings: first, self-awakening—realizing that the nature is truly eternal and...

First, awakening from delusion and falsehood. Second, awakening others: by exercising unconditional compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), one delivers the multitudes of sentient beings. Third, the perfection of the practice of awakening:

having exhausted the source and reached the ultimate depth, the practice is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled. As for "Dharma," it refers to the essential points of the pure Dharma taught by the Tathāgata according to the capacities and natures of beings;
when sentient beings rely upon it with faith and practice it, they attain great liberation and will certainly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. If...

Explaining it according to its meaning: "Dharma" (dharma) has the sense of being a guide and a support. That is to say, it guides so as to produce understanding in beings and maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
All phenomena each maintain their own intrinsic nature, whether they are relinquished or not;

each maintains its own intrinsic nature, just as water flows downward and fire rises upward—their natures are each determined. This is the essence of dharma. "Guide" (*viniścaya*) means a model or standard that can produce [understanding].
Understanding things is like using fire to cook food or water to float a boat; each takes its own principle, which constitutes the application of the Dharma (*dharmaprayoga*).

Regarding the term "Bhikṣu-saṃgha," it contains three meanings and possesses the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*), as explained previously. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are five kinds of saṃghas:
first, the shameless saṃgha, which consists of those who break the precepts; second, the sheep-like saṃgha, which consists of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) of dull faculties.

1. Those lacking wisdom, like a flock of sheep gathered in one place, who do not know the *poṣadha*, do not know the *poṣadha-karman*, do not know the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-vācana*), and do not know the Dharma assemblies;
these are the three types of separate communities that perform various *karman* separately within a single boundary.
2. The pure community of ordinary persons who maintain the precepts. 3. The true community of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa), it is this person who is the object of veneration here; specifically, one pays homage to the latter two types of Saṃgha.

This is because the *tattvika-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha in its ultimate sense) enables the ultimate True Dharma (*paramārtha-saddharma*) to endure for a long time, while the *viśuddha-saṃgha* (the pure Saṃgha) enables the conventional True Dharma (*saṃvṛti-saddharma*) to endure for a long time.
As for the phrase "now expounding the Vinaya rules," "now" refers to the actual time of reciting the precepts, excluding the past and future. "Expounding" (*vyākaroti*) means...

This proclaims its circulation. The Sanskrit term *vinaya* translates here as "extinction" (*miè*). However, extinction has three meanings: first, the extinction of unwholesome karma (referring to such acts as not stealing;

thus, within the Vinaya, there is the *vinaya* regarding offenses and the *vinaya* regarding disputes); second, the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*) (since afflictions are the root that gives rise to karma, the Vinaya states that one must subdue greed and other passions until they are exhausted;

for this reason, the Tathāgata established the training in higher morality); third, the attainment of the fruit of extinction (therefore, a sutra says: "With pure precepts and wisdom, one shall attain the foremost path").

King Seonjo said: "To translate *vinaya* as 'extinguishing' (*mie*) or 'subduing' (*tiaofu*) is to name it according to its function; it is not the correct translation. The correct translation is 'law' (*lü*).
'Law' means 'dharma. It is named according to its teaching. It adjudicates the gravity of offenses, what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts.
Without the dharma, there would be no certainty. Among the nine schools of worldly learning, the school of dharma occupies one; thus, it is called 'worldly law' (*shifalü*)."

All [matters] are determined by the penal statutes. Since the Way differs from secular custom, the terminology of the penal codes is distinct; yet, as for adjudication, one must invariably rely on established law.
Therefore, this Vinaya was translated. Regarding the phrase "so that the True Dharma may abide long": the True Dharma is the supramundane, untainted Path of the Sages.
When the True Dharma abides in the world, the three aspects of teaching, practice, and fruition are all fully complete. This is due to the administration of the *karmavācanā*.

Through the purification of the *poṣadha*, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is perfected, concentration and wisdom arise, and one may hope for the attainment of the untainted fruits of the noble ones (*anāsrava-āryaphala*).
If the *poṣadha* is neglected, the practice of ethical discipline becomes impure, and there will be no day when the True Dharma (*saddharma*) does not perish.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The *vinaya* is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; as long as the *vinaya* endures, the True Dharma will endure for a long time. Therefore, it is said:
Now I shall expound the Dharma of the Vinaya so that the True Dharma may abide for a long time.
The precepts are like a boundless ocean; they are like jewels sought without satiety. Desiring to protect the wealth of the Noble Dharma, all you gathered here, listen as I speak.
Commentary: This single verse consists of two lines above that reveal the merit of the precepts, and two lines below that exhort one to listen so as to obtain benefit.
The *Khandhaka* states: "The waters of the ocean possess eight extraordinary qualities, for which reason the asuras dwell there in enjoyment."
First, all streams flow toward it and enter it. Second, its tides do not miss their appointed limits.
Third, when the five great rivers enter the sea, they lose their original names. Fourth, though rivers and celestial rains all flow into it, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Fifth, it has a single uniform salty taste. Sixth, it does not accept corpses. Seventh, it produces many rare treasures.
Eighth is the dwelling place of great forms. Within my Dharma there are likewise eight wonders, by which all disciples, having seen them, find delight therein.
First, my disciples study the precepts progressively and all return to my Dharma.
Second, my disciples abide within the precepts and do not transgress them until death. Third, the four...

First, they abandon their families and surnames, all calling themselves śramaṇas. Second, within my Dharma, with firm faith, they leave home to study the Path and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder;
yet in that realm of nirvana, there is neither increase nor decrease. Third, they share the same taste of liberation.
Fourth, those who violate the precepts and harbor evil dharmas, though they sit among the assembly, are always far removed from the Saṃgha.
The community of monks is also far removed from that. Seventh, there is the abundant production of precious treasures, namely the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Eighth, there is the attainment of great forms, namely the four stages of approach and the four fruits of realization. The Fundamental Vinaya states:
The great ocean of the Vinaya has shores so vast and boundless that they are difficult to know; its diverse characteristics are infinite—how could I possibly detail them all?
The Great Master’s ocean of the Vinaya teachings is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; therefore, it is said that "the precepts are like an ocean without shore."
As for "one who seeks jewels without weariness," the jewel refers to the pure King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*) within the ocean.

It can, according to the requests of sentient beings, rain down all the requisites of happiness throughout Jambudvīpa in every moment of thought, yet the substance of the jewel never suffers any depletion.
Within the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, the *śīla* (ethical discipline) is as bright and pure; it can, in every moment of thought, give birth to...

Regarding all the sublime and virtuous factors—such as the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, up to the noble fruits of the three vehicles—the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*) never undergoes change; it is like that king of jewels which never tires of bestowing its gifts.
As for the wealth of the noble Dharma, briefly stated, it consists of seven factors: faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame; extensively stated, it is...
These are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path. Yet, these treasures of the Dharma cannot be guarded without precepts.

Precepts possess the merit of preventing what is wrong and ceasing evil; they are like a strong army and valiant generals who can subdue hostile enemies, or like a sturdy city with deep moats that can resist demonic thieves, not allowing them to find an opening or to commit acts of aggression. Therefore, one who desires—
"Guard this noble wealth of the Dharma. Let the assembly listen as I speak. "The assembly" refers to four or more pure bhikṣus, up to hundreds or thousands.
"Gathered" means that body and mind are harmoniously assembled. "Listen" means that the faculty of hearing gives rise to consciousness and hears.
"As proclaimed according to the Vinaya" means that each bhikṣu seated there receives and upholds it exactly as spoken.
To eliminate the four *pārājika* dharmas, And to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, Which obstruct the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules— I shall now speak;
may the assembly listen.
This one verse clarifies listening to the precepts in order to remain free from transgressions. The "four abandonments" (*catur-pārājika*) refer to the four fundamental root offenses. The *saṃgha*...
The *śeṣa* (residual) offenses consist of the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*; the *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* consist of the thirty [offenses involving forfeiture].

These are explained as in the section on "Restraint through Observance" (*sthiti-dhāra*). Now, regarding the five categories of the precepts (*śīla-dharma*), only three are mentioned here because the remaining two are minor;

their texts are abbreviated, yet their meanings are subsumed. How much more so, then, can the hearing of the precepts give rise to all manner of wholesome qualities and protect the wealth of the Dharma?

Since karma that can truly be permanently severed is neither pure nor defiled, one who wishes to eliminate, discard, extinguish, and cease residual obstacles and falls should cause the Saṃgha to assemble in harmony.
Listen as I proclaim this, so that you may distance yourselves from such faults.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni—
To these World-Honored Ones of great virtue, I speak this matter for you;
listen all together, O worthy ones, as I now wish to explain it well.
Commentary: The preceding verse summarizes the seven Buddhas; the subsequent verse describes the instruction and requests their attention.
Vipaśyin is also called Vīkṣin. This name has four meanings: because his wisdom is as perfect as the moon, he is called "All-Seeing" (Vipaśyin);
because his delusions are exhausted and eliminated, he is called "Pure Vision" (Vīkṣin); and since he is both perfect and pure, he is called "Supreme Vision" (Vīkṣin).

He is also called *Śikhin*, which is also named *Śikhi*; this translates as "Fire" and also as "Topknot-Holder," meaning that non-discriminative wisdom is most supreme and dwells at the crown of the heart. *Viśvabhū* is fully expressed as *Viśvabhū*.

He is also named Viśvabhū, which translates as "Pervading All with Sovereignty. Because his wisdom is perfect and his fruition is complete, he is honored as the most venerable among two-legged beings.
The three Buddhas mentioned above appeared in the world at the end of the past *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa* (Adornment Eon).
Kṛkī (Kakutsunda) translates as "That Which Should Be Severed," and is also translated as "Adorned by Function," meaning that he is able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Afflictions are forever extinguished without remainder; he is adorned with ten thousand virtues. Kanakamuni—this translates as "Golden Silence" or alternatively "Golden Immortal.
"Gold" signifies a firm essence; among the five colors, yellow is supreme, and its radiance is most brilliant and blazing.
"Silence" represents unimpeded wisdom that is tranquil and unmoving. This means that this World-Honored One has attained firm, unsurpassed, and unimpeded [wisdom].
Wisdom is tranquil and unmoving. Kāśyapa is translated here as "Drinking Light" (飲光), meaning that the radiance of his body is so magnificent it eclipses all other lights.
Śākyamuni is also named Śākya-muni; this is translated as "Capable Sage" (能儒) and also as "Capable Benevolent One in Silent Stillness" (能仁寂默).
Because he is silent and still, he does not abide in birth and death—this is the meaning of self-benefit. Because he is capable and benevolent...
Not abiding in nirvana is the meaning of benefiting others. Internally, he realizes the principle of wisdom; externally, he proclaims the transformation of virtue.

Because wisdom and compassion are practiced in tandem, this auspicious title was established. The four Buddhas mentioned above appeared in succession at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa to transform beings through the Way.
As for the reason why these seven Buddhas are spoken of in various places: first, it is because they appeared within a single hundred minor kalpas. Pure...

Because he dwells where gods and humans have never before seen him. Second, it refers to the fact that our Original Teacher cultivated the karma for the marks and signs beginning from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
The World-Honored One (Bhagavān) is fully endowed with the ten titles;

revered by the nine realms, he is the teacher of gods and humans, the king among all sages, and the peerless, supreme honor among both the mundane and supramundane worlds. "The Virtuous One" (Mahātman) means:

"The various World-Honored Ones rescue all sentient beings; they possess the virtue of great compassion and exercise the teachings of subduing and gathering through their possession of great majestic power.
Therefore, those who speak of this matter for my sake" — this phrase clearly elucidates the transmission between teacher and disciple, demonstrating that it is not a mere fabrication.
"I" refers to the one currently present among the assembly who recites the precepts, speaking of himself. "This matter" refers to the four matters and the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses].
The matters range up to the one hundred rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*). Regarding the phrase "well-spoken" (*svākhyāta*):
it means speaking in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, such that the words and phrases are free from error or confusion.

The phrase "all you virtuous ones, listen together" serves to exclude the possibility of a discordant assembly. "All" refers to those starting from the newly ordained monks (*upasaṃpanna*) who have no years of seniority (*anvaya*), up to...

All those who have attained one hundred years of seniority (śatavarṣa-sthavira) should assemble to listen. Beginning from the *Śīlaskandha* (the introductory section on precepts) up to the verses of the Seven Buddhas, they should cleanse their thoughts, join their palms, and listen with single-minded attention.
"Worthy" (*bhadra*) is a designation for those possessing virtue; it is equivalent to what is called the "Venerable Sangha" (*mahā-bhadanta-saṃgha*).
Now, because the World-Honored One is honored as "Venerable" (Bhadanta), the Saṃgha has replaced that term with "Worthy Ones" (Āyuṣmats).
Just as a person whose feet are destroyed is unable to travel anywhere, so too is one who destroys the precepts unable to be born among gods or humans.
If one wishes to be born in the heavens or, if born in the human realm, [to attain excellence].
One should always protect the feet of the precepts, And not allow them to be damaged or destroyed.
(This is the first verse. The first two lines establish a metaphor; the latter two lines apply the Dharma to it, clarifying how obstacles arise on the path to the good realms.
The subsequent verse: the first two lines indicate birth in the happy destinies; the latter two lines provide the Dharma and the metaphor.

This is stated as a pair to admonish one to protect wholesome causes. "For example" (*tadyathā*) is a term used for hypothetical illustration. "Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) means to ruin; "trampling" (*kramaṇa*) means to tread upon.
"Heavenly beings" (*deva*) refers to the various devas of the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness. "Human beings" (*manuṣya*) refers to the human race within the four continents.
As for the statement that they are "born among humans and heavenly beings," it is because the people of the Western Regions (India) mostly seek pleasure.
They are reborn in the heavens. When a Buddha appears in the world, he preaches the causes and effects of human and celestial realms according to their inclinations;
however, this is not the ultimate intention of the Noble Ones, nor is it the core purport of the Vinaya. Although he speaks of "human and celestial," his true aim is *nirvāṇa*. As it is said:

"First, one uses the hook of desire to entice them, and later leads them into the Buddha-wisdom. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Whether they aspire for the human realm or seek the heavenly realms..."
Those who diligently practice the holy life (brahmacarya) attain birth among humans or devas and experience temporary happiness; yet after their lives end, they enter the hells.
Therefore, one should seek nirvana in order to practice the holy life, rather than delighting in the realms of humans and devas which lead only to toil and suffering.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "There are two perilous paths: first, birth in the heavens; second, the evil destinies. Although one may be born..."

Even if one experiences all manner of supreme pleasures as a deva, once that retribution is exhausted, one falls back into the evil realms. Thus, the states of humans and devas are not what one should truly desire.
Furthermore, the precepts are likened to feet; there is nowhere they cannot reach. Their significance lies in their profound depth, meaning that the "feet" of the precepts must not be destroyed.
If they are destroyed, one cannot even be reborn among humans or devas, let alone attain nirvāṇa. Moreover, one must be fully endowed with...
The practice of the precepts is the supreme primary cause for rebirth in the Pure Land.
In a single moment of thought, one may approach and make offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions, and upon returning to one’s own land, listen to the wondrous Dharma.
Such inconceivable power of spiritual transformation is entirely brought about by guarding the precepts without impairment.
"Just as a driver entering a perilous road Is anxious when the axle breaks and the linchpin fails, So too is it with one who has violated the precepts;
At the time of death, they harbor fear.
This is one verse. The first two lines establish a metaphor, while the latter two lines demonstrate the recognition of its faults. The preceding...
The verse cites the Vinaya, which refers to the realms of humans and devas as "perilous paths. Here, however, it specifically designates the three miserable destinies (*durgati*) as perilous paths.
The axle is the pivot upon which the chariot wheels turn; the pin is the iron bolt at the head of the axle.

At the moment of death, one realizes for oneself that one has broken the precepts and will inevitably fall into the evil destinies—just like losing the pin or breaking the axle midway on a perilous path, one is struck with terror and panic.
They are without support and without refuge. The *Chapter on Vows and Practices* states:
"To close the gates of all evil destinies and to open and reveal the true path to humans, devas, and nirvāṇa is truly due to the efficacy of strictly maintaining the prohibitive precepts."

As when a person looks into a mirror, Joy or grief arises from what is beautiful or ugly; So it is with the recitation of the precepts: One feels sorrow or delight based on their being complete or violated.
This one verse consists of two lines that establish a metaphor, and two lines that reveal the integrity or deficiency of the precepts. As...
When a person looks at their own face in a mirror, they rejoice if their features are upright and feel sorrowful if their appearance is ugly.
Now, at this very time of reciting the precepts, having heard them, you should reflect upon and examine the precepts you have received and uphold.
If they are entirely pure and without flaw, you will harbor joy within and feel no shame before others; if there is anything that has been violated or defiled, then...
Within, one gives rise to sorrow and distress; without, one feels shame before others.
Just as when two armies engage in battle, the brave advance while the timid retreat, so it is with the recitation of the precepts:
purity and defilement give rise respectively to peace and fear.
Commentary: This single verse consists of two lines that establish a metaphor, followed by two lines that clarify the gain and loss regarding the precepts.
It is like two armies engaged in mutual combat: the brave advance with vigor, while the cowardly retreat in fear.

Now, when the assembly gathers to recite the precepts, it is precisely a time of waging war against the demonic army of the afflictions (*kleśa*). If the precepts are pure, this is the power of firm adherence.
The valiant one dwells together with the assembly; body and mind are both at ease. The defilement of the precepts refers to the timidity of one's resolve in practice.

Although such a person lives among the community, their heart is truly afraid of sensual desires; they cannot subdue the army of the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) and, on the contrary, are overcome by those afflictions.
Among those in the world, the king is supreme; Among all streams, the ocean is supreme; Among all stars, the moon is supreme;
Among all noble ones, the Buddha is supreme. Among all the various codes of discipline, The Sūtra of Precepts is the highest and most supreme.
The Tathāgata established these prohibitions and precepts, To be recited every half-month.
Commentary: This preceding verse cites a metaphor to praise his virtues. Anyone who receives the bhikṣu precepts is called a "Great Śramaṇa.
The Sanskrit term is *mahā*, which is translated here as "Great" (*dà*). This term "Great" encompasses three meanings. First, it signifies greatness.
Because he is the most honored among devas and humans; second, because he is abundant, possessing both merit and wisdom; third, because he is supreme, transcending all non-Buddhists.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "Among the assembly of devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, the śramaṇa, the son of the Śākyas, is the foremost.
Now, the first phrase is a praise based on a great analogy, while the next phrase is...
The third line praises by means of many metaphors; the fourth line praises by summarizing through many, great, and superior metaphors.
The final verse correctly applies these to the Dharma: that among all codes of discipline (*vinaya*), the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is the supreme and most excellent.
This refers to the fact that even the secular laws of worldly nations and the heterodox doctrines of non-Buddhist paths each have their own [codes].

The Vinaya cannot cause people to be liberated from their fetters and exit the realm of transmigration; only the Buddha’s Vinaya can rescue sentient beings, enabling them to transcend the mundane and enter the state of sainthood.
Furthermore, the five precepts, eight precepts, and ten precepts within the Buddha’s Vinaya are not equal to the full set of Bhikṣu precepts.
Moreover, the *samādhi-saṃvara* (meditative restraint) and *mārga-saṃvara* (path restraint) are not equal to the *Prātimokṣa* precepts. [The root...]
The Fundamental Vinaya states: "The Buddhas who realize Bodhi, the Pratyekabuddhas with pure body and mind, and the Arhats—all are accomplished through the practice of the Vinaya.
All the sages and saints of the three periods of time, who have distanced themselves from the bonds of conditioned existence, take the Vinaya as their foundation."
Because it can lead one to the place of peace and security, it is said that among all the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*), the Sūtra on Precepts (*śīla-sūtra*) is supreme and foremost.
Since the precepts received are supreme and foremost, those who receive them likewise become supreme.

When the Tathāgata establishes the prohibitions and precepts, this demonstrates that the precepts are ordained solely by the Buddha and are not something others are capable of establishing. It is like the rewards, punishments, and edicts of a state.
If one does not follow the king, ministers will overstep their bounds and commoners will lose faith; ruin will come before long. The Buddha-dharma is likewise:

if it permits other doctrines, sentient beings will not uphold it, and the Dharma will not endure for long. For this reason, the prohibitions and precepts were established solely by the Buddha himself.
As for the instruction to recite them every half-month, it uses the waxing and waning phases of the moon to symbolize the two aspects of good and evil.

Regarding karma: one desires that the black be exhausted and the white perfected. Furthermore, "white" represents the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while "black" represents the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Therefore, this fixed period was established as the foundation for reciting the precepts. In the *Vinayakṣudraka-vastu*, the Buddha said:
"I command you all to recite the *Prātimokṣa* every half-month; you should know that this is your great [precept]."
The Teacher is your refuge; it is no different than if I were dwelling in the world.
△ This explains the Preface to the Precepts (divided into four expositions):
"Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts. Listen attentively and reflect well."
Reflect upon this. If you know for yourself that you have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it; if you have not committed an offense, remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that the Venerable Ones are pure.

Explanation: "Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts. This marks the fundamental principle and establishes the formal framework, informing the assembly so that they may take note.
Now that the time for the recitation of the precepts has arrived, each person should restrain the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) and be careful to avoid distraction.
"Venerable" (*bhadanta*) is explained as before; it is a respectful title used in the Vinaya. *Prātimokṣa*...
This is translated as *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

"Individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*) refers to the gradual and successive abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions—ranging from the lowest of the low to the highest of the high—by practicing according to the instructions of this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, such that one never regresses."
Because one attains liberation from all afflictions, it is called *Prātimokṣa* (Individual Liberation).

It is also called "preserving liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), meaning that when the precepts are pure and free from flaw, concentration and wisdom are generated; for the Tathāgata guarantees that one will certainly realize *nirvāṇa*.
"Listen attentively" means to listen with truthfulness and reality so as to enter into the meaning of the words, thereby accomplishing the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Well done!
As for "contemplating," it means one should contemplate according to the meaning; one should recollect it without forgetting in order to accomplish the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Having heard and contemplated to discern the meaning, one should abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome in order to accomplish the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
If one knows for oneself that one has committed an offense, one should immediately repent of it oneself. This means that one must know for oneself whether one is defiled or pure; how could...

One may conceal [a fault]. If there is a transgression for which one has never previously confessed and sought repentance before others, at the time of this recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one should immediately speak of it oneself, confess the offense, and then be permitted to hear the precepts. One must not remain apart from the assembly;

do not wait for another to raise the matter so as to cause an obstruction. As for "confession" (*kṣamāpanā*): "confessing" (*ksama*) means to cultivate the future, and "repenting" (*pana*) means to reform.
"Past" refers to what was done in former days; because it was base and evil, one feels remorse for it.

"Repentance" (懺) means that all wholesome dharmas abandoned in the past shall henceforth be diligently cultivated according to one's vows. Abandoning the past and seeking the future—these combined are termed "repentance" (懺悔).
As for those who have not transgressed, they remain silent. "Not having transgressed" means that from the beginning there was no transgression; or, [if there was a transgression,]...
Having thus spoken of repentance, you should listen with single-minded silence and utmost sincerity. By remaining silent, the Venerable Ones acknowledge their purity;
this signifies that the Saṃgha is pure and harmonious, and it is therefore appropriate that the precepts be recited according to the Vinaya and the Dharma.

If others should ask him, he should answer in the same way. Thus, if a bhikṣu remains among the assembly and, even after being asked three times, remembers having committed an offense yet does not confess it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has declared that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the path.
Commentary: If others should question one, one should answer in this same manner.

That is to say, just as one answers truthfully when questioned by others at other times, so too should one answer truthfully when questioned during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. "In this way, the bhikṣus... and so forth.
The term "bhikṣu" refers to the person who has committed an offense. "In the midst of the assembly" refers to the pure community of monks gathered before one's eyes.

The phrase "three times" ensures the completion of the formal inquiry, avoiding both prolixity and brevity; for if it were too brief, those who are dull-witted would find it difficult to grasp immediately, and those lacking a sense of shame would fail to give rise to remorse.
Conversely, if it were too prolix, there would be fear that the time would be drawn out excessively, causing the assembly to grow weary from sitting.
According to the Vinaya, the formal procedure for the *dharmas* consists of only three questions.
If one remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose and repent it, one incurs the offense of intentional lying (*saṃprajāna-mṛṣāvāda*).

However, even if one does not speak, because the verbal action is manifested through bodily gestures, there is no offense of lying even if one previously committed an offense but now no longer remembers or knows of it. Within each individual question, according to...
If one remembers the offense when asked three times, and yet commits three instances of false speech, this constitutes an obstructive dharma.
For the Buddha has taught that intentional lying obstructs the first *dhyāna* through to the fourth *dhyāna*; it obstructs the first fruit through to the fourth fruit;
and it obstructs the path to *nirvāṇa*.
If that bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purity, he should perform confession; through confession, one attains peace and happiness.
*Explanation:* This means that if a bhikṣu endowed with a sense of shame and remorse remembers having committed an offense and desires to purify his body of precepts...

Regarding purification: one should, as a matter of principle, personally confess and repent. It is not out of fear of being interrogated by others or receiving punishment that one openly declares one's confession and attains peace and happiness.

"Peace" means that body and mind are tranquil and stable, such that afflictions do not invade; this constitutes peace. To be "far removed from faults and transgressions" means to distance oneself from errors and non-virtue.
To realize the fruit of the Path—this is what brings joy.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times. Venerable sirs, because you are silent, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall it be held.
Commentary: This concludes the inquiry. "The introduction to the Sūtra of Precepts" means that this serves as the preamble to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in its two hundred and fifty articles.
It is called the "preliminary" because it enables the subsequent teachings to arise.
"Regarding this matter, 'thus it is held' means it is understood as such. Having questioned the assembly three times, all are pure.
Because the entire assembly is pure and remains silent, I now understand this matter in this way and am fit to proclaim the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Having recited this introduction to the precepts and having finished reciting the characteristics of the precepts in their proper order, he further summarizes, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have already recited the four pārājika dharmas;
I have already recited the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas; I have already recited the two aniyata dharmas; I have already recited the thirty naiḥsargika..."
The *Śaikṣa* Dharmas. The ninety *Pāyattika* Dharmas have been explained. The four *Pratideśanīya* Dharmas have been explained.
The *Saiksa* Dharmas have been explained. The seven *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* Dharmas have been explained.
These were spoken by the Buddha and are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Whatever other teachings of the Buddha there may be, they are all contained herein.
"Be in communal harmony; this is how you should train.

Commentary: This passage concludes the preceding exhortation to practice. It means that one should not merely assemble together every half-month to hear and recite the *Prātimokṣa* precepts and maintain them strictly without transgression; there are furthermore further regulations established within the various *Khandakas*.
Regarding these dharmas, as well as the methods of the Sūtras, Abhidharma, concentration, and wisdom—one should diligently practice them all therein.

This is what a bhikṣu ought to study: that both [the teacher and the student] may be in harmony, exerting themselves with diligence in cultivation, so that there may be an increase in virtue, an increase in mind, and an increase in wisdom.
△ This explains the verse of the Seven Buddhas:
Patience is the supreme path; the Buddha has taught that non-action is foremost. One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Commentary: As for "patience," it is only when one can bring peace to the internal mind that one is able to endure external objects of insult.

Patience is of two kinds: first, patience regarding sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*); second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Patience regarding sentient beings is further divided into two:
first, being able to endure without attachment amidst favorable circumstances of respect and offerings, so that arrogance does not arise;
second, being able to endure amidst adverse circumstances of anger, abuse, beating, and harm, so that resentment, malice, and vexation do not arise. This is called patience regarding sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). First is that which pertains to non-mental phenomena, namely cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Second is that which pertains to mental phenomena, namely anger, grief, lust, pride, and so forth.
If one can endure these two types of phenomena without being moved, this is called patience regarding phenomena. Furthermore, one observes the nature of arising phenomena with right wisdom.
The nature of phenomena is empty; patience cannot be apprehended. Since suffering is empty and without self, who is there to exercise patience?
When patience itself is empty, the principle of non-arising is revealed, and one immediately realizes nirvana. This patience is the shortcut to nirvana, and is therefore called the foremost path.
Nirvana is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is described as profoundly tranquil and eternally quiescent, free from all fabrication, and transcending existence.
This is the realm for which he strives. He has transcended the stream of birth and death; there is no dharma superior to this, and thus it is called "supreme" (*agra*).

As for the term *śramaṇa*, the *Āgama* Sūtras state: one who has abandoned affection and love, left the household life to cultivate the Way, restrained the faculties, remained untainted by external desires, maintained a heart of loving-kindness toward all beings without causing harm, and neither rejoiced in meeting with pleasure nor... [encountered suffering].
One who does not grieve in suffering and can endure like the earth is therefore called a śramaṇa.

If one leaves the household life yet fails to practice patience, instead seeking revenge and vexing others, then one violates the Way of Non-contention; how could such a person be said to follow the conduct of a śramaṇa?
If you wish to attain the supreme path, you must not afflict others. If you hope for the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), you must fulfill the conduct of a śramaṇa.
Thus, patience is the cause for transcending the world, while the unconditioned is its fruit.
Afflicting others is the cause for birth and death (*saṃsāra*), while failing to be a śramaṇa is its fruit. Good and evil are both clearly manifested. Purity.
When the impurities have been removed, those who possess wisdom should discern and follow [the path]. "Vipaśyin and the others" refers to the Dharma previously explained;
this now clarifies the Buddhas who are able to teach it. All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess both general and specific names;
"Vipaśyin" is a specific name, as explained previously. "Tathāgata, Arhat," and so forth...
"Perfectly Awakened One" (Sambuddha) is a general title. In the Sanskrit language, *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus Come One.
In the Sanskrit language, *Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings," and is also translated as "One Free from Attachment.

In the Sanskrit language, *Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Perfectly and Fully Knowing One," and is also translated as "Equal and Perfect Awakening. These are three of the ten epithets [of a Buddha]. Regarding the latter six...
The titles of the Buddhas and Śākyamuni are to be understood accordingly;
they need not be elaborated upon here. Just as a person with clear vision is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths, so too can a wise person in this world remain far removed from all evils.
This is the *Śīla-sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin.
Commentary: The first two lines present a simile; the latter two lines apply the Dharma to the case at hand.

This means that if there is one in the world who is wise, who can have faith in the Buddha and hear the Dharma, and for whom right view is manifest before them, they will immediately know what is the path and what is not the path. As for that which is not the path:

The six realms of existence are perilous paths; this Way is called the level thoroughfare of the Eightfold Noble Path. Perilous paths are brought about by unwholesome causes, while the level thoroughfare is reached by relying on superior wisdom.
Therefore, one must distance oneself from all evil causes and strive to cultivate the essentials for transcending the world.
In the end, one arrives at the place of eternal bliss, Nirvana. It is like a person with clear vision whose path before them is bright and distinct;
they do not take a dangerous route, distance themselves from all fears, and ultimately reach a place of peace and security.
"All evils" refers to the delusions of the three realms, such as views, afflictions, and ignorance. The two names—general and specific—of the Tathāgata Śikhin are as explained previously.

Regarding the explanation: the *Vinayaviniścaya* states that when the Buddha Śikhin appeared in the world, many of his śrāvakas practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of rebirth in the heavens, seeking to enjoy sublime celestial pleasures in future lives.
At that time, the Buddha, wishing to provide an antidote for his assembly of disciples, preached this concise teaching.
Do not slander, nor be envious; one should practice the precepts with diligence. Know moderation in food and drink, always delighting in solitude.
With a concentrated mind, take joy in energetic effort—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
Commentary: Slander is an action of speech; envy is an action of mind. To wish to be free from these two, one should practice and uphold the precepts.
When the precepts are pure, the three types of action are instantly abandoned; what cause for concern would there be regarding the impurity of speech and mind? Food and drink pertain to the mouth.
One who constantly delights in focused attention and is content will cease their deluded pursuit; one who dwells in seclusion will find all discursive thoughts naturally stilled.

Through this, the mind becomes clear and enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*), giving rise to wisdom (*prajñā*) to sever afflictions. Only those who delight in diligent effort and the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) are able to dwell in seclusion;
such a place is the tranquil site of an *araṇya*. By relying on this location and diligently cultivating the gates of concentration, one will certainly attain [realization].
The noble fruit (āryaphala). The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time follow this same track in instructing their disciples; therefore, it is said:
"This is called the teaching of all Buddhas. The general and specific epithets of "Buddha" are explained as before.
Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Neither destroying its color nor its fragrance, But taking only its nectar and departing;
So too should a bhikṣu enter a village, Not interfering with others' affairs, Observing neither what is done nor what is left undone,
But observing only his own conduct, Whether it be right or wrong.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Commentary:
It is like a wandering bee gathering from flowers; it takes only the nectar and departs, without damaging the color or fragrance of the flower.

It is the same when a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for alms. He must not act contrary to the affairs of others. "Contrary" (wei) means opposition; "contrariness" (li) means transgression or offense.
That is to say, when a bhikṣu begs for food, he should seek only what is sufficient to sustain his body and assist the Path, accepting whatever is offered according to the generosity of others.
Being content, he returns home. He must not over-reach or act contrary to others' needs, thereby destroying their pure faith and respectful mind. This is exactly the same [as the previous case].
A bee gathers nectar from flowers without destroying their color or fragrance. Regarding "not observing whether one acts or does not act":
this means that since one should not oppose others, one must likewise refrain from observing the gains and losses of others, which would disturb the mind and body and hinder the practice of the Way.

Rather, one should only observe the conduct of one's own body and examine it. If one is personally free of fault, then the person is pure and upright; if there is a transgression, then one should [rectify] the action.

Because it is defiled and deviant, it is said to be "whether correct or incorrect. These two names of the Buddha—the general and the specific—are to be understood according to the previous explanation.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "When the Buddha Krakucchanda appeared in the world, many of his śrāvaka disciples longed for gain and honor and became arrogant regarding their virtuous qualities. To restrain them, he proclaimed this brief teaching."
Do not be negligent in mind; you should diligently train in the noble Dharma. Thus, free from sorrow, with a concentrated mind, one enters Nirvana.
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.
Commentary: Because of heedfulness, one is able to diligently train in the Noble Path. Because of training in the Noble Path, the afflictions of sorrow and distress are eliminated.
Because these afflictions such as sorrow and distress are eliminated, the mind becomes tranquil and enters right concentration.

By attaining meditative concentration, one realizes *nirvāṇa* and delights in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This constitutes the severing of the origin of suffering, the cultivation of the path, and the realization of cessation.
If the mind is negligent and accumulates evil causes, it will invite the bitter fruit of sorrow and lamentation.

If one does not cultivate the path, perceive the truths, and realize cessation, then even if one attains a concentrated mind, afflictions and delusions remain undestroyed; one will continue to transmigrate through the three realms of existence, beset by sorrow.
How can one be liberated from suffering? These are the general and specific names of the Buddha, as explained previously:
Commit no evil whatsoever; Practice all that is wholesome; Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Commentary:

"All evils" refers to the afflictions of the three poisons, which give rise to the various offenses—both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*)—committed through body and speech.
"All virtues" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all gateways to the Dharma. "Refrain from evil and do not commit it" means to abstain from these transgressions.
This precept uses the precepts to guard and prohibit the seven branches [of bodily and vocal action]. The poisonous natures, karma, and obstructive karma are all rendered pure.
Strive to practice this diligently. This precept increases the cultivation of the three trainings, extensively accumulates manifold virtues, and brings the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to completion.

To benefit oneself and save others, and to purify one’s own will and intention, means to rely upon and uphold the *vinaya*, to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and to give rise to the truth.

Uncontaminated wisdom destroys all false inversions and realizes that delusions are unborn; the mind is fundamentally pure from the start, free from the marks of defilement and impurity, and all things are empty.
Therefore, it is said: "One purifies one's own will. Although the ocean of Dharma is vast, these three [precepts] encompass it entirely.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have saved sentient beings according to their capacities, no differently than this. Therefore, it is said: "This is the teaching of all Buddhas."
Thus it is. The general and specific explanations of this Buddha’s name follow the previous pattern.
Guard well your verbal expressions; Purify your own intentions; Commit no evil with the body.
When these three paths of action are pure, One who can practice in such a way Traverses the path of the Great Sages.

This is the *Pātimokkha* Sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the community of monks who were free from affairs during the twelve years [following his enlightenment]. From this time forward, it shall be explained in detail.

For those bhikṣus who delight in the Dharma, who delight in being śramaṇas, and who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame while delighting in training in the precepts, they should [apply themselves] therein.
Commentary on the Study: When the Buddhas appear in the world, they observe the capacities of sentient beings and establish their teachings; thus, the Dharma is not fixed.

The World-Honored One appeared during this age of the five turbidities and evil times, when people were fond of contention, failed to guard their speech, and possessed heavy defilements of mind. Even if [the faults] were not manifest...
Regarding objects, one recollects past experiences and gives rise to desire and volition, thereby performing unwholesome physical actions.
For this reason, the Tathāgata warns against them, so that they may be prevented in their nascent state through gradual cultivation.

If one can thus guard oneself well, refraining from unwholesome acts and purifying oneself, then the three types of action will be pure and the dharma of the ten paths of wholesome conduct will be accomplished. Now, as for these ten paths of wholesome conduct:
The Dharma. There is not a single being among humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or Buddhas who does not rely upon it;
therefore, it is called "the path of the Great Sage. The Tathāgata is the God among Gods, the Sage among Sages, and the Honored One among Men; thus, he is titled the "Great Sage.
The two names of Śākyamuni Tathāgata—the general and the specific—have already been explained previously. For twelve years...
Regarding the statement, "To the monks of no-affairs (*avastuka*), he preached this Sūtra of Precepts": "monks of no-affairs" refers to those who do not transgress the precepts.
Prior to the fifth year after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, the assembly of monks all practiced with contentment;
there were no affairs to be transgressed and no precepts to be established. He merely set forth the general principles and briefly instructed them. From the fifth year thereafter, among the monks...
Defiled phenomena arise; in order to sever those defiled phenomena, he extensively established two hundred and fifty rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
Within these, there are further fundamental derivations, including permissions and prohibitions, as well as matters of gravity and lightness. These are what a bhikṣu receives and upholds.
It is said that during the twelve years [of the Buddha’s ministry], the teachings of the Āgamas were subsumed within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. This Āgama, in its entirety...
This is the twelfth discourse. Regarding those who take delight in the Dharma as śramaṇas: "Dharma" here refers to the Dharma of the precepts.
Pure observance of the precepts is the cause of the śramaṇa’s outflow-free state; the realization of arhatship is the fruit of the śramaṇa’s outflow-free state.
If the causes are not complete, the fruit cannot be established. Therefore, it is said that one delights in the Dharma and delights in being a śramaṇa.

Those who possess gradual progress and a sense of shame (*hrī*) delight in training in the precepts. *Hrī* is internal self-reproach; *apatrāpya* (shame before others) is the disclosure of one's faults to others.
If these two qualities of *hrī* and *apatrāpya* did not exist in the world, all would transgress the pure path of the noble ones and head toward various evils.
This is a perilous path. However, this *prātimokṣa* precept cannot be firmly believed in or joyfully studied by those who are shameless, lacking in conscience, or ignorant.

Those who should study within it—namely, within these two hundred and fifty rules of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-vinaya*) and the *Saptabuddha-saṃkṣipta-śīla-sūtra*—should practice them with diligence and exertion, guarding them carefully without transgression.
By means of this, one transcends the great suffering and afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and likewise does not fall into the censure of being like a mute sheep.
This clarifies the dedication verse at the end of the scroll (divided into six expositions).
The wise person who can guard the precepts Will obtain three kinds of happiness:
Renown and material gain, and upon death, rebirth in heaven. One should contemplate such states:
The wise who diligently guard the precepts, Whose purity of precepts brings wisdom, Shall attain the supreme path.
Commentary: The preceding verse concerns the causes and effects of the mundane world; the subsequent verse concerns the causes and effects of the supramundane.

By citing the mundane, the supramundane is revealed. "To understand clearly" means to realize that the three miserable realms are summoned by evil karma, while the blissful states of humans and devas are evoked by wholesome karma; therefore, one should abandon evil and cultivate goodness. This is the precept.
This is the root of all virtues; only those who are wise and discerning can protect it, for it cannot be maintained by the foolish and deluded who fail to distinguish between cause and effect.
As for the three kinds of pleasure: first, fame; second, praise; and third, gain. These are the pleasures of the present, which are like the blossoming of flowers.
After death, one attains birth in the heavens; this is the pleasure of future retribution. "Name" refers to being accorded credit for one's virtues, while "praise" refers to renown.

This refers to praise and gain. Regarding the four reliances and the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*): those who are able to uphold the Dharma according to the Vinaya possess the fragrance of ethical discipline (*śīlagandha*), which is wafted far and wide.
The four requisites that aid the path arrive spontaneously without being sought. One should contemplate such matters as follows:
even worldly fruits of happiness cannot be obtained without ethical discipline; how much more so, then, the supramundane noble path?
How could one be apart from the precepts? Those who possess wisdom should diligently and strictly protect them.
When the body one has received is pure and free from blemish, all states of existence can be transcended; therefore it is said that with pure precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.

Just as the Buddhas of the past, And those of the future, And the World-Honored Ones of the present— Who are able to overcome all sorrow— All together revere and honor the precepts; This is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If there be one who acts for their own sake, Desiring to seek the Buddha-way, They should respect and honor the True Dharma.
This is the explanation given by all the Buddhas.
The first one and a half verses cite the common attainment of the path by all Buddhas as proof;
the final verse demonstrates that those who seek Buddhahood should revere the True Dharma, thereby exhorting them. As for "able to overcome all sorrows," [it refers to] all afflictions...
It is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) because it vexes sentient beings by binding them with the fetters of various afflictions.

It is called "supreme" (*jyeṣṭha*) because the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all revere the *prātimokṣa*; being utterly pure, perfectly luminous, and having exhausted all afflictions, they attain great liberation.
"Acting for one's own sake" means that one exclusively seeks the path of Buddhahood for the sake of this body alone, in order to transcend birth and death. It is not...
One may aspire to maintain the categories of ethical discipline for the sake of temporary happiness; however, the intended meaning herein is profound and subtle.

It distinguishes this from the prātimokṣa vows of the two vehicles, as it is intended to bring the nature of ultimate ethical discipline to fruition. Students must not mistake its fundamental purpose and thereby fall into the pit of partiality and inferiority.
Those who are deluded should quickly reproach themselves and reflect upon their errors to clear away the sin of their derision and disparagement. Even if...

Yet, while his outward traces appear small, his fundamental intent is truly to guide beings back to the Great Vehicle. How much more so when the ocean of precepts is boundless, its measure equaling the vast void;

it accords with sentient beings to bestow benefit, dispensing equally without distinction. Although there are differences in the capacities of roots—some great and some small—the Dharma itself has no division of breadth or narrowness.
Desiring to escape the deep abyss of the two deaths, one should swiftly cast oneself onto the shore of the single reality.
If one can thus act for oneself without transgression, there will be hope for seeking the Buddha. The True Dharma (*saddharma*) is precisely the Dharma of the Precepts (*śīladharma*).

As it is said, as long as there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts, the True Dharma shall not perish from the world; for the precepts are the vessel and the oar for crossing the ocean of suffering.
The path to nirvana is not like the heterodox and deviant codes of external paths, nor is it the technique for governing the world through the ten wholesome acts of a wheel-turning monarch;
therefore, these Buddha-precepts are specifically termed the "True Dharma."
The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have extinguished all fetters and defilements, have preached this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts;
through them, one attains liberation from all bonds and enters into Nirvāṇa. All frivolous play is forever extinguished.
The Honored One, the Great Sage, has spoken these precepts praised by the noble sages, which are to be practiced by his disciples.
Commentary on Entering Quiescent Nirvāṇa:
The preceding one and a half verses refer to the disciples of the Buddhas who, having upheld the Sūtra of Precepts and attained liberation from all bonds, have entered nirvāṇa;
thus, these are cited as proof. The subsequent verse refers to the present disciples of the Buddha who revere the Buddha.
As it has been taught: by practicing in reliance upon the precepts, one attains the blissful fruit of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, this is shown as an exhortation.

"The fetters and proclivities" (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) refers to those various afflictions that drive the mind and spirit of a person, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms and fail to attain liberation;
hence they are called "fetters and proclivities. Briefly, there are ten proclivities; extensively, there are eighty-eight proclivities, up to eighty thousand.
These are the four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). The Seven Buddhas, as guides of the world, preached this *Śīla-sūtra* for the purpose of extinguishing the fetters of their disciples.

When the disciples practice it, they are thereby liberated from all afflictions and fetters, realize the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda-phala*), and enter *nirvāṇa*, wherein all conceptual proliferations of existence and non-existence are forever extinguished.
Indeed, the sutras spoken by the seven Buddhas, the Great Sages, are the precepts praised by all the worthy and holy ones.

Now, among those who are disciples of the Buddha, if they are able to practice according to the teachings, there will be none who do not realize and enter into the nirvana of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
"Quiescent extinction" (*ji-mie*) is a term that expresses both the Chinese and the Indic [Sanskrit] meanings together.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he gave rise to great compassion and assembled the community of bhikṣus, giving them this instruction:
"Do not say that with my parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity will have no protector.
I have now spoken the Sūtra of Precepts and have also well explained the Vinaya; even though I have entered parinirvāṇa..."
One should regard it as the World-Honored One; thus shall this sutra long abide in the world.
When the Buddha-dharma flourishes in such a manner, one attains entry into Nirvana.
If one does not uphold these precepts as they should be for the poṣadha, it is like the time when the sun sets: the world is entirely shrouded in darkness.

Commentary: The first verse clarifies that the Buddha bestowed his instructions. After the Tathāgata had taught the Dharma for forty-nine years and his work of transforming sentient beings was complete, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa;
he once again entrusted the precepts to his disciples, earnestly charging them with their preservation.

His instructions were repeated with earnest exhortation. Thus we know that this precept is truly the fundamental basis of the Buddha-dharma, the authentic life-line of wisdom, the safeguard for attaining sainthood, and the essential path for benefiting sentient beings.

If one does not receive and uphold it with the utmost reverence, one will not only willingly sink into the ocean of birth and death, but will also fail the Tathāgata’s entrustment. One should reflect upon this with compassion.

"Instruction: To honor the bequeathed Dharma while forgetting one’s own body; to exert oneself in the resolve of faith and to revere the *vinaya* for the rest of one’s life—this is what it means to know gratitude and repay that kindness. Do not say that because my *nirvāṇa* is so intensely blazing, I have entered *nirvāṇa*.
These two and a half verses clearly demonstrate the teaching. [The Buddha said: 'O Bhikṣus, you must not...'"

"Until the world is entirely shrouded in darkness"—this single verse reiterates the admonition through analogy. It means that the practitioner of purity possesses protection;

If one does not observe the *poṣadha*, by what could one rely for protection? Then, defilements and stains will increase daily, and wisdom will be lost.
To lack clarity and fail to perceive the Noble Path is to fall into the three miserable realms. This is like the sun setting into darkness;
because nothing can be seen, one immediately falls into pits and ditches.
One should guard these precepts as a yak protects its tail;
sitting together in harmony, as the Buddha has taught—this verse admonishes one to maintain firm resolve in observing them. That is to say, a bhikṣu should protect the precepts for himself.

Precious one! Firmly resolve your faith and intention; it would be better to die than to transgress. Just as the yak loves its tail and disregards its own life, this is what is called "observing the regulations and upholding the precepts.

it refers to the power and function of both the prohibitions (*saṃvara*) and the prescribed practices (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) that arise from strictly guarding the purity of each individual precept. This is what is called "merit."

If one follows the path of the Śrāvakas, why speak of dedicating [merit] toward Buddhahood? This refers to the period after the revelation [of the truth], at the time of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*’s final testament.

there is only the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), neither two nor three. Furthermore, while the precepts originally serve to prevent wrongdoing and cease evil, how could they alone constitute the path of a Śrāvaka?
[The term] "solely upholding" [applies]. The essence of a *bhikṣu* encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. How could it be merely a designation for an Arhat?

This meaning is based on the fact that for a śrāvaka, self-deliverance is the priority; thus, merely ceasing [unwholesome conduct] is termed "maintaining. For a bodhisattva...

The arising of *sattva* is the root. If one does not extensively perform various good deeds, it is termed a transgression. This is a direct reprimand of those with small minds who seek only their own benefit as a fault;
it does not refer to those of great mind who benefit others and together strive for the Buddha-way.

Even if one speaks of self-benefit, it inherently includes the benefit of others; thus, within each and every precept, there is nothing that does not involve protecting others. This is truly as [the Buddha taught].
This is a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). He secretly tied the jewel within his robe so that it might ultimately serve a great purpose.
People today do not understand the Sage’s intention and thus give rise to speculative debates. Once the meaning is understood and revealed, there will be no doubt.
As this verse says: "I now dedicate whatever merit exists in reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra to all sentient beings, that we may together..."

**The Method for Confession and Declaration when Monks Have Jointly Committed an Offense**

The Buddha said: "If the Saṃgha assembles for the recitation of the precepts, one who has committed an offense may not participate in the recitation, nor may they hear the precepts, nor may they confess their offense to another who has committed one;
likewise, the offender may not accept the confession of another. That bhikṣu, having made a formal motion, shall then perform the confession.
He should make the following formal motion:"

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This entire assembly of monks has committed an offense. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that this entire assembly of monks shall perform confession. Thus is the formal announcement."
Having made this announcement in this manner, one then recites the fundamental text of the Prātimokṣa. One does not further repent for the original offense.

*Commentary:* Regarding the phrase "one does not further repent for the original offense" within this legal code (*vinaya*): this refers to offenses such as the *pāyantika* (single downfall) and the rules of decorum (*śaikṣa-dharma*).
Because, when approaching the *poṣadha*, one reflects upon the noble prohibitions and finds them difficult to set aside, there is an urgent desire to recite [the text] together with the community.

They each felt shame and remorse, confessed their faults, and sought purification. This is precisely in accord with the intent of the *poṣadha*—the relinquishing of all evil and unwholesome dharmas and the ultimate holy life—and thus further repentance is not required.
However, this does not apply by analogy to violations of the first two categories of offenses (*pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*), nor to the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
Regarding the ritual for monks to confess a doubtful offense collectively:

The Buddha said, "If, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, there are those among the entire Saṃgha who have doubts concerning an offense, they should make a formal announcement (jñapti) as follows:"

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let this assembly of monks themselves declare their doubtful offense. Thus is the motion (jñapti).

Thereafter, the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is recited. This refers only to the disclosure of offenses; once the *Poṣadha* has been heard, the original offense must still be confessed after it has been declared.
[Commentary: The aforementioned "one who recognizes the offense" means one who knows it clearly and without doubt. This [present case] refers to "one who has doubts regarding the offense."
Because one does not personally know the names and characteristics of the categories of offenses, doubt arises as to whether an offense has been committed or not.

When it is time for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, one should first disclose the matter and wait until the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made; once the recitation and listening are finished, one must still consult someone who knows the Dharma to resolve the nature of the offense committed.
He himself says he seeks repentance. This consciousness doubts two dharmas; both are created for the sake of human dharmas, and they pertain to both the public and the private.
○ Regarding the method for a nun to dispatch someone to request instruction:

On the day of the *poṣadha*, the assembly of monks is gathered; their consent is sought and the circumstances are inquired about. The response is: "Appoint a person to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of requesting instruction.

Then the formal motion (*jñapti*) is made, as explained: "Regarding the day of the *poṣadha*: according to the Vinaya, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to perform the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day. [As for] the bhikṣuṇī..."
Regarding the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day: if there is a specific reason, the bhikṣus may perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day while the bhikṣuṇīs perform it on the sixteenth day;

this is called the "boundary-binding through mutual dependence of the two assemblies. Now, following the standard procedure for the Great Assembly (bhikṣusaṃgha) on the fifteenth day for the recitation of the precepts (*pravāraṇā*), the bhikṣuṇī community shall assemble within their own boundary and appoint a person to make the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, on behalf of the community of bhikṣuṇīs, once every half-month to the community of bhikṣus to seek instruction. This is the formal motion.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, once every half-month to the community of bhikṣus to seek instruction.

Venerable Sisters who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, once every half-month to the community of bhikṣus to seek instruction, remain silent. Who does not?

The *kṣānti-vādins* declare: "The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so] to go, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, once every half-month to the assembly of bhikṣus to seek instruction.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Vinaya-mūla states: After one person has been appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, he should go alone to the monastery;
however, as he would be unprotected, two or three more people should be appointed as companions to accompany him.
Commentary: Regarding the instruction to "further appoint two or three nuns as companions," this is a skillful means (upāya) to command their attendance for protection;

it does not involve the formal procedure of a motion (*jñapti*) for appointment. One must select those who are experienced and observant of the precepts to go together, rather than merely requiring a numerical count of two or three nuns.
According to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, if a nun has five faults, she should not be taken along as a companion on a journey.
1. One person, Xita, goes ahead; 2. another, Xita, follows behind; 3. the third, Xi, intercepts and cuts off people's speech; 4.
they do not distinguish between good and bad speech—failing to praise well-spoken words while extolling evil ones; 5. they accept gains obtained through lawful means at improper times.
If one avoids these five faults, one may listen to the Sangha’s appointment of a companion, so that both may obtain benefit and be free from all [obstacles].
Having suffered harm, she went to the bhikṣu to whom she had entrusted her request. According to the principle of the matter, a person should have been appointed to receive it;

that nun who had made the entrustment should have fully stated her request and waited until the sixteenth day, after which she would again go to the monastery of the monks to seek permission. If she obtained it...

All the nuns received it with palms joined and heads bowed. There is no textual authority for this in the *Vinaya*, but according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the text and meaning are as follows. If the *saṃgha*...
The two assemblies of nuns must consist of at least five persons before they may perform this rite; therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states:
