Commentary: If both the assemblies of monks and nuns desire to joyfully rely upon and practice this dharma according to the regulations, each must consist of at least five persons;
only then may the two groups perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to appoint an official. The fundamental Vinaya clarifies this for both assemblies:

even if they are in harmony, the number is insufficient; or if the number is sufficient, they are not in harmony. On the day of the *poṣadha*, the nuns should merely pay their respects by going to the assembly with reverence.

By adhering to the Eight Respectful Precepts, one shall not dare to violate them for as long as life lasts. This single *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the Dharma and thus belongs to the public.

It is not [invalid] due to "non-persons" (i.e., those who do not count as members), meaning that the assembly is deficient in number or lacks harmony, or because one acts alone without a companion; other invalidations are to be judged according to the preceding rules.

Regarding the method for instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, the Buddha said: "When the Saṃgha is reciting the precepts, the Elder shall ask: 'Whom has the community of bhikṣuṇīs sent here?'"

Yes. Now, let us simply ask those who recited the precepts at that time. The one who received the entrustment immediately rose, fully assumed the proper dignified demeanor, and made this announcement to the Sangha:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The community of bhikṣuṇīs at [place name] is in harmony.
The Saṃgha has appointed the bhikṣuṇī [name] to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha every half-month and to request instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs.

Having spoken thus three times, the meaning is further supplemented as follows: "She should go to the place of the Elder (sthavira) and say: 'Venerable Sir, out of compassion, are you able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?
If he answers that he is incapable, she must inquire of each one individually, starting from those with twenty years of seniority (*varṣa*) and below.
If there is no such person, she returns to the place of the Elder and reports: 'I have inquired among the entire Saṃgha, and there is none.'"
If there is someone capable, the Elder should briefly instruct them in the rules of discipline and inform the person who will give the formal assignment, saying:
"This assembly has no one capable of acting as an instructor; tomorrow the nuns will come, so please invite them at an appropriate time. [The assignee] should reply:
"Last night I invited the nuns extensively, but there was no one capable. Nevertheless, by the Elder's command, I shall instruct the community of nuns to practice with diligence."
The Way: Be cautious and do not be negligent.

The above explains the brief instruction for those who are incapable. If it is asked whether there is anyone [capable], the bhikṣu who has received the commission returns to the place of the Elder and reports, saying:
"Among the assembly, such-and-such (the Venerable Elder) is capable of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs."
According to the Vinaya, this was initiated by the group of six monks. The Buddha said: "From among the Saṃgha, appoint a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
The motion (*jñapti*) shall be made as follows:"
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, [I propose] to appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] shall instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Which elders approve of the Saṃgha appointing this bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs? Those who approve, remain silent; those who do not approve, speak.
The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Since the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Buddha said: "One who accomplishes ten qualities may then receive the authorization to instruct bhikṣuṇīs. First, being fully endowed with extensive learning; second, having mastered the recitation of the two sets of precepts;
third, possessing the ability to resolve doubts without hesitation; fourth, being skillful in preaching the Dharma; fifth, having renounced the world from a noble family;
sixth, having a handsome appearance such that the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs feels joy upon seeing one; seventh, being capable of [instructing] the bhikṣuṇīs..."
An *upāsikā* (nun) preaches the Dharma to encourage them to rejoice. Eighth, one commits a grave offense if they don the dharma robes without having left home for the sake of the Buddha.
Ninth, if she is exactly twenty years of age; tenth, if she is over twenty years of age. Furthermore, the *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
"There are five qualities by which a nun should be instructed: first, she must fully observe the *prātimokṣa* precepts; second, she must be learned and skillful."
Third, being eloquent in the three languages; fourth, committing a grave offense while not having gone forth as a monk under the Buddha;
fifth, having twenty years of seniority (*vassa*), or more than twenty. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There are five qualities for which one should not be appointed [as a teacher];

if already appointed, one should be dismissed: first, reciting the sūtras and precepts yet frequently forgetting them; second, having incomplete faculties; third, having excessive desire; fourth, manifesting evil characteristics."
[The Buddha] prohibited the five classes of bhikṣuṇīs from associating with evil persons.
Commentary: This refers specifically to the formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the continuous assignment [of duties].

The ritual procedures are fully recorded in the *Jièjì bǐqūnì zhèngfàn* (The Correct Model for Instructing Bhikṣuṇīs). This one *karman* is a public legal procedure; it is clearly not the case that all [procedures] are identical to those mentioned above.
There is no difference.

The Buddha said regarding the procedure for declaring purity: "On the day of the recitation of the precepts, if guests arrive and are few in number, one should declare that the resident bhikṣus are pure; it should be done in this manner."
He shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure" (stated once).

If this statement is made only after the introduction to the recitation of the precepts has been concluded, then there must certainly have been an offense; having thus exposed the transgression to the Saṃgha, the remainder...
This is explained in sequence.
The *poṣadha* is fundamentally intended for reforming past transgressions and eliminating faults, so that one may diligently cultivate purity.

Nevertheless, if one is traveling due to circumstances and encounters a community of monks reciting the precepts at a certain location, it is reasonable that one should attend to listen; one must by no means disregard this. Once the assembly of monks has gathered...
Having finished reciting the preceding verses, one need not announce purity (*pārisuddhi*). One should instead perform the formal salutation, arrange the seats, and sit down.
If the recitation reaches the end of the *Nidāna* (the introductory section), then since the announcement of purity has already been requested during the seating, one should now state these words.

It should be understood that this is because the detailed exposition involves requesting purity at eight locations. If one knows for oneself that there is an offense, one should first acknowledge the fault and inform the Sangha; as for the remainder...
Listen to the end according to the order of seating, and then seek repentance in accordance with the offense committed. This single dharma is performed for the sake of the Dharma;
it belongs to the private sphere.
○ The Method for Recognizing and Disclosing Offenses.
The Buddha said: "One should go to a pure bhikṣu, assume the proper deportment, and state the name and category of the offense committed.

One should say: 'Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. I, [so-and-so], have committed [such-and-such] an offense and have developed doubt regarding it. I now disclose it before the Venerable sir. Afterward, as [previously described]...
The Dharma Confession (recited three times).

This method must be employed by one who remembers [an offense] at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). If one confesses according to the Dharma at other times, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"A bhikṣu who has already made a disclosure need not disclose it again."
Commentary: Regarding "one who remembers during the recitation of the precepts": this excludes those who were aware of the offense on the preceding day but did not repent.
Here, it refers to one who, upon encountering the *poṣadha*, suddenly recalls the transgression committed; thus, this method is employed so that they may be permitted to hear the precepts.

Once the recitation is concluded, they should immediately request its removal. If, at other times, one recognizes an offense or gives rise to doubt, one should disclose it to seek a resolution and perform repentance according to the Dharma.

Regarding the citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: it means that if one has already confessed a transgression prior to the day of the *poṣadha*, there is no need to confess it again at the time of the actual *poṣadha*;
one need only listen to the recitation of the confession.
○ The Method for Confessing Doubtful Offenses.

In the Vinaya-mūla, it is stated that when a bhikṣu has committed an offense and harbors doubt, yet the time for the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) is imminent, the Buddha said: "He should confess his fault and then be permitted to hear the precepts.
According to the interpretation of this principle:
"Venerable sirs, please take note: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed [an offense] at [a certain place] and now harbor a doubt regarding it; I now confess it before the Venerable ones."
[The Master] Lù said: "One must wait until after the time of no further doubt, and perform the repentance according to the Dharma (recited three times).
*Explanation:* "Must wait until after the time of no further doubt" does not mean to allow it to be drawn out indefinitely; rather, it refers to the period following the conclusion of the listening.
Regarding the rule for confessing a remembered offense during the *poṣadha* assembly:

According to the original Vinaya texts, while one is seated upon the platform for the confession ceremony, if one suddenly remembers a past offense, they should confess it to a fellow monk. [If this is not done], the entire assembly will fall into confusion and disorder.
The Buddha commanded that one should disclose what has been thought in the mind.

This should be interpreted according to the principle as follows: The Vinaya states that at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), there was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense and was seated among them.

He thought, "The World-Honored One has established that one who has committed an offense may neither recite nor listen to the precepts. What shall I do? He then spoke to the one reciting the precepts.
People said, "Stop, stop! Do not speak of the precepts. I have committed such-and-such an offense and wish to confess it before the Elder.
The entire assembly became noisy and chaotic. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If that person remembers their own offense and reveals it, that bhikṣu should say to those nearby: 'I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now confess it before the Elder.'"
Furthermore, he should think: "If I speak to others, I fear it will disturb the assembly of monks and prevent the recitation of the precepts from being completed.
That bhikṣu should reflect in his mind that once the session has concluded, he must perform a formal confession according to the Dharma.

Having done this, he may hear the precepts. Now, following the method of mental reflection, the voice must be kept low so as not to be heard by the assembly. This should be understood according to the underlying principle.

I, [Name], have committed [a certain] offense. Because the recitation of the precepts is being pressed upon me and I fear it will cause disturbance among the assembly, I shall confess it once the session is concluded. (Recite three times.)
Cases involving doubtful offenses are to be judged according to this principle.

Explanation: The three aforementioned methods are all performed for the sake of the Dharma; thus, they pertain to the private sphere. ○ A Brief Exposition of the Method for the Uposatha (Sīla-uddesa).
The Buddha said: "If there are kings, thieves, water, fire, the sick, non-humans, evil insects, or other such circumstances;

if the seats are insufficient; if it is exposed to the dampness of rain; if the *poṣadha* has lasted many nights and is already late; or if there have been long periods of quarreling or preaching the Dharma—then the precepts shall be recited in brief."
Commentary: This clarifies the opening conditions. First, the eight difficulties are enumerated. 1. **The difficulty of kings**: A king possesses sovereign authority.
If he has faith, he will cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; if he lacks faith, he will destroy the Triple Gem. 2. **The difficulty of bandits**: "Bandit" is a term for those who inflict harm.
Bandits are the kings of the forest; they are capable of performing acts that bring no benefit. 3. **The difficulty of water**:

The "oceanic calamity" refers to tidal surges and floods that rush forth and overflow. The "calamity of fire" refers to the nature of fire being unstable and dependent upon various conditions, capable of burning down forests and wilds.
The "calamity of disease" refers to the prevalence of illness within the same boundary, making it difficult to accommodate the assembly at the place where the *śīla* (precepts) are recited.
The "calamity of people" refers to laypeople who lack faith, or those who come and go [disturbing the community].
Wandering for sightseeing disturbs and hinders monastic affairs; it may give rise to improper intentions and obstruct the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Seventh, the difficulty of non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) refers to either mountain spirits manifesting wonders or malevolent demons appearing in form.

Eighth, the difficulty of evil insects refers to the appearance of predatory beasts whose sounds and sights terrify people. These are called the eight difficulties. "Few beds and seats" means that [the number of] the multitude is small.
"Congested quarters" means that the bedding and mats are insufficient. "Exposure to dew and rain" means that the covering is incomplete, fearing one might be caught by wind and cold.
"The *poṣadha* has lasted many nights already" means that the final watch of the night is nearly over and the time approaches the following morning.
"Quarreling" refers to disputes involving speech, which are like water and fire. "Expounding the Dharma" refers to the teaching being too protracted. Such are the remaining circumstances.
Furthermore, when encountering the eight difficulties, the abbreviated recitation of the precepts is permitted in all cases.

Both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* provide for this due to many circumstances, opening the allowance for an abbreviated recitation. The preliminary procedures (*pūrvakalpa*) are also performed as in the full recitation;
one should recite them either extensively or briefly according to the urgency of the situation.
Commentary: This citation from another school clarifies the conditions for the suspension of the precepts (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). It is identical to our own Vinaya.

Although it says "briefly explained," once the assembly has gathered, one must certainly perform the preliminary ritual (*purva-kalpa*). If there is time, one may explain in detail; if it is urgent, one explains briefly.
Thus, while the extent of the explanation is not fixed, the performance of the preliminary ritual is mandatory.

the first is the recitation of the *Pratimokṣa* introduction; the second is the recitation up to the four *pārājikas*; the third is the recitation up to the *saṃghāvaśeṣas*; and the fourth...

The four *pārājika* rules, up to and including the *śaikṣa* rules, are likewise omitted; these are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
When recited, the preceding and following sections are supplemented, and each item is asked about individually: "In this matter, are you pure?"
The above has been explained in detail according to the text. If a sudden obstacle should arise, one should say, as appropriate for the location reached: "It has been said up to [place name]";
the remainder is what the Saṃgha hears regularly. If the circumstances of the obstacle are so imminent that the introduction cannot be recited, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

Then each may depart as they please. According to the Vinaya-mūla, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one must not fail to perform the recitation.
If there is no [monk] present, it is also permissible to recite the Dharma or chant the sūtras.
Commentary: Delusive afflictions give rise to various unwholesome karmas, such as those produced by the three poisons and committed through the seven branches of misconduct;
therefore, the Buddha established the precepts to prohibit them. Although this citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is brief, its meaning already encompasses the extensive details.

purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. One must not fail to preach this. This method of abbreviated recitation without formal instruction was temporarily permitted only because there was no one to preach it;

Having personally heard the Buddha’s regulations, we committed them to memory and recited them orally; they have now been compiled and the Sanskrit texts have been transmitted to the East, with the Vinaya volumes preserved in the Tripiṭaka.
Even if one cannot recite them from memory with fluency, one should nevertheless expound them by referring to the scrolls. This is also called the "Dharma-conformity Poṣadha.

The source states: Shi Sengfan of Dajue Monastery in the eastern capital of Ye during the Qi dynasty was pure and lofty in his observance of the precepts, maintaining them without flaw.

He frequently stayed at other monasteries with the intention of hearing the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. On the night of the fifteenth day for the recitation of the precepts, the assembly collectively decided to suspend the recitation and instead hold a "Dharma Assembly.
When someone ascended the seat and intended to establish a formal discourse, he introduced it by saying: "Establishing a Discourse on the Dharma..."
The monk Xiāng deeply understood the sacred teachings and was constantly heard reciting the *poṣadha* ceremony. He was renowned for his skill in debate and challenging opponents.

Suddenly, he saw a deity, over ten feet tall with a most majestic and imposing appearance, towering and startling to behold. The deity came before his seat and asked the one expounding the doctrine, "What day is this today?
He replied, "It is the *poṣadha* day. The deity then struck him with his hand and dragged him down from his seat.
He was utterly exhausted and on the verge of death. Next, he questioned the Elder; the dialogue was the same as before.
After having harmed two or three Elders, the spirit shook its sleeves and departed. At that time, monks and laypeople alike witnessed this phenomenon more than once. Master Fan saw this marvel.
He then personally applied diligent effort and exhorted the great assembly; throughout his entire life, he did not dare speak of desire.

Even when he was so ill as to be unable to endure being carried on a sedan chair, he would request monks to come to his bedside and reverently recite the precepts. Thereafter, he greatly promoted the Dharma of the precepts.
For this reason, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one must not willfully neglect the recitation of the precepts in order to lecture upon the Dharma.
○ Continuation of the Method for Reconciliation at an Improper Time:
This follows the outline of the *ekajñapti* (single motion). Now, it is continued here according to the *Śikṣāpada-vastu* (Section on the Exposition of Precepts).

The Buddha said: "The Saṃgha has been split into two factions. At that time, the bhikṣus wished to [perform the procedure] in Śrāvastī (the mention of the kingdom of Śrāvastī is based on the *nidāna*; here, however, it follows...).
Regarding the matter of formal assembly (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*): from this time forward, it is permitted that after the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, one may then enter into formal assembly.

Once the Saṃgha has gathered, if there is a reason for which one cannot grant consent (*chanda*), one should reply: "The Saṃgha is in formal assembly; the *karmavācanā* shall be performed as follows. Thus is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Regarding the matter of dispute that has caused the Saṃgha to quarrel and become discordant, that person committed an offense;
he was formally accused, and his offense has now been resolved. The defilement of the Saṃgha has been extinguished. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
The Saṃgha is in harmony. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Commentary: Having made this announcement, they continue to dwell together within the same boundary for the sake of the Dharma-food.
This single *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of individuals; thus, it belongs to the public.

It is not [the case that] non-humans are [included]. This means that in the present instance, there is no distinction regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*) or the rules for assembly (*sannipāta*), etc. It should be understood that the remaining points are not the same as those previously mentioned.
○ The Dharma for the Extinction of Disputes and the Recitation of the Precepts.
Continuation: This follows the outline of the *śuddha-vidhi* (single-announcement rite). Now, it is continued here according to the *Poṣadha-vastu*. The Buddha said:
"If there is a matter on account of which the Saṃgha falls into dispute and lacks harmony;
if the Saṃgha is broken apart, defiled, and divided into two factions—if one can therein reform and repent, and no longer incite [others to quarrel]..."
This is called the Saṃgha being in harmony through the Dharma. From this day forward, it is permitted to recite the Prātimokṣa after first making a formal announcement (jñapti).
Once the assembly has gathered, one must not grant consent (chanda) by proxy; rather, one should answer: "The community of monks wishes to recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
One should make the announcement in this manner.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Regarding the matter of dispute that has caused the Saṃgha to contend and lack harmony, that has broken the Saṃgha, defiled the Saṃgha, and divided the Saṃgha into two factions—that person has recognized their own offense and now repents.
They have removed the defilement from the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of forbearance, grant its consent so that we may recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
The announcement is made as follows.
Having made this announcement, the Saṃgha then performs the Poṣadha in unison.
Commentary: This is the method for the intermediate Poṣadha for harmonizing the Saṃgha; it is not necessary to proclaim the harmony again as is customary.

It is said: "Therefore, it is stated that after this announcement has been made, the Saṃgha then performs the recitation of the Prātimokṣa together. This *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of the Dharma;
thus, it belongs to the public [the community]. It clearly shows that, unlike the previous case, the full requirements must be met.
○ First Supplementary Method for Reciting the Precepts; Second Supplementary Method for Reciting the Precepts (Continued).
These two methods follow the framework of the *jñapti* (single-announcement) procedure. They are now included here following the *Pratimokṣa-vastu* (Section on Prohibitions). The Vinaya states:

At that time, there were many bhikṣus from another location who, on the day of the *poṣadha*, heard that in their place there were bhikṣus who delighted in quarreling and reviling one another, mutually slandering each other, and whose mouths produced swords and blades. They wished to come here for the *poṣadha* ceremony and asked, "How should we proceed?
They immediately went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If such a situation arises, you should perform two or three kinds [of procedures]."
Regarding the *poṣadha*: if it should be recited on the fifteenth day, one should do so on the fourteenth; if it should be recited on the fourteenth, one should do so on the thirteenth.
If one hears that [the monks] are coming today, one should immediately assemble in one place for the *poṣadha*.

If one hears they have already arrived within the boundary (*sīmā*), one should go outside the boundary to perform the *poṣadha*. If it is said they have already entered the monastery, one should sweep the bathhouse.

Having prepared the bathing requisites and asked the elder [monk] whether he has already lit the fire, when those visiting bhikṣus enter the bathhouse to bathe, they should each exit the boundary of the bathhouse and recite the *poṣadha*.
If a visiting bhikṣu calls upon a resident bhikṣu to recite the *poṣadha* together with him, he should reply:
"We have already recited the *poṣadha*. If the resident bhikṣus have already finished reciting the *poṣadha*, the visitor...

If a bhikṣu obstructs the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), the obstruction is not valid. If, however, when visiting bhikṣus are reciting the precepts, resident bhikṣus obstruct the recitation, the obstruction is valid.
It is well if they can act in this manner; if they cannot, they should postpone the day for the recitation by making a formal announcement (jñapti).
They should make the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha shall not recite the precepts now; they shall be recited during the dark fortnight. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

One should make such a motion and then postpone the recitation of the precepts. If a visiting bhikṣu remains waiting and does not depart, that bhikṣu should make a second formal motion to postpone the recitation of the precepts. It should be made as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen. The Sangha will not recite the *Prātimokṣa* now; it shall be recited when the bright fortnight arrives. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
It should be announced in this manner for the second postponement of the recitation. If the visiting bhikṣus do not depart until the bright fortnight arrives..."
The resident bhikṣus should, in accordance with the Dharma, insistently engage the visiting bhikṣus in a formal exchange of questions and answers.
Commentary: Regarding "insistently engaging in questions and answers": this means the resident bhikṣus should strike the gong to assemble together and question the visiting bhikṣus, saying:
"The Buddha has given clear instructions, enjoining this procedure of 'informing after returning' (*pratideśanā*). Why do you wait so long and not depart? You are causing us distress."
They disturb the community of monks and thereby obstruct the *poṣadha*. If they should reply that they will not go, the resident monks should say to them:
"If you do not go, we shall follow the Vinaya to discipline and punish you, and only thereafter shall we perform the pure recitation of the precepts.
The fault lies with you, not with us. This is why it is said that they are "forcibly engaged in question and answer. These two *karmavācanās*...

The *mala* (powder) is prepared for the sake of human needs; thus it belongs to the public. This clarifies that it is not the same as the aforementioned [provisions]. [The rules] concerning the methods for insanity and delusion are here explained in conjunction with the preceding.

These two methods follow the framework of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation). Now, they are incorporated into the sequence following the *Poṣadha-vastu* (Section on the Bi-monthly Confession) according to the Vinaya.

The original text says: At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose mind was distracted and who suffered from insanity; sometimes he remembered the recitation of the precepts, and sometimes he did not remember it;
sometimes he came, and sometimes he did not come. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
For that bhikṣu, perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) for mental derangement and insanity.

Appoint a person within the Saṃgha who is capable of performing the *karman* to carry out the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*), and respond by saying: "The *karman* for insanity shall be performed. The motion (*jñapti*) should be made as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane. He sometimes remembers the *poṣadha* ceremony and sometimes does not remember it;

he sometimes comes and sometimes does not come. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this bhikṣu the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one who is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane—whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come—and let the Saṃgha perform the formal act.
The precepts. It is announced as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane; he may or may not remember the recitation of the precepts."
Whether he comes or does not come, the Saṃgha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the monk [Name] who is mentally deranged and insane.
Whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come, we shall perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
Which Elders consent to the Saṃgha performing the *karmavācanā* for this [Name], who is mentally deranged and insane, whether he remembers or does not remember, or whether he comes or does not come?
The one who proclaims the precepts remains silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak.

The Sangha has consented to perform the *karmavācanā* for the bhikṣu [Name], declaring him to be of deranged mind and confused, whether he remembers or not, and whether he comes or not. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of those who are deranged or insane. First, those who, when the *poṣadha* is being recited, are unsure whether they remember it or not, and whether they will come or not.
Second, there are those who are deranged or insane but come to the *poṣadha*. Third, there are those who are deranged or insane and do not remember the *poṣadha*, nor do they come.
Regarding these, the Saṃgha should grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to the first; as for the second and third types of the deranged or insane..."
One should not grant this *karmavācanā* to such a person.

Explanation: Regarding these three types of insanity and delusion, the first refers to one who at times loses consciousness and does not remember [the offense], yet remembers and recognizes it when not in that state.
Because the illness is unstable, the *karmavācanā* is granted. As for the second, the illness is mild; he remembers [the offense] each time.
"Come. This was because he was so severely ill that he did not remember the assembly at all; therefore, the Dharma should not have been conferred upon him.

If it were conferred, the Saṃgha would be at fault. One must weigh the situation carefully. According to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vinaya*), "If one sees fire and grasps it, it is no different from gold."
Seeing excrement, he grasps it as if it were sandalwood, no different; this is called a mind deranged by folly.
This one *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of an individual and pertains to private matters.
"Non-human" means it is not so; that is, the faculties do not correspond to the Dharma and so forth. Other "non-" [cases] are to be judged according to the preceding.
Regarding the procedure for insanity and delusion, the Buddha said:

"If one who was insane has been granted the *karmavācanā*, and later the illness of insanity or delusion ceases, one should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) for them."

The *karmavācanā* for the lifting [of the penalty] should be performed as follows. That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], previously suffered from the affliction of insanity. At the time of the recitation of the precepts, I sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember;
I sometimes came and sometimes did not come. The Saṃgha performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for me regarding this insanity.
Having performed it, I have now regained right mindfulness and request the lifting of the formal act for insanity. (Thus, three times.)"

The monk appointed as the *karmakāra* (the administrator of the formal act) shall solicit the consent of the assembly and inquire regarding the circumstances, responding: "I am performing the formal act for the release from the affliction of madness and delusion.
He then makes the following motion:
"Venerable Sangha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] was previously afflicted by the disease of madness and delusion; when the *poṣadha* was being recited, he sometimes remembered..."
Whether he does not remember, or whether he comes or does not come, the Saṃgha performed the *unmattaka-karman* (the ritual for one who is insane) upon him.
Having performed it, his madness and illness have now ceased. He now seeks the lifting of the *unmattaka-karman*. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for the removal of the insanity affliction is announced as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] was previously afflicted by the disease of insanity; at the time of the recitation of the precepts, he sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember, and sometimes came and sometimes did not come.
The Saṃgha has performed the formal ritual of insanity for him. Having performed it, he is now no longer insane."

The illness of delusion has now been brought to rest. We now request the Saṃgha to perform the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the formal act concerning the illness of madness and delusion for [Name] Bhikṣu.

Which Elders among you who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the formal act concerning the illness of madness and delusion for this Bhikṣu, remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak.
The Sangha has already consented; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the lifting of the suspension from the monk [Name] due to insanity is completed.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Vinaya-mūla states: "If one further becomes insane or deluded, and while under the influence of such insanity or delusion, the *karmavācanā* is performed for them; once the insanity ceases, it is revoked.
○ The Method of Confessing the Precepts Face-to-Face.

The Buddha said: "If there is a single bhikṣu residing at a monastery, on the day of the *poṣadha*, he shall go to the *poṣadha* hall, sweep and sprinkle it until it is clean, spread out the seating mats, prepare the water for washing and the water jars, light the lamps, and prepare the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
If visiting bhikṣus arrive, if there are four or more, they should announce and perform the recitation. If there are exactly four, they should assemble and announce the *poṣadha*."
There are three persons who may not receive the consent (*chanda*); each should recite the precepts with three utterances, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind: today is the fifteenth day for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts; I, [Name], am pure."
The other two persons should likewise recite this three times. If there are two persons living together, it should be conducted according to this same rule.
If one has committed an offense, they must confess it before a pure person; only after the confession has been made may the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) be performed.
If one has an offense and does not confess it, they do not accord with the pure Dharma.

Commentary: Regarding those who have committed an offense—meaning at the time of the *poṣadha*, whether they remember having committed one, recognize having committed one, or suspect having committed one—they must disclose it according to the monastic rules previously explained. In such cases, the rite of purification (*pārisuddhi*) should not be conferred.
Only if the individual has already repented prior to the *poṣadha* day may the rite of purification be conferred. However, if an offense has been committed and has not yet been disclosed...

Regarding confession (*pratideśanā*): to add [procedures] beyond what is prescribed is contrary to the Dharma. This Dharma is performed for the sake of the Dharma; it is the private within the public.

It is "non-human" (or "not of a person") when, for example, three people receive the *chanda* (consent). It is "non-Dharma" when, for example, one falsely adds the [status of being] pure (*pariśuddha*).

Regarding the matter of what is not [proper]: this refers to the lack of preparation and other such factors within the two types of boundaries (*sīmā*). The remaining four non-characteristics are to be understood by analogy.
The Dharma for announcing the *Poṣadha* through mental intimation:
The Buddha said that on the day of the *Poṣadha*, a single bhikṣu should prepare the communal requisites as previously described and wait for visiting bhikṣus. If...
[The respondent] says: "There is nothing to report.
[The proclaimer] says: "Today is the fifteenth day for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts. I, [Name], am pure. (This is said three times.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: After performing the aforementioned procedure, one who has committed an offense should confess it before the Saṃgha of the four directions.

Commentary: In the "Chapter on Establishing Boundaries" (*Sīmābandha*) of the *Five Hundred Questions*, it is stated: "If there is a boundary at a single residence, even a single bhikṣu may strike the *gandī* and extensively recite the precepts.
First, he should repent before the Saṃgha of the four directions; thereafter, he may also [recite] three times."
"Recite three times" means to speak three utterances. The current text states, "having added the aforementioned method," which means that it may likewise be recited three times;

this refers to the *cittotpāda* (mental resolve) for the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*). Having recited three times, one sits alone and recites the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Dharmaguptaka* school in full.
Regarding "one who has committed an offense should repent before the Saṃgha of the four directions": this means that if there is a transgression, one should wait for a visiting monk.
If a pure bhikṣu arrives, one should confess openly before him. If no one has arrived, one should perform a mental confession, saying:
"I, [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I shall wait for a visiting bhikṣu to arrive and then perform the confession according to the Dharma."
Thereafter, one sits alone and recites the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* until its conclusion. This is now cited for the sake of convenience according to the circumstances.
The terms for *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* are distinguished; all other wording is the same as above.
Commentary: Regarding the precept-dharma, the assemblies are divided into the Great and Small Vehicles. As for the principle of the *poṣadha*, it must apply universally to all ranks;

the only difference lies in their respective designations. If one were to claim that the three lower assemblies do not have a *poṣadha*, then one would remain ignorant of the categories of pure and defiled precepts during the fortnightly purification.
That which is prohibited by the Vinaya for the purpose of upholding the discipline is intended to ensure that one does not become unacquainted with the Dharma of the Great Saṃgha.

The phonetic gloss for "yè" (鄴) is pronounced "yè."

*Asura*, translated into Chinese as "Non-Gods" (*fēitiān*), are so called because their karmic retribution is most excellent; they rank immediately below the various devas, yet are not gods.
There are four types, as they are born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or through transformation.
Miǎo (pronounced miǎo) means a vast expanse of water.

Xì (pronounced xì) means a brilliant crimson.
*He* (Hè): entering tone; it denotes brilliance and flourishing. It also denotes loftiness, clarity, and manifest abundance.
*Jian* (Jiàn): departing tone; it means to feign or pretend. It also means to overstep or transgress.
"Bǐ" (pronounced like "bǐ") means "thin" or "slender.

"Yù" means "to govern" or "to regulate."

Dǐ (pronounced dǐ) means "to reach" or "to arrive.
Máo (pronounced máo) refers to the tail of a cow, which can be used for banners (*jīngmáo*). Jīng (pronounced jīng) and máo (pronounced máo) refer to the banners; feathers are split to form them.

The *jing* (banner) refers to the analysis of bird feathers to form the top of the staff, to which a *mao*—the tail of an ox—is attached. The purpose of the ox-tail at the head of the banner is to inspire the soldiers to diligence.
The height of the Son of Heaven’s banner is nine *ren*; that of the feudal lords is seven *ren*; and that of the great officers is five *ren*.
“Ni” (擬) means to imitate sounds; “yin” (音) means ants;
“chuai-duo” (揣度) means to estimate or conjecture. *The Fourth-Part Vinaya of the Dharmaguptaka School: A Revised and Supplemented Manual of Rituals According to Circumstances*, Fascicle Nine.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Chongyi Temple in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty.
Continued Explanation by the Junior Monk Duti of Huashan, Jinling:
Chapter Six, on the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*) for the Assembly.
The preceding section clarified that the *poṣadha* is performed twenty-four times each year; this section clarifies the summer retreat during the four seasons.
The ninety-day summer retreat (*varṣā*) is a fundamental duty for bhikṣus; it is indeed a rigorous regulation for earnest practice.

As for the phrase "the various assemblies," the Vinaya permits five groups, while the Dharma opens the way for four types. These categories form the body of this work, and the introduction stands as the sixth chapter.
At that time, the bhikṣus were wandering about at all times, trampling and killing living plants and grasses, and severing the life-faculties of various sentient beings.
The people of the world censured them, and insects and birds gathered in swarms. The Buddha said: "One should not wander about at all times;
I authorize a three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*). There is both a general censure and a specific regulation, which is found in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*."
Commentary: This first cites the circumstances for the establishment of the rule. The Vinaya states: At all times—spring, summer, and winter—the group of six bhikṣus traveled through the human world.
During the summer months, when the heavens rained heavily and the waters swelled, they lost their robes, bowls, bedding, and needle-cases, and they trampled and killed living plants and trees.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged them, saying: "These śramaṇas..."

The sons of the Śākyas lack a sense of shame and modesty; they wander about at all times, losing their robes and requisites, trampling and killing living grass, and severing the life-force of other beings.
Even the non-Buddhists observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat, and even insects and birds have nests and dwellings where they reside.
How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas act in such a manner? Those monks who possess a sense of shame and delight in upholding the precepts [were distressed].

This was reported to the Buddha; therefore, he established the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*). The text states that there are both general prohibitions and specific regulations, the latter appearing in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

Regarding the general prohibition: it means that bhikṣuṇīs likewise should not travel through human settlements at all times, up until the permission granted for the three-month summer retreat. Regarding the specific regulation: it is found among the eight weighty precepts (*gurudharma*) for bhikṣuṇīs.
Seventh, a bhikṣuṇī must not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) where no bhikṣus are present.
Eighth, when a bhikṣuṇī has completed her retreat, she should request the three matters of self-examination—regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected—from the community of bhikṣus.

Now, although the eight rules of respect for bhikṣuṇīs were established later, while the regulations for the bhikṣu retreat were established earlier, it is said here that they are universally censured.
Why? For the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is a universal regulation for the monastic community. To censure one group is to censure all five groups.

Regarding the rules for the *varṣā*, as the Buddha taught, there are three types of retreats: the early retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), the middle retreat (*madhyamavarṣā*), and the late retreat (*paścimavarṣā*). The early retreat...
Regarding "those who dwell": those who dwell during the first three months [of the rainy season] are called "early retreaters" (*pūrvavārṣika*);

those who dwell during the latter three months are called "late retreaters" (*paścimavārṣika*). Commentary: As for "retreat" (*varṣā*), the stilling of body and mind is termed "peace" (*an*); the formal commitment to reside here is termed "lock" (*vāra*).

Contemplating the correct path in a quiet place requires that one set aside days to pursue merit, exhorting and advancing one’s mental conduct as circumstances permit. One should entrust oneself to these conditions.
In this regard, one’s resolve should be solely directed toward what is beneficial. One must not permit the mind to wander or become distracted, as such paths obstruct spiritual practice.

Therefore, while the Vinaya generally regulates all three seasons, the texts specifically focus on the summer months because the origin of the rule arose from circumstances concerning three specific faults.

Nevertheless, when these are divided into the three periods of the year, why is it that only three months are prescribed for the single four-month summer retreat? This contains two meanings: first, [it concerns] the conditions of birth and death; second, [it concerns] the waiting period.
Because physical forms must rely on nourishment, the three-month period [of the rains retreat] is established first, and one month is opened afterward to provide for robes for the body.
Second, if the retreat were concluded at the end of the fourth month, it could only be successfully completed on the sixteenth day of the fourth month;

should there be any lapse or omission, the conclusion would not be achieved. Such a teaching would be too urgent and difficult to apply consistently. Thus, the Tathāgata skillfully accords with the needs of sentient beings.

Regarding the *kī* (the rainy season retreat): one month is opened for it, and it is continued and completed [over the following month]. Furthermore, within that same month, three types of *vassa* (rainy season) retreats are permitted.

The first day of the sixteenth of the fourth month is the commencement of the *pūrvavārṣika* (early retreat); from the seventeenth onwards until the fifteenth of the fifth month is called the *madhyavārṣika* (middle retreat);
and the first day of the sixteenth of the fifth month is called the *paścimavārṣika* (late retreat). This refers to the *pūrvavārṣika*.

Those who remain until the fifteenth day of the seventh month are said to be in the "first three months. Those in the "later retreat" (paścimā vārṣikā) remain until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, which is called the "last three months.
As for those in the "intermediate retreat," they complete the three months by remaining from the latter part of one period to the former part of the next.

According to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), among the translators of the sūtras and vinaya in previous generations, some referred to this as "sitting out the summer" (*zuo xià*). Or...
The so-called "sitting wax" (zuo la) practices all originate from the divergent customs of frontier regions, where they do not understand the standard pronunciation of the Central Kingdom.
Perhaps local dialects have not yet been harmonized, leading to errors in transmission and translation; it should properly be called "sitting in the rains retreat" (anju).

Nevertheless, there are those today who, at the time of entering the retreat, fashion figures out of wax, intending to examine their merits and faults for the summer by observing them on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. How could this be...?
This halts delusion and restrains transgressions; furthermore, it does not distinguish between *la* (years of seniority) and *la* (wax).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Buddha ordained that the five assemblies must all observe the *varṣā* retreat (*anugamana*). The Vinaya says: "If a bhikṣuṇī does not observe the *varṣā*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other four assemblies, including the bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
Commentary: Regarding the citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this clarifies that it includes the minor schools (*hīnayāna*).

According to the fundamental Vinaya, if a nun does not observe the *varṣā* (rain-retreat), she commits a *pāyattika* offense, because this violates the strict instructions of the Eight Respectful Precepts. As for the other four [rules], one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense, due to failing to avoid worldly censure and suspicion.
The regulations are thus established; there has never been one who, having failed to observe the *varṣā* at the end of summer, could still be called a "Son of the Śākya" (*śākyaputra*).
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If there are no five faults, one may enter the rains retreat (*varṣāvāsa*) therein. First, being too far from a village makes it difficult to obtain what is needed.
Second, being too close to a city wall hinders the path of cultivation. Third, having many mosquitoes and ants [causes harm] to both oneself and others."
[If there is] loss; or if there are four kinds of persons who cannot be relied upon— namely, those who do not cause one to hear what has not been heard,

those who do not purify what has already been heard, those who cannot resolve the net of doubts, those whose understanding is obstructed and lacks fluency, and those who lack right view— or if there is no donor to provide medicine and food,
in all such cases, one must not enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Commentary: Among the monastic community during the Buddha’s lifetime, some accepted invitations to enter the retreat, while others selected specific locations to observe the summer rains retreat (*varṣā*).
The present text cites five faults from the *Śāstra* to clarify that only by acting in accordance with the Dharma does one truly accomplish the retreat.
The first fault refers to the fatigue incurred by traveling back and forth for alms, which causes both mind and body to fail in tranquility. The second fault refers to householders...

Coming and going, one remains silent for fear of inviting ridicule, yet speaks again because it obstructs the Way. Thus, time and effort are wasted in vain while one's fundamental practice remains unaccomplished.

The first three faults are said to harm living beings and violate compassion, as well as contravene the original precepts and conditions. The fourth fault is that, having heard and understood, one expects to enter [the path] [but fails to do so].

Instruction must necessarily derive from a teacher. The meanings of cessation and cultivation are profound; without study, one cannot comprehend them. Therefore, one should select a person endowed with virtue as a reliance.

The five faults refer to the four requisites for sustaining life, all of which depend upon faithful donors. If one resides where there is a lack of patrons, then the assistance of the Path will be difficult to achieve;
thus, these five faults exist. In such cases, one must not remain in retreat. Conversely, if these conditions are met, one may practice.
One gains benefit on the Path, and it is also beneficial for those living at home to establish fields of merit.

The *Vinaya-mūla* states: "There are four types of *varṣā* (the summer retreat): first, the face-to-face (*saṃmukha*); second, the mental recitation (*manasikāra*); third, the completion through forgetfulness (*vismṛti-siddhi*);
and fourth, the reaching of the boundary (*sīmā-prāpti*). Each has its own supporting conditions, which are listed in detail below."
Commentary: This is the general heading; what follows is the detailed enumeration. However, the ritual procedures for this *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) are not complete across all schools;

they were personally observed and heard by the Vinaya Master Yijing during his travels to the Western Regions. Having practiced them himself on numerous occasions, he later requested the Sanskrit manuscripts and returned to the Tang dynasty to translate and record them. We now continue to follow these practices accordingly.
Continuation: According to the *Ekottarakarma*, it is said: "The *an-shu* (rainy season retreat) begins tomorrow; today, one receives the counting-sticks (*śalākā*).

These sticks must not be coarse, inferior, crooked, or twisted. They should be washed with scented water and placed peacefully within a bowl, covered with fresh flowers and then further covered with a clean cloth.
(Text). According to the regulations below, one should [perform this] on the fifteenth day of the fourth month at the place where the assembly gathers. Correctly...
On the upper part of the central section, provide a seat for Śākyamuni Buddha, the Original Teacher and Lord of the Sahā World.

On the lower part of the center, provide a seat for the Dharma-protecting Vajrapāṇi Deva. To the left and right, arrange seats for the assembly of monks. Ring the mallet to assemble the monks within the boundary.
Set up a low table in the center and place the counting-board tray upon it. The presiding elder (upādhyāya) should then request the *chanda* (consent) and inquire [of the assembly].
The cause. The answer is: the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of receiving voting sticks (*śalākā*). One who is capable of performing the formal act within the assembly makes the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today, on the sixteenth day, the Saṃgha intends to enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha receive the voting sticks today and enter the retreat tomorrow. Thus is the motion.

Having made this announcement, if there is no one in the assembly who has previously received the appointment, one should appoint them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion and one proclamation) according to the tenth chapter.
If there is someone who has already received the appointment, the *sthavira* asks: "Who is able to distribute the *śalākā* for the Saṃgha?
He replies: "I, [Name], am capable. Thereupon, he rises from his seat with the proper decorum and pays homage to the *sthavira*.
He returns once more to his original seat, joins his palms, and says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing, I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall conduct the *śalākā* (lottery/counting sticks) on behalf of the Saṃgha.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). (The single-announcement procedure [*ekajñapti*] states: "In conducting the *śalākā*, there must be an announcement; this is precisely that.")

Having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), he rises from his seat. The person holding the counting tray (*śalākā-patra*) goes before him, while the person collecting the counting sticks follows behind with an empty tray.

First arriving before the Buddha’s seat, he hands the counting tray to the collector. Performing the ritual with full decorum, he prostrates three times and, holding the counting stick, kneels and says:
"On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], at this assembly for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the Teacher of the Sahā World, our Original Master Śākyamuni..."
The Muni Buddha received the first tally. Having spoken and performed one prostration, he rose to stand by the side. He took the two bowls in his hands.
The other [monks] prostrated themselves and withdrew the tallies, each still holding them aloft. Next, they proceeded to stand before the senior monk (upādhyāya).
The senior monk left his seat and squatted down to receive the tallies from him. When the distributor reached the second seat, the collector...
Approach the senior elder (sthavira). The senior elder places the tally-stick (śalākā) into an empty bowl. In this manner, they proceed to collect them until the last person.
If there are novices (śrāmaṇera) observing the rains retreat, their preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) shall receive the tally on their behalf.

Afterwards, go before the Vaisravana deity, hold the tally, bow, and declare: "On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], within this assembly for the rains retreat, I am a protector of the Dharma..."
The Vajrapāṇi Deva receives the final tally-stick, which is also collected according to the previous ritual procedure.
Once the distribution is complete, he counts the number of sticks in a secluded place. Then, returning before the *upādhyāya*, he announces:

"On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], at this residence, there are this many bhikṣus who have currently received the tally-sticks, and this many śrāmaṇeras. Having finished speaking, he further says: "I, [Name]..."

A) When the distribution of the *śalākā* (voting sticks) for the Saṃgha has been completed, the Elder replies, "Well done" (*sādhu*). He should then place the counting tray back in its original position.

Having performed prostrations, they return to their positions. When the assembly has finished chanting in unison the "Merit of Receiving the Counting-Sticks" (Shouchou Gongde Shusheng Xing) and other verses, they rise to prostrate to the presiding elder (*upādhyāya*).
Then, each member returns in order to their respective places. This is called "gathering and continuing" in order to complete the ritual protocol.

○ Regarding the legal procedure for *pratyekasīmā-vārṣika* (the rains retreat in the presence of another): The Vinaya text states that one should address the person upon whom one relies, saying: "I shall observe the rains retreat at this location.
[Explanation: This clarifies the first type of method for the rains retreat. Anyone who comes to the monastic boundary (*sīmā*) to observe the retreat should first...
Addressing the presiding *vinaya*-master, one says: "I wish to observe the three-month summer rains retreat (*varṣā*) at this location.

Although the *Vinaya* merely mentions speaking these words, I now add the ritual procedures to manifest that it is performed according to the Dharma. Having first made this declaration, when the appointed time arrives, one fully assumes the dignified posture, prostrates, kneels with the right knee on the ground, joins the palms, and speaks as follows:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now enter the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) based on [the name of] a certain monastery or village in order to repair dilapidated dwellings.

(Recite this three times. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that the person who has been informed should say: "Know this; do not be negligent. (The respondent says: "I accept and uphold it. (The *Vinayamūla* states:

During the summer, one must rely on a fifth-teacher (*pañcamo dharmaśāstrī*) who can recite the two sections of the Vinaya in detail. To violate this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. During spring and winter, one relies on a fourth-teacher (*caturtho dharmaśāstrī*). To violate this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is the principle.)
According to the intent of the Vinaya, one should ask him: "Upon which master of the Vinaya do you rely? (He replies: "I rely upon Master So-and-so. (The master of the Vinaya says:
"If you have a doubt, you should go and ask him. (He replies: "Yes."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: The Buddha said, "One should observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) with one who upholds the Vinaya.

If the location is cramped or crowded, one may mentally rely on a distant teacher provided that one can travel back and forth within seven days. If one observes the retreat in a donor’s village, the wilderness, a forest grove, a mountain crag, a dwelling, or similar places, it is all the same as the preceding text;
the only difference is that 'monastery' (*saṃghārāma*) is substituted for [the previous term]. If one is repairing..."
Regarding the speech for breaking [the boundary]: it is restricted to the monastic residence and measured according to the specific circumstances.

As for the ritual procedures for the fourfold assembly, one merely changes the terms—substituting *bhikṣuṇī*, *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī* for [the male counterparts] to distinguish them; all other wording is the same as above.

Commentary: If the location is cramped and crowded—meaning it is congested and lacks tranquility—one may, for the purpose of restraining the mind and body and exerting oneself toward the Path, take seven days to travel back and forth.
One should then form a mental resolve to rely on the *anvaya* (remote) *varṣā* from afar.

However, if one avoids the assembly out of weariness with toil or acts according to one's own whims and desires, forming a mental resolve to rely on the *anvaya* from afar in such a manner, the *varṣā* is not validly established.

Regarding "repairing dilapidated dwellings," according to the *Mūla-vinaya*: prior to the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), the Saṃgha appoints persons of fivefold virtue to distribute the rooms by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
First, they address the Elder (*sthavira*), saying: "Venerable Elder, please take this room and bedding as you see fit.
This is announced in the same manner down to the fourth Elder. At that time...
There was a bhikṣu who obtained a dilapidated room and thought to himself, "I will not accept this room, for fear that I must repair it.
The Buddha said, "You should accept it and repair it according to your ability. The present text follows what is prescribed by the regulations.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if there is a dwelling that is broken or leaking, it should be repaired at the end of spring (that is, during the month prior to the sixteenth day of the fourth lunar month). If...

If grass or tiles appear, one should follow this by repairing them. However, since temples in the Eastern lands all establish meditation halls (zen-dō), even if they become dilapidated, the monastery’s permanent endowment (jōzō) will manage the repairs.
For those who come to observe the summer retreat (an-gyo), such matters do not arise;
therefore, these words need not be spoken. To speak of them would be merely empty. If there were actually someone responsible for maintenance, then one may explain it according to the text. This—
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) takes the advancement of the Path as its principle, the prohibition of wandering as its purpose, and the protection of all living beings as its function;
this belongs to the private within the public.

Non-human [faults] are not [permissible]. This refers to cases where the basis [of the residence] violates established regulations and so forth. Faults regarding the matter refer to the five transgressions, such as failing to exercise discernment, and so forth.
Other faults are of a similar category to those mentioned previously. ○ The Method for the Later Retreat (Kārttika-vassa).

In the Vinaya, there is a case concerning a bhikṣu who wished to enter the *pūrvavāsa* (early retreat) on the sixteenth day of the fourth month but did not reach his destination until the seventeenth day.
The Buddha said that he should enter the *paścimavāsa* (late retreat). As stated in the preceding text, one should observe the three-month summer retreat during the latter part of the period;
the remaining text is as above. This applies likewise up to the method for the *paścimavāsa* beginning on the sixteenth day of the fifth month.
The same applies as before.
Explanation: Regarding the three types of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat), one should change the phrasing for the [first] four months to "the summer *vassa* of the third month.
This is because, since there is already a preceding [period], it thus opens up the subsequent [period]. At another time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
The Venerable Kāśyapa, there are three types of *vassa* (the rainy season retreat). Thus, altering the middle three months is not without basis.

This was initiated by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana within the Vinaya: when these two honored ones did not employ their supernormal powers to fly through the air and arrive swiftly, they came on foot just like ordinary people.
Failing to meet the appointed time, they requested that the Buddha grant an exemption; this was truly an exercise of great skillful means (*mahopāya*).
This is manifested as a model to be followed for future generations. This method possesses three conditions; its manifestation and non-manifestation are both based on the aforementioned rules.
○ Regarding the Method of Mindful Residence (Cittānuvartana-varṣā):
The Buddha said, "If there is no person upon whom one can rely, one may announce it and perform the mindful residence. The text states:
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat (varṣā) at the monastery of [Name] (the remainder is as stated above).

**Explanation:** This clarifies the second type of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat). It concerns the procedure of formal declaration (*sammukhībhāva*) and mental reflection (*manasikāra*). Regarding the conditions established in the Vinaya:
at one time, there was a bhikkhu residing in a place where no person was available to rely upon; he became doubtful, not knowing whether his *vassa* was validly established or not.

The Buddha said, "It is established. It is for the sake of the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat). From this day forward, if there is no person upon whom one can rely, I permit the *vassa* through mental resolve (*cittena vassam upagantun*).
As for the phrase 'the mind constitutes the *vassa*,' it means to firmly resolve upon the ninety-day period and to cultivate diligently without slackening."
This practice is to be observed only by those who have entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) rains retreat; it does not serve as a precedent for those in the *aparavārṣika* (later) rains retreat.
This rule pertains to private matters, and the circumstances for its application are the same as those mentioned above.

1. Non-fault regarding the person: because there is reliance, mindfulness and so forth are not at fault. 2. Non-fault regarding the dharma: the middle and subsequent ritual procedures and so forth are not at fault.
3. Non-fault regarding the matter: the three types of action are not disrespectful and so forth. The remaining four are combined with the "taking" (ādāna).

○ Regarding the case where the boundary for the rains retreat (*varṣā*) was not formally established: when various bhikṣus arrived at their place of residence to enter the rains retreat, they forgot to establish the boundary. The Buddha said:
"If they have come specifically for the purpose of the rains retreat, the retreat is thereby established."
Commentary: This clarifies the third type of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat). This rule was established as an extension from the practice of mental recollection (*manasikāra*).

According to the Vinaya, at one time the bhikkhus wished to enter the retreat at their dwelling places, but because they lacked someone to address for formal notification (*ñatti*), they forgot to perform the mental recollection of the retreat.
Having doubts as to whether the retreat had been validly entered or not, they reported this matter to the Buddha. Therefore...
This is to permit the hearing of this Dharma.
In the Vinaya, for a visiting bhikṣu who has previously made an agreement to rely on a dwelling place, there is an allowance for the establishment of boundaries even if he forgets to do so;
provided there is already a resident, it is not restricted by the general rule. If there was originally a skillful means, it applies to both the guest and the host.
Commentary: Master Xuanzu feared that the established practices of resident bhikṣus might be followed; therefore, he again clarified the distinction between the general and the specific.
He stated that when a visiting bhikṣu first sets out, his original intention is already fixed upon advancing on the Path.

Having come from abroad to seek lodging in this place, once arrived, he finds no one to rely upon with whom to make a formal declaration, and furthermore, he has forgotten to mentally resolve upon the *anvārohaṇa* (the formal entry into the rains retreat). Thus...
The Buddha’s resolution of doubts confirms this: if a dwelling must have a resident who relies upon it, then that person is not included within the general scope of this rule.
However, since this rule applies exclusively to guests, if the root Vinaya contains a provision allowing for it, then it may apply to both guests and residents.
Furthermore, regarding the method for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*) within a monastery precinct (*sīmā*) and a garden (*ārāma*):
at one time, there was a bhikṣu who went to another place to enter the retreat; he placed one foot inside the garden and the precinct, and then the dawn appeared.
If both feet have entered the garden and the boundary, and then the dawn appears;

or if both feet have entered the garden and the boundary, and then the dawn has already passed—the Buddha declared that in both cases the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) is successfully established. According to human interpretation, the latter two methods should be applied during the sixteen days preceding or following [the full moon].
If one observes the mid-term retreat (*antarāvassa*), the formal act of establishing it may be performed on any day.

Commentary: This clarifies the fourth type of boundary for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). It refers to the formal *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), which also serves as the limit for the storage of robes.

It has markers at its four cardinal points and belongs internally to the community of monks (*saṃgha*). The Sanskrit term is *ārāma*, which translates here as "Garden of the Multitude"; it refers to a monastic monastery.
The boundary encircles the exterior of the garden, while the garden is situated within the boundary. Although there is a distinction between near and far, they constitute a single [unit].

If one foot enters within the boundary while the other foot remains outside the boundary, or if one foot enters the temple gate while the other foot remains outside the gate, and then the light of dawn appears—the "light of dawn" meaning that the stars fade away and the east becomes bright—then it is so.
It is the same when both feet enter the garden or the boundary; likewise, if both feet have entered the garden or the boundary and then the light of dawn passes by.
[The] signs: as the rising sun was about to ascend, they came for the purpose of entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*), and thus all successfully entered the retreat.

According to human interpretation, regarding these two methods of entering the monastery and the boundary: if one comes for the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) on or before the sixteenth day of the fourth month, it is precisely on the morning of the seventeenth day of the fourth month;
if for the later retreat (*aparavarṣā*) on or after the sixteenth day of the fifth month...

Come. It is precisely on the morning of the seventeenth day of the fifth month. According to the Vinaya regulations, the periods for the preceding and succeeding retreats (*pūrvavāra* and *paścimavāra*) each last for only one day.

5. Abandonment through the severance of expectation: If a bhikṣu, having accepted a *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining one, and that bhikṣu then goes to the place where he hoped to obtain the robe, but upon seeing it, does not obtain the robe and his expectation is severed—having no further place of expectation—his expectation being severed, he loses the *kaṭhina* robe.

Commentary: This refers to the intention of departing the boundary after having finished receiving the robe through formal combination (*saṃghāṭī*). It means that one expects to certainly obtain the materials for a robe from a certain donor and departs to make the robe;
however, upon reaching that place, one begs but does not obtain the robe, and there is no other place where robe-material can be sought.
When that bhikṣu’s hope is severed, the *kaṭhina* (功德衣) is likewise lost. The calculation of days is as stated above.

Sixth, loss through hearing. If a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to make a robe, and having finished making it, hears that the Saṃgha has discarded the *kaṭhina*, he loses the *kaṭhina* robe upon hearing that news.
Commentary: This refers to having finished receiving the robe through formal assembly. While outside the boundary making the robe, one maintains mindfulness;

as soon as the robe is completed, one returns to the boundary. Even if the robe is completed but one has not yet returned, one hears that the *kaṭhina* robe has already been suspended by the Saṃgha within the boundary.
Upon hearing this, he immediately loses the *kaṭhina* robe. These cases, as well as the two following, all refer to the completion of the full month, and are not the same as the five preceding cases.

Seventh, relinquishing by going outside the boundary: if a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary and finishes making his robes [and returns], the count [is complete].

[The monk] forms the intention to return. While the community of monks outside the boundary is distributing the *kaṭhina* robe, he remains outside the boundary and loses his claim to the *kaṭhina* robe.

Explanation: This refers to one who, having completed the formal reception of the robe through a harmonious assembly, goes outside the boundary and takes a long time to make the robe, only after a great deal of time [does he complete it].

It is accomplished. Even if one repeatedly forms the intention to return, but does not actually return to the boundary, and the Saṃgha within the boundary has cast out the *kaṭhina* robe, he who remains outside the boundary also loses the *kaṭhina* robe.

Eighth, the common relinquishing. If a bhikṣu, having accepted a *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to make robes, and whether those robes are finished or unfinished, he returns to his residence, that bhikṣu’s community shall together relinquish the *kaṭhina*.
These are the eight matters.

Commentary: This refers to having finished receiving the robe through formal assembly. One goes outside the boundary to seek the materials for the robe, and due to the circumstances of making it, many days pass.

When the time limit of the four winter months is nearly reached, whether the robe being made is finished or not, one must quickly return to the original boundary, join with the community, and together perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony. This is [the rule].

This is for the purpose of distributing robes in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding these eight matters, the first five are explained by means of mental reflection (*manasikāra*), following the precedent of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations).

The causal origins (*nidāna*) in all the Vinayas are identical: they were established because [monks] failed to relinquish the five types of benefits derived from the *kaṭhina* robe out of excessive greed.
Among these, if the date of the robe’s loss is known, or if the four months of winter have been completed—[in all such cases, the procedure applies].

If one keeps [the robes] beyond the prescribed time and so forth, one commits an offense in all such cases; they are to be dealt with according to the fundamental offense. The seventh section, "The Chapter on the Self-Examination (Pravāraṇā) of the Assembly," is concluded.
This concludes the ninth volume of the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (Continued Commentary on the Vinaya), including the phonetic glosses.
Section on the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*). "Tà" (踏) is pronounced as "tà," meaning to tread upon.

"Shì" (市) is pronounced with the third tone; it refers to a marketplace, a place for buying and selling. "Shì" (市) means to rely upon; one relies on it to provide for and sustain the elderly and the young. Thus... [it is not].
It means "to cross.
The pronunciation of *she* (涉) is *she*. It refers to crossing water while traveling on a path. In ancient times, one did not bathe naked when crossing water;
therefore, one would wear clothes while crossing. When the depth reaches up to the clothing, such a crossing is called *li* (厲).
"Niè" (捩) means to twist; it signifies breaking.
"Zé" (迮) means to press; it signifies confinement.
"Náo" (鐃), with the departing tone, means lack of tranquility.
Kuò (括) is a word of the first entering tone; it means to examine or inspect.
Yū (迂) has the pronunciation yú; it means distant.
From the "Chapter on Self-Indulgence."
*Zì* (pronounced with a departing tone) means to let go or to release. *Xiāo Hé*’s biography uses the phrase "to release and point out.
*Kuǎn* (pronounced with an entering tone) means respect or intimacy.
*Yán* (sound like *yán*) means to follow downstream.
*Jiān* (緘) means to seal or close.
*Jù* (懼) means to fear or be terrified.
*Nruò* (懦)—the initial rhyme is *gè*; the pronunciation is *ruì*—means weak or yielding.
*Jīn* (pronounced *jīng*): To be conceited and self-important.
*Wěi* (pronounced *wěi*): The withering of grasses and trees.
*Zhǎn* (with the third tone): To roll or turn; to thresh grain.
*Śan-chui-yang* (Fanning and Blowing Up).
