Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Chongyi Temple in the Capital of Tang.
Continued Explanation of the Section on the Distribution of Various Robes, Part Eight, by the Later Scholar Bhikṣu Duti of Mount Hua in Jinling.
Explanation of the Six Harmonies of the Renunciants: Equal distribution of benefits constitutes one harmony. To embrace the Way without greed is called being a true Śākyaputra. Regarding robes:
In the *Khandhaka*, the Buddha compassionately issued repeated prohibitions; herein, within this compilation, our patriarch further elucidates them in detail.

You should contemplate with a mind intent on gathering and supplementing these teachings, rather than speaking with superficiality or indifference. To act upon these matters as they arise is of the utmost urgency and importance;
therefore, I have compiled the rules for the distribution of robes and placed them in the eighth chapter.
Within this, there are two ways in which gifts are acquired: first, those given by the seven classes of followers for the sake of the Saṃgha;
second, those given by monastics and laypeople for the sake of those currently present. If categorized according to conditions and timing, they do not exceed six types.
Commentary: Here, the seven assemblies are precisely the monastics and the laity; the monastics and the laity are precisely the seven assemblies.

Because their respective motivations for generating the aspiration differ, there are two distinctions. First, when one generates the aspiration to practice giving so as to reach those coming from the ten directions, it is said to be "for the sake of the Sangha.
Second, when one generates the aspiration to give only to the assembly present here, it is called "for the sake of those present. This applies universally.
Regarding the "ten directions": when distributing [the property] through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to those present, it merely illuminates the specific lineages of individuals;
thus, there are explanations based on conditions and timing that do not exceed the six types [of distribution]. These are detailed and clarified in the subsequent sections.
Regarding the method for the two assemblies of monks receiving offerings:

at one time, there was a residence where the two assemblies of monks had acquired a large quantity of divisible clothing and requisites. At that time, the community of bhikṣus was numerous while the bhikṣuṇīs were few.
The Buddha said: "Divide it into two portions. If there are no bhikṣuṇīs, even if there are only śikṣamāṇās, [the same rule applies].
It shall be divided into two portions. If there are only śrāmaṇerikās, they too shall be divided into two portions.

If there are no two assemblies [of bhikṣus], the bhikṣu-saṃgha alone shall divide it. If the bhikṣuṇīs are numerous and the monks few, or if there are none at all, it shall be divided into two portions.
Even if there are no śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣuṇīs shall receive the items; once they have arrived, they shall all be distributed within their own respective groups.

Explanation: One must perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution. If the two assemblies of the great *saṃgha* have no portion to bestow upon the two assemblies of the minor *saṃgha*, then those minor assemblies are subordinate divisions of the great *saṃgha*.
Thus, the minor assembly shall receive from the great *saṃgha*, just as a son receives the father’s property.

This clarifies that both divisions may receive the offerings. Regarding the case where, having received the items, they arrive within the boundary of their respective division, this is based on two principles:

first, that the Great Assembly (the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*) carries the items to the boundary of their own division; second, that the Small Group (the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*) returns the items to their original residence.
If there is a boundary of the Great Assembly, or if the Small Group arrives from outside, should they encounter a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for distribution, [they shall proceed accordingly].
When objects appear before them, each has its own portion; this clarifies the further subdivision within the [original] portions.
It is called "obtained by the Saṃgha" because the donor’s intention is universally impartial toward all things, extending throughout the ten directions.

As long as there are monks and nuns, they all partake in its portion; therefore, it is called "obtained by the Saṃgha. Furthermore, it must require the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha to exclude those who might arrive from the ten directions.
Once the procedure has been performed, the current distribution of the portion follows as described below.
Commentary: This passage investigates and explains the meaning of "attained by the Saṃgha" (*saṃghalabdha*). As for why it is so named:
the "Saṃgha" refers here to the two great divisions of the monastic community within the sphere of the World-Honored One’s single dispensation.
To designate such a vast domain, [it is understood that] the donor, having generated a mind of universal impartiality, bestows limitless objects of charity throughout [the entire assembly].
This is likewise true throughout the ten directions. Since there are only monks and nuns, they all partake of their respective portions;
therefore, it is spoken of in reference to a single monastic jurisdiction (*sīmā*), and thus it is called "obtained by the Saṃgha. This distinguishes it from a gift made to those present.

Furthermore, it must involve the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*); the convention of the *karmavācanā* serves to restrict subsequent claimants and facilitates the distribution of the shares. If...
At the time when the mallet is struck, those who have arrived from the ten directions have a share in the presence [of the assembly].

If the *karman* (formal ritual act) has already been completed, those who arrive from the ten directions cannot obstruct it and have no share. Therefore, it is said: "Once the procedure has been performed, the *karman* of those present is finalized;
as for those who come later," which accords with the sixth section on the procedure for distributing gifts obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time.
2. The Method for Receiving Offerings in the Presence of Both Assemblies.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained in meditative seclusion for three months, with the exception of a single attendant.
There were sixty *dhūta* monks who went to the Buddha’s dwelling and were praised by the Buddha; meanwhile, those monks who were not *dhūta* abandoned their robes.
It formed a great accumulation. The Buddha said: "It should be given as a gift to the community of monks (saṃgha).
If it is given to a single person, it may be granted to a bhikṣuṇī as non-clothing. If a bhikṣu is performing parivāsa or mānatva, he should divide it and distribute it.

For the seven types of persons undergoing formal acts (karmavācanā), it should be placed on the ground for them to take. If one has another give it, or if it concerns a śrāmaṇera, it should be distributed equally; or half may be given."
If three parts are given and one part remains, the monastery attendant should be given an equal share.
If it reaches four parts and one part is to be given, if it is not given, it should not be divided; if it is divided, it should be done according to the Dharma.
Commentary: The World-Honored One’s essence is true as delusion is exhausted; movement and stillness are one and the same. Yet he said, "I wish to sit in meditation and contemplate for three months;
do not allow outsiders to enter, except for a single person who provides offerings. He praised the dhūta practices alone, yet permitted people to pay their respects at will.
Within this praise, there is censure and exaltation; it is precisely this that restrains and removes people's greedy attachments and gives rise to [right] understanding.

To inspire pure faith, he then revealed the origins of his undertaking. Consequently, upon seeing and hearing this, there were no non-dhūta bhikṣus who did not aspire to emulate the twelve dhūta practices. Some came to dwell in araṇya hermitages;
some refused invitations and constantly practiced alms-gathering; and some abandoned the robes offered by donors to wear robes made of discarded rags.
There are those who renounce extra robes and maintain only the three [monastic] robes; even some who practice constant sitting and refrain from lying down.

For this reason, they renounce their clothing, resulting in a great accumulation [of discarded items]. In the Sanskrit language, *dhūta*; translated here as "shaking off" (*dǒusǒu*), it means one is able to shake off the dust and defilements of affliction;
that is, it is diligence (*vīrya*). As for the twelve practices (*dhūtaguṇa*): first, dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage).

That is to say, a bhikṣu should dwell in a secluded and tranquil place, far removed from bustle and noise, untainted by the dust of desire, forever severing all objects of attachment, and seeking the path to liberation;
this is the dhūta practice. Second, he constantly practices begging for food.

It means that a bhikṣu remains free from all craving and seeking; he does not accept invitations from others but constantly practices alms-gathering to sustain his physical body and assist in accomplishing the work of the Path.
When he receives food, whether it be good or bad, he gives rise to no thoughts of discrimination, increase, or decrease.
Even when he does not receive food, he feels no resentment. Whether he obtains food or not, his mind never wavers. This is called...
The dhūta practice of begging for alms in successive order: when a bhikṣu goes on his almsround, he does not despise sentient beings nor discriminate between the poor and the wealthy;
with an impartial and single-minded heart, he begs from house to house in regular sequence. This is the dhūta practice.
Fourth is eating at a single session. This means that a bhikṣu practicing the Path should reflect: "I seek but a single meal, yet even this involves much restraint;
how much more so regarding food before and after the small meal! If I do not diminish my own food intake, I shall lose half the merit of the day."
It is difficult to accomplish the work of the Path without a single-minded focus; therefore, one repeatedly abandons eating at all times and adopts the practice of eating only once a day.
This constitutes a *dhūta* practice. Fifth is the regulation of food quantity: a monk shall divide the alms he has received into three portions.
He gives one portion to those who are hungry and destitute, and places another morsel of food in a secluded, quiet place.
When giving to birds and beasts, if one does not see them in distress, one should eat only two-thirds of the food and leave one part behind;

one must not consume it all. In this way, the body will be light and at ease, easily digested and free from ailment, thereby manifesting compassionate virtue and extending pity to all sentient beings.
This is a dhūta practice. Sixth, among the transgressions, not drinking *pāna* (liquids). *Pāna*...
This refers to honey-meadow drinks and the like. That is to say, on the days a bhikṣu cultivates the Path, if various kinds of juice-drinks are consumed after midday, he must not drink them at all.

If he drinks them, he will delight in their flavor and greedily crave them without satiety, being unable to restrain his mind and failing to apply himself diligently to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
Therefore, by not drinking such drinks, this constitutes a dhūta practice. Seventh is wearing tattered rag-robes (pāṃsukūla), which means:

A bhikṣu does not love finery nor seek fine garments; rather, within the village, he gathers discarded old items, washes them clean, and makes them into patched robes (*kaṣāya*) to ward off cold and heat and avoid exposing his body.
If one craves new and fine things, one will be driven to excessive seeking, which can also invite thieves and robbers; therefore, that which he wears is but a tattered patched robe.
To practice the dhūta austerities: the eighth is "possessing only the three robes. As for the three robes, they are the nine-strip, seven-strip, and five-strip *kāṣāya*.
This means that a bhikṣu, being one of few desires and contented, takes only enough clothing to cover his body—neither too much nor too little.
Thus he differs from laypeople and is not the same as non-Buddhists. The disciples of the Buddha abandon these two extremes and accept only the three robes; this is the dhūta austerity.
The ninth is dwelling among burial mounds (*śmāśānika*). This means contemplating impermanence, suffering, and emptiness; it is the initial gateway for entering the path of the Buddha’s Dharma.
It enables one to cultivate weary detachment from the three realms and to refrain from clinging to the four great elements.

When a bhikṣu dwells among burial mounds, he constantly beholds corpses—putrid, decaying, and strewn about, pecked by birds or consumed by fire. Thus, the contemplation of impermanence and impurity is easily accomplished.
Thus, he sits among burial mounds; this constitutes the dhūta practice. Tenth is sitting under a tree: it means that a bhikṣu has few affairs and delights in silent cultivation.
He resorts to an undecorated, lush tree merely to shield himself from rain and dew and to avoid the scorching sun.
When the time comes, he goes for alms; returning, he sits cross-legged and contemplates with single-minded focus, having no further concerns. In this way, the work of the Path may be hoped for.
Because he has achieved this, he sits beneath a tree; this constitutes a dhūta practice. Eleventh is sitting in the open air:
it means that after a bhikṣu has finished his meal during the day, he practices walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), and at night he spreads his bedding and sits in the open.

With the wind fresh, the moon bright, the environment tranquil, and the mind at ease, one can, through such a vast and open disposition, easily enter the signless right concentration (*animitta-samādhi*). Therefore, [the practice] is performed in the open air.
Sitting is the dhūta practice. Twelfth is "sitting only and not lying down. This means that a bhikṣu, intending to sever the five hindrances, first dispels sleepiness;
thus the master is not deluded and the thief finds no opportunity. With diligent vigor and a pure body and mind, he gives rise to true, untainted concentration and wisdom.
Except for begging for food and attending to the calls of nature, he sits constantly day and night. This is...
This constitutes the practice of dhūta austerities; it is a brief explanation of the twelve dhūta practices.

One should understand that the aforementioned rule states that the two assemblies of the Sangha receive offerings because this applies universally to the Sangha of the ten directions. This present rule, however, states that the two assemblies receive offerings when they are present before one.
Because it does not pertain to the Sangha of the ten directions, the Buddha said: "One should give to the assembly of monks;
if given to a single person, it is permitted to give to a bhikṣuṇī, provided it is not a robe. "Non-robes" refers to alms-bowl bags, needle cases, waistbands, hats, towels, and so forth.
If one is practicing the two types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* penance, the portion of the robe should be divided and given to him, so that he may practice the rite of begging out of a sense of shame.
In order to comply with the Saṃgha and hope for purification from the offense, the seven *karman*-officiants should place the robe on the ground and give it to him, or have someone else give it.
Since the distribution of the robe belongs to the Saṃgha, they cause it to be placed on the ground or have someone else deliver it.
This is done to administer the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), so that he may recognize his error, repent, and quickly seek the lifting of this *karman*. Thus, the *śramaṇa*...
"Equally, or half, or one-third, or one-fourth" means that if the community is in harmony, it should give equally to the assembly;
if they permit giving half or a small portion, it should likewise follow accordingly. It is the same for those who guard the monastery;
they should give equally, or if it reaches four parts, they should give one part, and so forth. If there are śrāmaṇeras or those who guard the monastery, if they do not... [text ends]

That which is given should not be divided; if it is divided, it must be handled according to the Dharma. That is to say, if the Saṃgha acts contrary to the Buddha’s word, they all incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (dharma-vyatikrama).
○ The method for receiving offerings that appear at the three times.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in one place, resided in another place.

Not knowing from which location he should take his share of the goods, the Buddha said: "It is permitted to take [the share] from the place where he has resided for the greater number of days. If he has resided equally in both places, it is permitted to take half from each.
If a large amount is obtained that can be divided, it should be distributed according to the number of people, or by means of counting sticks (*śalākā*), and so forth."
One person directly undertakes [the observance];
he does not form a mental resolve regarding the Dharma. Commentary: This practice begins from the sixteenth day of the fourth month.

Regardless of whether one is within the boundary (*sīmā*) or engaged in intensive cultivation, should there be circumstances requiring one to leave the boundary, all those who are co-residents in this location during the retreat are present before him; they are counted as being within the retreat.

Because the donor originally gave rise to the intention to provide for the monks dwelling in this location during the summer retreat, it is said that "the gift is obtained by those present at the time.
The alms and requisites obtained during this single summer are only to be distributed once the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is completed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The text states: "Having completed the summer retreat (varṣā), if one dwells in another location," this refers to the permission granted for relocation due to specific circumstances.
Consequently, there is a share in the property of both locations; however, it is permitted that one takes [the portion] from the place where one has resided for the greater number of days.
This involves relinquishing the small for the sake of the large, without regard for the original transfer.

If it is permitted that both parties may each take half when their portions are equal, this means that, based on the share obtained by others present before one, one takes only half of that single portion;
since the two portions are combined, they still correspond to the measure of one original portion. If there is a large amount to be divided, it should follow the persons currently present.

Regarding the counting: it says to take one full portion, or alternatively, "to fall into the division by tally-sticks" (*śalākā-bhāga*). This is different from the "untimely casting of tally-sticks" mentioned below;
the former is spoken in order to prevent discord during the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), while the latter is taught for the sake of equitable distribution among those present.

According to the Vinaya, when the Saṃgha was split into two factions during the *varṣā*, the Buddha ordered that each group should take [the property] according to their respective tally-sticks, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "one person, etc.": In the Vinaya, there was a householder who gathered the monks from various locations at a bhikṣu residence, provided them with food and drink, and offered robes as alms. The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it is given to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu-saṃgha should divide it; if it is given to a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha should divide it."
If it is given to two groups, the two groups should divide it; if it is given to one person, it should belong to that one person.

This does not involve the formal procedure of *cetanā* (mental resolve). The present text uses the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) because, in practice, it employs the procedure for a single person; thus, the rest is abbreviated.
Since the donor provides only the items for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) for one person, it is permitted for that one person to take them directly without the formal procedure of *cetanā*.
This may be done; it is not like the case where the Sangha receives an offering at a later time.
○ Fourth, the method for receiving an offering that is present before the assembly at an improper time:
When the Sangha present at the proper time obtains a large quantity of divisible clothing and goods, the Buddha said: "I allow you to count the number of people. If there are ten..."

If there are ten people, they constitute one unit; up to one hundred people, they constitute one hundred units. If good and bad qualities are intermingled, those who have not yet seen [the matter] should be made to cast lots to divide them;
it is improper to perform a *karmavācanā* [formal act] [without such division].
Commentary: This teaching concerns gifts bestowed at times other than those during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Such gifts are to be divided among the resident bhikṣus;
they do not extend to the *daśadig-saṃgha* (the Sangha of the ten directions). Therefore, it is called "gifts obtained by the *pratyutpanna* (present) community at non-seasonal times.
According to the Vinaya, there was a donor who sent various fine robes to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not know what to do with them.
"What is it? he asked the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should count the number of people. If there are ten people, divide into ten portions; up to a hundred people, divide into a hundred portions.
When the robes are being distributed, good and bad items should be mixed together. At that time, those distributing the robes might take their own portions.
The Buddha said, 'One should not take one's own portion. One should have another person distribute them and have another person take the portion.'"
Regarding the distribution by casting lots: that bhikṣu cast the lot himself. The Buddha said, "One should not cast the lot oneself.

It is permitted for one who does not see [the names] to cast the lot. This means that the names of the bhikṣus should be written upon the lots and entrusted to another bhikṣu who does not see those names to cast them.
The intention is to ensure impartiality and freedom from favoritism, to settle disputes, and to manifest harmony through mutual benefit.
[The distribution] is equal. Once divided in this manner, it is not permissible to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) [to alter it].
Regarding the fifth rule, the method for when the Saṃgha receives offerings:
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who departs before the summer robes have been distributed. Later, when the robes are being distributed, he is unable to return; furthermore, he has forgotten [the matter].
It is not [considered] distributed. If a practitioner does not know whether their portion has been distributed or not, the Buddha said: "It counts as a distributed robe.

They should wait for one another, and they should also have that portion brought out and divided by means of a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), according to the procedure for gifts received by the Saṃgha at an improper time."
Commentary: The third [category] is called "receiving offerings while present" (*pratyakṣa-lābha*).

This fifth [category], called "the Saṃgha receiving offerings while present," differs from the former rule, which was restricted solely to items present at the original site of the retreat and did not extend to the ten directions.
This [fifth category], however, applies to all monks in summer retreat, whether they have left their original boundary due to some necessity or whether others have arrived from elsewhere.
When robes that have come into view are encountered, all shall receive their shares; therefore, a separate section is established.

The text cites two conditions to clarify that among those in the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), even those not present should receive their share of the offerings. The Vinaya states: "There was a certain bhikṣu..."
Before the summer robes had been distributed, he departed. After the robes had been distributed, he returned and asked, "Have the summer robes been distributed?
They replied, "They have been distributed. He asked, "Did you take my portion? They replied, "We did not take it. That bhikṣu became angry and rebuked the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus wondered, "Does this constitute a valid distribution of robes? The Buddha said, "It constitutes a valid distribution of robes; one should have waited for him."
Upon returning, he should also receive his portion from that [remaining] share, and he should also entrust the subsequent person with the receipt of his summer robe portion.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, before the summer robes had been distributed, went away and entrusted a bhikṣu, saying, "Please take my share of the summer robes for me.
When the bhikṣus were distributing them, they asked, "Who took the robe portion of such-and-such a bhikṣu? The bhikṣu who had received the entrustment had forgotten it.

[He] took [it]. He asked in return, "Has the robe-cloth been divided? [The other] replied, "It has already been divided. [He] asked, "Have you not taken my share of the robe-cloth? [The other] replied, "I have not taken it.

These descriptions refer to products produced in the Five Indias (*Pañcāla*). In Sanskrit, this is called *kūṇapa*, translated as "small" or "tiny."
Objects: including the razor, robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle-case, and so forth—these are items that may be distributed.
This is the definitive judgment according to the Vinaya texts of our own school (*mūla-nikāya*).

As for other items not mentioned here, one should consult the Vinayas and treatises of the various schools to determine whether they belong to the category of distributable or non-distributable items according to our own school. If one relies on the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*...

The Vinaya states: If there are items such as a *saṃkakṣikā* (translated as an inner garment, resembling a modern short skirt), a single-layered cloth, an undergarment, a needle case, a water-strainer, large and small alms bowls, or a door hook—such objects are subject to distribution; the monks currently present should all divide them among themselves.

However, if there are items such as brocade, damask, a rain-bathing robe, a wound-covering cloth, a mosquito net, or a mat for walking meditation used to shield against walls, these are not to be divided.
Wind-bells, single-layered sitting mats and beds, containers for medicinal substances, umbrellas, and staffs (*khakkhara*)—these are indivisible and should belong to the communal use of the Saṃgha.

The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states: "If there are male or female slaves, they should be released and allowed to go; if they are not released, they shall serve as *śuddha-karmika* (pure workers) for the Saṃgha.
Camels, horses, oxen, and donkeys shall be used for the transport and maintenance of the monastery’s permanent property. This refers to the deceased bhikṣu.
If there are any items with interest accruing outside [the monastery], one should have the *śramaṇoddeśa* (lay-attendant) of the monastery search for and recover them.
Once recovered, they shall enter the permanent property (*ātyayika*) of this monastery’s resident Sangha. All items made of iron that are divisible include:
iron hooks, iron shackles, wedges, axes, knives, scissors, iron staffs, incense burners, braziers, bowls, and incense tubes. (*Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha*)

It is said: If, after the death of a *bhikṣu* who served as an administrator, his personal belongings are intermingled with those belonging to the Three Jewels such that they cannot be distinguished, these possessions of the deceased shall be shared equally by the Three Jewels.
Now, according to what is clarified in the aforementioned Vinaya and Śāstras, this is adjudicated by applying the same principles to its own category.

One should examine the intent of the Vinaya texts; they do not tolerate laxity, haste, or self-deception. If one desires to know this in full detail, it is as explained in the *Liángchù chóngqīng wùyí* (The Ritual for Determining the Weight of Objects).
Regarding the statement that "the intent of the Vinaya texts does not tolerate laxity, haste, or self-deception": in all cases of deceased property, one must be thorough and precise.

Having secured the items, the funeral procession shall return to the monastery, where the assembly of monks shall divide them. If one delays for many days, there is a fear that private corruption may arise;
yet if one settles matters too hastily, there is a risk that items will be forgotten.

For those who desire to know this in full detail, including the regulations regarding the gravity of the offenses, this ritual manual is one section of the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao*. It states: "The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* divides [the distribution] into four types."
Regarding the permanent endowment (*sthāvara-vastu*): in Sanskrit it is called *saṃghika*, which is translated here as "property of the Saṃgha of the four directions.

First is the "permanent-permanent" [endowment], referring to the monastic community's kitchens and storehouses, temple buildings and communal utensils, flower gardens, fruit orchards, fields, groves, servants, livestock, and so forth.
Because their substance is restricted to that specific location and does not extend to other boundaries, they may only be used; they cannot be divided or sold.
Therefore, "permanently abiding" (changzhu) is mentioned twice. Second is the "permanently abiding of the ten directions," such as the regular food provided by a monastic community for the Sangha;
its substance extends throughout the ten directions, yet it is restricted to its original location. These two are called *saṃghika* property. Third is the "present before one" (*pratyutpanna*).
This refers to property obtained as an offering for the Saṃgha, which is given specifically to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present Saṃgha) of this location.

Fourth is that which belongs to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* of the ten directions, such as the light personal belongings of deceased members of the five groups. If the *karman* has not yet been performed, one incurs an offense with respect to the *saṃgha* of the ten directions;

if the *karman* has already been performed, one incurs an offense with respect to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha*. These two are called "property of the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha*" (text). This is to be understood accordingly.
The fourth [offense] refers to the property of the deceased community, which belongs to the Saṃgha and is not yet determined as belonging to either new or resident members.

If, prior to the striking of the gavel to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one privately intends to retain it, or exchanges the old for the new, and obtains goods worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—or less than five—this constitutes stealing the property of the Saṃgha of the ten directions.
The offense is established according to the value of the goods. If the gavel has already been struck and the ritual performed...

Regarding the time of the Dharma: if one falsely claims that a gift was given, or deceitfully asserts a debt, and acquires property—whether much or little—the offense is established according to the calculated value.
This is stealing the property of the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes. One must reflect that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are subject to decay;

all things are ultimately empty. Impermanence, suffering, and emptiness—whom among humans can escape these? It is precisely appropriate to contemplate these objects and apply antidotes, binding the mind in diligent cultivation. How can one afford to be so deluded?
The mind becomes attached; because of objects, non-virtue arises. This is called losing one's human form beneath the *kāṣāya*, or turning back into bondage within liberation itself.
When the wise behold this, they realize that both person and environment have returned to themselves. Since "that" has perished in this way, "I" am likewise the same.
Thus, as a superior condition for increasing application, one performs the remedy for transcending suffering through authentic cultivation. Objects—
Although there are portions [of the property], the intention does not lie therein. Because the substance arises from the gathering of conditions, the assembly has come together.
Therefore, the *gandi* is used as a portion for deceased items; its role in providing exhortation among them is truly beneficial for those present.
Regarding the eight measures of merit for awarding goods, the Buddha said:
"If one accomplishes five dharmas, one should be granted clothing and requisites for the sick; therefore, it is known that if these are not complete, one shall not receive the reward.
First, one must know what the sick person may eat and what they may not eat; if it is permissible to eat, one should provide it."
Commentary: Medicine and food should correspond to the illness; only then will there be profound benefit. If the medicine and the illness are incompatible, there will be no benefit and only harm.
For this reason, one should not follow the whims of the patient, but rather rely solely on skillful methods of treatment.

If something is unwholesome to eat, even if the patient feels anger or resentment, it should not be given. If it is wholesome to eat, even if the patient finds it distasteful, one should encourage them all the more to consume it.
Thus, while illness requires treatment through medicine, nourishment by food takes precedence. Since disease arises because of food, abstaining from food is fundamental;
this constitutes the primary virtue of one who tends to the sick.
Second, not to despise the excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit of the sick.
Commentary: When one lies prostrate upon a pillow and mat due to a chronic illness, rising and sitting are indeed difficult; being defiled and impure, they truly suffer from affliction.
If one can take pity on them, changing their bedding and washing it morning and evening, and cleaning the spittoon at dawn and dusk, so that the patient may rest in peace.
Their body and mind attain peace; they do not cause distress by increasing filth and suffering through the lack of bedding. This is the second virtue of nursing the sick.
Third, they possess a heart of compassion and do not act for the sake of food or clothing.
Commentary: When renunciants live together in community, they take the precepts as their kin. In times of well-being, they practice together; in times of illness, they look after one another.
Were it not for a heart of compassion, how could there be such mutual concern for each other’s pain and itching?

It is because of harboring thoughts of pity that they provide medicine and nursing—not waiting for inquiries out of a desire for food or clothing—but by rising to strike [the bed], and rubbing [the patient] while lying down. This is the third virtue of tending to the sick.
Fourth, one is able to manage medicines until the patient recovers or dies.
[Commentary: The local flora consists of plants whose natures are either warm or cool. The physician is well-versed in prescriptions and pulses, distinguishing between various types of beings.

For pills and powders, they are administered according to the proper seasons; for decoctions, the fire must be regulated as "gentle" or "vigorous. If one can manage these matters, the illness relies [upon such care].
When the medicine takes effect, even if one encounters fixed karma that is difficult for the masters Qí and Huáng to cure, one must exert oneself from beginning to end until the patient’s passing;
this is the fourth virtue of tending the sick.
Fifth, he is able to preach the Dharma to the sick. He himself increases in wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*).

[Commentary: Grass roots and tree bark merely treat physical ailments; the unsurpassed medicine of the Dharma (*anuttara-dharma-bhaiṣajya*) alone removes the chronic disease of karma (*karma-ābādha*).
By employing physical medicine in conjunction with the medicine of the Dharma, one brings peace to the body so as to bring peace to the mind. Thus, the patient attains clarity.

Understanding suffering as empty, one is free from attachment; remaining within one’s own sphere, one is able to contemplate all things as illusory transformations and enter the principle of ultimate truth.
Because of this, the two benefits [of self and others] arise, and one is praised for the six points of harmony. This is the fifth virtue of tending to the sick.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five circumstances under which it is difficult to tend to a patient: first, having a wicked nature such that one cannot converse with them; second, tending to...
The instructions for the patient: first, they do not believe or accept the teaching; second, they consume food and drink that is unsuitable for their illness;
third, they do not know how to moderate their own intake; fourth, they are unwilling to take medicine; fifth, they are unwilling to exercise self-restraint and moderation.
If one reverses these five conditions, then the patient is easy to care for.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are four kinds of temporary labor: labor performed because the Saṃgha has appointed one, labor performed out of a personal desire for merit, and labor performed as a means of wrong livelihood;
none of these are worthy of reward. However, if it is for the benefit of a sick person and with the wish to cause them to recover quickly—even down to lighting a single lamp—it is permissible.
Regarding those who pass away while engaged in work, they shall receive these items.
Commentary: First, "temporary work" refers to that which is performed incidentally rather than being undertaken with a deliberate resolve;

since it lasts for no more than a few days, it does not merit a reward. Second, "work assigned by the Saṃgha" refers to tasks performed within a shared boundary (sīmā) by one who is ill and ought to be cared for.

If one looks upon others [with such concern], yet the assembly is crowded and arrives in disarray, it will instead increase confusion and disorder. Therefore, regarding the assignment of duties, those on duty shall attend to the medicinal decoctions according to their assigned days.
If one fails to tend to the sick, the *Vinaya* censures such lack of compassion as a fault; the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* further binds this as a minor secondary offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*).
An ancient master exhorted the monastic community regarding nursing the sick, saying: "A sick bhikṣu has no home within the four seas; a solitary lamp shines alone by his broken bed."
The solitary mind dwells amidst groans; for porridge and medicine, one must rely upon fellow practitioners of the Way.
It was for this reason that he was dispatched to attend to the sick, and thus it was not appropriate to reward him. Third is the practice of creating merit for one's own benefit:

among the eight fields of merit, the field of compassion (karuṇā-kṣetra) yields the greatest merit. Reflecting on the teachings clarifying the karmic retribution for nursing the sick, [the practitioner] shall remain free from calamity for many kalpas. Thus spoke the Buddha Dhataraṭṇa.
"Massaging the hands" is also obtained by stroking [the patient] out of compassion for their illness. Since this is done with the intention of seeking merit, it does not deserve a reward.
Fourth is "acting through wrong livelihood," which means that one originally lacks a compassionate heart or pity for suffering, and does not act out of a desire to seek merit;
rather, seeing that the patient has an abundance of medicine and food and that their storehouses are overflowing, one feigns the role of a caregiver.
He harbors internal malice and greed. Not only is there no praise or reward for such conduct in principle, but by the nature of the law, he ought to be censured.
Suppose, however, that a bhikṣu truly intends to benefit the patient, skillfully managing their medicine and food according to the illness with the desire to effect a swift recovery.

One must not cause that person’s illness to become chronic. Such a compassionate mind is so urgent that even if one only burns a single lamp, should the patient’s life come to an end, one will immediately obtain this object.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If many people tend to the sick, [the reward] is given to the one who attends to them until the end."
Explanation: This has two meanings. First, it refers to cases where a long-term illness persists and the caregiver becomes utterly exhausted;

since there must be someone to relieve their fatigue by taking turns, many people take turns in caring for them. Second, it refers to cases where the caregiver themselves is pulled away by other circumstances and cannot fulfill the task from beginning to end, so many people are employed to care for the patient in succession. Since there are many caregivers, it is difficult to reward each one individually; therefore, this regulation was established.

It is granted only to the "ultimate" recipient. If, at the time of a patient's death, there are two or three people present who are both designated as "ultimate," the reward shall be distributed equally among them.
The Vinaya states: "One should provide [the patient] with robes to wear and maintain. If one does not know [how to do so], one should provide the utmost care for their medical treatment.
One should provide them with the three superior robes (tricīvara), and according to whether they require upper, middle, or lower grades, the provision of robes is likewise."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "one who maintains [the robe]," this distinguishes it from a surplus robe (*atireka-cīvara*). A surplus robe belongs to the Sangha and may be distributed among those entitled to shared property.
If one does not know whether a robe is one that is maintained or not, it should be measured and given to the attendant according to their virtue.
If they apply themselves with utmost diligence in seeking out medicines and are moreover skilled in preaching the Dharma to comfort the patient, then—

If one possesses all five virtues, they should be given the superior set of three robes (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi*). Among those with five virtues, if one cannot preach the Dharma but possesses only three or four, they should be given the middle set of three robes.
If one possesses only one or two, lacking the final fifth virtue, they should be given the inferior set of three robes.
This refers to bestowing robes upon a person by examining their character when the specific requirements for the robes are not known.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one does not trust [the caregiver], give them six items that are neither good nor bad.
Commentary: "If one does not trust" refers to a caregiver who claims to possess all virtues and has frequently preached the Dharma for the sick person.
The Sangha should examine that person; if it appears at first glance that they have studied little and are not yet familiar with the Vinaya, then [one should not trust them].
From among the six items, one should select the medium-quality ones and give them to him. This applies specifically to cases where the person’s own words are difficult to trust.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state: "When a bhikṣu is ill, he may receive [offerings] from two assemblies; when a bhikṣuṇī is ill, she may receive them from three assemblies."

Commentary: This clarifies that the two divisions and five groups each have their own distinct categories. Since there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools, it is difficult for objects to be mixed or taken indiscriminately.

Alas, those born in this degenerate age cast wooden fruits at the right time; they form intimate friendships with laypeople (*avadātavasana*) and, after death, distribute their white shrouds among householders.
Thus, they instead recognize worldly relatives as kin. How could they know that the favors bestowed upon the laity during life have already been transformed [into merit]?
Regarding those who fall into the state of being a donor, they are ultimately provided with their share; yet, some still steal monastic property to solicit others.

If even for monks and nuns who have left the household life there are prohibitions based on this principle, how can the belongings of the deceased be handled according to one's own private whims? Does not anyone who knows the Vinaya feel indignation at this?
The *Mātṛkā* states: "When a layperson nurses the sick, they should be given a small portion; the same applies to the three groups of nuns.

Commentary: "Layperson" refers either to a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) employed by the monastery to perform services, or to a private attendant who has been kept as a youth-in-training (*kṣullaka*) for personal service.
Since the Sangha lacks such merit, one should simply give rise to a virtuous intention; having deliberated with the assembly on what is appropriate, one should provide a small amount.

As for the claim that "the three groups of nuns caring for a bhikṣu’s illness should be treated according to this same principle," during the Buddha’s lifetime the community of nuns maintained the precepts with pure excellence.
There were even nuns who were relatives who attended to the sick, acting out of compassion and kindness, and honoring the Sangha as they would the Buddha himself.

This is not universally applicable; one must necessarily observe the individual. However, in the present age of defilement (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), among the monastics, who is like those trained by the Vinaya?

Since nuns have not been accorded equal status with monks, even if a nun maintains pure precepts and integrity, she should not be permitted to attend to [a monk] at the point of death. One must avoid the risk of public censure and scandal.
One should merely understand this; be careful not to practice such a thing. As for the citation in the current text, it is intended to clarify the broad scope of nursing the sick.
This is a regulation.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a caregiver goes outside on behalf of the patient to beg for food, clothing, or medicine, they should be left behind to wait until their return, at which point these items are to be handed over to them.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "A caregiver who attends to a patient outside the monastery boundaries shall be rewarded according to the law."

The *Śāriputrābhidharma* (or *Śāriputra-śāstra*), representing the Sarvāstivāda school, states: "If a caregiver leaves the boundary [of the monastery], it is not due to his own cause, but was originally for the sake of the patient;

having endured the toil of travel, when the patient has passed away and the Sangha is distributing the goods, one should set aside a portion as a reward to wait for him upon his return and hand it over to him.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu within the boundary falls ill, and a bhikṣu from another boundary comes to visit him..."

Although their places of residence were different, through their mutual affinity in the Way and their shared understanding, they could not bear to abandon one another. Out of compassionate pity, he went in person to behold him.
Both of these cases involved the sincere recommendation of one’s heart in accordance with virtue; therefore, they are cited as evidence to serve as a model for later generations.
△ Clarifying the Method for Bestowing Rewards:
The Buddha said, "One should grant six items to the attendant who nurses the sick: namely, robes, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a needle case, and a container for storing robes.
They should be granted in this manner."

Commentary: Following the usual procedure, one should respond with the preliminary formalities as follows: "The *karmavācanā* for the distribution of the deceased monk’s property should be performed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

Listen, Venerable Saṃgha! The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. Whatever he possessed—his three robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and containers for storing clothing, as they existed at that time—"
[This] is to be distributed among the present Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The Saṃgha now bestows [this] upon the monk who attended to the sick. The motion is thus.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen: the bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. His three robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and garment-storage container—[are hereby offered].
This should be divided among the present Sangha. The Sangha now bestows [it] upon the monk who attended to the sick.

Which elders approve of the Sangha’s bestowal of the three robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing container upon the monk who attended to the sick? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
The Sangha has approved and completed the bestowal of these requisites upon the monk who attended to the sick. The Sangha approves and remains silent.
Therefore, this matter should be maintained in this way.
The Vinaya-mūla clearly explains that those possessing virtue are worthy of reward, whereas for those without virtue, it is logically improper to grant such favors.

If one knows that a task involves labor but provides no benefit according to the Dharma, it may be included in the procedure for light items (*laghu-dravya*). Thereafter, one should harmonize with the Saṃgha in accordance with the Śāstra. As the case may require...

**On Bestowing Rewards and Gifts.** This *karmavācanā* for bestowing rewards upon those who have performed meritorious deeds is intended for public matters; it is not for the sake of a single individual. There are two types of invalidity: 1.

**Invalidity regarding the person:** This refers to cases such as when one nurses the sick despite lacking merit, or when the assembled community is small and lacks harmony. 2. **Invalidity regarding the dharma:** [This refers to] the formal procedure itself being improper.

This refers to the three types of non-proper conduct regarding the handling [of robes]: failing to maintain proper decorum, using language that violates the Vinaya, and other such irregularities. The three matters of non-proper conduct regarding the robes themselves refer to errors concerning quality—such as possessing or giving robes that are superior or inferior—and other discrepancies such as length.
The four subsequent categories of non-proper characteristics are to be understood by analogy with the preceding ones.
Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā* on the Dharma for Distributing Light Objects in Nine Parts:
"When five people live together and one dies, a sequential distribution (*krama-vibhāga*) may not be performed.

The rules set forth in the *Vinaya* are incomplete in this regard. Now, following the *Karma* for the Community’s Receipt of Offerings at Improper Times, the sequential distribution is fully established."

Regarding these words, when there are five or more people, this method must be employed. According to the Vinaya text, one person should be appointed to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) to distribute [the items] in this manner.
Some maintain that three rounds of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) should be performed; however, this interpretation is not definitive.
Others maintain a two-round procedure. Now, according to the text of the *karman*, it fully contains both the entrustment and the distribution.
Dharma. It is not mentioned here because others do not exist [in this context]. According to the *Vinaya-karman*, the commentary states:

First, the *Mātṛkā-vibhaṅga* is cited as evidence regarding persons and dharmas; next, by way of analogy, it is extended to successive cases, and thus the "non-timely gift obtained by the Saṃgha" is cited.
This "successive extension" refers to what is stated in the following text: "The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles and gives them to [the next person]."
"O [Name], you must return this to the Saṃgha. If one employs this method, it must involve five or more persons;

only then does one avoid falling into an improper act and successfully accomplish the task. According to the *Mūla-vinaya*, one person should be appointed to perform the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Some authorities maintain that there should be three recitations of the *karman*, while others maintain two recitations; furthermore, some omit the preliminary announcement (*jñapti*).

Regarding the term "transference" (*parivarta*): this arose because the text was not finalized when composed through unwholesome reflection. Now, according to the *Karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) texts, it fully contains two methods—entrustment (*arpaṇa*) and distribution (*vibhāga*).
As for the remaining two [methods], there is no authoritative basis for their prohibition; therefore, they are not set forth here.
According to the *Saddharmakarmavācanā*, it says:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. All his robes and personal effects should be divided by the present Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and personal effects and gives them to the bhikṣu [Name], who shall then return them to the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. All his robes and personal effects should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now takes these robes and effects and gives them to the bhikṣu [Name], who shall return them to the Saṃgha. Which elders...?
The monk [Name] has passed away. All his robes and requisites should be divided by the present Saṃgha.

If the Saṃgha now holds these and gives them to the monks [Name and Name], who intends to return them to the Saṃgha, let those who consent remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented;
it has been decided that these robes and requisites are given to the monks [Name and Name] to return to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha consents.
Because he remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed this rite, one should take the robes and requisites according to the number of persons present and distribute them accordingly.
It is not appropriate to give them separately, as that would invite further defilement; for it is not the Buddha’s injunction.

Commentary: It is improper to distribute [the property] separately, as this would further invite defilement. This refers to taking communal property as one's own and using what belongs to the community for private purposes.
Since this is not in accord with the harmony of the assembly, it will inevitably invite the suffering of falling into the three miserable realms.
To act arbitrarily by transgressing established regulations further commits the offense of defiling non-action (*avijñapti*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If [the property] is not sufficient for all, the Saṃgha shall give it to one monk who has no robes.
Commentary: This refers to the case where a monk with no acquaintances passes away and there is a large quantity of property but few items.

Although it says "give it to one monk who has no robes," it must still be determined through consultation by the harmonious assembly of monks; it is not permitted to act according to personal whims or cause disorder.
This is the established rule.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a single robe is of excellent quality, it need not be cut or torn. If all members of the community possess such robes, they should be distributed starting from the senior-most;
if someone requires one, it shall be given directly."

Commentary: "Extremely fine garments" refers to expensive, superior-quality robes. Regarding the items to be distributed, those of high and low quality were mixed together and divided equally without partiality.
Now, since everyone has already received their share, if there remain any other expensive garments...
In this case, there is no need to divide or distribute [the items]. One should allow them to be passed down in order from the four senior monks among the Sangha;
if they are to be used, they should be handed over directly. According to the underlying principle, there are two points: first, to cherish the offerings of the donors so that they are not wasted;

second, to manifest freedom from greed and to take pleasure in honoring the venerable ones. For the mind is not the object itself. To verify contentment, one must understand that the mind does not shift in accordance with changing circumstances. Thus...
This is called "upholding the precepts. This one *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed for the purpose of appointing a person to distribute items; thus, it pertains to the public.
It is not improper for a single individual to do so, provided that the distributor does not harbor feelings of hatred or attachment, and there are no obstacles (*pratikṣepa*) among those assembled.

1. Faults regarding the person (*pudgala-vipatti*): this refers to cases such as sending [a messenger] and so forth. 2. Faults regarding the dharma (*dharma-vipatti*): this refers to not stating that [the offense] is transmissible, or errors in the wording and phrases, and so forth.
3. Faults regarding the matter (*vastu-vipatti*): this refers to treating what is grave as light, and so forth. The latter four [categories] are to be understood by analogy.
△ Regarding the method of distribution among four people, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If there are only four people, one should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of direct distribution.
As for the items to be awarded as compensation for nursing the sick, the principle is that the three [remaining] members reach a consensus by entrusting the robes with these words."

Commentary: When four persons constitute the full number for the Saṃgha, they should perform the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakalpa*). They must not receive or confer *chanda* (consent), nor engage in the question-and-answer procedure.
Regarding those who perform the direct distribution by *karmavācanā*—meaning there is no exchange of verbal messages—one among the four persons attends to the sick.

As for the method of distributing the reward goods, according to the underlying principle, the three [other] persons may only agree orally; they hand over the robe to that person, saying: [as follows].

Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind: I now take up the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and other items [as applicable] belonging to the deceased bhikṣu [Name], and offer them to the bhikṣu [Name] for his care. (Recite this three times.)
As for the remaining light items, one should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution of their value.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, [the name] the bhikṣu has passed away;
all his clothing and requisites should be divided by the Saṃgha present before us. This is the motion."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. All his robes and personal effects should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
Which elders approve that the Saṃgha now divide these robes and effects? Those who consent, remain silent. Those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has approved the division of these robes and effects. Because the Saṃgha consents through silence, this matter is thus upheld.
If the robes are relinquished, or if the robes are distributed, or if guests arrive, all cases are to be judged according to the above.
Explanation: This *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) pertains to public matters;

it is not for a single individual. "Not for one" means that [the person] has not come to announce their *chanda* (consent), etc. "Non-validity of the two procedures" refers to the performance of the *jñapti* (motion) and the *anujñā* (authorization).

The three matters of "transformation and so forth" are not [the case], meaning that objects do not intermingle with one another and so on. The latter four characteristics of disintegration should be understood by analogy with the constant [characteristics].
△ The Dharma of the Distribution of Many People's Shares.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: When four people live together and one dies, they should divide [the property] among themselves in succession. After the robes have been relinquished, according to the method for rewarding labor, two people may, by mutual agreement, take possession of them, saying: [“We shall keep these.”]

Venerable Sir, please bear this in mind: we take these robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage vessel belonging to the deceased bhikṣu [Name] and give them to the bhikṣu [Name] who attended to the sick.
After the three recitations have been made, regarding those light items, according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, they should be received and shared together through three verbal declarations.
One should say:
"May the two Venerable Ones listen. These robes and personal effects of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to us. (This is to be said three times.)

It is the same for others. In the case of two people, one must also follow the above principle. When the reward for labor has been paid with three words, although the distribution of goods is finished and they have not yet received them in hand, if a guest arrives, one must share a portion with them.

Commentary: If an object has already entered the hands [of the community], it belongs to the owner; therefore, it is the property of the *sāṃghika* (present) Saṅgha, and one need not give it to a guest who arrives.
If it has not yet entered their hands, no owner exists; therefore, it is the property of the *daśadig-saṃgha* (Saṅgha of the ten directions), and a guest has a share in it.

One must carefully weigh the causes and effects of sin and merit. This is a *saṃmukha-vinaya* (face-to-face legal procedure) for a single assembly; because the matter pertains to the public, it is made manifest.
It is not the same as the cases mentioned above.

△ First, regarding the Dharma of Mindful Recitation (cittānuvartana-dharma) according to the *Vinayamātṛkā*: "As for the 'Dharma of Correspondence' (sāmagrī-dharma), when two people live together and one dies, the survivor takes [the deceased's requisites]."
The one who wears the robe speaks with his mouth, saying: "This property of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to me.
Having made these three declarations, he takes hold of the object with his hand; therefore, others who arrive later may not obtain it.
○ Tenth, the method for receiving robes:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one seeks medicine, clothing, or food for a sick person, or for the sake of stūpa affairs or the affairs of the Saṃgha,
one should receive a share even if they are not present at that time.

Commentary: The preceding section on the Ten Recitations already clarified that when one goes outside to beg for food, clothing, or medicine on behalf of a sick person, these items should be kept and returned to them.
This section is presented again here to provide further corroboration based on the merit derived from such activities as the construction of stupas and service to the Saṃgha.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bhikṣu from outside the boundary enters, he must also be given a share. This refers to the time of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

The reason this point, which was already clarified above, is restated here is to ensure that one understands the regulations for both parties are identical, thereby preventing any doubt or hesitation.
In the Vinaya, it is stated that if a bhikṣu is absent, or if the assembly is incomplete, the distribution of robes is not valid.
Furthermore, regarding gifts made in the presence of the community, one may give an equal share or half a share to śrāmaṇeras and lay attendants (karmadāna), as distinguished previously.
Commentary: There are cases where monks, while perceiving themselves to be in a single community, divide the robes separately and thus fail to accomplish the distribution.

According to the Vinaya, there are six permutations; this passage briefly cites the third. First: In a certain residence, there are monks, and they perceive themselves as being with other monks, yet they divide the robes separately.
The Buddha said: "The distribution is not accomplished; one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Second: In a certain residence... [text continues]
1. In a monastery where there are monks, if one has the perception that there are monks and distributes the robes separately, it is not valid; the offense is as stated above. 2.

In a monastery where there are monks, if one has the perception that there are no monks and distributes the robes separately, it is not valid; there is no offense. 3. In a monastery where there are monks, if one acts with the perception that there are no monks and distributes the robes separately, it is not valid;
there is no offense. 4. In a monastery where there are no monks, if one has the perception that there are monks and distributes the robes separately, it is valid; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Fifth: if there is a residence where no bhikṣus are present, yet one suspects that there are bhikṣus, and one distributes the robes separately, it is an offense as described above.
Sixth: if there is a residence where no bhikṣus are present and one has the perception that there are none, and one distributes them, there is no offense.
Furthermore, regarding "the distribution among those present" and so forth, this example applies to others: the śrāmaṇeras and lay attendants (*karmadāna*) are also given a share.
This may be known from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states: "If a bhikṣu has entrusted his robes and bowl to a bhikṣuṇī and she dies, the bhikṣu shall reclaim them;
those who saw him first shall divide them."

Commentary: Among the ten types of methods for distributing [relics] mentioned previously, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* has already been cited regarding the case where the object is entrusted to a person rather than a location:
if a bhikṣu entrusts it to the place where another bhikṣu resides, that bhikṣu need not take possession of it, as it belongs to the Saṃgha of that specific location.

However, in the case where it is entrusted to the place where bhikṣuṇīs reside, since bhikṣuṇīs are a subordinate assembly and are not entitled to receive the robes and bowls of the great Saṃgha, the rule was established that they must take possession of them.

Regarding the distribution of items belonging to one's own original community: even if one is not currently living together with them, if one was previously seen to have requested a share, one must attend the assembly to receive a portion along with the rest of the community.

If death occurs in the home of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), light items shall be distributed among the five groups of monks (*pañcavargīya*) present there; heavy items may be disposed of as one pleases for distant locations.
Recently, a monk was entrusted to a temple.
Regarding the phrase "the five assemblies appear before one and divide [the property]": this refers to the time of death; among the five assemblies—

Regardless of the order of arrival, those who arrive first shall receive their share in person. As for property entrusted to a monastery according to the rules of the Saṃgha, one must exclude places that lack formal boundaries, such as monasteries without *sīmā* or dwellings for only two or three people;

rather, it refers to a place where the *dharmasīmā* has been formally established, where the *karmavācanā* can be performed, and where monastic affairs are conducted. The heavy valuables left by the deceased should be delivered to such a place to serve the Saṃgha.
This refers to property permanently held by the Saṃgha.
If there are no members of the fivefold assembly (pañcavarga), the precepts dictate that faithful lay donors (*dānapati*) should take charge of it.
If no members of the fivefold assembly come forward, it should be sent to the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) of a nearby location. The remainder is as explained in the *Yao* (Digest).
Commentary: This citation from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* is combined with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to clarify the nature of light items. Regarding the term "faithful devotee" (*dānapati*):

"faith" means that the principles of cause and effect are clearly discerned, such that one is not deluded regarding self and other; "devotion" means that one makes offerings to the Triple Gem without begrudging one's own wealth.
Only such a person may be entrusted with the deceased’s belongings to await the arrival of the five assemblies for their distribution.

If, after the designated date, no one has arrived, the items should be sent to a neighboring monastery and divided according to the Dharma. The remaining details are as explained in the *Chao* (Commentary).

This passage demonstrates the criteria for determining whether the distribution of goods is correct; this is clarified in the *Chao*. Examine those who have left their homes to enter the monastic life:
they discard worldly attachments as if they were mucus or spittle, regard honor and wealth as worn-out sandals, and weary of the realm of sensual desire.

The mind does not follow after [worldly things]. It washes away the taints of habitual defilements and constantly wears the Way upon its breast. By diligently cultivating accumulated practices, one repays the four debts of gratitude;
as virtue gathers in profound depth, one is then able to benefit both self and others. Valuing only the Way and holding it in high esteem, what cause for concern is there in bodily poverty?

Even if circumstances suddenly converge such that offerings from donors appear like a cluster of arrows, one should think of repaying such generosity as if carrying a heavy stone—accepting whatever is obtained accordingly.
Purify accordingly. Entrust yourself to the two fields [of merit]; do not covet, do not hoard, and provide only for the sustenance of the four great elements.

If one’s virtue is exalted and no surplus remains, then one’s fragrant name will endure for a thousand ages, and all who see or hear of it will look up to it as a model; this may truly be called the Jewel of the Sangha.

In these times, however, religious practice is insufficient and defiled habits have not been cast off; people scheme to cultivate social connections and hoard beyond measure without satiety. I can only urge you...

The laity relinquish their possessions to break their stinginess, yet they themselves take no pleasure in practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). When the light of their eyes falls to the ground [at death], they do not consider what they should do;

only when their belongings are emptied from their bags and brought forth does it become manifest how deluded and miserly they were in their hoarding. This is the case for those who die within a monastic temple.

One should obtain an equitable distribution according to the monastic laws. If one dies in a lay residence, the five groups of practitioners shall divide the property together in accordance with the regulations.

In this way, not only will the deceased receive benefit and the living be relieved, but you may also enjoy peace and leisure; furthermore, the merit of the offering will increase, allowing for vast rewards.

However, should the patient become critically ill and lose consciousness, and the property be privately concealed, or if the distribution is handled improperly, [the consequences would be grave]. I fear...

To claim things as one's own is to fall into ruin through greed; such theft drags others along, causing both to enter the *niraya* hells, where the retribution for their actions results in extreme suffering.
Indeed, the Buddha spoke with his own lips that material things are poison; he repeatedly taught in his instructions that this poison harms the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).

Therefore, know that those who have left the household life to become monks must not poison themselves or others, nor wound the life-force of wisdom, thereby bringing about the destruction of the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*).
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If a bhikṣu uses the property of the Saṃgha to sustain his own life, he is likewise a thief.
Therefore, all property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions must not be used privately.

However, regarding the rise and fall [of practices] mentioned in the *Chao*, the general principles of right and wrong are similar to this. For now, I shall briefly explain one category to supplement the *Chao*.
Thus it is said. The eighth chapter, "The Method for Dividing Various Robes," concludes.

The eight fields of merit consist of the Buddha, the noble ones (*ārya*), and the Saṃgha; these three are the fields of merit to be revered. [The others are] the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the teacher (*ācārya*).
These four—parents—are fields of merit through their kindness. To rescue and provide for the sick is a field of merit for the ill; it is also called the field of compassion.
As for the single field of the Buddha, this refers to one whose equipment for awakening is complete and who has attained the ultimate fruit.
Being the most supreme and peerless in both the mundane and supramundane realms, if a person can reverently make offerings to such a one, they will not only obtain all blessings, but also...
It extinguishes all sins; therefore, it is called the Buddha-field of merit (*buddha-kṣetra*).

Second is the field of the noble ones (*ārya-kṣetra*), referring to Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas who have transcended the three realms, realized the Noble Path, and are endowed with immeasurable merit.

When a person of wisdom respectfully makes offerings to them, they immediately obtain supreme blessings; therefore, it is called the field of the noble ones. Third is the Sangha-field of merit (*saṃgha-kṣetra*).

The Sangha refers to those who are harmonious; "assembly" means being among the multitude. To be in accord, respectful, compliant, and free from contention—such people who are disciples of the Buddha can receive offerings with reverence and thereby obtain merit and benefit; thus they are called the "Sangha Field of Merit.

Fourth is the "Upādhyāya Field of Merit," which refers to the fact that for one who has left the household life, it is through the power of the teacher’s instruction that the Dharma-body grows and develops; therefore, the teacher's kindness is truly profound.
If a person can provide offerings and show respect, they will immediately obtain blessings and merit; therefore, the *upādhyāya* is called a "field of merit.
Fifth is the field of the *ācārya*, which refers to a teacher who can correct the conduct of their disciple—namely, a teacher such as one who instructs in the attainment of the precepts.

Because one relies on these precepts to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), their kindness is truly profound. If a person can provide offerings [to them], [they will likewise obtain blessings and merit].
By showing reverence, one immediately obtains benefit and merit; therefore, he is called the "Ācārya Field of Merit. Sixth is the "Father Field":
the father is the beginning of one's physical form and possesses the virtue of procreation and birth. From childhood until adulthood, he provides instruction, admonition, and nourishment.
Their kindness is boundless. As a filial son, one ought to serve and support them with all one's strength; how could there be any thought of seeking blessings?
If one’s heart is characterized by ultimate filial piety and purity, then blessings will be obtained naturally. Therefore, parents are called "fields of merit."
The seventh field of merit is one's mother. This refers to the mother from the moment she conceives and gives birth, through the nursing and nurturing that protects and raises her child;
her compassionate toil and kindness are boundless. As a child, one ought to serve and support her with all one’s strength—how could there even be a thought of seeking merit?
Yet, if one’s heart is characterized by the utmost filial piety and purity, then it is likewise [a field of merit].
One naturally obtains blessings; therefore, it is called the "Field of Merit of Parents. Eighth is the "Field of the Sick":

when one sees a person who is ill, one should immediately contemplate their suffering and apply oneself to curing them by providing medicinal decoctions; thus one can obtain blessings, and it is therefore called the "Field of Merit of the Sick."
