Chapter Nine, Part Two: The Section on the Method for Repenting the Six Classes of Offenses.

○ Regarding the continuation of the three methods for repenting *sthūlātyaya* offenses, there are two types of causal conditions. First, it clarifies that there are three distinctions within independent *sthūlātyaya* offenses, such as the schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha (*cakrabheda*).
Stealing four *kārsāpaṇa* coins, stealing food belonging to the Saṃgha, and so forth, are termed "upper-grade" offenses.
Commentary: Although the name of the offense, *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression), is one, there are two types of conditions for its commission.

First, to clarify the standalone (*mukhya*) *sthūlātyaya*: this is distinguished from those arising from other offenses; it is committed independently and is also called a "natural" (*svabhāva*) *sthūlātyaya*. This refers to the standalone [offense].
There are three grades: superior, middling, and inferior. Within the superior grade, there are also three divisions. First, regarding the schism of the *saṃgha* (breaking the wheel of the Dharma):
this is obtained by originally generating the intention to cause a schism in the *saṃgha*. If the *saṃgha* is not split, the offense may be expiated;

once the *saṃgha* has been split, the offense cannot be expiated. Second, regarding the theft of four coins: in the Western Regions, four large coins correspond to six [coins] according to the standards of this land.
Fourteen small coins: this refers to the initial arising of the intent to steal, where one steals only such an amount. Third, regarding those who steal the food of the Saṃgha:
this refers to all food and drink offered by faithful donors to the Saṃgha, for it belongs to the present Saṃgha of the ten directions.

If one does not use the communal provisions with a private mind but eats them secretly—whether in large amounts to satisfy one's hunger or in small amounts just enough to swallow—they are all termed stealing the Sangha’s food.
As for the word "equal" (等), according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it refers to cases such as:

if out of anger one breaks a vessel that has been formally maintained, breaks the three robes that have been formally maintained, destroys a stūpa of the World-Honored One, or destroys the dwellings of the Saṃgha; in all such instances, there is simply the presence of anger.

This includes the superior grade. However, one who destroys a stūpa of the Blessed One incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; the retribution for the karmic consequences of this action involves more suffering than other [offenses].
These are called the three types of independent (*mukhya*) superior-grade offenses.
If one causes a schism in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Saṃgha, steals less than three *kārsāpaṇas*, or has mutual contact with clothing, these are termed "middling offenses.
Commentary: This explains the three types of middling offenses that occur independently (*mukhyaka*). First, regarding "causing a schism in the *karmavācanā*":

this refers to turning away from harmony to form a separate faction, while remaining within the same legal jurisdiction (*dharmabhāga*), and performing separate *karmavācanās* and reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) within a single boundary (*sīmā*). Regarding "stealing less than three [kārsāpaṇas]":...

"Less than this" refers to stealing three coins or two coins. If one originally intended not to steal four or five coins of property, yet there is mutual contact with clothing, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The second case refers to "with an interval"; that is, contact occurs while an interval remains.
Why are they not included among those arising from contact (*āśrayaja*), but called "independent" (*mukhya*)?

It is because the original intention was not to experience sensual pleasure through direct contact without an interval, but rather to act in such a manner. Furthermore, this involves contact with the upper part of the body;
these are called the three types of middling independent [contact].
If one reviles the Sangha with an evil mind, steals a single coin, uses human hair, eats raw meat and blood, goes naked,
or wears the robes of non-Buddhists, these are classified as inferior offenses.

Commentary: Regarding "one who with an evil mind reviles the Saṃgha": this refers to a bhikṣu who cultivates his person through loving-kindness and ought to possess a spirit of humility and reverence.

If, however, he harbors anger and utters coarse and violent words, thereby insulting and defiling his fellow members of the Saṃgha, he is no longer part of the community that is like water and milk; therefore, this rule was established.
Regarding the theft of a single coin: according to the standards of this land, it corresponds to sixteen small coins. Although the object is minute, it is incompatible with the precepts.
Regarding the use of human hair: it is because one treats another’s discarded body with disrespect. Regarding the eating of raw meat and blood: it is because it lacks compassion and fosters hatred.
"Wearing the robes of non-Buddhists" refers to all those who manifest heterodoxy to delude the masses;
it does not refer specifically to black robes as prescribed by the regulations, but rather to any such attire, which is collectively termed "the robes of non-Buddhists.

As for the word "etcetera," according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, keeping a stone bowl and shaving the hair from the pubic region and the armpits are both considered minor *sthūlātyaya* offenses. This refers to the three minor independent [offenses].

If one initially intends to take four *kārsāpaṇas*, but takes two or three and then returns them, it is likewise. If one sends a messenger to take another's property, there is a light *sthūlātyaya* at the time of giving the instruction.

Regarding the sixth precept: if one is constructing a hut or applying a final layer of mud, as long as the work is not yet finished, it constitutes a heavy *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the seventh precept, the gravity of the offense is the same as the sixth. Regarding the eighth and ninth precepts:

if, out of a mind of malice, one goes to that person and slanders them, but the speech is not fully articulated, it is a heavy *sthūlātyaya*. This excludes the four matters [of the pārājikas]. Furthermore...
The same applies to slandering [a monk] by claiming he has committed a non-existent offense. The same also applies to slandering a nun by means of these eight matters.

Regarding the latter four precepts, if one does not relinquish [the offense] after the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) has been completed, it constitutes a *triple-sthūlātyaya*. This is how the grave offenses arise within these two categories.

Regarding the two cases where a light offense is incurred: the *Śāstra* states that within the first precept, if one has a lustful mind and initially moves the hand toward the organ and then withdraws it, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya*.

Within the second precept, if one has a lustful mind and intends to approach a woman to touch her for sensual pleasure, with every step taken toward her, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya*; this also applies if one touches the woman’s clothing.

[The offense is] complete. If, while harboring desire in one's heart, one draws back after having nearly touched [the woman], it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the third precept on coarse speech (*pāruṣya*):
if one uses finger-signs or dispatches a messenger to convey a signal so that the woman understands, each instance of instructing her constitutes a light *sthūlātyaya*.
If one utters coarse speech while suspecting that one is uttering coarse speech, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. The fourth precept...

Regarding the offense of lightness: it is the same as the third precept. Within the fifth precept, if one acts as a matchmaker or sends a letter, for every syllable [of the message], there is a light *sthūlātyaya*.
If one makes a sign to convey the intent, even before it reaches the recipient, for each instance there is a light *sthūlātyaya*.
Within the sixth precept, when leveling the ground or marking the boundaries of the land, from the second clod of earth until the work is finished...
Returning [to the point of departure], these are all light *sthūlātyaya* offenses. Regarding the seventh precept, a light offense arises; it is the same as the sixth precept.
Within the eighth and ninth [precepts], if one, with a mind of hatred, intends to slander a pure person, from the first step taken until reaching the person in question—

At every step, there is a light *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the latter four precepts, if one confesses after the assembly has been gathered and the single motion (*jñapti*) is completed, it is one light *sthūlātyaya*;

if one confesses after the single motion and the first *karmavācanā* are completed, it is two light *sthūlātyayas*. These constitute the light offenses arising from the two categories [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The method for repentance is the same as that for the *pāyattika* [offenses]. The method for repenting the independent *sthūlātyaya* [offenses] is also determined according to their origin.
There are superior, middling, and inferior methods of repentance."
Commentary: This cites an example from the treatises regarding the methods for repentance for *sthūlātyaya* offenses. The various schools established no differing methods for repentance;
however, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it is the same as for *pāyattika* offenses. Nevertheless, within this similarity, there are differences:
if a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has become light, or if it is an independent (*mukha-mukha*) lower-grade offense, one should repent before a single bhikṣu. This, then, differs from—
The *pāyattika* [offenses] are the same. This is why, in the first section, only the framework for the confession of *sthūlātyaya* dharmas is listed within the headings.

As for what is said to be "not the same": if it is an offense from the first category (*ādi-pada*) that is grave, or a primary (*mukhya*) high-grade (*uttama-prakāra*) offense, one must confess before the entire community of monks (*sarva-saṃgha*).
If it is a light offense from the first category, a grave offense from the second category, or a medium-grade (*madhyama-prakāra*) primary offense, one should...

Repenting before a group of four bhikṣus outside the boundary is a formal procedure for the Saṃgha, specifically a *pratideśanīya* (confession before a group). This is equivalent to the confession for a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;

it is not merely a *pratideśanīya* (confession before an individual). Detailed reflection reveals that the methods for performing and maintaining these rites have been lost to tradition, making them difficult to comprehend through mere analogy.
Therefore, I have now compiled these rules according to the procedures for confession.
△ Requesting the Method for Confession before the Sangha:

If one has committed an offense of the first category (*āpatti-prathama*) that gives rise to grave consequences, or an independent (*mūla*) offense of the highest grade, one must confess before the entire community of monks (*sarva-saṃgha*).
As usual, the gong is struck to assemble the monks. The offender should then go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, and remove his leather sandals.
Kneeling on the ground with palms joined, one should speak these words of request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a sthūlātyaya offense. I now request the Saṃgha to grant me the opportunity for repentance.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], the opportunity for repentance. (Recite this three times.)

△ Having requested the master of confession to seek absolution from the Saṃgha, one should request a monk who upholds the Vinaya and acts in accordance with the Dharma to serve as the presiding master of confession within the assembly of monks.
The procedure for making this request is as follows: [Insert the formal request here.]
Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a [certain] sthūlātyaya offense.
I now request the Venerable sir to act as my master of confession. May the Venerable sir act as my master of confession out of compassion for me.

When the three requests have been completed, the preceptor for the confession (sāntika) shall not grant permission immediately. He should first announce to the assembly of monks present: "Does the Sangha consent to hear this?

△ The method for making the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: the Elder in the midst of the Sangha should perform the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakaraṇīya*) and respond, saying: "The *karmavācanā* for the confession of a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
Having received the prostrations from the presiding master of the confession and having been seated as the senior, he speaks alone:
"Venerable Sangha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a certain *sthūlātyaya* offense. I now beg the Sangha for its confession."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name].
This is the formal announcement. Having performed this *jñapti-karman* (formal announcement), the assembly of monks joins their palms and replies in unison: "So be it. The assembly...
Once the Saṃgha has granted permission, one may then perform the ritual procedure.
△ Regarding the formal method of confession,

the presiding officiant (sāṃghika-vinayadhara) should know that the various offenses, such as concealment and so forth, are categorized into eight classes, as described above for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses].

The Method of Confession. According to the section on subsequent *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, this text clarifies only the method for confessing the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*). One should assume the proper deportment and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a [certain] *sthūlātyaya* offense. Now, before the Venerable sir..."
I confess and reveal my transgressions; I dare not conceal them. To confess brings peace and happiness; not to confess brings no peace or happiness.

Recalling my offenses, I reveal them; knowing them, I dare not conceal them. May the Venerable One bear witness that my body of pure precepts is complete and that I have performed the *poṣadha* with purity.
(Having said this three times, the one receiving the confession should say to him: "Reproach yourself and give rise to a sense of weary detachment. (He replies: "So be it."
**Explanation:** This commentary on the meaning of the text for repentance will be clarified later in the section on *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).

It is not the case that other [rules] do not follow the general standard; rather, they differ only in their legal status (*dharmatā*). That is to say, what would otherwise be light is treated as heavy, such as when [an offense] is committed alone or without sharing [the guilt].
△ The Method for Repentance Before Four Bhikṣus:

If an offense of the first category (pārājika) is committed with light intent, or an offense of the second category (saṃghāvaśeṣa) is committed with heavy intent, or if there are offenses of the middle grade committed independently, four pure bhikṣus who understand the Dharma within the boundary (sīmā) should take the offender outside the boundary to perform repentance. According to the underlying principle, this is not required [in cases other than these].
Having performed the preliminary rites, as there are no other assemblies to be gathered, he performs the ritual of requesting confession before four bhikṣus.

The wording for both the request for the presiding confessor (*kṣamāpaka*) and the confession itself is the same as above; however, instead of reciting the response aloud, one should respond orally to those standing nearby when asked.
If you three elders would permit me to accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name], I shall accept it. (The three bhikṣus say: "So be it.

The procedures for the interrogation, concealment, and so forth regarding minor offenses by the one receiving the confession, as well as the formal confession of the primary offense itself, are all identical to those described above without difference.

Non-human non-compliance refers to those who are beyond the four [classes] or fewer than that. Non-compliance regarding the Dharma refers to questioning the harmony of the assembly or the matter at hand.
Non-compliance regarding the matter refers to remaining within the boundary and not departing, and so forth. The remaining four [factors] must be combined and complete.
△ The Method for Confessing Before a Single Bhikṣu:

If one has committed two categories of offenses that are light, or if they are minor *duṭhullā* (grave) offenses occurring independently, one should go before a pure bhikṣu who understands the Dharma.
The manner of requesting the host and the procedure for confessing the offense are both as described above; however, the location is not restricted, provided there is someone present.
The distinctions have been heard.

What preceded this was a continuation of the explanation of the three repentances; however, due to omissions in the source text, they were not recorded. Hereafter, the methods will be listed according to the text.
If a ritual is present in the [ritual manual] but absent from the [explanatory] text, it shall be made clear in its own context as the text proceeds.

Regarding the method for confessing *pāyattika* offenses, the confession applies both to the community (*saṃgha*) and to individuals. Therefore, the preceding list of thirty [offenses] is based solely on face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*).

The subsequent list of ninety [offenses] is divided into two categories because they arise from greed and pride, and involve matters of wealth that differ in gravity; thus, they are distinguished by these two types of mental states. Both confession and relinquishment (*pratyaya*) apply to these two cases.

Commentary: Regarding the *pāyattika* (pāyattika) precepts for bhikṣus, there are one hundred and twenty rules; this section occupies the third position. When the categories are expanded, they are divided into four.
The first two lines of this text indicate the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture), while the following two lines indicate the simple *pāyattika*.

Although the offenses are essentially one, they are divided into three groups of ten and nine respectively. The first thirty are so designated because the mental karma arises from excessive greed for material goods.

Thus, the gravity [of the offenses] differs. Regarding the ninety offenses committed through the influence of pride, the mental karma is light; therefore, the compilers of the canon divided them into two categories.
For the ninety offenses, one merely confesses the transgression, and the rite requires only a face-to-face confession. For the thirty offenses, one must additionally relinquish the material object.
Repentance applies to both the Saṃgha and the individual, as clarified according to the Vinaya. Both confession (*pratideśanā*) and relinquishment (*niḥsargika*) are based upon this.

Regarding the aforementioned confession and relinquishment of the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, the Buddha stated: "One who has committed the offense of relinquishing a robe must not give it away to others to be made into the three robes; it must be made into a *pārikkāra* (miscellaneous) item."
Regarding robes: if one repeatedly wears and uses a robe, one must first relinquish it as a formal gift (*pariṇāmanā*) and then perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*).

This robe subject to forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pācattika*) must be relinquished to the Saṃgha—whether to a large group or to a single person—and it must not be relinquished to a separate faction of the community.

If one relinquishes [the offense] but the relinquishment is not accomplished, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; thus, one should know that there are three methods of confession. Furthermore, offenses are divided into two categories:
those common to the Saṃgha and those pertaining to specific boundaries; these should both be examined and reflected upon in detail.

Commentary: Regarding the violation concerning the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, this refers to the first of the thirty [offenses] as well as the third offense regarding robes kept for more than one month, which are explained in detail within the section on "Ceasing and Maintaining" (*zhi-chí*).
Here, we shall discuss it solely in terms of the violation incurred by keeping it beyond the permitted period.

This robe may not be made the object of a formal act of purification (*viśuddhi-dāna*), nor may it be accepted and maintained as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be used for any other miscellaneous purposes.
Regarding robes: one must not wear them so frequently that they become damaged. One must not perform a *parivatta* (reciprocal) purification gift.
Rather, one should relinquish them according to the Dharma, and only thereafter perform two types of purification gifts. The Sanskrit term *niḥsargika* is translated as "relinquishment.
When relinquishing this robe, it should be given to the Saṃgha; even if the number of monks is insufficient, it should be relinquished to a large group of individuals. That is to say:
If there are three bhikṣus, or two bhikṣus—if there are not two or three bhikṣus—one should relinquish it to a single bhikṣu.
The jurisdiction of the dwelling place shall be determined according to the number of people. If there is a saṃgha that relinquishes it to three, two, or one bhikṣu;
if there are three bhikṣus who relinquish it to two or one bhikṣu; or if there are two bhikṣus who relinquish it to one bhikṣu.
Regarding the term "qiu" (mound): if one abandons [the offense] but does not complete the formal act of abandonment, one is to be dealt with according to the *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) offense.

Thus, one should know that among the three types of confession methods, there are offenses that apply to both the *saṃgha* and the *gaṇa*, and these are further divided into two categories based on the boundary (*sīmā*). One must examine these matters in detail and reflect upon them;
the ritual action and the Dharma must necessarily correspond.

Regarding the essential method for performing repentance within the Saṃgha, one must have at least five persons acting as the recipients of the repentance. Within the Saṃgha, there are three aspects to the forfeiture and expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*):

first, the clarification of the forfeiture of material goods, which refers to the removal of the conditions for the offense; second, the clarification of the relinquishment of the mind, which refers to the removal of the causes of the offense; and third, the clarification of the forfeiture of the offense itself.

This eliminates the karma of birth and death. Regarding these three methods of repentance through relinquishment (*prahāṇa*), their principles and categories are universally applicable throughout the tradition.
To explain this method of repentance within the Saṃgha: it requires a minimum of five persons.

Among them, one must be requested to serve as the presiding master who receives the repentance, while the remainder must constitute a full quorum of the Saṃgha. If the number is not complete, this rite cannot be performed.

The present text first sets forth the three types of relinquishment (*tyāga*) so that one may understand their application in achieving salvation. Should one be ignorant of even one of them, it will conversely invite the grave fault of violating the teachings.

Generally speaking, when an offense against the precepts occurs, external sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) serve as the conditions for the transgression, while internally arising thoughts of greed and grasping act as the cause of the transgression.
Through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, the karma one has created is completed, resulting in retribution within the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*) and suffering.
This is twice the worldly punishment; therefore, one is first commanded to abandon the conditions for transgression. Once these conditions no longer adhere, the mind is likewise free from greed.
When the greedy mind is extinguished, there is no basis for the retribution of sin. Thus, the karmic suffering of birth and death can be severed and eliminated.
Now, these three types of relinquishment truly constitute the fundamental path of the thirtyfold method of repentance; their principles are comprehensive and sufficient.

△ First, regarding the explanation of the forfeiture of wealth within the thirty rules for forfeiture: among these, the three precepts concerning begging for cotton to make robes, and the storing of goods belonging to the Three Jewels, do not apply to the Sangha.
All others apply universally to all three types of objects. Now, I shall extract those most frequently violated as representative headings. Forfeiture.
There are three dharmas: first, items exceeding five in length; second, robes separated from their formal acceptance; and third, miscellaneous items such as those to be relinquished.
Having determined these three points through formal proclamation, one shall proceed to the midst of the Saṃgha.
Commentary: This clarifies the distinctions within the category of relinquishment (*niḥsarga*). Regarding "one who begs for cotton to make clothing":
if one commits the eleventh offense of making a new bedding (*śayanāsana*) from wild silkworm cotton, this must be relinquished.

If one uses an axe to finely chop it and mixes it with mud to plaster walls or mounds, the Vinaya states that "bedding" (*śayanāsana*) is a general term for clothing. Regarding "possessing goods": gold, jade, and so forth.
It is said: "Goods. If one commits the nineteenth offense, which is variously buying and selling precious objects or the Three Jewels;
or if one commits the eighteenth offense, which is taking money, gold, or silver with one's own hand—these accumulated goods and seized treasures must be relinquished.
One should speak to a faithful and devoted garden-keeper or an upāsaka, saying: "These are not for me to possess; you should [take them]."
Understood. Of these three types of precepts, the first is relinquished through self-abandonment; the second is relinquished in the presence of a layperson, not before the Saṃgha;
once relinquished, the offense should be confessed. As for the remaining twenty-seven precepts, if one commits any of them, they all apply across the three spheres of objects.
Now, I shall extract and list the rules for those who frequently commit offenses, taking as the primary example the case of intentionally keeping extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*).
This is based on the twenty-seven rules for relinquishment (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*), which contain three distinct categories. First, there are five types of long-term items:

namely, the first, the offense of keeping an extra robe beyond ten days; the third, the offense of keeping an extra robe beyond one month; and the second, the eight-day emergency robe (*akālacīvara*).

Subsequently, there are the rules regarding the keeping of requisites: the twenty-first, the rule against keeping an extra alms-bowl; and the twenty-sixth, the rule against keeping medicinal medicine for more than seven days.
These constitute the five rules concerning "extra" items. Second, the separation from receiving robes: that is, the second [rule] regarding the three robes.

The precept regarding staying overnight apart from one’s robes (the twenty-ninth) and the subsequent precept regarding being separated from one’s robes for more than six nights during the last month of the rainy season;
as well as the remaining miscellaneous rules concerning forfeiture and so forth—excluding the aforementioned three sets of seven—are included here.

If a bhikṣu commits any offense among these thirty, and desires to seek confession in order to restore purity, he must first prepare the three items that must be forfeited according to the regulations.
Having spoken thus, he shall then proceed to the midst of the Saṃgha.

The Buddha said: "When relinquishing [the object] to the Saṃgha, take it to the midst of the Saṃgha; bare your right shoulder, remove your leather sandals, pay homage to the Elder, then kneel with your right knee on the ground and join your palms. You should make this declaration of relinquishment."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe beyond the permitted period; I have committed an offense involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

[I have also] committed an offense involving forfeiture by staying overnight separated from my saṃghāṭī robe. I have committed an offense involving forfeiture by purchasing a single robe for myself. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha. (Recite once.)

Commentary: Within this section on relinquishment (*pratyāstaraṇa*), there are only three [rules] for the text, while the precepts and their applications number seven. One should follow the sequence of offenses as they appear in the text;
let this serve as the model. Now, as for the listing of the numbers one, three, five, eight, and four, these clarify the permissions and prohibitions regarding the conditions for an offense.
Master Xuan was concerned that future bhikṣus might know only that there is a ten-day limit for keeping extra robes and that there are restrictions regarding cloth and wealth.

For those who are insufficiently informed, I permit the practice according to the one-month rule. However, they may not understand the various conditions for transgression regarding what is timely or untimely, what is permitted or prohibited, and the duration of such practices.
Therefore, these four characters are set forth within the text on relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*), so that future generations may clearly understand what is permitted and what is prohibited.

This is for the purpose of practical application, so as not to result in negligence or transgression of the regulations. The numbers one, three, and five are permissive provisions; the number eight is prohibitive.

"One" refers to the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*); for a monk who does not possess the *kaṭhina* robe, the standard limit of ten days is waived, and he is permitted to keep extra robes for one month.
Should he exceed this period, he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). This is the rule regarding forfeiture.

The third precept: During the three months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), before they have concluded, one is permitted to receive an "urgent offering robe" (*ātyayika-cīvara*) during the ten days preceding the end of the retreat.
If one receives it after that period or retains it beyond the permitted time, one commits an offense. This is the twenty-eighth *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
The fifth [precept]: When the summer retreat has concluded, for a monk who possesses a "meritorious robe" (*kaṭhina-cīvara*), a period of five months is permitted.
Within this [period], one may keep extra robes; once the period has passed, one commits an offense. The eighth refers to the eight circumstances under which the *kaṭhina* robe is lost;
keeping extra robes then constitutes an offense. This is a prohibition. The eight circumstances for losing the robe are as explained previously in the section on receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.
Although the distinctions between what is permitted and prohibited regarding the keeping of extra robes are extensive, they are fully encompassed by the numbers one, three, five, and eight.
Thus, he was seen to have excised the redundant and extracted the essential; in the mastery of literary expression, none surpassed the Master (the Buddha).

Regarding the single item among the various *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses—namely, "an article of clothing purchased with money or gems received by oneself"—he specifically highlighted this one offense to clarify the forfeiture.
As for the other miscellaneous *naiḥsargika* offenses, they are to be cited according to their respective transgressions.

If one knows the number, one should state it according to whether it is many or few. If the robes and materials are numerous, one may say, "I do not remember the number," with the sole exception of the three robes (*tricīvara*), as these must have a fixed number.
If the robes and materials are in many locations, one should relinquish them in each respective place before performing the confession of the offense;
this is because the transgression involves pervasive defilement. This applies even when the names of the offenses are many or few.
Explanation: According to the Vinaya, it is as stated above; one must not harbor doubts regarding its application.

If the materials for robes are kept in multiple locations—meaning that the robes and materials one possesses are deposited in several places—one must relinquish them one by one at each respective location before collectively requesting absolution for the offense. Only then will the transgressions be entirely cleared away. Should...
There is one factor that is not relinquished: even if one confesses their transgressions, they will not be extinguished.

Although the objects and locations differ, because the offense was committed through a single defiled mind of greed, confession cannot bring about purification. Regarding the number of offenses to be recorded in detail:
if one has committed a single matter, record the name of that one offense; if one has committed many matters, record the names of those many offenses. There is no room for omission.

[怡-台+龍]tong. Fearing one might fall into a semblance that is not the Middle Way, the Vinaya provides this standard. One must not act out of doubt; should one act while harboring doubt, [it is a transgression].
This meaning borrows from the *Book of Yu*: "When a crime is doubtful, treat it as light; when a merit is doubtful, treat it as great.

△ In the middle section, it clarifies the mind of relinquishment according to the Sarvāstivāda: first, the robe has already been relinquished and the offense has already been confessed, yet the intention to possess it is not severed. On that very day...

If one obtains both the original property and extraneous property on the following day, it constitutes an offense because both were acquired through mental defilement. Second, regarding the forfeiture of robes when the offense has not yet been confessed but the intention to keep them has ceased:
if one obtains both the original property and extraneous property on that very same day, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Explanation: "Original wealth" refers to that which was previously desired and sought to obtain. "Extraordinary wealth" refers to that which was unexpected and not sought after.
If one has already relinquished the robe and confessed the offense, yet the intention to possess it persists—meaning the covetous mind continues in succession—[it constitutes a transgression].
The intention of keeping [the extra cloth] still persists. On that same day or the following day, one further obtains the original or a different cloth or wealth.

This subsequent cloth, together with the previous cloth, constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (expiation involving forfeiture). Because it is subject to the same defilement, the offense is incurred.

If the cloth has already been forfeited but the offense has not yet been confessed, and the intention to keep it ceases—meaning that greed is rebuked and seeking is abandoned on that very day—and one subsequently obtains the original or a different cloth or wealth again: [End of passage]
One commits a *duṣkṛta* offense because one has transgressed the Vinaya by failing to observe the rule regarding the non-interruption of the matter.
Now, according to the various Vinayas and Śāstras, the forfeiture and the returning of the property both depend upon the deliberation of the Saṃgha; one does not act on one's own authority.

Whether it be permanently discarded, permanently transferred to the Saṃgha, returned to the original donor—whether monastic or lay—or distributed among the seven classes of followers, it is as prescribed in the Vinaya-mūla.
This refers to such matters as the practice of cutting up [the object] before it enters the storehouse. Therefore, the mind of relinquishment must be firm, never harboring lingering attachments.

If the original property is returned, it is treated as if newly acquired; one should perform the ritual of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification) according to the Dharma. Such purification should correspond to the fundamental white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
Commentary: This citation from the Vinaya-śāstra clarifies that the Dharma is without disorder.

When the Noble One established the forfeiture of fallen items (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), it was intended to cut off greed and eliminate attachment, to exhaust defilements and clear away transgressions. If even a slight trace remains, the root of karma still persists;

all such matters must be measured and decided by the Saṃgha, and one may not take personal initiative or propose them arbitrarily. As for those who have permanently renounced [the item], it is like seizing a treasure.

Regarding the precepts, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Saṃgha should perform a formal motion with a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint one bhikṣu as the person to discard gold, silver, and money.
That bhikṣu should discard these items by placing them in a pit, or in flowing water, or in the wilderness."
It should not be recorded as such. Regarding "permanently entering the Saṃgha": it is like making an article from mixed wild silk cotton (*kośika-tūla*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It should be relinquished to the Saṃgha; it must not be relinquished to any other person. The Saṃgha uses it to spread upon the ground.

With the exception of the monk who relinquished it, all other members of the Saṃgha sit according to their seniority. Regarding "returning to one's original status as a layperson or a monastic": it is like requesting robes.

Regarding the sixfold rule for returning the robe: if one has stood silently before the donor four, five, or six times and still does not obtain the robe, one should go to the place where the price for the robe was received and say, "Please take this back.
As for giving to all seven classes of followers, it is as in the precept regarding the handling of precious objects.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If an object subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) has been forfeited within the Saṃgha, it may not be returned to that person."
The *bhikṣu* saṃgha should likewise not divide [the property]. If there is a large amount, it should be placed among the "inexhaustible goods" (*akṣaya-vastu*).
By "inexhaustible goods," one refers to the treasury of goods belonging to the Saṃgha of the ten directions. According to this, these apply only to gifts made to the five groups of renunciants;

as for the mention of "seven," this is an error in transcription by later scribes, as seen in the examples in the Vinaya texts regarding the forfeiture of items that have been cut or destroyed and entered into the treasury.
Furthermore, this passage uses the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* as an analogy for other schools to prove that [the relinquishment of property] is entirely a matter of monastic deliberation.

Therefore, once the intention to relinquish has been resolved, there should not be even a single thought of lingering attachment to prior conditions. If the original property is returned, it is treated as if newly acquired;
one should immediately perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) according to the Dharma and use it. Regarding the method of performing this *śuddhi* according to one's own circumstances:
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) according to the original Vinaya text.
In this Vinaya school, these words are not established in vain. Since the robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha, one’s mind is no longer bound to it; therefore, the Vinaya text states:
"If one does not return the robe, or if one wears it until it is worn out or destroyed, or if one accepts it to make it into the three robes (*tricīvara*), one commits only a *duṣkṛta* offense."
This refers only to the offense of losing the object.
*Explanation:* This clarifies that the monastic regulations do not allow for the relinquishment of an object when there is no owner.

Therefore, if the Sangha does not return robes and such items, it merely incurs the offense of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); this is simply the offense of failing to perform the method for returning [lost property].
△ The Dharma for Abandoning Offenses:
The Buddha said, "Once he has finished relinquishing the robe, he shall immediately perform repentance within the Saṃgha.
○ The Dharma for Requesting Repentance:
This is extracted from the subsequent text of the *Vinaya-mūla*.

It should be requested in this manner. Commentary: This refers to the method for repenting transgressions. According to the first division of the *Vinaya-mūla*, as set forth in the subsequent text, one must first make this request.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept [a number of] extra robes, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Now, there are [a number of] *pāyattika* offenses; I beg the Saṃgha for confession.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], the opportunity for confession. (Recite this three times.)"
△ Requesting the Master of the Dharma for Confession:
The Buddha said, "If all the monks in a single residence have committed an offense together, one may not confess toward another who has also committed the offense.
One who has committed an offense may not absolve another of their guilt. However, if a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is pure and free from offense..."
Regarding the offender: they should go before each person individually to confess. If no one comes, they should go to a nearby assembly of pure monks and confess.

This bhikṣu should then return to his original residence. The other bhikṣus should speak of the name of the offense to this bhikṣu and perform the confession. One who acts in this manner is called "pure."
Commentary: In general, when practicing wholesome qualities for the benefit of others, if one is not oneself pure yet wishes to cause others to be pure;
or if one has not personally ceased and severed greed and pride yet desires to cause others to do so—none of these are possible.
One should therefore request a single Dharma-abiding monk who maintains the precepts from within the Sangha to serve as the presiding master for receiving the confession.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If there is a circumstance involving a threat to life, the Buddha permitted that whether an offense was committed or not, the confession may be accepted;
if there is no such circumstance, it is not permitted. Therefore, the Vinaya says: "There are two kinds of delusion: namely, not seeing one's own offenses."
The offender shall repent. Explanation:

This refers to when the time of death is imminent and the mind is acutely distressed by the fear of transgression. If one were to maintain a total prohibition without making an exception, then urgent distress could not be rescued.
Therefore, the Buddha, out of compassion, temporarily permits such a person to be gathered and saved. If there are no such causes and conditions, it is not permitted.
Therefore, one should perform a public confession for intentional offenses. Consequently, I have cited the Vinaya and applied it accordingly, while further following the spirit of sincerity.
Although the Vinaya lacks the specific ritual for requesting [forgiveness], one must now speak according to the underlying principle.
Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [so-and-so], now request the Venerable one to act as my master for the confession of a *pāyattika* offense.
May the Venerable one act as my master for the confession of the *pāyattika* offense out of compassion.
He requests three times. If he does not receive an answer, may it be as he desires?

Regarding the procedure for seeking agreement (*sāmagrī*) and asking for consent (*jñapti-karman*): once the agreement has been sought and asked for, one replies, "I accept the *pāyattika* (pāyattika) confession ritual."
Commentary: The text provides a general response. One should respond according to the specific offense committed. To speak in terms of both the general and the particular:

the request for consent and the inquiry for harmony constitute the *jñapti* (formal motion) for harmony among the Sangha performed by the presiding elder (*sthavira*). This is to be personally proclaimed by the presiding master of the confession (*pratideśaka*). He should make the proclamation as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] intentionally kept many [number] extra robes and committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Within this, there are [number] *pāyattika* offenses. I now request the Saṃgha for confession.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name]. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
This being so, after making this formal announcement (jñapti), he informs the assembly of monks, who reply, "So be it. [The commentary] explains:
the host of the confession is requested because there must be a witness to certify that [the practitioner] is pure; thus, although the request is made three times.

One must not grant permission arbitrarily; one must inform the Sangha and obtain their consent before accepting the repentance. This means that the assembly of monks also acts as witnesses for the presiding master of the repentance ceremony.
△ The Formal Rite for Abandoning Offenses.
In the common practice of careful recitation, there are many redundancies and excesses; yet upon examination, no such faults exist, so one must not point them out recklessly.

As for the concealment of offenses and their application in usage, these are spoken of according to the specific transgressions committed; I hope they may be excised. Should any remain, they are as follows.
Commentary: This text demonstrates the clarification of erroneous teachings. "Jin" (謹) means single-mindedness. "Song" (誦) refers to what has been circulated.

It is said that those who currently oversee the Vinaya rules and perform the confession and relinquishment of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses generally focus exclusively on repenting the eight categories [of offenses], circulating this as a matter of routine. However, this is often excessive and superfluous.

One should first interrogate the practitioner’s capacity and examine their transgressions; if none exist, one must not point out offenses recklessly. It must be understood that concealment (*praticchādana*) applies universally.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous application [of the rules] and those offenses not shared [with others], one should proceed to eliminate them step by step. If such [an offense] exists, it is as follows:
the method for confessing before a single person. This is the formal relinquishment of the fundamental *pāyattika* (falling offense). One should speak as follows:

Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* by intentionally retaining numerous extra robes for more than the permitted period.
These robes have now been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Regarding the numerous *pāyattika* offenses incurred, I now confess and repent before the Venerable one.

I do not dare to conceal it. To confess brings peace and happiness; not to confess brings no peace or happiness. I call to mind my transgression and disclose it; knowing it, I do not dare to conceal it.
May the Venerable One bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure.
(After this has been recited three times, one should say: "Self-reproach arises in your heart, and you feel weary detachment. (The response: "So be it."

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "repentance leads to peace and joy," there are three aspects. First is the cause of peace and joy, which refers to upholding the precepts and knowing what is improper;

in the Vinaya, such a person is called a "wise one. Although the body dwells amidst outflows (*āsrava*) and the mind is equal to that of ordinary beings, their past habitual tendencies are already deep.
When manifest afflictions are easily aroused, one can possess a sense of shame and speak openly, sincerely washing away transgressions like laundering old clothes;
once the grime is exhausted, they become pure again. The ritual procedures of the Vinaya are likewise: not distancing oneself from the assembly, yet not being mixed with the assembly.

Therefore, one attains peace and happiness. Second is the peace and happiness of the provisional reward (*puṇya-vipāka*): this refers to the five [faculties] already being purified and the three [remaining faculties] not yet having fully matured;

thus, without traversing the evil paths, one provisionally receives celestial blessings and thereby attains peace and happiness. Third is the peace and happiness of the ultimate retribution (*vipāka*):

this means that the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) without outflows serve as the cause, and *nirvāṇa with remainder* is the fruit. *Nirvāṇa* is eternally free from all afflictions and does not involve receiving further existence.

Therefore, it is said that through repentance there is peace and happiness. If one commits an offense and conceals it, there is no way to avoid the two retributions, and one will inevitably go to the three miserable realms; thus, it is said that without repentance there is no peace or happiness.

To "mindfully recall the offense, disclose it, and knowing it, not dare to conceal it" precisely clarifies that the confession is made by oneself and was not brought to light by another. "May you remember my pure precepts."
"Endowment of the body" refers to the petitioner’s request for another person to act as his witness. "The aggregate of precepts" (śīla-kāya) is the essence of the precepts;
it is called "endowed" because it is untainted and without deficiency. Due to this purity and endowment, one is permitted to participate in the *saṃgha*'s *karmavācanā* and *poṣadha*.
Regarding the instruction from the presiding master (*karmadāna*) to generate self-reproach and a sense of weary detachment: this is from the Vinaya.
Regarding the method for rectifying transgressions, the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "In general, there are five causes and conditions for violating the precepts:

first, a lack of a sense of shame; second, a lack of reverence for the teachings; third, a mind of negligence; fourth, an inherently dull and ignorant nature; and fifth, the loss of right mindfulness.
Now, one must reproach such mental states within oneself, give rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*), and be careful not to let them arise again. By means of this...
Regarding the transgression of the noble precepts, he answered for himself: "I feel profound shame and remorse;
I hereby make a vow that even at the cost of my life or through any circumstance, I shall never commit such an offense again."
○ The Method for Returning Robes:
The Buddha said, "That robe subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) should be returned to the bhikkhu. If it is not returned, one commits an offense. There are three methods for returning it:

namely, for those such as the five extra robes that have a valid reason, they may be returned through mutual exchange; for those that are not among the five extra robes, they should be returned immediately at the very seat."

Returning: If there is no reason [to stay], the five elders shall return on the following day; this is because the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*) requires a one-night interval, and the meaning must be distinguished accordingly.

Regarding "returning from the very seat": in the Western Regions, when the Saṃgha assembles, seats are spread upon the ground; in this land (China), seating is not considered regardless of the occasion.
Stand up. However, as long as the assembly has not dispersed, you must immediately return the robe.
△ First, the method for transferring [the robe] while remaining seated:
The Buddha said, "If the community of monks is difficult to assemble, and this bhikṣu has a matter of necessity and wishes to travel far away..."
One should ask: "To whom do you give these robes? and they should be given according to their response.

Among these, there are five rules concerning surplus items—namely, the month-long robe, the urgently offered robe, keeping a bowl beyond the limit, medicinal remains, and surplus robes—which are to be returned according to this method.

Commentary: Based on these conditions, [the Buddha] granted permission for two reasons: first, because the boundary (*sīmā*) is vast and the number of people is great, each having their own karma and activities, making it difficult for them to assemble;
second, because individuals have personal affairs and wish to travel far away urgently, unable to remain here.

Therefore, he opened this allowance so that both parties may accomplish their business without hindrance to their obligations. The Sangha should ask: "Regarding these articles of yours, within the assembly present here..."

"To whom do you wish to give it? One should give it to whoever is mentioned. If it concerns the five rules regarding extra robes, such as the one-month robe, they should all be returned according to this method by speaking as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] intentionally kept many [number] extra robes and committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and gives them to the bhikṣu [Name];
the bhikṣu shall return them to this bhikṣu. The motion is thus made.
Venerable Sangha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] intentionally kept many extra robes [in number], thereby committing an offense requiring forfeiture.
These robes have already been forfeited to the Sangha. The Sangha now bestows these robes upon the bhikṣu [Name]. Bhikṣu [Name] shall return them to this bhikṣu.
Which elders among you consent to the Sangha bestowing these robes upon the bhikṣu [Name]? Bhikṣu [Name]...
"Let those who agree that this robe should be returned to this bhikṣu remain silent; let whoever does not agree speak.

The Saṃgha has agreed to bestow this robe upon [Name] bhikṣu. [Name] bhikṣu shall return it to [Name] bhikṣu. This matter is thus settled, for the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent; thus it shall be upheld."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Once a knowledgeable bhikṣu has obtained this robe within the saṃgha, he shall deliver it in a secluded place.

Commentary: "To divide" (*fen*) means to bestow; "to deliver" (*fu*) means to hand over. When one obtains clothing or requisites within the saṃgha, they belong to oneself. To bestow them upon another in a secluded place is a matter that does not concern the saṃgha as a whole.

One should be instructed to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) or to have the recipient take formal possession (*dhāraṇa*). If one does not perform the ritual of *śuddhi*, [there is an offense].

One must not store it away. If one does not apply the [prescribed] method, one must not don it. That is to say, if the original property is returned, the matter is treated as if it were newly acquired.
△ Next, the method for direct bestowal on the spot is explained.
If it is not one of the five long robes, all shall follow this rule. If it is one of the five long robes that has been kept overnight, it shall be dealt with according to this text:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The bhikṣu [Name] has intentionally stayed overnight separated from his saṃghāṭī (the other two robes, up to the returning of property belonging to the Saṃgha, shall all be dealt with accordingly), thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha now takes this..."
"I return this robe to the bhikṣu [Name]. Thus do I announce it. Venerable Saṃgha, listen:
the bhikṣu [Name] has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) for intentionally sleeping apart from his saṃghāṭī robe.
This robe has already been forfeited to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha now returns this robe to the bhikṣu [Name]. Which elders of the Saṃgha consent to the Saṃgha returning [this robe]?"
If you approve of returning this robe to the bhikṣu [Name], remain silent. Whoever does not approve, speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and completed the return of the robe to the bhikṣu [Name]. Because the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Commentary: In this *baiwen* (formal announcement), it is redundantly stated that "the remaining two robes... up to returning property belonging to the Saṃgha shall all be treated according to this.

"Treat" (*zhuo*) means to supplement. This is why, regarding the thirty rules for forfeiture within the section on "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*zhichi*), each case is indicated by stating, "This is detailed in the section on 'practicing what is prescribed' (*zuochi*).
This is because they are all based upon the aforementioned forfeiture procedures and follow these same *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas).
One should amend and supplement according to the specific circumstances and record the names for appointment; the remaining texts are all identical and without difference.
As for the seven points concerning the avoidance of faults, they have already been clarified in the first chapter; therefore, they are not shown again here among the three sets of nine dharmas.
○ Explanation of the Procedure for Confession Before Four or Fewer Persons (Pratideśanīya-dharma):

This heading provides a dual indication. Regarding the timing and the specific regulations for its performance, the text follows the established precedent; while it includes the methods applicable to the *saṃgha*, it specifically clarifies the procedure for confession before a few persons.
If one confesses before four persons, the procedure for relinquishing the property is the same as above. For the confession of the offense, one must orally harmonize with the three others;
a *śuddhaka-vidhi* (single announcement) alone is not permitted. When returning the property, it may be paid directly; the *karmavācanā* is as described above.
Commentary: There are four types of *saṃgha* that constitute a quorum. The previous section clarified the *saṃgha* of five or more members; these latter three types of *saṃgha* follow.

This present case of confessing before four persons refers to the first type of *saṃgha*. Regarding the formula for relinquishing property, which is the same as above: when there are four persons present, one should address them as "the *saṃgha*" when relinquishing [the object].
As for the confession of offenses, it requires verbal consensus (*mukha-sāmagrī*) and does not require a formal motion (*jñapti*); one person receives the confession.

Confession. If three members are deficient and the quorum is not met, yet the property can be returned and the transaction performed directly, once the confession of the offense is completed, the count reaches the required number of one plus three.
Therefore, the *karmavācanā* is as described above for the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. This refers to the precedent involving the *saṃgha*;
hereafter, it will explicitly demonstrate the *sāṃghika-dharma* and the *pratyekamukha-dharma*.

The Buddha said: "If one wishes to repent before three bhikṣus, one should go to the place where three pure bhikṣus reside and, as in the previous method of repentance, fully cultivate the proper deportment and speak these words of relinquishment."
Venerable sirs, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept many extra robes and have committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
I now relinquish them to you, venerable sirs. (Recite this once.)
Having performed this relinquishment in such a manner, one should confess the original offense. First, one should invite a master of confession;
the text for this invitation is no different from that used when inviting within the Saṃgha. Therein, the master of confession should ask the other two bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, if you, the elders, would permit me to accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name], I shall accept it. [The two bhikṣus reply: "So be it."
He then addresses the one confessing their transgression, saying, "It is permissible. The procedure for returning the robe before two persons is likewise the same.

*Explanation:* The confession of all transgressions follows this method. Regarding the phrase "the procedure for returning the robe before two persons is likewise the same," this is now also clarified by analogy for practical application.
If it concerns the five types of extra robes (*pañca-ātiriktaka*) or those that are not the five types of extra robes, they are to be handed over directly; this should be understood accordingly.

"Listen, you two elders: the bhikṣu [Name] has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) for intentionally keeping an extra robe beyond the permitted time. This robe has already been forfeited and given to us.
If you two elders consent, we shall now take this robe and return it to the bhikṣu [Name]. (The two bhikṣus reply: "So be it."
It may be so. ○ Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) for confessing before a single person, the Buddha said:
"If one confesses before a single bhikṣu, one should go to a pure bhikṣu and act as follows:"

Regarding the Dharma Confession (dharmapratideśanā): in the practices of the present day, face-to-face confessions (pratyakṣa-pratideśanā) are most common. Therefore, it is necessary to clearly establish a fixed procedure so that those who consult this work may easily examine and practice it.
[Commentary: The passage from "in the practices of the present day" to "easily examined and practiced" refers to the instructions of Master Seon-jo (宣祖).

At that time, those who perform the rituals remarked that although these individuals claim to uphold the Vinaya rules, none of them know the distinctions between the various types of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).
Most simply perform the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) in a uniform manner.
Therefore, it is necessary to clearly establish the fixed formulas for the fivefold distinctions, so that future practitioners seeking the methods of confession may easily understand them.
If one practices with diligence, one may avoid transgression and obtain benefit. This method is called the "Formal Procedure before the Assembly" (*saṃgha-pratimukha*).

It means that although one ought to assemble the Saṃgha, one does not confess before the entire assembly; rather, one should confess face-to-face with a single counterpart, rather than before a separate group. This differs from the "Single Offense" (*pāyantika*).
One must perform these repentances in a secluded place, either face-to-face (*pratimukha*) or before a formal assembly (*parṣad*).
As for what are called the "five fixed procedures," this refers to applying the methods used for a formal assembly and the face-to-face method across these five types of repentance.

First, if one repents within a community of five or more people, one employs the single announcement (*jñapti*), the acceptance of the repentance, the method of successive transmission (*saṃkramaṇa*), the direct entrustment (*sākṣāt-pratipādana*), and the returning of the object.
All [of these] are permissible. Second, if one confesses before four people, one should merely verbally harmonize with three;

the object must be returned directly, and neither the *śuddhaka-vidhi* (single-announcement) nor the *pārāyaṇa-dvaya-vidhi* (two-fold successive method) should be employed. Third, if one confesses before three people, one should verbally harmonize with two;
the method of returning the object directly may likewise not be used. Fourth, if one confesses before two people...
In this case, one should orally harmonize with a single person. Fifth, if one confesses toward a single person, there is no one else with whom to harmonize;

one simply accepts [the confession] and that is it. Although such a form of confession lists five variations of *karmavācanā*, it is definitively a *saṃgha-dharma* (procedure for the assembly) performed as a *pratyekamukha-dharma* (face-to-face procedure).

Regarding the method for relinquishing robes (*cīvara-utsarga*): one should take a single bhikṣu to the *prakṛti-sīmā* (natural boundary) or to the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (formal boundary), and all must assemble there.
Commentary: Although this text refers to a single person, the relinquishment must necessarily take place within the *prakṛti-sīmā* or [the *śīma-kaṇḍa*].

Regarding the phrase "within the boundary" (*sīmā*): this meaning implies a gathering of five or more persons. If there are four, three, or two people, because they would have to abandon [the rite], one knows that as long as there are others present, one may not perform the rite separately from the assembly.
Thus, the procedure for the fivefold confession (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*) universally encompasses all such cases; therefore, it is said that "all must assemble together."
Gather the items that were acquired through the offense and bind them together in one place. Having properly adjusted your deportment, speak these words of relinquishment:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept many extra robes (or intentionally stayed overnight separated from my saṃghāṭī), thereby committing an offense involving forfeiture.
I now relinquish them to you, Venerable sir" (recite this once).

Please perform the confession for the presiding master of the Dharma. The text for this is as explained above. The presiding master of the confession should distinguish the names of the offenses, their categories (*jāti*), and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

"Name" refers to the distinctions among the six classes of offenses. "Category" refers to the differences between such matters as keeping extra robes or being separated from one's robe for thirty days.
"Characteristic" refers to the distinction between a single instance and multiple instances. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "A single name may have many categories, abiding in various distinctions."
Explanation of the Names: Regarding the distinctions among the six classes [of offenses], they are: (1) four *pārājika* offenses; (2) twenty-three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses;
(3) *sthūlātyaya* offenses arising from [the aforementioned]; (4) one hundred and twenty *pāyattika* offenses; (5) four *pratideśanīya* offenses;
and (6) one hundred rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*). However, when these names are combined, there are only five causes that require a presiding master (*pratideśaka*) for confession.
Through analytical investigation, it is discussed from the perspective of its opening; thus, there are six categories. "Category" (*jāti*) refers to the nature of the offense itself;
because the defiled minds that commit them are not uniform, they differ in thirty respects regarding the keeping of extra robes.
Thus, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this category of offenses is not the same as the intrinsic nature of that category of offenses.

If one extends this reasoning further, each of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga-āpatti*) likewise possesses distinct characteristics. Regarding the difference between "one" and "many": these characteristics refer to the specific nature of the offense committed.

There are cases where committing one precept results in a single offense, and there are cases where committing one precept results in multiple offenses; therefore, the Vinaya is cited [to illustrate this].
It says: "One name has many kinds of distinctions in its dwelling. This appears in the third section, the *Pudgala-vastu*. The Buddha said:
"If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, whether one knows the number of days or does not know the number of days; whether one knows of the concealment or does not know of the concealment;
whether one knows of equal concealment or does not know of equal concealment—this is called 'one name with many kinds of distinctions in its dwelling regarding self-nature and non-self-nature.'"

The Buddha said: "If one has committed an offense ranging from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *duṣkṛta*, and is known to have concealed it, one should first instruct them to perform a confession for the *duṣkṛta* offense, and subsequently perform the confession according to the Dharma.
Therefore, it is known that one must first inquire in detail before instructing them in repentance."

Commentary: Previously, within the outline for the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), it was stated that "the essential points reveal the six categories of offenses (*ṣaṭ-saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharmāḥ*).
This title was established based on this [text], and it encompasses the two types of confession methods mentioned below.
○ Clarifying the Method for Confessing Offenses:
According to the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, there are eight categories; for *duṣkṛta* offenses, there are two categories. These originate from the root [offenses] as listed below.

Regarding concealment (*praticchādana*), there are six categories in total: the first two categories involve concealing the original *pāyattika* offense that has arisen; the middle two categories involve concealing...
The offense of wearing impure robes arises [at dawn]; the latter two offenses—concealing a fault during the *poṣadha* recitation and remaining silent when one should speak—arise [at dawn].
In all cases, the calculation is based on having passed the first watch and the second watch of the night.
△ First, one should confess the eight categories of minor offenses committed since birth. One should collectively request a single master of confession;

the ritual text is the same as that for the *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture), differing only in that the master of confession is designated for *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Next, one performs the formal confession of the concealed offenses.
Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], intentionally kept many extra robes (*dīrghacīvara*), thereby committing numerous *pāyattika* offenses.

Having concealed them overnight, I continued to conceal them successively night after night and wore them; thus I committed the *dukkaṭa* offense of forfeiture regarding the robes (*cīvaranissaggiya dukkaṭa*).

Having concealed them overnight, I continued to conceal them successively night after night, and by remaining silent during the Sangha’s recitation of the precepts, I committed the offense of false speech. I have committed these *dukkaṭa* offenses. [I confess them.]

[This constitutes] a *duṣkṛta* offense. Having concealed it for a night, and having continued to conceal it for successive nights (this is stated based on the fact that [the offenses] exist), one commits *duṣkṛta* offenses for each instance.
I do not recall their number; I now confess and repent before the Venerable One. I shall not dare to do so again.
May the Venerable One bear me in mind. (Recite once.)
The remaining methods for punishing offenses and establishing vows are as described above.
△ Regarding the method for repenting the two fundamental minor offenses, the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Shanjian lun) states:
"If one commits an offense involving the forfeiture of a robe (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), and wears it without having forfeited it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (transgression). The Vinaya says:
When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, if one remembers an offense even after being asked three times but does not disclose it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind: I, [Name], a bhikṣu, have committed the offense of wearing an impure robe, as well as the offense of lying by remaining silent during the recitation of the precepts by the Saṃgha;
both constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses, which I did not previously remember or count. I now disclose them before the Venerable One."
I repent; I dare not do it again. May the Virtuous One remember me (one recitation).
The remaining wording is the same as above. These [procedures] are all stated with reference to those who have committed an offense.

From the beginning of this life, the fundamental Vinaya combines the two types of repentance—prior and subsequent—but does not set forth the formal text. Now, by applying the principles of various forms of repentance, the underlying logic and precedents can be understood. Therefore...
Establish the correct ritual procedure; do not harbor doubts or confusion regarding its application.

*Explanation:* This text resolves doubts concerning the precedents of the Dharma. That is to say, the preceding section has combined the eight minor offenses (duṣkṛta) that constitute the root of arising transgressions according to the Vinaya, and it is appropriate that these be preceded by both types of repentance (the formal confession and the mental recollection). Although this is not explicitly stated in the main text, it is so intended.

Since transgression is the beginning and repentance follows from that which precedes it, the present method accords with various repentance rituals; its principles are consistent and without contradiction, and its practice can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, I have established this formal liturgy for those who would examine it; may there be no further doubt or hesitation among those who might otherwise join in it indiscriminately.
The treatise states: "It is necessary that both [the subject and object] be absent for the principle to be universally applicable; this is the definitive rule.
○ Regarding the method for repenting fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*), one should address the presiding master (*karmavācanācārya*) as follows:
Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [so-and-so], have kept an extra robe beyond the permitted period without declaring it as pure;
thus I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This robe is now relinquished to you, Venerable sir. Furthermore, there are numerous *pāyattika* offenses;
I now confess and repent them before you, Venerable sir, and dare not conceal them.

The remaining text is as above regarding the Sangha; even the methods for reprimanding, administering discipline, making vows, and returning the robes are all to be conducted according to the preceding articles.

As for the forfeiture of property that has already been used up or destroyed, one must detail its specific characteristics; furthermore, the ninety matters are all identical to the procedure for confession.

Commentary: Regarding those who have committed offenses involving forfeiture of property (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*): this refers to having committed an offense requiring forfeiture, where a long period of time has passed and the items have been worn out through use.
One must, according to the specific offense committed, confess each individual transgression by its characteristics; this is identical to the procedure for the ninety matters (*navati-vastu*).
Therefore, one must perform confession (*pratideśanā*). Previously, within the context of the "mind of relinquishment" (*tyāga-citta*), only the relinquishing of the robe was clarified;
the confession for the offense of possession (*parigraha*) was not yet performed. When the mind of possession is severed but the robe has not been relinquished, the offense is not yet confessed.

When the mind of possession is severed but the robe has not yet been destroyed, both the mind of possession remains unrelinquished and the offense remains unconfessed. Thus, the three principles of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) are fully established, leaving nothing unexhausted.

The procedure for the *pātayantika* offenses following confession is largely the same as that in the [Prātimokṣa] Thirty; the only difference is the absence of the forfeiture of material goods (*naiḥsargika*). Regarding the eight types of offenses arising from the preceding category, they may or may not exist.

For example, in the case of new robes exceeding the prescribed measure, both wearing and using them constitute an offense; logically, one must perform confession accordingly, just as in the case of lying.

Regarding the offense of digging the earth without cause, it need not necessarily apply to all cases simultaneously; rather, one should confess according to the actual number of offenses committed and state the facts as they are.

It must not be included within the root category [of the *pārājika*]. This is because the Buddha’s precepts were established first. If one confesses the root offense, there is an allowance for a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*), but this does not apply to the thirty [offenses of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
Commentary: Regarding the ninety matters herein, if one performs confession, one must know whether or not the eight types of minor offenses arising from the preceding category apply;
one must not point to them recklessly. For example, "if new robes exceed the prescribed measure" is a general heading that subsumes within it:
the sixtieth precept, "obtaining robes without dyeing them"; the eighty-fifth precept, "storing cotton in beds and mats"; and the eighth [precept].
88. The precept on the excessive size of sitting mats; 89. The precept on the excessive size of garments for sores;
90. The precept on the excessive size of rain-cloaks; 91. The precept on the measurement of the Buddha’s robes.
These six matters constitute offenses when worn or used. Furthermore, there is the 84th precept on the excessive height of beds, and the 86th... [precept].
Regarding the precept on bone, ivory, needles, and tubes: one incurs an offense merely by using them, even without possessing them.
As for the remaining eighty-two matters, such as lying and digging the earth, since there is no reason to possess them, they do not necessarily apply to all cases;

rather, one should confess according to the actual number of offenses committed, declaring the truth, and perform the confession together with the preceding ones. If one confesses these fundamental *pāyattika* (downfalls), the two boundaries upon which they depend are distinct.
