The assembly attains opening [of the path]. This differs from the thirty [rules]; the confession applies to both the Saṃgha and the individual.

The text for requesting the master of confession is as explained above. If one sincerely confesses the original offense, there is a slight difference in the wording, which should be stated as follows:
Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, have committed the offense of intentional lying, a *pāyattika* (the remainder being recited as appropriate).

I do not remember the number [of times I have committed it] (if one has committed only a single *duṣkṛta* and does not remember the number, or if there are others, speak according to what exists—truthfully and without error).
I now disclose and repent before the Venerable One; I dare not conceal it.
The remaining wording is as above. This applies even up to the reprimands and the taking of vows.
○ Regarding the method for confessing the *pātideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession):
it refers to receiving food with one's own hands from a nun who is not a relative while in a village or street, or eating food assigned by a nun.
Commentary: This explanation of the characteristics of the precept is as clarified in the section on "Observance through Cessation" (*zhi-chí*). There are four types of collective prohibitions;
here, only the first two are explained, hence the word "etc. (*deng*) is used to include the third: performing the *karmavācanā* for a family (*śaikṣa-kula*) and receiving [food] when not ill.
Regarding eating: the fourth [case] concerns receiving food within a saṃghārāma when one is not ill.
All the Vinayas require that one person be appointed as the host to announce the name and category of the offense; once it has been announced, one stops. The wording is as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a *pāyattika* offense by eating food assigned by a bhikṣuṇī.
I do not recall the number of times this has occurred. Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable act that should not have been done;

I now repent before the venerable one. [The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states: The person before him should ask: "Do you see your fault? [He replies: "I see it. [He should then reprove him, saying: "Be careful not to do it again."
[The ritual] is performed. [The respondent] says: "I shall receive it upon my head. Explanation:

It is said that one person should be requested to act as the presiding master; the procedure for the text is the same as the aforementioned method. Among these, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Small Version) has no application at all.
For the others, perform them according to their presence. Based on the reality of the situation, first perform the repentance.

First, non-validity regarding the person: this refers to matters such as the person toward whom the confession is directed being excluded by prohibitions. Second, non-validity regarding the ritual procedure (*dharma*):

this refers to matters such as the formal announcement (*jñapti*) having three additional elements, or being erroneous or omitted. Third, non-validity regarding the matter (*vastu*): this refers to matters such as the offense committed being ambiguous, doubtful, or undecided.
The latter four cases follow the standard procedure.
○ Regarding the method for repenting *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses):
The Buddha said, "If one commits them intentionally, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense that must be repented; furthermore, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct."

If one does not act intentionally, one merely commits a *duṣkṛta*. Since the original Vinaya text clearly distinguishes between the two mental states of "intentional" and "unintentional," it specifies that the two offenses are distinct categories.

Yet, various masters have failed to consult the Vinaya sections; instead, they take the Fivefold Repentance as their primary authority and consequently follow suit in a uniform manner, treating all offenses—whether light or heavy—as identical and purifying them through a single repentance. Furthermore, the explicit meaning of the Fivefold Repentance applies only to specific occasions.

Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* and *pāyattika* offenses, their existence or non-existence, and their frequency vary; the established rules are not uniform. It is necessary that the underlying principles be made clear.
Ordinary speech is difficult to rely upon, whereas the words of the Sage are easy to believe.
Commentary: The original text of the Vinaya states: The Buddha said, "If one commits an offense intentionally, one should confess a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Because it was committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for improper conduct (*anācāra-duṣkṛta*). As for the statement "one should confess a *duṣkṛta*," this refers to the fundamental offense committed;
it is the actual commission of the primary offense. Because it was committed intentionally, one loses the integrity of the monastic discipline and simultaneously incurs [the secondary offense].
The *duṣkṛta* offense regarding improper deportment is such that it arises simultaneously [with the act]. When one commits it, the name of the offense is established separately;

when one performs the confession (*pratideśanā*), it is extinguished simultaneously [with the act]. If one does not act intentionally and merely commits a *duṣkṛta*, the original Vinaya texts clarify this through the hundred rules of training for the assembly (*śaikṣa-dharma*), which fully explain the two mental states of "intentional" and "unintentional. One should proclaim the request for repentance, and thus the two offenses are categorized as distinct.

Yet the masters of the Vinaya school themselves do not personally investigate or study the Vinaya texts; following established custom, they have discarded them and instead take the Five Repentances as their primary doctrine.

Consequently, they all follow suit, treating offenses of both light and heavy gravity with uniformity, collectively purifying them through these rites. Furthermore, regarding the meaning elucidated in these Five Repentances:

The first two sections of this [text] are extracted from among the *sthūlātyaya* offenses arising from [other categories]; one must distinguish those that are independent (*mukta*). Within the third section on the *pārājika*, there are cases where forfeiture (*niḥsarga*) exists and cases where it does not;
furthermore, there are differences regarding the gravity of the offense based on the number of factors, such as the three or nine [criteria]. For these reasons, the established rules are not uniform.
However, regarding this *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), how could it be limited merely to the specific primary transgression? Therefore, both intentional and unintentional cases apply equally.

This is true for all precepts as well; the principle must be made clear. Thus, the following cites the Vinaya to provide proof. For ordinary speech is difficult to rely upon, whereas the words of the Sage are easy to trust.

Therefore, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one acts intentionally, one confesses before another person; if one acts through negligence, one reproaches oneself. This method of confession is consistent with the Vinaya and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

How can you persist in your intentional adherence [to other views]? As evidenced by the Vinaya’s *Pravāraṇā-vastu*, the *Abhidharmadīpa*, the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, and other texts, each provides clear proof.
It is not merely a matter of suppressing conjecture; in principle, one must rely strictly upon these sources. The rest...
There are nine grades of distinctions based on the root of arising; these should all be determined by analogy with the examples provided above.
Commentary: "Not merely suppressing" means that one does not merely suppress the conduct of others while being self-centered in one's own estimation and display.
Since the principle is regulated in this manner, one must reverently rely upon and uphold it. Regarding the "nine grades of distinctions," it refers to:

The fundamental transgressions of negligence and the remaining eight categories are all as described above. One should deliberate upon each case individually and apply the corresponding methods of repentance to cleanse them.
○ The actual procedure for the ritual of repentance.

There is no specific textual passage in the Vinaya; one should follow the method previously established. In principle, this applies to the removal and extinction [of offenses]. As for the procedure for a formal act (*karmavācanā*), first request the presiding master (*sāṃghika-vinayadhara*) as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable sir to serve as my witness for the confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense."

"Venerable One, I pray that you will act as my witness for the confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense. Out of compassion, [please do so]. (Request three times). ○ Regarding the method for relinquishing an offense, it originates from its root;

one must possess two types of awareness. As for the various characteristics and their quantities, they must all be examined and scrutinized with full detail. One should respond to the person before them."
A person speaks thus:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally do not wear the saṃghāṭī robe in a neat and orderly manner [the remainder being determined by the same principle]."
I have committed one *duṣkṛta* offense. I now confess and repent before the Venerable One. I shall not dare to do it again.
May the Venerable One bear me in mind. (Recite once.)
The reprimand and the taking of the vow are as previously described.

There are three types of invalidity (*asādhutva*): first, invalidity of person (*pudgala-asādhutva*), which refers to cases where there is no single individual or where there is another group present; second, invalidity of dharma (*dharma-asādhutva*), which refers to instances such as the words of the reprimand being omitted or dropped;

third, invalidity of matter (*vastu-asādhutva*), which refers to cases where the offenses committed are mutually confused or mistaken. Other forms of invalidity should be understood by analogy with the standard rules.

Having mistakenly committed [this offense], one should perform the ritual of repentance by fully assuming the dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*), giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and speaking these words:
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have mistakenly worn the saṃghāṭī robe in a disordered manner, thereby committing a *duṣkṛta* offense. I now..."
Repenting with a sense of self-reproach (one interpretation).
Non-human [confession] refers to confessing one's faults before a person. Non-dharmic [confession] refers to mental recollection while remaining silent, and so forth.
The others are not as before. ○ The Procedure for Remaining Speech (Śeṣavāda) continues:

This follows the outline of the *śuddha-jñapti* (single motion). Now, according to the Vinaya, the method for continuing [the procedure] is as follows: namely, the first of the ninety matters (*navati-prakaraṇa*).

This is the twelfth precept concerning vexing others with irrelevant speech. The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu has committed an offense and the other bhikṣus ask him, 'Do you know that you have committed an offense?
he immediately answers the bhikṣus with some other matter, saying: 'To whom were you speaking? What was it you were explaining?
What principle were you discussing? Were you speaking to me, or to whom? Who is the one who has committed the offense? What is the offense?'"
"From what does this arise? I do not see any offense; why do you say that I have committed one? The Buddha said:

"From now on, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to formally announce [the case] and designate it as 'speaking otherwise' (anyavāda), according to the usual procedure. [The questioner asks: 'What is being sought? [The respondent] answers:
'The formal act (karmavācanā) for speaking otherwise. It should be announced as follows:"
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] has committed an offense. When the bhikṣus asked him, "Do you yourself recognize that you have committed an offense?
he replied to the bhikṣus with an irrelevant matter, saying, "To whom were you speaking? What matter were you discussing?"
To discuss what principle: for whom am I speaking? For myself, or for others? Who has committed an offense? From what does the offense arise?

I do not see the offense (*this is spoken according to the conditions of the transgression; however, when speaking according to reality, one should state it as follows*). If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience:
I shall designate the bhikṣu [Name] as one who speaks evasively. Thus is the motion.

The Vinaya states: Once this formal announcement has been made, it is termed "remaining speech" (*avasiṣṭha-vāk*). If one speaks in such a manner before the Sangha has made the announcement, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one speaks in such a manner after the announcement has been made, it is in all cases a *pāyattika* offense.
Non-human [non-offense]: this refers to cases such as when the administrator is not present. Non-substantial [non-offense]: this refers to cases such as joking speech or lack of intention.
Other non-offenses are to be understood by analogy with the preceding.
○ The Dharma of Annoying Contact.
Continuation: This follows the *śuddhaka-vidhi* (the single-announcement procedure) regarding the "net-pattern" [of offenses]. Now, according to the Vinaya, the method for continuation is as follows:

After [a monk] has previously engaged in irrelevant speech (*parāpudgalavāda*), he subsequently intentionally harasses the Saṃgha—such as by not coming when summoned or coming when not summoned. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, it is permitted that after the Saṃgha has made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), this bhikṣu shall be designated as one who 'harasses' [the community]. As stated in the usual procedure for assembly, questioning, and answering: [The text continues...]
Regarding the *saṃvāsanīyakarman* (the formal act of censuring for causing disturbance), one should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṅgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has been designated by the Saṅgha as one who speaks evasively, yet he causes disturbance to the community:
when summoned he does not come; when not summoned he comes; when he should rise he does not rise; when he should not rise he rises; when he should speak he does not speak."

One should not speak what ought not to be spoken (the truth being stated as a formal citation). If the Saṃgha is ready and the Saṃgha permits, let it be enacted that the bhikṣu [Name] shall be designated as one who causes provocation. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The Vinaya states: "If one does not come when summoned without having been formally notified, and so forth, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts after the formal notification has been completed, as in all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*. If an elder summons one and one does not come, it is *duṣkṛta*.
The exceptions are determined according to the above."

○ Continued: The Procedure for Appointing One to Confess a Gross Offense (*sthūlātyaya*). This follows the outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one proclamation). Now, according to the established procedure for continuation:

In the original Vinaya, Devadatta, for the sake of gain and honor, caused a schism in the Saṃgha; thus, he harbored an evil intent to harm the Buddha. Furthermore, he instructed Ajātaśatru to kill his father. At that time—

The Venerable One addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "You may be appointed. Śāriputra addressed the assembly of laypeople, saying, "Whatever is done by Devadatta is not a matter of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha;
it is the doing of Devadatta himself. A formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) should be performed to appoint him.
When appointing him, one must solicit his consent and inquire about the circumstances. The response shall be: 'I am appointed as the messenger. Thus it is done."
He addressed them, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.

We now appoint the bhikṣu Śāriputra to go before the assembly of laypeople and declare that the deeds performed by Devadatta are not the deeds of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; it should be known as such."
This was done by Devadatta. It is announced as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu Śāriputra to go before the assembly of laypeople and explain the deeds of Devadatta—that these are not the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, but were performed by Devadatta. Who [among you]..."

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣu Śāriputra to speak before the assembly of laypeople regarding the deeds of Devadatta—which are not the affairs of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha—should remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has consented to appoint the bhikṣu Śāriputra to speak before the assembly of laypeople regarding the deeds of Devadatta, which are not [the affairs of] the Buddha... [and so forth].
The section on the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is concluded. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
*Explanation:* This refers to the seventh of the ninety matters concerning the precept against confessing offenses to laypeople; it excludes the formal *saṃghakarma*.
Since this specific case does not exist today, it has been appended here as a continuation so that one may understand the conditions for its application.

**Commentary on the Method for Caring for the Alms Bowl** This follows the outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one proclamation). It is now appended here according to the Vinaya;

it is the twenty-second of the thirty rules (*triṃśad-śikṣāpada*). It concerns a nun who, while her bowl has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, seeks a new bowl because she considers the old one to be inferior.
This is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it. [The Saṃgha] shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among those present and give it to him to hold;
he must continue to hold it until it breaks. Now, following this, the method for maintaining the protective bowl is set forth.

Previously, there was the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the granting of a bowl and the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) for the distribution of bowls; these rules are listed here according to the Vinaya, and the ritual procedures should be supplemented according to their underlying meaning.
Practice.
△ First, the explanation of the method for giving a bowl:
This rule is one of the twenty-seven rules concerning the returning of robes. First, one should relinquish the invitation and perform repentance.
The censure for the offense and the taking of the vow are as previously described; all such dharmas are identical to those before. The difference therein is that giving [the robe] is not permitted.
It should be given by many people to one person. In this residence, the Saṃgha likewise does not perform the successive transfer on the spot.
There are two methods for returning [the bowl] directly. Once the bowl has been relinquished and the offense expiated, the Elder should announce within the assembly:
"Tomorrow, the Sangha shall gather to return the bowl. However, while the underlying principle is clear in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the textual evidence is missing.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Let one person proclaim within the Sangha: 'Venerable sirs, at such-and-such a time, each of you should bring the bowl you have been using.'"
"Come! If one does not call out [the announcement], one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If any bhikṣus further receive an inferior bowl and bring it along, they likewise commit a *vinayātikrama* offense. Once this proclamation has been made, the gavel is struck at dawn.
At that time, each bhikṣu takes his own bowl, places it in his bowl-bag, hangs it over his shoulder, and proceeds to the assembly.
In the Vinaya, the Buddha said: "If this bhikṣu’s bowl is of high value and fine quality, it should be retained; one should take the lowest and most inferior one and give it to him.
This should be done by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."

**Explanation:** Because the mind that commits the offense of violating the precepts is originally characterized by greed for what is desirable, the present regulation of withholding the desirable from those of lower standing is precisely intended to exhaustively purify this mind.

Once the Saṃgha has assembled, they should sit according to the usual order of seniority (*pūrva-vṛddha*). The Elder (*sthavira*) shall solicit the consent (*chanda*) and inquire about the circumstances.

He replies, "The *pātra-karman* (the formal act concerning the bowl) is to be performed. He further asks, "Who among the assembly is capable of performing the *karman*? If there is anyone [capable], [he should be appointed].
He replies, "I am capable, Venerable Sir. Since the Elder is indeed capable, he should perform the ritual according to the Vinaya.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] intends to employ means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, persisting in his resolve and refusing to relinquish it.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent to address him with a formal admonition so that he may relinquish this matter:
"Bhikṣu [Name], you must not break the harmony of the Saṃgha by persisting in your refusal to relinquish it. You, bhikṣu [Name], should live in harmony with the Saṃgha. May there be joy.
"May we rejoice without contention, like water and milk blending as one, and dwell in peace within the Buddha-dharma.
Having thus made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the officiant of the *karmavācanā* should admonish them, saying:

"Venerable one, I have finished the announcement. There remains the formal act (*karmavācanā*). You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform a formal act against you and cause you to incur a further grave offense."
If they accept this proposal, it is well. If they do not accept it, the first *karmavācanā* is performed as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] intends to adopt the practice of causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persists in it, refusing to relinquish it."
Now the Saṃgha admonishes you, [Name], to relinquish this matter. Do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by persisting in your refusal to relinquish it.
You, [Name], should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and without dispute, as one with water and milk, dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Which elders among you who consent to the Saṃgha’s admonition of the bhikṣu [Name] to relinquish this matter, remain silent?
"However, let whoever does not approve speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed this first *karmavācanā*, one should admonish him, saying:
'Venerable sir, I have finished the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā*; two *karmavācanās* remain. You should relinquish this.'"
Do not let the Saṃgha perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against you again, whereby you would incur a grave offense.
If you heed these words, it is well; if you do not heed them, as stated above, the second *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Once the two *karmavācanās* have been completed, one should admonish him, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have already completed the first of the two formal acts (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Only one formal act remains.
You should relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform the formal act against you once more and you incur a grave offense."
If he is able to relinquish it, that is well. If he does not relinquish it, proceed as previously described. Perform the third *karmavācanā* (formal act), concluding with:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to give this admonition to the bhikṣu [Name] to relinquish this matter. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, it is so."
One should maintain the matter in this manner.
Regarding the abandonment [of the offense] through admonition: if one abandons it before the initial proclamation (*jñapti*) is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one abandons it once the proclamation is finished, it is one *sthūlātyaya* (light offense). If one abandons it after the proclamation and the first *karman* have been performed, it is two *sthūlātyayas*.
If one is restrained and then relinquishes [the offense] through a *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion), it is a *tri-guṇa-sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not relinquish it after the third *karman* is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one does not relinquish it at all before the *jñapti*, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Commentary: This section exclusively continues the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) for schism. Since such a matter does not exist now, the refutation is not explicitly stated. The same applies to the following section on assisting in the breaking of the Saṃgha.
[The Method of Admonishing Those Who Assist in Breaking the Saṃgha]
Continuation: This follows the outline of the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations). Now, according to the eleventh *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule, the continuation of the procedure is as follows.
The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu acts as an unlawful partisan and assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, that bhikṣu should be admonished by the others, saying:
'Venerable sir, do not speak such words; this bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma.'"
"This monk speaks according to the Dharma; this monk speaks according to the Vinaya. What this monk has said, we accept.
Yet, this monk does not speak according to the Dharma, nor does he speak according to the Vinaya. Do not, O Venerable Ones, cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
You should support the unity of the Saṃgha. Let the Saṃgha be harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute, like water and milk mixed together, under the Buddha."
Within the Dharma, there is the addition [of merit], peaceful dwelling, and that which may be relinquished by comparison; do not be censured by the Saṃgha, nor commit further grave offenses.
If you follow these words, it is well. If you do not follow these words, the Saṃgha shall admonish and exhort you to relinquish this matter;
therefore, the formal motion and threefold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) are performed.
Explanation: There are two kinds of compliance: first, compliance with the Dharma, which refers to receiving instruction in the Dharma, reciting it, and upholding it;

second, compliance regarding robes and food, which refers to providing the four requisites. Having thus assembled the Saṃgha and appointed those for the *karmavācanā*, one should perform the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*) and respond as follows:
"Grant [him] assistance in breaking the Saṃgha," and perform the *tarjanīyakarman* (act of reprimand). As...
He speaks thus: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This group of bhikṣus, being in accord with [so-and-so], speak as follows:
'You bhikṣus should not admonish [so-and-so]. Why? Because [so-and-so] is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and the Vinaya.'"
Speak to the bhikṣus: "We approve of what [so-and-so] has said. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
The Saṃgha now intends to reprove [so-and-so] and his faction for the purpose of making them abandon this matter.

You must not say that [so-and-so] is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya, and that 'we approve of what [so-and-so] has said'; for [so-and-so] is not in accordance with the Dharma."
He addresses the monks according to the Vinaya: "Monks, do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. You should assist the Saṃgha in reaching harmony, O Venerable Ones.
Be united with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, like water and milk blended together. Within the Buddha-dharma, there will be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Once the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, the officiant of the ritual (*karmakāraka*) should admonish him, saying:

"Venerable sir, I have completed the formal motion; the rest of the ritual remains. You should relinquish this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Saṃgha nor further commit a grave offense."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, one should perform the first *karmavācanā* as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This group of companion monks, following [the lead of] [Name], speaks thus:
'O monks, do not admonish [Name]. [Name] is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma; [Name] is a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya.'"
(a) What has been said by [so-and-so] we accept and approve. Now, the Saṃgha is admonishing the partisan bhikṣu [so-and-so] to abandon this matter.
Venerable sirs, do not speak thus: that [so-and-so] is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya;
that what [so-and-so] says we accept and approve; yet [so-and-so] is not a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma nor one who speaks according to the Vinaya.
"O bhikṣus, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha. You should assist in bringing about harmony in the Saṃgha. Venerable ones, be in harmony with the Saṃgha;
be joyful and free from dispute, like water and milk mixed together. Within the Buddha-dharma, this will lead to increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness."
"Whichever elders among you who consent to the Saṃgha’s admonition of the monk [Name], the partisan, so that he may relinquish this matter, remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, please speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*."
Having performed this first *karmavācanā*, one should admonish him, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have completed the first *karmavācanā* proclamation; two more remain.
You should relinquish this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, perform the second *karmavācanā* as above.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, you should further admonish them, saying:
"Venerable one, I have already completed the first of the two formal motions (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Only one motion remains.
You should relinquish this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Saṃgha nor further commit a grave offense."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, as previously described, the third *karmavācanā* is performed, concluding:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to reprimand and admonish the partisan bhikṣus [named so-and-so], commanding them to relinquish this matter. The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent.
Therefore, this matter is to be upheld in this way.
Regarding the admonition to relinquish [the offense] therein, if one does not relinquish it, the procedure for punishing the offense is the same as above.
○ Admonishing those of a wicked nature.
The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu is of evil character and refuses to accept the words of others, that bhikṣu should be admonished by the others as follows:
'Venerable sir, do not make yourself one with whom it is impossible to converse; you should become one with whom it is possible to converse.

Venerable sir, admonish the other bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the other bhikṣus shall likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma. Venerable sir, such is the way for a disciple of the Buddha.'"
The assembly of disciples shall attain increase. They shall instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent before one another.
"Venerable sirs, you should abandon this matter; do not be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense. If they comply with these words, it is well.
If they do not comply, it is permitted for the bhikṣus from this time forward to assemble the Saṃgha and [deal] with this bhikṣu.
One should perform the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to issue a reprimand for abandoning this matter.

Once the community of monks has assembled, a monk shall be appointed from among them as the *karman-maker*. Having performed the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakalpa*), he should respond, saying: "I shall perform the *karman* of reprimanding one of evil character.
He should then make the formal motion (*jñapti*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] is of an evil nature and does not accept the words of others.
Although the bhikṣus have instructed him according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, he himself makes himself unapproachable for conversation.
He says to the bhikṣus: 'Venerable sirs, do not speak to me whether it be good or bad; nor will I speak to the venerable sirs whether it be good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist.'"
There is no need to instruct me. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:

the Saṃgha now intends to carry out a formal admonition against the bhikṣu [Name] so that he may relinquish this matter. You, [Name], must not act as one who is uncommunicative; you should act as one who is communicative.
[Name], you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus shall likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma. As...
The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples has attained increase. They instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent before one another.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, the *karmadāna* (the officiant) should further inquire as follows:
"Venerable sir, I have finished the formal announcement (*jñapti*). There remain three *karmavācanās*. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter;
do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense."
If he complies with what is said, it is well. If he does not comply with what is said, the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] is of evil character and will not accept the words of others.

Although the bhikṣus instruct him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he himself acts in such a way that he cannot be spoken to. He says to the bhikṣus: 'Venerable sirs, do not speak to me.'"
Whether I am right or wrong, I shall not speak of my own rightness or wrongness to the Venerable Ones. Venerable Ones, please desist; there is no need for you to instruct me.
Now the Saṃgha is performing a formal reprimand and admonition against the bhikṣu [Name] so that he may relinquish this matter.

You, [Name], must not yourself act in a manner that makes one unfit to converse with others; rather, you should act in a manner that makes one fit to converse. You should admonish others in accordance with the Dharma.
"O Bhikṣu, the other bhikṣus shall also admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase as they mutually instruct one another, mutually admonish one another, and mutually confess their faults.

Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu [Name] to abandon this matter? Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*."
Having performed this first *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
"Venerable sir, I have completed the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā*; two *karmavācanās* remain. Venerable sir, you should relinquish [the matter]."
Regarding this matter, do not allow yourself to be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense.
If you comply with these words, it is well; if you do not comply, perform the second *karmavācanā* as described above.
Once the second *karmavācanā* has been performed, you should again entreat [the Saṃgha], saying:
"Venerable sir, I have already completed the first of the two formal motions (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). One motion remains.
Venerable sir, you should desist from this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, as described above, perform the third *karmavācanā* and conclude by saying:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out this formal admonition for the bhikṣu [Name] to abandon this matter; the Saṃgha consents, as indicated by its silence."
"Maintain this matter thus. Commentary:
In this context, the procedure for admonishing one to relinquish [the offense] and the punishment for failing to relinquish it are to be applied according to the above.
If there are other bhikṣus who instruct [the offender] not to relinquish the *sthūlātyaya*, or if bhikṣuṇīs so instruct, it is likewise.
It is not other; it is not based on the permanent; it is only the negation of a different entity—meaning that playful discourse is not the truth. It is countered by actual facts and so forth.
○ Admonishing against evil and heterodox teachings.

Continuation: This follows the outline of the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three proclamations). Now, according to the procedure for the sixty-eighth offense of the *pāyattika* (offenses entailing expiation), the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu gives rise to such a wrong view as this: 'I know that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is such that committing sexual misconduct does not constitute an obstacle to the path,' that bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: 'Do not speak thus.'"
[He] said: "Do not slander the Blessed One. To slander the Blessed One is unwholesome; the Blessed One would never speak such words.
By means of countless skillful means, the Blessed One has declared that the practice of sexual desire is an obstructive dharma to the Path.
You should now abandon this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses. It is well if you accept these words; if you do not comply with them, listen to [the following]..."
"Monks, from this day forward, assemble the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure against that monk for the purpose of making him relinquish this matter through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Having assembled the Saṃgha, appoint those to perform the *karman* and carry out the preliminary procedure, declaring:
'We shall perform a formal act of admonition and censure against one who holds evil and heterodox views. Then, make the formal motion (*jñapti*) as follows:"
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] speaks thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha;
engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.

The Saṃgha now intends to carry out a formal admonition against this bhikṣu [Name] to make him abandon this matter. [Name], do not speak such words. Do not slander the World-Honored One. To slander the World-Honored One...
"Venerable sir, it is not right; the Blessed One does not speak thus. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path.
To commit sexual misconduct is itself an obstruction to the path. This is my formal statement."
Once the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, the officiant of the ritual (*karmakāraka*) should admonish him, saying:

"Venerable sir, I have completed the announcement; the formal act (*karman*) remains to be performed. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter, lest you be censured by the Sangha and commit further offenses."
If he follows what is said, it is well. If he does not follow what is said, the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] speaks thus: 'I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is such that the commission of sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path.
The Saṃgha now grants him a formal reprimand to make him abandon this matter. [Name], do not do so!"
Do not speak thus. Do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not say such a thing.

Through countless skillful means, the Blessed One has declared that sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path; if one commits sexual misconduct, it is indeed a dharma that obstructs the path.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu [Name] for the purpose of making him relinquish this matter, remain silent.
Those who do not consent, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*."
Once the first *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should admonish him, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have finished the first proclamation; two proclamations remain. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter;
do not commit further offenses so that you may be rebuked by the Saṃgha."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, perform a second *karmavācanā* as described above.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should again admonish them, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have already completed the second of the two *karmas*. Only one *karman* remains. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter;
do not commit further offenses so as to be censured by the Saṃgha."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, perform the third *karmavācanā* as described above, concluding by saying:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal admonition against the bhikṣu [Name]. Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
In this regard, if one relinquishes [the matter] before the motion (*jñapti*) is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one relinquishes it after the motion is completed, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If one relinquishes it after the first *karmavācanā* following the motion has been performed, it is two *duṣkṛtas*.

If one relinquishes it after the second *karmavācanā* following the motion has been performed, it is three *duṣkṛtas*. If one does not relinquish it after the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one speaks these words before the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is all *duṣkṛta*.

If the community of monks exhorts him, yet other bhikṣus obstruct him, saying, "Do not abandon this matter," it is all *duṣkṛta*. It is the same if a bhikṣuṇī or those of the three lower groups of nuns obstruct him, saying, "Do not abandon it."
Commentary: This *karmavācanā* (formal act) of admonition is for the sake of leading persons toward the correct path and for the sake of the Dharma; thus, it pertains to private matters.
Among the three types of schisms, this constitutes a schism of view (*dṛṣṭibheda*), and it is shown not to be the same as the aforementioned "evil nature" (*duḥśīla*).
○ The Two Methods for Admonishing and Expelling a Wicked and Erroneous Śrāmaṇera (Continuation) This follows the framework of the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations).

Now, based on the seventy rules of the *pāyattika* (offenses entailing expiation), these two methods first clarify the admonition to renounce [the error], and subsequently clarify the performance of the expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*). Both concern the breaking of views and are *karman* performed without the offender being present. (Vinaya)
It is said: At that time, there were two śrāmaṇeras who engaged in unchaste conduct together. They said to one another, "We have heard the Dharma from the Buddha;

for one who engages in sexual desire, it is not an obstacle to the Path. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them, saying, "You yourselves said to one another, 'We have heard the Dharma from the Buddha; engaging in sexual desire is not an obstacle to the Path. The bhikṣus...
The Bhikṣu Kāśyapa reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to reprimand such a śrāmaṇera and cause him to abandon this matter.

It should be performed as follows: Having assembled the Saṃgha, appoint a person to perform the formal act. He shall carry out the preliminary procedure and respond, saying: 'To [the one with] evil and heterodox views...'"

The śrāmaṇera undergoes the formal act of admonition (hōkan-katsuma). Leading this śrāmaṇera to stand before the assembly of monks in a place where he can see them but cannot hear what they say, the following announcement is made:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Those śrāmaṇeras have said among themselves: "I have heard the Dharma from the Blessed One that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant leave, let this śrāmaṇera be reprimanded so that he may abandon this matter.
You, śrāmaṇera, must not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One. To slander the Blessed One is unwholesome.

"World-Honored One, you do not speak such words. Śrāmaṇera, the World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, declared that the practice of sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path. It is so stated."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Those śrāmaṇeras have said among themselves: 'I have heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One that engaging in sexual desire is not an obstacle to the path.
The Saṃgha now addresses this śrāmaṇera with a formal admonition to cause him to abandon this matter.
You, śrāmaṇera, must not slander the World-Honored One; it is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One, for the World-Honored One does not speak such words."
The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, declared that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.

Which elders among you who consent to the Saṃgha’s present censure of this śrāmaṇera and its command that he abandon this matter, remain silent? Who does not consent, let them speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*.
(The second and third are spoken in the same manner. The Saṃgha has already consented to the censure of this śrāmaṇera. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, it is so.
Maintain the matter thus. Commentary:
This dharma is called "admonition" (*codanā*). According to the Vinaya, this refers exclusively to the admonition to relinquish [a fault] within the formal motion (*jñapti*) itself;
it is not the same as the sequential admonition involving one motion and three *karmavācanās* used for admonishing monks and nuns.

Non-human [invalidity] means that [the instruction] was not conveyed or heard, or that it was given in a secluded place and so forth. Invalidity regarding the Dharma means that [the formal act] was carried out through a mere motion (*jñapti*) or a suspension of admonition (*pratyanuyoga*).
Other forms of invalidity are as previously described.

The Buddha said: "If this śrāmaṇera, having been rebuked by the community of monks, still does not relinquish his evil view, the Saṃgha should perform the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the expulsion of this śrāmaṇera for not relinquishing his evil view. It should be carried out as follows:

Having assembled the Saṃgha, they should appoint an official for the *karman* and perform the preliminary ritual, declaring: 'We shall perform the [procedure] for the śrāmaṇera for not relinquishing his evil view.'"

Regarding the *nihsarana-karman* (act of banishment): Having brought the śrāmaṇera before the assembly of monks and stationed him in a place where he can see but not hear, one makes the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This śrāmaṇera has been censured by the Saṃgha, yet he does not relinquish his evil view. If the time is right for the Saṃgha..."
May the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of banishment for this śrāmaṇera due to his failure to relinquish evil views.
From this day forward, this śrāmaṇera must not say, "The Buddha is my World-Honored One," nor may he follow other bhikṣus.
While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you are no longer permitted to do so. Depart! Be gone! Do not remain!
"You should abide in this. [The motion] is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This śrāmaṇera has been censured by the community of monks, yet he does not relinquish his evil view.
The community of monks now performs the formal act of *niḥsaraṇa-pārājika* (expulsion for not relinquishing an evil view) against this śrāmaṇera. From this day forward, this śrāmaṇera shall not..."
"You may say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One,' but you should not follow after other bhikṣus.
Just as śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you are not permitted to do so now. Get out! Be gone! You should not remain here.

"Which elders among you approve of the Saṃgha performing this act of *pravāsanīya-karman*—the formal act of banishment—for this śrāmaṇera who holds an evil view and refuses to relinquish it? Those who approve, please remain silent. Who..."
"It is approved; it is spoken. This is the first *karmavācanā* (the second and third are likewise spoken).
