If they comply with the instruction, it is well. If they do not comply, perform the second *karmavācanā* as before.
Once the second *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should again speak as previously stated (and so forth).
If she complies with these words, it is well. If she does not comply, after the third *karmavācanā* has been performed as above, the conclusion is made thus:
"The Saṃgha has consented to carry out the act of censure against the bhikṣuṇī [Name] so that she may abandon this matter; the Saṃgha consents by its silence."
Therefore, this matter should be maintained in this way.

Commentary: Herein, the relinquishing or non-relinquishing [of the offense], as well as the instruction not to relinquish it and the disciplinary measures for the offense, are all characteristics of the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (methods for settling disputes). All are to be determined according to the aforementioned rules.
○ Continued: The Dharma for Admonishing the Practice of Associating with Householder Sons.
This follows the outline of the *jñapti-caturtha* (formal motion followed by three proclamations). Now, based on the ninety-ninth rule of the *bhikṣuṇī-pācattika*, the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī associates closely with householders or the sons of householders and dwells with them, engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma."
The other bhikṣuṇīs admonished her in this manner, yet she still refused to live separately. She informed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*) against that bhikṣuṇī for the purpose of making her abandon this matter.

It should be performed by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) as follows: Having assembled the Saṃgha within the boundary (*sīmā*), one should appoint an official to perform the ritual and summon those who have consented."

Question on the formal cause. Answer: It is said that the *karmavācanā* of censure and admonition has been performed against a certain son of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati-putra*) with whom [this nun] has been associating. She makes this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so] has been living in close association with a lay devotee and the son of a lay devotee."
She does not act in accordance [with the teaching]. Other bhikṣuṇīs admonish her, saying: "Sister, do not associate with householders or the sons of householders and engage in such improper conduct.
Sister, you should live separately. If you live separately, there will be progress in the Buddha’s Dharma and you will dwell in peace and happiness.
Yet that bhikṣuṇī still does not reform. If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, grant [the formal act] to the Saṃgha...

That bhikṣuṇī [Name] has issued a formal reproach, commanding her to abandon this matter: "Sister, do not associate with householders or the sons of householders, nor dwell with them in conduct that is discordant.
Sister, you should live separately. If you live separately, there will be growth in the Buddha’s Dharma and you will dwell in peace and happiness. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, one should further say:
"Sister, I have finished the announcement; the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) remains. You should relinquish this matter, lest you be censured by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses."
If she follows these words, it is well. If she does not follow these words, the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) shall be performed:
"Listen, noble sisters of the Saṃgha. This bhikṣuṇī [Name] associates with and dwells together with laymen and the sons of laymen, engaging in conduct that is improper.
Other bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her, saying: 'Sister, do not associate with or dwell together with laymen and the sons of laymen.'"

She remains and continues to act in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma. "Sister, you should now dwell separately. If you dwell separately, there will be growth in the Buddha’s teaching and you will abide in peace and happiness.
Yet she does not change her ways. Now the Saṃgha is performing an act of censure against this bhikṣuṇī [Name] for the purpose of making her abandon this matter.
"Sister, do not associate with or live together with householders or the sons of householders, acting in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma."
Acting in accordance [with the teaching], you, sister, should dwell separately. If you dwell separately, there will be increase in the Buddha-dharma and you will abide in peace and happiness.
Which of you, venerable sisters, approves of the Saṃgha’s granting of a formal reprimand to that bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so] so that she may abandon this matter?
Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Once the first *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should again speak as above (and so forth).
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, one should perform the second *karmavācanā* as above.
Once the second *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should again speak as above (and so forth).
If she complies with these words, it is well. If she does not comply, after the third *karmavācanā* has been performed as above, the conclusion is made thus:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal act of censure against that bhikṣuṇī [Name] so that she may relinquish this matter; the Saṃgha consents by its silence."
"Because it is so. This matter is to be maintained as such.

Explanation: Regarding this, the instruction on relinquishing or not relinquishing—that nothing should be relinquished—is all based on the above. One incurs only the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*). The distinct manifestation of "not [relinquishing]" is also the same as above.
○ On the Method for the *Pātra-paryādāna* (Setting Aside the Alms Bowl) The appointment of a messenger to announce the *pātra-paryādāna*; the method for rescinding the *pātra-paryādāna*.

These three methods follow the general outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement). They are now included here following the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Section). There are three regulations;
the underlying cause is the same matter, yet it is a *karman* performed in the absence of the parties concerned. The Vinaya states: At that time, there was a certain...
Kauṣṭhila was angry with other pure bhikṣus and instructed his friends and acquaintances to slander them with groundless charges of impure conduct.
When the Saṃgha had assembled, he went there and spoke [of this]. The Buddha ordered the bhikṣus to interrogate that speaker:
"Do not slander pure bhikṣus with groundless charges of impure conduct; you shall incur a grave and heavy offense. He replied: "A certain bhikṣu..."
“Venerable One, you are pure; there is no impure conduct in you. This is merely what a certain bhikṣu has taught me. The Buddha said:

“From this day forward, perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning-over of the bowl) against him. Do not engage with him in conversation or exchange words. Perform the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for this purpose.”

There are five conditions under which a lay household should be subject to the *pātra-pratikṣepaṇa* (the overturning of the bowl). That is to say: they are unfilial toward their father; they are unfilial toward their mother;
they do not respect śramaṇas; they do not respect brahmins; and they do not serve bhikṣus.

There are five conditions under which one should not subject them to the *pātra-pratikṣepaṇa* (the reverse of the above five). Furthermore, there are ten conditions under which the Saṃgha should subject them to the *pātra-pratikṣepaṇa*. First: [text continues]
1. To revile and slander bhikṣus; 2. to cause harm to bhikṣus; 3. to act without benefit to them; 4. to employ means to deprive them of their dwelling place;
5. to incite strife among bhikṣus; 6, 7, and 8. to speak ill of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in the presence of bhikṣus;
9. to slander a bhikṣu with groundless charges of impure conduct; 10. to commit adultery with a bhikṣuṇī. As [in the previous cases]...
Regarding these ten dharmas, if even one is present, the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-āvarta* (turning-over of the bowl) karmavācanā against that person. It should be performed in this manner:

after striking the gong to assemble the Saṃgha, a *karmakāraka* (officer for the ritual) is appointed. He solicits the consent (*chanda*) and inquires about the circumstances. Having received the response, he announces: "I shall perform the *pātra-āvarta* karmavācanā against him.
Then he makes the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This lay follower (so-and-so) has slandered a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges of a pārājika offense.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now performs the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl) against this lay follower, such that they shall not associate with one another.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This lay follower (so-and-so) has slandered the pure bhikṣu (so-and-so) with a groundless *pārājika* offense.
Now the Saṃgha shall perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl) for this lay follower, such that they shall not associate with one another.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *pātra-nyāsa* for the lay follower (so-and-so), so that they shall not associate with one another, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Saṃgha has [acted].

The Saṃgha has granted the *pātra-āvartana* (the overturning of the alms-bowl) against the lay devotee [Name], and they shall henceforth not have mutual dealings. Since the Saṃgha remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Commentary: This *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of an individual; it pertains to the public.
Non-human [objections]: these refer to those such as laypeople appearing before the assembly. Matters [of objection]: these refer to secular slanders that are not grave, and so forth.
Other "non-" [objections] are as usual.
△ The Procedure for Appointing Messengers to Announce the Covering of the Alms Bowl.
The Buddha said: "Once the *pātra-ovaddha* (the overturning of the bowl) has been performed for him, the Saṃgha is permitted to appoint a messenger to go to the householder and speak thus:
'The Saṃgha has performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* of overturning the bowl for you, such that you shall not have mutual dealings.

If a bhikṣu possesses eight qualities, he should be appointed to go: he is able to listen, able to explain, understands it himself, can cause others to understand, is able to receive instruction, and is able..."

[The text] recalls and maintains [the teachings] without error, distinguishing between the meanings of the wholesome and the unwholesome. Regarding the appointment by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), the commentary states:
first, the one who is able to listen, meaning one who is entrusted with the Sangha’s command and hears and retains [the teachings] without outflows (*anāsrava*); second, the one who is able to speak.

1. This refers to one who has no timidity or fear when facing those of great wisdom. 2. Third, "one who understands by oneself" means that one's own mind understands [the teaching] spontaneously, such that there is no need to request further instruction. 3.
Fourth, "one who can cause others to understand" means that one knows what others harbor in their minds and speaks in a way that accords with their intentions.

4. Fifth, "one who can receive the teaching" means that when receiving the benefits of instruction from another, one’s speech does not cause harm or diminution. 5. Sixth, "one who can remember and retain" means that...

He must be thoroughly conversant with the meaning of the teachings and well-versed in the Vinaya. Regarding the seven points free from error: his speech must accord with reality and his words must not be confused.
Eighth, he must distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful; that is, when questioned, he remains unshakable and guides others toward joy.
However, this messenger need not be questioned by the entire assembly; rather, one who possesses such qualities should be selected and entrusted with the task.
The one who upholds the Dharma shall announce the *karmavācanā* as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as an envoy of the Saṃgha to go to the householder [Name] and say:
'The Saṃgha has now performed the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over of the bowl) against you; there shall be no coming or going between us. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
Thus it is.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu [Name] as a messenger for the Saṃgha to go to the householder [Name] and speak these words:
"The Saṃgha has now performed the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl) against you; there shall be no coming or going between us. Which elders approve of the Saṃgha’s action?
The monk [Name] has been appointed as the messenger for the Saṃgha; he remains silent. Whoever does not approve, let them speak.
Since the Saṃgha has approved the appointment of the monk [Name] as the messenger for the Saṃgha, he shall go to that householder [Name] and say:
"The Saṃgha has completed the act of overturning the bowl for you, such that there is no longer mutual interaction. Because the Saṃgha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Commentary: This refers to the procedure for appointing a messenger after the *pātra-āvartaṇa* (the overturning of the bowl) has been performed, before the Saṃgha has dispersed.

If the appointment is made after an overnight interval, one must again assemble the Saṃgha and perform the preliminary formalities (*purākaraṇīya*). Then, one declares: "I shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the appointment of a messenger to announce the *pātra-āvartaṇa*.
Therefore, this rite may pertain to both the complete assembly (*sabhikṣuka*) and the individual (*ekabhikṣuka*).

The Buddha said: "When the appointed bhikṣu goes there wearing his robes and carrying his bowl, and that layperson sees him, comes forward to welcome him, and invites him into their home, he should reply:
'I shall not enter your house to accept the offerings of a seat, food, or drink. If the person asks why, he should answer:
'The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātra-nyubja* rite against you; therefore, we do not associate with you.'"
If he asks, "For what reason? the bhikṣu should explain the cause and conditions.
If, upon hearing this, he becomes extremely distressed, pained, and remorseful, thinking, "By what means can I resolve my *pātra-āvartana* so that we may once again associate with one another?"
The bhikṣu says: "You should go and confess; the Saṃgha may then grant you release. Commentary:
This *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed by appointing a person for a specific task; it belongs to the public domain.

It is not otherwise, nor is it as described above; it is solely the fault of the person who is different [from the qualified]. That is to say, it refers to those lacking virtue who are selected for appointment, or those to whom affairs are entrusted through erroneous appointment, and so forth.
△ Explanation of the Method for Covering the Alms Bowl (Pātra-āvarana).

The Buddha said: "If a layperson has complied with the Sangha and does not dare to oppose them, and later requests from the Sangha to have the *pātra-nyāga* (the overturning of the bowl) lifted so that they may resume mutual interaction, the Sangha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) to lift it. It should be performed in this manner:
the assembly is gathered within the boundary, the preliminary procedures are carried out, and it is announced: 'We shall perform the *karman* to lift the *pātra-nyāga*. The proclaimer then says:"
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Now the Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-āvarta* (turning-over of the bowl) for the lay follower [Name], such that they shall not come or go [with one another].
He has conformed to the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-āvarta* and the ritual of non-intercourse.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of patience, grant its consent. The Saṃgha now performs the lifting of the *pātra-āvarta* for the lay follower [Name], so that they may once again come and go [with one another]. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Thus it is.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-āvartana* (turning over of the bowl) against the lay follower [Name], such that they do not associate with one another.

He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-āvartana* and the cessation of the formal act (*karman*) of non-association. Now the Saṃgha...
The lay follower [Name] has had the *pātra-āvaraṇa* (the bowl-covering) lifted; he shall henceforth associate with and come and go among the community.
Which elders approve of the Saṃgha’s lifting of the *pātra-āvaraṇa* for the lay follower [Name], so that he may associate with and come and go among the community?
Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak. Since the Saṃgha has approved and remains silent, this matter is thus settled.
This is the upholding.
Commentary: This means that one should not be reproached for ignorance, but rather acknowledge one's errors and repent. One should aspire to plant roots of merit.
Nevertheless, the Vinaya regulations require that one possess redoubled deep faith and maintain pure conduct within the Saṃgha before such [rites] may be performed.
Not a non-human; not [a case of] insincere remorse or lack of earnestness; begging monks lacking respect, etc. The rest is the same as above.

○ The Ritual of Censure (Nigarhaṇīya-karman) and its Explanations and Continuation. These two rituals follow the outline of the Fourfold Proclamation (Jñapti-caturtha). Now, they are entered here following the Kṣudraka-vastu (Minor Matters), specifically the Section on Censure (Nigarhaṇīya-khandhaka). The Buddha...

It is said: If there are bhikṣus who delight in quarreling and mutual abuse, whose mouths produce swords and blades as they seek out each other's faults, and if there are other bhikṣus who likewise engage in such abuse, one should go to them and urge them, saying:
"Exert yourselves well; do not be inferior to others. We shall act as your allies so that no dispute arises within the Saṃgha."

There was contention; and since there was contention that had not been extinguished, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) of censure against that bhikṣu.
It should be performed in this manner: having assembled the Saṃgha, one should first carry out the formal act of *utkṣepana* (reproval) against him;
having carried out the *utkṣepana*, one should effect the *smṛti* (remembrance); having effected the *smṛti*, one should assign the offense. From among the assembly, [one should] appoint..."
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: the formal announcement (*jñapti-karman*) that effects the threefold suspension (*tri-udghāta*).
This regulation is the most stringent among the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Now, first we shall cite the Vinaya to clarify the rule;

hereafter, all matters shall follow this precedent without further elaboration. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One who accomplishes five qualities is qualified to suspend another: [they must be] pure in body..."
[One should be] pure in bodily action, pure in verbal action, and maintain a right livelihood; one should be well-versed in the Abhidharma and well-versed in the Vinaya.
If one’s own bodily action is impure yet one censures another, that person should say: "Venerable sir, your own bodily action is impure; why do you censure another?"
One should first purify one's own bodily actions before censuring others. Even if one has heard only a little of the Vinaya yet censures another, that person should say:
"Venerable sir, why do you censure another’s offense when you have heard so little of the Vinaya?
You do not even know in which country, village, or city this precept was established, nor for what reason it was enacted. It would be well, Venerable sir, [if you were more learned]."
One who wishes to censure another should first become extensively learned in the Vinaya, and only then censure others. Furthermore, there are five methods:

there is censuring after having reviled, which means that after first having reviled [the person] with harsh words, one subsequently cites one or another of the five classes of offenses (the five classes of offenses for bhikṣus established by the Buddha). There is censuring before reviling, which means that first [one cites] the five classes...

Regarding offenses: there are those who, after having raised a specific offense, subsequently revile [the person]; that is, they raise the charge and immediately revile them, saying, "You have committed such-and-such an offense.
There are those who revile but do not raise the charge; that is, they utter various kinds of abuse without raising the offense.
There are those who raise the charge but do not revile; that is, among the five classes of offenses, they raise one or another [offense] but do not [revile].

This refers to abusive speech. Among these, the first four types of monks should neither question nor accept [such accusations]. If one raises an accusation without using abusive language, they should investigate the matter.
When wishing to accuse another, one should first say: "Venerable sir, I wish to raise a formal charge; will you permit me to do so?
If the other person says, "If you wish to raise a charge, you may do so," yet one proceeds to raise it without having asked for permission, one commits an offense.
Regarding the Vinaya offenses, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has not first requested permission, one may not raise another's offense to cause them to reflect upon it;
if one does so, it is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression). This offender must be instructed in the five practices within the Saṃgha:

first, rising from one's seat; second, baring the right shoulder by adjusting the robe; third, removing one's leather sandals; fourth, placing the right knee on the ground; and fifth, joining the palms."

Previously, there was one who raised a charge against another; that person likewise abides in these five qualities. When requesting permission to speak, there are five matters for requesting permission.
One should say to them: "I shall now speak to you; I shall now show you; I shall now charge you; I shall now cause you to remember; listen to me.
There are five matters for granting permission. One should say to them: "Speak to me; show me; charge me."
"Make me remember; listen to you. Furthermore, there are five kinds of things that are manifest before one: how do you charge me?
Is it by what was seen, heard, suspected, by the body, or by speech? Having spoken thus regarding what is manifest before one, fear arises.
There are five matters for providing consolation when they are present: "Do not fear; do not be startled; do not conceal your offense;
do not flee; do not form factions. When one is being thus consoled, if that person speaks in a contrary manner, they should be investigated using five methods:
they should be sternly rebuked with sternness, and they should be made to rely upon reliance.
Cease. One who should be expelled shall be expelled; one who should be made to humble himself shall be made to humble himself;

one for whom an offense must be sought shall have his offense sought (these five methods of investigation collectively encompass the seven formal acts [*karmas*]. Within the "harsh admonition" (*tarka*), four are included: namely, reprimand for not seeing [the fault], not repenting, and not relinquishing [the wrong view]. "Humbling oneself" refers to prohibiting [the offender] from going to the homes of laypeople, as well as dependence and expulsion—these constitute the seven).

Now, following the established principles, the ritual is added as follows: First, having struck the gavel to assemble the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu who formally charges another with an offense shall emerge from the assembly in full ritual decorum.
Having paid homage to the senior monks (upādhyāya), he shall join his palms, kneel, and say:

"I, [Name], now within this Saṃgha, charge the bhikṣu [Name] with an offense" (this constitutes the preliminary formal charge). Upon hearing this, the accused shall likewise emerge from the assembly in full ritual decorum and pay homage.
Once the senior monk among the assembly has been addressed, [the accused] should join their palms, kneel, and say: "Virtuous One, how do you charge me? Do you see it? Do you hear it?
Or do you suspect it? Is it an offense of the body? Or an offense of the speech? The one who brings the charge should reply: "Virtuous One, do not be afraid; do not be alarmed."
"I have seen the Venerable One performing such-and-such an act in such-and-such a place. You should recollect what you have done; speak directly and do not conceal it.

(This refers to having performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* and then having the offender recollect their deed. Whether based on what was heard or suspected, one must state the facts as they are. Once he has been made to recollect and has bowed his head in submission, one speaks again, saying:
"The offense you committed is such-and-such a crime; you should acknowledge and repent for it. (This refers to having performed the recollection and then assigning the specific offense. The Elder.
Always cause both the accuser and the offender to stand up together. Having performed the preliminary rites, one should respond by saying: "I shall perform the *karma* of censure for him.
Then, having appointed the officiant for the *karma*, one should announce it as follows:

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name]—[if there are two or three such persons, they may be mentioned, provided their number does not exceed that of the assembly]—delights in quarreling and reviling, uttering words like swords and blades, and seeking out the faults of one another.

Having already engaged in mutual strife themselves, whenever there are other bhikṣus who quarrel, he immediately goes to them and exhorts them, saying: "Exert yourselves; do not be inferior to others! You..."
You possess great learning and wisdom, and your wealth is also superior; you have many friends and acquaintances.
We shall act as your allies so that disputes may arise where none existed before, and existing disputes may not be resolved.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu [Name]. Should he subsequently engage in further quarreling...
Regarding those who engage in mutual quarreling and verbal abuse, the Saṃgha shall further increase their punishment. The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] delights in quarreling and mutual verbal abuse; his mouth utters swords and blades as he seeks out the faults of others.
Having already engaged in such quarreling himself, if there are other bhikṣus who likewise engage in quarreling..."
He then went back to them and exhorted them, saying: "Exert yourselves; do not be like others. Your wisdom and learning are great, and your wealth is also superior;

you have many friends and acquaintances. We shall act as your allies so that the Saṃgha, which previously had no disputes, will come to have disputes, and those disputes already existing will not be extinguished. For the sake of the monk [Name]," [he said].
The *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is performed. Which elders approve that the Saṃgha perform the *tarjanīya-karman* against the bhikṣu [Name]?
Furthermore, if he should again engage in quarreling and mutual abuse, the Saṃgha shall increase his punishment.
Those who approve, remain silent; those who do not approve, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*. (The second and third are recited in the same manner. The Saṃgha has approved.
The *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) has been performed for [Name]. Since the Saṃgha remains silent, it is accepted; this matter is thus maintained. The Buddha said:
"Once the *tarjanīya-karman* has been performed, one should not engage in the 'seven groups of five' matters.

That is to say, one should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, and so forth, up to: one should not dispute with virtuous bhikṣus. (This refers to the thirty-five matters previously forfeited. There is...
When the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) is performed against three [types of] persons, it is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya;
the formal act is not accomplished, and there is no formal accusation, no formal reminder, and no confession of guilt.
Furthermore, there are three factors that constitute a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) which is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and thus the karman is accomplished (namely,
the opposite of the aforementioned factors).
There are five factors that constitute a formal act of censure which is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, and thus the karman is not accomplished.
When one is present before the assembly and does not declare oneself to be pure, it is an illegal separate assembly (*adharmika pṛthaggaṇa*).
Furthermore, there are five factors by which a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is performed that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and thus the *karman* is accomplished— namely,
the opposite of the aforementioned five factors.

1. Non-validity regarding persons (*puggala-ayutti*): this refers to cases such as when the assembly is not in harmony or when it is incomplete. 2. Non-validity regarding the matter (*dhamma-ayutti*): this refers to cases such as when the action violates the regulations or resembles what is prohibited.

(These two types of non-validity—regarding persons and matters—comprehensively encompass the seven types of *kamma* that should not be performed, as set forth in the first chapter on the Sangha’s legal procedures. 3. Non-validity regarding the object (*vatthu-ayutti*): this refers to cases where the action undertaken is inappropriate, such as an improper act of censure (*tajjaniya-kamma*).
Other forms of non-validity should be understood by analogy.

△ Regarding the legal procedure for the *karmavācanā* of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*), it is said: If the community of monks is at the time of the morning meal or the midday meal, or when the Dharma is being preached, or during the *poṣadha*,
the person subject to the *karmavācanā* of censure shall adjust their robes, remove their leather sandals, stand to one side, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and join their palms.
He addressed [the monks], saying: "Venerable Sirs, please accept my confession. From this day forward, I shall reproach myself with a contrite heart and cease from such actions henceforth.
I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure). The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If one complies with the Saṃgha and does not oppose it, and seeks the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*, the Saṃgha is permitted to grant the lifting. This should be done by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations)."

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: there are seven sets of five factors for which one should not perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure). These range from [the case of] conferring the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon another person, up to disputing with a virtuous *bhikṣu*.
There are seven sets of five factors for which one should lift [the censure], ranging from not conferring the full precepts upon another person, up to [the case of] not [disputing].
If one disputes with a virtuous bhikṣu,
that bhikṣu who has been subjected to the formal act (karman) should go before the Saṃgha. Waiting for the striking of the gong and once the assembly has gathered,
he should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the karma of censure.
I now comply with the Saṃgha and do not oppose it; I beg the Saṃgha to revoke the karma of censure for me.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, revoke the karma of censure for me. (Thus, three times.)
The monk appointed as the *karmakāraka* performs the preliminary formalities and declares: "I shall grant the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
Thus it is announced:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the *tarjanīya-karman*, and that bhikṣu has complied.'"
The community of monks has not acted in opposition. [I] request from the community the lifting of the *karma* of censure.
If the time is right for the community, may the community, out of compassion, grant its assent to lift the *karma* of censure for the bhikṣu [Name]. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] has had the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu has complied with the Saṃgha and has not opposed them in any way. He now requests the Saṃgha to revoke the *tarjanīya-karman*.
The Saṃgha now revokes the *tarjanīya-karman* for this bhikṣu [Name]. Which elders consent to the Saṃgha revoking the *tarjanīya-karman* for this bhikṣu [Name]?
Those who approve of the lifting of the *karma* of censure remain silent; those who do not approve should speak. This is the first *karma*; the second and third are spoken in the same manner.
The Saṃgha has approved the lifting of the *karma* of censure for the bhikṣu [Name]. Because the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Commentary: Having understood this according to the Dharma, one is capable of performing the seven groups of five matters; one may act as one pleases without restriction.

This does not apply to other cases, which are not the same as those above; it applies only to cases where the matter is improper, meaning the request for alms is insincere, or the act of taking away involves the ten types of items, and so forth.
○ The Method of Banishment and its Subsequent Reinstatement:
These two methods follow the framework of the *jñapti-caturtha* (formal motion with three proclamations). Now, according to the *Kṣepaka-vastu* (Section on Rebuke), the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu resides in dependence upon a village and commits evil deeds that defile the families of others, and this is both seen and heard, [the community] shall inform him."
"O monks, from this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) for the purpose of suspending that monk.
It should be performed in this manner: [the procedure] beginning with the formal charge (*ukṣepa*) up to the imposition of the offense."
Commentary: According to the Vinaya, one who practices evil conduct refers to one who personally plants flowering trees, or even gives them to others, as well as instructing others to do so.

Within a village, there are four ways of defiling a household by associating with women: sitting or rising together, eating or drinking from the same vessel, engaging in speech and laughter, and performing songs, dances, or acts as a performer. The first is defiling a household by relying upon it. From the first...
When a household acquires goods and gives them to a family, those who hear of what was acquired are not pleased;
yet those to whom the goods were given think they ought to repay the kindness, thinking, "If he gave to me, I shall repay him; if he did not give to me, why should I give?
Second, there is defiling the family through gain and offerings: if a bhikṣu obtains gains in accordance with the Dharma, even as much as what is in his alms bowl—
Or otherwise, [he may] associate with one householder and not another; those whom he favors think of repaying his kindness as described above.

Third, regarding corrupting a household by relying on friends: if a bhikṣu relies upon a king or a great minister, or acts for the sake of one householder and not another, those whom he serves think they ought to repay him; "He has done this for me, and I shall [repay him]."
Regarding offerings: "I shall not offer to those who do not give to me. Fourth, regarding monasteries that defile households:
if a bhikṣu takes flowers or fruit from a monastery and gives them to one layperson but not to another, he immediately forms this thought:
"To those who give to me, I shall offer; to those who do not give to me, I shall not offer. This...
Regarding the four ways of defiling a household by practicing such conduct: one must go together with at least five other persons to that dwelling place.
If that village is a "separable natural boundary" (*prakṛti-sīmā*) and there are other bhikṣus residing within it.

One should first announce the time for the assembly. If there is no one residing [there], one should go alone. Once the Saṃgha has assembled together, one first performs the formal act of *karma* against him, up to the point of inflicting the punishment (the ritual procedure is as before).

Having performed the preliminary formalities, one replies, saying: "I shall perform the *karma* of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*). One who is qualified to perform the *karma* then makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*), saying:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name], residing in [Village or City—insert the specific location as appropriate], has defiled the families of others.
He has committed evil conduct; he has defiled other families, which we have both seen and heard; he has committed evil conduct, which we have both seen and heard.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against this bhikṣu [Name]: "You have defiled other families and committed evil conduct;
you have defiled other families, which we have both seen and heard; you have committed evil conduct, which we have both seen and heard. You should depart from here."
"Go to another dwelling; you need not remain in this dwelling.
It is announced thus: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] in [Place] village has defiled families and committed evil deeds.
That he has defiled families is both seen and heard; that he has committed evil deeds is also both seen and heard. The Saṃgha now [acts] for the sake of this bhikṣu [Name]..."
The formal act of banishment is performed: "You have defiled the families and practiced evil conduct.

You have been seen and heard to have defiled the families, and you have been seen and heard to have practiced evil conduct. Depart from this residence; you must not remain here. Which elders [agree]?"
The Saṃgha consents to performing the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* against the bhikṣu [Name]. Those who consent remain silent;
those who do not consent speak. This is the first *karman*; the second and third are likewise recited. The Saṃgha has completed the *pravāsanīya-karman* against the bhikṣu [Name].
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Buddha said: "Regarding those who perform the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), they should not perform seven sets of five matters. If there are three or five factors present, performing this formal act of banishment will not be accomplished;
it is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya. If there are three or five factors present, performing this formal act will be accomplished;
it is according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya—all as stated above, and the censure is no different."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, [the person] is placed at the edge of the saṃghārāma to reside there.
It is not otherwise; it is not the same as the aforementioned cases. It is not a different matter, meaning that jesting and the like are not considered truthful."

△ Admonishing and Expelling One Who Slanders the Dharma (This one rule was originally listed under "Aiding in Subversion" in the table of contents; however, for the sake of conforming to the characteristics of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, it has now been moved here following the sequence of the rules.

Furthermore, the formal act of expulsion and its subsequent resolution are listed separately so as to conform to the *Khandhaka*, wherein all seven types of *kamma* possess a resolution. The Vinaya states:
When the bhikṣus went to that place as described above and performed the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīyakarman*), at that time, that bhikṣu was among the Saṃgha.
In the midst [of the assembly], they spoke thus: "The Saṃgha possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. There are other bhikṣus who have committed the same offense;

yet some are expelled while others are not, and I alone am being expelled. When the bhikṣus had completed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) according to the Dharma, they returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and reported these circumstances to him. The Buddha, through various skillful means, rebuked them from afar.

He rebuked him and addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure and exhortation (karma-vācanā) consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) against that bhikṣu.
Other bhikṣus should first exhort that bhikṣu, saying: 'Venerable sir, you have defiled families.'"
He has been seen and heard engaging in evil conduct. This matter should be abandoned; do not commit a grave offense again after being rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, [the formal act shall proceed].
Once the striking of the gong has gathered the monks, the preliminary ritual actions are performed, and it is announced: "The *karman* of censure and admonition shall be carried out for him.
The officiant of the *karman* makes this formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] was residing in [Place Name]. When the Saṃgha was performing the *karman* of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against him..."
He then spoke these words: "The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion. There are bhikṣus guilty of the same offense as this, yet some are expelled while others are not.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
the Saṃgha now formally reprimands and admonishes the bhikṣu [Name] so that he may abandon this matter. Do not speak thus: 'The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear...'"
There is delusion. There are bhikṣus who have committed such an identical offense; some have been expelled and others have not.

Yet these bhikṣus are without attachment, without hatred, without fear, and without delusion. You have defiled families and engaged in evil conduct. That you have defiled families has been both seen and heard;
that you have engaged in evil conduct has also been both seen and heard. "You have defiled families and engaged in evil conduct"—thus is the formal announcement made.
Having performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the officiant of the ritual (*karmakāra*) should further address them, saying:

"Venerable sirs, I have already performed the announcement; there remain three formal acts (*karman*). You must relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense."
If he renounces it, that is well. If he does not renounce it, the first formal act (karmavācanā) should be performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] was residing in [Place] village when the Saṃgha performed the formal act of banishment against him."
He then says: "The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion; there are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The Saṃgha now addresses this bhikṣu [Name] with a formal reprimand and admonition so that he may abandon this matter:
"Do not speak thus, saying that the Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion, and that there are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense [yet are treated differently]."
There are those who are expelled and those who are not expelled. Yet the bhikṣus are without attachment, without hatred, without fear, and without delusion.
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to defile families, and you have been seen and heard to commit evil deeds.
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds. Which elders, O Venerable Ones, would consent to the Saṃgha’s formal act of censure against the bhikṣu [Name]?
Those who advise abandoning this matter remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should further seek [the response].
"Venerable sir, I have already performed the proclamation and the first *karmavācanā*. Two *karmavācanās* remain. Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter;
do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense."
If they comply with these words, it is well. If they do not comply, perform a second *karmavācanā* as described above.
Having performed the two *karmavācanās*, one should again request [their compliance] as described above, and so forth.
If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, then after the third *karmavācana* has been performed as described above, the formal act is concluded.
It is declared:
"The Saṃgha has consented to carry out this formal admonition for the bhikṣu [Name] to abandon this matter. The Saṃgha consents, because of its silence."
"Maintain this matter thus. Commentary:

In this context, whether one is exhorted to relinquish [the offense] or not, and whether one is instructed not to relinquish it, the adjudication of the offense is as previously described. Furthermore, the manifestation of the characteristics of non-compliance is also to be understood according to the previous rules.

△ Regarding the legal procedure for revoking the suspension (*pārivāsika*), the Vinaya states: That suspended bhikṣu came into the boundary (*sīmā*) of his own accord without being summoned. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not allow him to come into the boundary without being summoned. It is permitted for him to remain outside the boundary; rather, one should send a suitable companion to bring him [into the assembly]."
Within the Saṃgha, one should announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, I confess my transgression. From this day forward, I shall reproach myself and never do so again.
That bhikṣu, complying with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, requests from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karma* of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

The Saṃgha should grant him the revocation through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). There are seven groups of five factors for which the revocation should not be granted, beginning with those who have conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others.
Even to the point of quarreling with virtuous bhikṣus—these seven sets of five things he shall not do. He should be granted reconciliation.

That expelled bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha; once the gong has been struck and the assembly gathered, he should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīyakarman*).
I now comply with the Saṃgha and do not dare to oppose it; I beg the Saṃgha to grant me release from this act of suspension.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, release me from the act of suspension. (Thus, he says three times.)
The Saṃgha appoints a person to perform the *karmavācanā*. Having performed the preliminary formalities, he declares: "The Saṃgha shall grant the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the suspension.
He makes this formal motion (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the *karmavācanā* of suspension. He has conformed to the Saṃgha..."
I dare not disobey. I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *karma* of suspension. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
The Saṃgha now performs the *karma* of lifting the suspension for the bhikṣu [Name]. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment).

He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of that *pravāsanīya-karman*. The Saṃgha now intends to lift the *pravāsanīya-karman* for this bhikṣu [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s lifting of the *pravāsanīya-karman* for this bhikṣu [Name], let them remain silent. Who...?
If you do not consent, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā* (the second and third are recited in the same manner). The Sangha has consented;
the *karman* for the revocation of the suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for the bhikṣu [Name] is completed. Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Commentary: Having explained the method according to the Dharma, the matter of deprivation is still permitted as being capable [of restoration]. This shows that it is not the same as the aforementioned cases.

○ The rules for dependence (*niśraya*) and the subsequent methods are both explained here. Regarding these two methods, following the outline of the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations), we now rely on the *Kṣepana-khandhaka* (Chapter on Censure) for the subsequent method. The Buddha...

He said: "If a bhikṣu is deluded and ignorant, frequently committing many offenses—namely, those concerning the last three categories of the *vinaya* and the rules of decorum—and living in close association with laypeople, not conforming to the Buddha-dharma, [the Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus: 'From this day forward...'"

The Sangha shall perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for him to act as his *niśraya*. Having assembled the Sangha, one should proceed with the formal acts of censure (*ud-dhuraṇa*) up to the imposition of the offense (according to the ritual procedures of the Huai region).

Having performed the preliminary formalities, one replies: "I shall perform the *niśraya-karman* for him. Then, having appointed those capable of performing the *karman*, one makes the following proclamation (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu [Name] is foolish and ignorant; he has committed many offenses and dwells in close association with laypeople, not conforming to the Buddha’s Dharma.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this bhikṣu [Name] the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*). This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] is foolish and ignorant; he has committed many offenses and dwells in close association with laypeople, not conforming to the Buddha’s Dharma.
The Saṃgha now intends to perform an *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) for the bhikṣu [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *niśraya-karman* for the bhikṣu [Name], remain silent. Who...
If you do not consent, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā* (the second and third are likewise spoken). The Saṃgha has consented;
the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for [the name] as a monk’s place of dependence is completed. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha said: "One who performs the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman) should not perform seven sets of five matters.

There are three dharmas and five dharmas by which, if this karman is performed, it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and is not accomplished. There are three dharmas and five dharmas by which, if performed according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya, it is accomplished. All are as stated in the aforementioned rules."
The Vinaya states: There are those who designate a specific direction for the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), yet that direction is destroyed and its people become rebellious.
There are those who designate a kingdom, yet that kingdom is destroyed and its people are scattered. There are those who designate a residence, yet the people of that place are destroyed.

There are those who designate a person, yet that person is either subject to the three types of schism, the three types of formal accusation (*utkṣepa*), or the two types of expulsion (*pravāsanīya*); thus, they are unable to increase [the community].

This further increases the qualities of a śramaṇa; it is called "entering the rains retreat" (varṣā). When that person for whom the *karmavācanā* has been performed attains wisdom during the rains retreat, the Buddha said:
"One should not perform a formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) by using such designations. From this day forward, I allow you to say:
'You should receive dependence.'"

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Even if one has been [ordained] for a hundred years, one must defer to a preceptor who maintains the precepts—even a ten-year bhikṣu who knows the two divisions of the Vinaya.
Upon rising in the morning, one should inquire after his well-being, provide him with the vessels for excrement and urine as well as the spittoon, and place them back in their usual locations.
One should provide him with tooth-sticks, sweep the ground, receive food, wash his robes, and fumigate his bowl; all such services should be performed."
[It is] granted. With the sole exception of prostrating and massaging—though during times of illness, one may allow for massage—one should instruct them in both divisions of the Vinaya.

If they are unable to do so, instruct them in one division. If they are still unable, one should extensively instruct them in the precepts of the five groups (namely, the five categories of offenses).

One should instruct them to be well-versed in the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One should instruct them to be well-versed in the characteristics of offenses and non-offenses.

Regarding the characteristics of offenses, proper deportment, and improper deportment: once one has completed the training, it is said that one has "renounced" [the requirement of dependence] (meaning that one is permitted to leave the formal reliance).
The Mūlasarvāstivāda school states: A bhikṣu who relies on a foolish person due to ignorance should rely on a wise, junior bhikṣu to study the Vinaya;
he should provide all necessary services for him, with the sole exception of performing prostrations.
This is called the case of an elderly or junior bhikṣu;
it is not otherwise and does not conform to what precedes. It differs only in the matter, namely that the matter involves the first two [categories] and so forth.
△ Explanation of the Method for Relying on a Preceptor (Upajjhāya).

The Buddha said: "Regarding that person who has been subjected to the *karman* (formal act), if they study the Dharma and Vinaya under learned and wise bhikṣus who are their close friends, and thereby attain wisdom, becoming compliant with the Saṃgha and free from any opposition, they may request the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence).

The Saṃgha should grant the lifting through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). However, there are seven sets of five conditions—whether performed or not performed—for which the lifting should not be granted."
The procedure for granting absolution is as previously described. That monk who has been subjected to the *karma* shall go before the Saṃgha;
once the gong has been struck and the assembly has gathered, he shall assume the proper dignified posture, kneel with his right knee on the ground and palms joined, and address the Saṃgha as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have had the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) performed upon me by the Saṃgha.
I now comply with the Saṃgha and beg the Saṃgha for the revocation of the *niśraya-karman*.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, revoke the *niśraya-karman* for me. (Thus, three times.)

The monk appointed as the *karmakāra* (the one who performs the formal act) performs the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakarman*) and replies: "The formal act of granting release from dependence (*niśraya-karman*) shall be performed.

He then makes the following formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Sangha, listen! This bhikṣu [Name] has been granted the formal act of dependence by the Sangha. He is now compliant with the Sangha."
I do not dare to disobey. I request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *niśraya-karman*. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
The Saṃgha now lifts the *niśraya-karman* for the bhikṣu [Name]. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of dependence (*niśraya*).
He has complied with the Saṃgha and did not dare to oppose it. He now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the formal act of dependence.
The Saṃgha now grants the bhikṣu [Name] the lifting of the formal act of dependence. Which elders approve of the Saṃgha granting the bhikṣu [Name] the lifting of the formal act of dependence?
[The assembly] remains silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak. This is the first *karmavācanā* (the second and third are spoken in the same manner). The Saṃgha has already consented;
the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the *niśraya* (dependence) from the bhikṣu [Name] is completed. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Exegesis: Having understood according to the Dharma, one may take back the object without restriction and is capable of acting accordingly.

○ Not seeing [the offense], the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and the subsequent restoration (*abbhāna*). Regarding these two procedures, they follow the general outline of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal acts consisting of a motion and three proclamations). Now, based on the *Kṣepaṇa-vastu* (Section on Rebuke), the procedure for restoration is as follows.
The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu commits an offense and other bhikṣus say to him, 'Do you see that you have committed an offense? and he replies, 'I do not.'"

[The Buddha] saw this. He addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the purpose of censuring this bhikṣu for not acknowledging his offense.
It should be performed in this manner: Having assembled the Saṃgha, one shall carry out the censure, and so forth, up to the granting of the penalty (the ritual procedure is the same as above).

One asks for consent and inquires about the circumstances; the answer is: 'I grant my consent for the performance of the *karman* of censuring him for not acknowledging his offense. This is a valid *karman*."
