This is the first *karmavācanā*. (The second and third are spoken in the same manner. The Saṃgha has approved and completed the *karmavācanā* for the formal act of assigning a place of offense to the bhikṣu [Name]. The Saṃgha...
Because he has endured in silence, this matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha said: "There are three unlawful matters which, in accordance with the *karmavastu* and the *vinaya*, should not be performed:

one should not perform a formal accusation (*codanā*), one should not perform a formal recollection (*smṛti*), and one should not perform a formal self-accusation (*svayam-ukti*). There are three lawful matters which should be performed (the opposite of the above). Furthermore, there are three [other] unlawful..."

This is the Dharma. There is no offense [in this case], yet it constitutes an unconfessable offense (*āpatti-asaṃvaraṇīya*). If one has committed an offense and subsequently confesses it, there are three points that accord with the Dharma (the opposite of the above).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Once the formal act of 'seeking the characteristics of the offense' (*mṛṣādṛṣṭi-karma*) has been performed, this person must practice eight matters for as long as they live."
1. One must not ordain others. 2. One must not confer the full precepts (upasampadā) upon others. 3. One must not provide dependence (niśraya) to others.
4. One must not accept massage from bhikṣus. 5. One must not accept provisions from bhikṣus. 6.
One must not serve as a messenger for bhikṣus. 7. One must not be appointed in turn to attend assemblies. 8. One must not perform labor for the Saṃgha.
Regarding the speaker on this matter, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "This 'seeking of the offense' (*mṛṣā-vinīta*) is a *pratisaṃharaṇīya-vinaya*.

For all five categories of offenses and for all five groups of monastics, one should fully administer the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of a motion followed by three proclamations) for the actual seeking of the offense. However, the three minor groups [of nuns, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs] do not appear in person."
Commentary: These are not the [proper] characteristics. According to the Vinaya, all three sets of three and the seven types of *karmavācanā* in the first section should not be performed.
This concludes the nine methods for repenting the six classes of offenses in the Section on Dharma.
● Chapter Ten: On the Maintenance of Miscellaneous Rules (Zá-fǎ zhùchí piān). Commentary:
Regarding the essential principles of all *karmavācanā* (ecclesiastical acts), none exceed the establishment of goodness and the administration of punishment.
These have been detailed previously; here, those matters not yet included in the preceding chapters are further gathered and compiled as the tenth section. Examine them carefully.
The essential point for upholding the True Dharma is that the Precepts are not lacking in their foundation.

Regarding the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), although the relevant matters exist within the Vinaya, the textual meaning is scattered; the definitive version appears in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. However, that...
The words are concise while the meaning is extensive; furthermore, as this practice is widely prevalent in the present age, it is necessary to supplement the text with its underlying significance.

**First: Recollecting the Date and Number of Days.** The *Sengqilü* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya) states: "One should recollect and know the first day of the month, up to the fourteenth and fifteenth days; [distinguishing] whether the month is large or small."
[The Buddha] said: "It is small; you should all know this.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣus should know the number of half-months, know the date of the poṣadha, and purify themselves through confession."
The Vinaya states: One should be mindful of and know the two types of calendrical reckonings—the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight. If one enters a village, this must first be known;
this thus encompasses both the monastic and the lay traditions. One should make the following reflection: "Today is the first day of the small [lunar] month of the dark fortnight."
This is stated even up to the fourteenth day. If it is a "great" [fortnight], it is indeed great.
As for the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), because it consists entirely of great days, one simply says, "Today is the first day of the bright fortnight," and so on, up to the fifteenth day.

**Explanation:** Regarding "possessing both the monastic and lay dharmas": "The Way" refers to causing the ordained sangha to recollect the *poṣadha* (confession) of both the black and white [fortnights], to reflect upon their own virtuous conduct, and every morning to mentally note the date.
Knowing that as time passes, one's lifespan accordingly diminishes, they consider whether the practice of the Way is diligent or lax, and whether the precepts they uphold are pure.

If you are stained by defilement, strive to become pure again and cultivate further with joyful aspiration. If you are indolent and commit transgressions, you must feel shame and remorse, and perform repentance and purification.
To contemplate in this manner every day is what defines a *śramaṇa* who acts according to the Dharma;

it ensures that one does not sit idly waiting for the arrival of the Mara of Death. This teaching was specifically established for those who have left the household life. According to the *Śikṣāpada-vastu*, regarding...
On the day of the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts, there was an elder who asked a bhikṣu, "What day is it today?
The bhikṣu replied, "I do not know. The assembly of monks all felt ashamed. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, you must count the days."
After several days, he forgot again. Therefore, it was permitted to employ a method of counting by thirties: fifteen [units] were used to count the black [days] and fifteen to count the white [days].

During the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), one counted with the black units; during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), one counted with the white units. This was so that even if the king changed the date, there would be no confusion.
This follows the laws of kings. Therefore, whenever a bhikṣu enters a village, he must first understand this: when questioned, he should answer.
This rule is for the purpose of protecting against worldly censure and serves as a restraint; thus it is said to encompass both monastic and secular laws.
△ Second, the mindfulness of the place where food is obtained.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "At dawn, one should form the intention to give food, and so forth. Now, synthesizing the various schools, one should form the intention according to reality, saying: [insert appropriate formula].
I always beg for my food. Whether one says, "I always eat my own food," or "I always eat the food of the Sangha"—to explain:
"always begging for food" means not accepting invitations to dine and not following the offerings of the Sangha.

This is done to break down pride and manifest humility, so that one may cultivate pure conduct by not discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, and to cause householders to be relieved from hunger and famine. This...

This practice was transmitted by the sages of antiquity and should be emulated by the worthies of later generations; it is the fifth entry into the Right Path and follows the sequence of the four reliances.
It is the practice of shaking off [defilements]. Regarding those who always eat their own food: this means not accepting food offered through intermediaries, nor sharing out portions from one's bowl.
One relies on whatever conditions arise to sustain the body, renounces thoughts of excellence, cuts off greed and expectations, and aims solely for true cultivation.

This refers to those who have taken refuge as householders and constantly provide food offerings. Those who "always eat the food of the Saṃgha" are those who dwell together with the community, living in common with equal benefits;
they do not need to enter villages to beg for food when the time arrives. This refers to residing in a place belonging to the permanent endowment of the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
If one is not constantly in meditative concentration, one should reflect:
"I have no place to which I am invited; I am now begging for food.
This applies by analogy whether it be one's own food, or the regular meals provided by donors or the Sangha.
Commentary: The three types of mental resolve regarding the practice of eating by mindfulness described above are maintained by bhikṣus of firm resolve as a fixed practice.
What follows below concerns receiving food according to circumstances; therefore, it is said that these are "not always fixed. To know by analogy:
for instance, if one says, "Today there is no invitation to attend; I shall not accept protracted offerings, I shall not eat the food of the Saṃgha, and I shall not go..."
"I am a beggar for alms. Yet today I have donors who have sent offerings, and so I eat what has been provided.

If it is said that today no one has sent food, that I do not use the standing provisions of the Saṃgha, and that I do not beg for alms—then the Saṃgha should now assign me by rotation to attend a formal invitation for a meal.
If it is said that today there is no meal by rotation, that I do not beg for alms myself, and that no one has sent food—I [shall eat this]."
Now, one should eat together with the community of monks from the permanently established food (sthity-āhāra).
If it is said that there is currently an invitation (nimantraṇa), one may now rely on the exception (pratyaya).
The Buddha said: "During the month of Kārttika, whether it be the offering of robes (cīvara) or due to illness and so forth, the setting aside of the invitation is permitted."
Regarding the month of Kārttika: it spans from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month. "Kārttika" is a Sanskrit term;

in the language of China, it refers to the lunar mansion Ārdrā (the Ox Star), meaning that the Ārdrā asterism governs this month. "To turn one's back" (*pratyākhyāna*) carries the sense of a separate assembly.
This is because when the bhikṣus have completed their nine-month summer retreat and finished the three matters of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) arrive.
"Please accept this food. One must not dare to separate from the assembly. The Buddha, knowing the circumstances, permitted [eating apart from the group] during these seven occasions:
when making robes, when receiving donated robes, when one is ill, when traveling on a journey, when traveling by boat, when there is a great assembly, and when śramaṇas are distributing food.
Although these exceptions were granted, it remains that this is "timely food" (kālabhojana) and must not exceed noon.
Except during the month of Kārttika, if one eats separately from the community, one commits an offense of *pācittiya*.
However, if only two or three people accept an invitation to beg for food, there is no offense, as they do not constitute a formal monastic assembly (*saṃgha*).
If one says, "I have accepted invitations elsewhere; I now relinquish them to you," the Buddha said:
"If one has accepted many invitations on a single day, one may accept one invitation for oneself and give the remainder to others.
One should say:"
"Elder, I should go there; now I give this to you" (recited once). [Commentary:
This is the procedure for relinquishing an invitation through face-to-face confession (*pratideśanīya*).

It is the thirty-second rule among the ninety matters, established by the precept concerning eating in succession (*paryāyeṇa bhojana*). Aside from this, all others are mental acts of intention (*manasikāra-dharma*). If neither [party]...
If one is aware [of this], it is a violation of the law and improper.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"I have now obtained food; I shall give it to [the name of] a bhikṣu (or even a śrāmaṇerī). If one says:
"Venerable [Name], this morning a donor gave me a meal of proper food. I now transfer it as a gift to you, Venerable [Name].
The donor has no further claim upon me; I shall eat it. (Recite three times.)
Commentary: If a donor has specific attachments, this is a request based on attachment to signs (*nimitta*), and the gift cannot be redirected.

If, however, although there is a request, there is no such attachment, it is for the sake of the Sangha as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); since the intention is without discrimination, the gift may be bestowed as one pleases. One must, however, carefully distinguish and exclude the three types of "corruptions" (*bhedana*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "This mental recitation of the Dharma may be performed by only five kinds of persons:

namely, forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), those living alone, those traveling on long journeys, those suffering from chronic illness, and those staying with relatives during times of famine. It is only such individuals who may perform this mental recitation."
Commentary: This citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* serves as proof for the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya*’s method of mental recitation (*cittānujñāta*).

As for the *araṇya*, it is a secluded dwelling without companions. "Living alone" means not residing together with the community. "Traveling far" refers to going urgently due to pressing circumstances. "Long-term illness" refers to a lack of attendants to provide care.
Even those who reside near their relatives during times of famine are considered to be living in solitude; thus, we know that [this practice] exists.
A person must perform the transference of the precepts through face-to-face confession.
△ Third, regarding the mindfulness of the number of years since receiving the precepts (*kṣapaṇa*):
the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states, "Every day one should personally recall one's own seniority (*varṣāgra*). All other Vinayas and Śāstras are likewise. One should say:
I received full ordination on the [day] of the [month] of the [year], at the [time] (or "at such-and-such shadow-length"). I have no summer retreats to my credit yet.
Regarding the subsequent mention of "if there is a summer retreat," it refers to the number of years spent in the retreat, whether many or few.

Commentary: According to the Vinaya regulations, for all who have left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), seniority and juniority are not determined by birth year or social status, but solely by the number of years spent in the retreat (*vassa*).
One must record and remember the month, day, time, and shadow [at the commencement]. It should be understood that one without such a retreat...
There are those with *zha* (seniority) but no *xia* (summer retreat), those with both *xia* and *zha*, those with *zha* but no *xia*, and those with neither *xia* nor *zha*.

Those with neither *xia* nor *zha* are those who received full ordination after the fifteenth day of the seventh month and have not yet reached the *an-gu* (rainy season retreat) and *zi-zi* (invitation for criticism) of the following year.
Those with *zha* but no *xia* are those who received full ordination before the sixteenth day of the fourth month and immediately joined the assembly for the *an-gu*.

Having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, those who have observed the summer retreat (*varṣa*) and possess the seniority of a *kaṭhina* robe (*laba*) are said to have received full ordination after the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
They then proceed through the successive summer retreats until the next year’s *pravāraṇā*.

Whether it be one summer’s seniority, or the passage of several months, days, times, and shadow-lengths, even up to forty or fifty summers, they should likewise maintain mindfulness and awareness of this every day when assembling for practice.

As for sitting, the order of salutation according to *laba* (seniority) must be maintained without confusion in each instance. Those who have completed the summer retreat (*xiazhang*) but lack *laba*—referring to those who have not yet received full ordination (*yuanju*), such as *śrāmaṇeras*—are governed by the same regulations as the monks regarding the summer retreat;
however, they are counted only by their years of retreat (*xiashu*). Since they possess no *laba* to establish precedence, seniority is determined solely by their year of birth.
△ Fourth, mindfulness of the robes and bowl and their formal purification (*śuddhi*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should remember those three robes that are being maintained and those that are not being maintained but have been formally purified through donation."
I now possess three robes and a bowl, all of which I maintain as long-term property and have all been formally dedicated (*paryavadāpana*).

Should there subsequently be items that are neither maintained nor dedicated, one should, according to what exists, maintain them in mind and dedicate them in mind, whether the quantity be great or small.
Commentary: If one does not mindfully maintain awareness of the three robes and the alms bowl, it may happen that they are missing or separated from oneself without one knowing.
If one does not mindfully maintain awareness of long-term surplus wealth for which *śuddhi* (purification) has been declared, it may become a mixture of what is pure and what is impure.
By thus maintaining mindfulness day by day, one will not incur the fault of improper storage or deficiency.
△ Fifth, regarding mindfulness of eating with a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*):
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "One should be mindful of eating with a separate group. Furthermore, one should further reflect, saying:
"I am not eating with a separate group."
If one follows the Buddha’s words, when there are seven circumstances that permit eating in a separate group, one should announce before entering;
if there are no such special circumstances, one should announce before departing. If such circumstances exist, one should say: [announcement].
"I have a separate group of associates" (having made this announcement, one may eat).

Explanation: This further cites the regulations regarding entering and leaving [the assembly]. It is neither a *cetanā-dharma* (mental intimation rite) nor a *pratyekamukha-dharma* (face-to-face rite);

it is the formal statement (*jñapti*) addressed to the assembly. The seven conditions are as above, such as when making robes and so forth. Regarding "eating with a separate group": if there are four...
If there are more than four people: the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states that within the boundary, an invitation for four or more people is termed "separate-eating among a group.
If one encounters such an occasion where an exception is permitted, then whether it be four or more than four people, all are allowed to receive and eat the food.
If one also has a share in this particular occasion, one should request entry by addressing the assembly as follows.

Having so requested, one may proceed according to the order of the senior monks to receive food. If, however, one has no share in this occasion, one should immediately request exit by addressing the assembly, saying:
"I have no reason for a separate meal with the assembly. Having so requested, one does not receive food according to the order.
△ Sixth, mindfulness of the body’s strength or weakness:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One should be mindful of whether one is ill or not.
If one is not ill, one should say: "I am currently not ill; I am capable of practicing the Path. (If one is ill, one should say: "I am ill; I must receive medical treatment."

Commentary: To cultivate the karma of merit, one must rely upon physical strength and vigor. To cultivate the karma of wisdom, one must necessarily depend upon the mind and its objects in meditative observation.

Although merit and wisdom are distinguished as pertaining to body and mind respectively, when they are put into practice, both must be employed together. If the body is strong yet one is negligent regarding the path and its practice, [merit will not be realized].
How can one achieve success? If the body is frail yet one exerts oneself, the physical strength will find it difficult to advance toward accomplishment.

Therefore, the Tamer (the Buddha) bestowed his compassion, instructing the bhikṣus to contemplate the body every morning: when it is time to walk, they should walk; when it is time for treatment, they should receive treatment.
By relying upon this illusory body, they establish the virtue of Brahma.

**Explanation of the Procedure for Entering a Village Before or After a Meal, Announced with the *Jñapti* (Formal Declaration)** This follows the procedure for entering a village as set forth in the *Prātimokṣa* section on individual confession (*pratideśanīya*). It is the forty-second of the ninety offenses (*navati-śikṣāpada*).
If a bhikṣu visits other households before or after a meal, he commits an offense; therefore, it is permitted to enter [the village] after having made a formal declaration (*jñapti*).
First, the introductory context is cited:

At that time, within the city of Rājagṛha, there were many places where the Saṃgha was invited to receive offerings. All the monks were apprehensive and did not dare enter the city to accept these invitations.
The Buddha said, "I permit the bhikṣus to enter the city after having entrusted one another with their responsibilities; they should inform the bhikṣu who is being invited alongside them."
It is said thus:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], having previously accepted an invitation from [Name], now have a certain matter to attend to."
"If one intends to enter a certain village or go to a certain house, one should inform a venerable elder [once]. The Buddha said:
'If, after having made such an entrustment, one wishes to go to the village but returns midway; or if one goes to a place other than the house to which one entrusted oneself;
or if, having entrusted oneself to go to the house of a layperson, one instead goes to a storehouse or a nunnery—then one must immediately inform [the elder again]."

When one leaves the family home where the robes were offered, such instances as these all constitute a loss of the previous formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇa*). If one wishes to go, one must perform the entrustment anew.

With the exception of the time for the offering of robes—namely, the month of Kārttika and the five months following—during any other time, if one encourages the making of food offerings or the giving of robes, [the entrustment is lost]; however, during the month of Kārttika, it is universally permitted.

Commentary: "Furthermore, regarding 'going to the place where the storehouse is located' means that one has already arrived at the house of the layperson to whom the instruction was given, yet proceeds to the side room where rice and grain are stored; in such a case, the location does not correspond to the instruction.
Except for the five ordinary occasions, when one encourages others to prepare food or bestows robes, all must follow the formal entrustment. This applies during the *kārttika* period."
This is because the *anvārohaṇa* (re-entry) was not performed at the beginning of the retreat; thus, it is generally permitted. It is not invalid for one person alone;

this refers to the formal announcement (*jñapti*) made toward the minor laity. It is not invalid regarding the two dharmas; this refers to the threefold proclamation (*tri-kṛtva-vacana*) addressed to the Saṃgha.
Three matters are invalid: namely, when the entrustment and the arrival both deviate from the agreement. Other invalid cases are to be determined by analogy.
○ Explanation of the Procedure for Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
This rule is identical to the preceding one; it is the eighty-third of the ninety matters. If a bhikṣu...
If one enters a village at an improper time without having informed a bhikṣu, one commits an offense.

The Buddha said: "If you enter a village, you must inform a bhikṣu who dwells with you. However, the specific method for making such an announcement is not set forth; the same applies to the preceding rule. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"Even if the meal has already concluded early, if one enters [the village] immediately thereafter, it is termed 'improper time' (*akāla*). Since there is no explicit canonical text on this point, [the matter remains uncertain].
One should speak according to the facts:

"Venerable sir, I have entered the village at an improper time; I have gone to such-and-such a city or village, to the house of [so-and-so]. [The other] replies, "So be it. (According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*)... "I have arrived at such-and-such a city or village, at the house of [so-and-so].
[The other] replies, "It is well."
Commentary: If a bhikṣu enters a village frequently, it will hinder his authentic cultivation, stimulate old habits, invite worldly derision, and damage the pure faith of others.
However, if he encounters truly beneficial circumstances, he should inform [his preceptor] before departing, so that the community knows the destination of his coming and going;
thus he does not violate the precepts he upholds. This applies unless it is an improper time or the market is sparse.
The dark-robed stream thus manifests the purity and correctness of the Dharma-path; truly, the name "Sangha Jewel" is not in vain. Herein, it is not merely a formal imitation of the above.
[End of section. Performing the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food).
Explanation: This rule is one that requires only a formal confession before another person (*pratideśanīya*). It is the thirty-fifth of the ninety offenses.
If a bhikṣu has finished his meal and subsequently accepts an invitation, yet eats without performing the ritual for leftover food (*atiriktapiṇḍapāta-vidhi*), he commits a *pācittiya* offense.

The Buddha said: "There are two kinds of food for bhikṣus. The first is improper food (*akalpya-bhojana*), which refers to eating branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, oils, sesame, black rock honey, or finely ground powders;

or when rice porridge has just come out of the cauldron, such that one cannot draw a line through it with a blade of grass—this is neither 'food' (*bhojana*), nor 'invited food' (*nimantrita*), nor 'sufficient food' (*paryāpta-bhojana*).
The second is proper food (*kalpya-bhojana*), which refers to boiled rice, parched grain flour, dry rice, fish, [meat, and dried meat]."

Meat and so forth—these are invitations, these are meals, and these are satisfactions. If, during the formal meal or after having eaten one's fill, one changes one's posture without performing the *yavāpūrvaka* (the ritual for leftover food), and then eats what has been obtained, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense.
According to the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, if one has eaten enough to be fully satisfied during the morning meal and then discards the formal posture after every swallow,
eating further constitutes a violation of the rule against over-eating.

Furthermore, according to the Vinaya-mūla: when various bhikṣus who have undertaken the practice of *akṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa* (the dhūta-practitioner) see a senior elder approaching, they announce, "I have undertaken the practice of *akṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa*," and need not rise; they may then finish their meal.

Therefore, one knows that the preceding object is sufficient. If one wishes to eat more, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (rule for leftover food) must be performed. Furthermore, it is the same in the rule concerning the nuns' respect for the monks;
thus, one knows that nuns also have the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*.
Commentary on the One Hundred and Seventy-Eight *Pācittiya* Offenses, Number One Hundred and Seventy-Five: The Precept Regarding Arrogance Toward a Newly Ordained Bhikṣu.
It is said: "If a bhikṣuṇī sees a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to greet him, escort him, pay him respect, prostrate, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit.
To fail to do so, except for a specific cause, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. A 'specific cause' refers to when... [or one...]

If one eats while seated, or eats without performing the *yavaddhika-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food), or if one is ill, or has already eaten enough, one should say: "Venerable sir, please bear with me;
due to such circumstances, I do not violate the precept against showing contempt toward the Saṃgha. Thus, this is now cited as a precedent.

If one who has committed an offense (meaning one who has already abandoned their formal deportment) carries food to the presence of one who has not yet committed an offense (meaning one who has not yet abandoned their formal deportment), they should announce as follows:
"Venerable sir, I have already finished my meal; you know this, look at this. (Having taken a small amount of food, he returns it to him; if the other does not eat it, he may also say:
"Elder, I have already eaten; stop your greedy desire. (The other then takes and eats it.)

The Vinaya states: "First, regarding 'one meal' (ekapiṇḍapāta). As for the ritual procedure (vidhi) of the Vinaya, 'having already [performed] one meal' refers to those who have likewise eaten among all those who have completed their meal.

*Explanation:* This means that among the five types of "completed meals" (pūrṇa-piṇḍapāta), by relying on the Vinaya through the single practice of "one meal," once the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (the ritual of remaining food) has been performed, one is permitted to eat.
For all others among those who have completed their meal, it is the same: they must follow this same rule; having performed it, they may then eat.
The first "non-validity" (*na-yukta*) is when both parties abandon their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). The second "non-validity" is when one remains silent without accepting food.
The third "non-validity" concerns three matters: it is non-valid if it is not food, not an invitation, or not sufficient. The remaining four "non-validities" are to be understood by analogy.
The Method for Rebuking Disciples:

At that time, the disciples did not follow the dharma of disciples; they did not serve their *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, lacked shame and remorse, did not accept instruction, engaged in improper conduct, were disrespectful and difficult to converse with. With them...

He makes evil people his friends. He delights in going to the houses of prostitutes, the houses of women, the houses of unmarried girls, the houses of eunuchs, the monasteries of bhikṣuṇīs, the monasteries of śikṣamāṇās, and the monasteries of śrāmaṇerikās.
