"It is poverty-stricken. Who would dwell here? The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for one bhikṣu. Having assembled the Saṃgha, they should appoint a person to perform the *karman* and carry out the preliminary procedures."
The answer is as follows: A *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is made for the appointment of a monk to attend to the monastic quarters.
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made thus: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Now the Saṃgha grants this [certain] room to [certain] bhikṣu for his care.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. This is the announcement."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This room [named] so-and-so is assigned for the management of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha assigning this room for the management of the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, please speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to assign this room for the management of the bhikṣu so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents by its silence.
Therefore, this matter is to be maintained in this way.
[Commentary: Regarding the monastic quarters constructed by a donor (*dānapati*), they are intended for the community of monks from the ten directions to reside in.

If one were to manage them privately, it would lead to disputes; if they were left unattended and unrepaired, the donor’s faith would decline. Therefore, it is ordained that the *saṃgha* grant them through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
First, cause the assembly to be harmonious and to remain silent and patient so that the dispute may cease. Next, have the master take note and carry out repairs so that faith may increase.
Thus, both protection and prevention are fully prepared; such is the regulation of the mind. This *karmavācanā* is performed for the sake of a specific matter; it pertains to public affairs.

It is not others who are at fault, nor is it based on a constant rule; rather, it is only the person who is at fault. That is to say, their talent is deficient and they are unacquainted with the methods of maintenance and work, and they harbor much private interest and so forth.
○ The Method for Distributing Bedding and Requisites.
Continuation: This follows the outline of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation). It is now continued as the eighth of the thirteen matters.
In the Vinaya-mūla, because the Venerable Trapusa initiated such a method of appointment, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu is endowed with the five virtues—being free from partiality, hatred, fear, and delusion, and knowing what has been distributed and what has not been distributed—"

Listen as the assembly gathers for the formal motion with a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). From among the community, one who is skilled in the formal procedures (*karman*) shall perform the preliminary rites and respond, saying:
"The formal procedure for appointing a distributor of bedding and furniture (*śayanāsana-vastu-vyavasthāpaka*) shall be announced in this manner. One should speak as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent to appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha. Which elders consent?
The Saṃgha appoints (so-and-so) bhikṣu to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha; those who consent remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak.

The Saṃgha has already consented and completed the appointment of (so-and-so) bhikṣu to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Vinaya states: Regarding those who distribute bedding and requisites for the Saṃgha: if one is a forest-dweller, one should share with a fellow forest-dweller; if one is an alms-seeker, one should share with a fellow alms-seeker;
if one wears patched robes, one should share with a fellow wearer of patched robes; if one does not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* rite, one should share with a fellow non-performer of that rite;
if one sits in a single location, one should share with a fellow sitter in a single location; and if one takes food in a single mouthful, one should share with a fellow taker of a single mouthful.

They share the practice of sitting in cemeteries with those who sit in cemeteries; they share the practice of sitting in the open air with those who sit in the open air; they share the practice of sitting under trees with those who sit under trees;

they share the practice of sitting wherever they happen to be with those who sit wherever they happen to be; they share the practice of wearing the three robes with those who wear the three robes; and they share the quality of being learned with those who are learned.
Dharma-preachers are grouped with Dharma-preachers; those who uphold the Vinaya with those who uphold the Vinaya; and those who practice meditation with those who practice meditation.

Regarding the *Vinaya*, the Venerable One initiated this *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) with the aspiration to distribute the bedding and seating of the Saṃgha and to assign the order for receiving invitations to meals.
According to the headings [of the text], it merely says "assigning the distribution of bedding and seating"; therefore, the text of this *karmavācanā* [is as follows].

...omitted hereafter. The original scroll, at the end of the *Bai-er* (the second part of the *Prātimokṣa*), adds a supplementary note stating: "There should be distinctions [in the distribution]: the distribution of rice gruel (*yavāgū*) as light food (*khādya-bhojana*);

the distribution of *khaajja* (solid food); the appointment for the distribution of bedding and furniture; the distribution of bathing robes (*snāna-śāṭī*); and the distribution of robes that may be accepted.
These are assigned to appointed monks and śrāmaṇeras to manage according to the dwellings. This is the Buddha’s word following the *Karmavastu* (*Gandhaka*). If one encounters these eight kinds...

Regarding the procedure for its application: following the precedent of this *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement) method for appointing [an official], because the text is general and the matter analogous, only the specific details of the current case need to be inserted and modified.
This *karmavācanā* is performed specifically for the sake of an individual, yet it pertains to the public.

Non-human invalidation refers to those lacking virtue and so forth. Dharma invalidation refers to errors in the ritual procedure and so forth. Factual invalidation refers to what is improper and so forth.
The remaining four [types] are to be understood by analogy.

○ The Procedure for a Bhikṣuṇī to Inform Before Entering a Monastery (Continued) This follows the general outline of the *pratideśanīya* (confession) rules. Now, based on the one hundred and forty-four *pācittika* offenses specific to bhikṣuṇīs, this rule is added as a continuation.
The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣuṇī knows that there is a monastery belonging to the saṃgha of bhikṣus and enters it without having informed them [of her arrival], [she commits an offense]."
[If she does so], it is a *pāyattika*. Although the rule requires that she announce [her arrival], if the formal words of the announcement are omitted, they may be added according to the sense.

Whenever a bhikṣuṇī is dispatched to the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) to request instruction and admonition, or to seek the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*), she must go outside the monastery gate.
One must not enter abruptly. If no one comes out, the bhikṣuṇī should make a slight sound so that those inside may hear it;

she should not speak loudly or clamorously, as this would cause her to lose her dignified demeanor. If there is a bhikṣu outside, one bhikṣuṇī should approach him, pay respects with reverence, perform a single prostration, stand up, join her palms, and say:
"Venerable Sirs, we bhikṣuṇīs are now entering the monastery of the bhikṣusaṃgha, desiring to request instruction (or to seek *pravāraṇā*).
We pray that the Venerable Ones will, out of compassion, inform [the Saṃgha] on our behalf. (Having spoken thus once, the bhikṣus reply: "Very well."

When she hears the attendant’s announcement, she shall exit her quarters to be summoned before entering. Unless it concerns matters of immediate necessity, she must request permission based on the specific circumstances to enter. The Buddha said:
"Except for the purpose of paying homage at a stūpa of the Buddha or a stūpa of a Śrāvaka, there is no offense in entering a monastery without having requested permission.
In the final age, because nuns have long been deluded regarding this rule, many show arrogance toward the monks.
Furthermore, regarding those who look up to the monastic community from the secular world and seek to take refuge therein, it is for the sake of honoring the Way and its virtue.

As for monks who guide and transform the laity, they must maintain proper decorum and mindfulness; they must never harbor even the slightest thought of personal gain, but hold only the intention to fulfill compassionate salvation.

May it be so: when preaching the Dharma, may medicine and ailment meet; when receiving offerings, may the mind remain undistracted; when objects appear, may they not shift; and when conditions converge, may one know contentment.
How much more so for the silent, venerable teacher who need not preach! Yet even through such silence, he can propagate the transformation.

In the final age, bhikṣus who perform acts of merit through teaching often deviate from the established precepts and fail to protect the Way of the Dharma; therefore, I append these words of the Sage to guide myself.
Admonition: I also wish that those of like mind would exercise caution in this matter.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: If a bhikṣu acts as a teacher for a layperson, instructing them to cultivate merit, there are five things he must not do:
first, he should not reside in the house of this donor; second, he should not fix his mind on greed.
Regarding material gain: Third, one should not preach the Dharma in its entirety to a donor to instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden them;
rather, one should instruct them individually to practice other dharmas. These "other dharmas" refer to giving, observing the precepts, and receiving the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa);
one should explain each of these one by one. Fourth, one must not engage in playful entertainment or mutual amusement with householders. Fifth, one must not [be] bound...

The mind constantly desires to see one another, yet there are five matters for which this is not permitted: first, if a donor (*dānapati*) is not an old acquaintance, one must not go to them by forcing a pretense of long-standing intimacy;
second, one must not seek to exploit their influence to manage the donor’s household affairs; third, one must not... [text truncated]

We, your humble donors, have spoken in private: there are four things you must not say to a donor—namely, that it is an auspicious time and day for sacrificing to the spirits—and fifth, you must not make excessive requests of your close friends and donors.

The above was composed by the bhikṣu Daoxuan during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. Having traveled among various seminaries of the Vinaya (the character *si* being pronounced *yì*, meaning "to practice"), he extensively sought out diverse instructions.

However, he found that people merely recited the texts and placed their trust in the literal words; while the sections were arranged into established schools, when it came to discussing and reaching the essential points, they had never yet attained the correct principle.
Thereupon, he took up pen and ink and compiled [this work] according to the fundamental tenets. Although he did not exhaustively investigate the source or the branches, [he strove for accuracy].
I hope that these matters may be resolved for practical application, so that my humble contribution, like dust and dew, might be reflected upon by future generations for ten thousand years;
the reach of this aspiration is indeed far-reaching.
[End of Exegesis] This text is the preface recorded at the end of the original scroll, written by Emperor Xuan during the third year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty.
Having received full ordination, he states that it was during the Zhenguan era; this refers to a period when two emperors had succeeded and eight years had passed.

During this interval, he traveled to study various Vinaya texts and applied himself diligently to the training in *vinaya*. When the text says "extensively seeking divergent methods," this does not refer to extraordinary or esoteric arts;
rather, it means seeking the correct standards of the Vinaya regulations, as distinct from the erroneous traditions that had been handed down. The following two lines clarify this.
The purpose for initiating this compilation is that the Vinaya school is not comparable to the study of doctrinal philosophy (*abhidharma*).
If what was not prescribed were treated as prescribed, then the very foundation of maintaining the teachings would be obscured and lost; how could this not lead to their ruin?

Desiring to rescue declining customs and to clarify the turbulent waves, he did not follow contemporary teachers; rather, whenever he compiled a volume, he invariably verified it against the sacred words and established precedents.
Was this not so that, by providing a correct standard, he might instruct future generations? Thus, relying on the fundamental principles of the school, he arranged the sequence of the texts.

Exhausting the source and investigating the branches, his practice and application found their proper destination. He synthesized the great achievement, skillfully attuning it to the requirements of the times. It was as if...

He was no mere lion emerging from its den, nor a king of geese selecting milk from water; who else could establish the Southern Mountain as the preeminent lineage and cause the Vinaya to resound throughout the Western Regions?
Though he said that his vows were like fine dust compared to Mount Tai, or a drop of dew compared to the vast ocean, he took this very principle as his standard for upholding the Dharma.
It illuminates ten thousand generations. Yet the Master’s aspiration did not stop at this alone;

he truly wished that the True Dharma might endure forever until the end of the future, benefiting sentient beings without interruption. Therefore, it is said that "the reach of his aspiration is far-reaching.
All those who succeed the lineage and propagate its teachings enter the Master’s vow, together riding the vessel of precepts and morality—thus it is said. (Chapter Ten)

It is like holding a life-preserving bag (*fu-nang*) wishing to cross the great ocean; the life-preserving bag is the vessel for crossing the sea. Formerly there was...
A merchant was crossing the ocean with an inflated life-belt. A rākṣasa in the sea begged him for the life-belt; the man would not give it to him.
Then he begged for half of it, but this too was not permitted. When he begged for even a single thread, the man still did not grant his wish. Why was this?

Because life is contained within the bag; if it were torn, one would never reach the shore. This serves as a metaphor for a person who maintains the precepts and wishes to cross the ocean of birth and death.
Even if they encounter the rākṣasa of passionate attachment and seek a single boon, it will ultimately not be granted.
Why? Because life depends upon the precepts. If the precepts are broken, one will drown in the ocean of birth and death, never again to emerge.

Therefore, it is like the case where tying a garment with grass results in the loss of life yet constitutes no offense. Long ago, there was a thief who, having plundered goods, encountered a bhikṣu on his way home.

"Qì" (憩) is pronounced *qiè*; it means to rest.
*Yǔn* (pronounced *yǔn*) means to perish; it is synonymous with "to pass away.
*Bāo* (with the second tone) means to praise or extol.
*Biǎn* (pronounced *biǎn*) means to censure or suppress.
Ying (應) is pronounced like yīng; it means to respond with words to a question.
Ta (沓) is pronounced like tà; it means to be layered or repeated.
Yi (擬) is pronounced like yǐ; it means to deliberate and wait.
"Chuai" (揣度) means to measure and estimate.
"You" (猷) has the pronunciation "you" (由) and means the Way (道).
"Ai" (閡) is the same as "ai" (礙); it means obstruction or hindrance.
The pronunciation of "fà" in "fàxíng" (發硎) is "xíng. "Fàxíng" refers to the ultimate refinement in carving and slicing.
The pronunciation of "yù" (唹) is "yú"; it means to smile.
The pronunciation of "xúnxún" (循循) is "xún"; it means orderly sequence. The *Lúnyǔ* states: "The Master was xúnxún-rán, skillfully guiding others."
*Cù* (蔟): pronounced *cù*; it means to gather or cluster together.
*Pí* (疲): pronounced *pí*; it means physical exhaustion from labor. *Kuìjuàn* (困倦):
it means the extreme state of fatigue and the depletion of one's strength.
*Mao* (pronounced *mào*) means forgetfulness due to senility. One becomes senile (*máo*) at eighty or ninety years of age.
*Tié* (with the entering tone) refers to the age of eighty, when the skin turns black like iron; it is also the ultimate stage of life.
*Nián* (pronounced like "male"): *nián-nián* means to speak much. *Jué* (pronounced like "decide"):
refers to essential methods of arts and techniques. *Zhì* (same sound as *zhì*):
refers to the binding and sequencing of book scrolls. *Zhí* (same sound as *zhí*): refers to the arrangement of book scrolls.
It is also an opportunity.
